https://sourceforge.net/apps/phpbb/free-cad/viewforum.php?f=4

just a reminder- I'm not sure that the core devs are receiving pull requests via this medium so:

https://sourceforge.net/apps/phpbb/free-cad/viewtopic.php?f=17&t=3781

Thank you!

What is the reason to have?
Lib64Dir = FreeCAD.getHomePath()+'lib64'

Usually FreeCAD is installed under /usr/lib/freecad/... (or maybe /usr/lib64/freecad) and the output of FreeCAD.getHomePath() should be /usr/lib/freecad (or /usr/lib64/freecad respectively) but not just /usr.
FreeCAD's own libraries then go to /usr/lib/freecad/lib or /usr/lib64/freecad/lib respectively.

So, do you have a system where the FreeCAD package is configured to return just "/usr" as home path?
And if yes, does it actually find all its workbenches and resource files?

I'm still learning git but here is how I would do it:

```
$ git checkout predeformation2
$ git rebase -i 9dc13ef48c6d80811857c831d36bddc4ef7fd101^
```

Then an editor pops up. Change the word "pick" to "edit" in the first line.
Save the file and exit the editor.

```
$ git reset HEAD^
$ git status
```

This should show something like this.

```
interactive rebase in progress; onto 1507ef2
Last command done (1 command done):
   edit 9dc13ef Prescribed displacement working the same as other boundary conditions
No commands remaining.
You are currently splitting a commit while rebasing branch 'predeformation2' on '1507ef2'.
  (Once your working directory is clean, run "git rebase --continue")

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git checkout -- <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)

        modified:   src/Mod/Fem/FemPrescribedDisplacement.py

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)

        .excludes
        CMakeLists.txt.user
        FreeCAD_trunk.cbp
        data/Mod/
        deformationdec.json

        ....
```

If only the FemPrescribedDisplacement.py should have been modified in this commit then:

```
$ git add src/Mod/Fem/FemPrescribedDisplacement.py
$ git commit --amend
$ git rebase --continue
```

And this will push to and overwrite the online repo.

```
$ git push -f
```

That is all.

You should also sync your feature branch with upstream.

Two more remarks:
IMO it's plain wrong to add any entries to ADD_DEFINITIONS inside the FindNetgen file. The proper way is to set it to a variable and let the programmer add this variable to ADD_DEFINITIONS where needed.
It can be done like this:
SET(NETGEN_DEFINITIONS "-DNETGEN_V5")
...
 ADD_DEFINITIONS(${NETGEN_DEFINITIONS})

Second remark:
This was already wrong in the original file. Preprocessor macros must not be added to the list NETGEN_INCLUDE_DIRS which you then add to include_directories() because this may easily fail with future cmake versions. The correct way is to add them to the variable NETGEN_DEFINITIONS.

Great work but this strikes me as a bit unconventional for FreeCAD...  

1) While this PR is for users building with MacPorts, typically [the dependencies](http://www.freecadweb.org/wiki/index.php?title=CompileOnMac/es#MacPorts_Dependencies) are installed separately according to the aforementioned instructions that cover both MacPorts and HomeBrew.

2) Building MEDFile is already handled by [Travis using a homebrew formula](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/master/.travis.yml#L146) for the continuous integration builds posted to the [FreeCAD GitHub Releases](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/releases/tag/0.17_pre)

I would suggest the following:

1) Move the CMake MedFile logic to a MacPorts portfile and submit it to MacPorts for inclusion as a supported port.  I am sure the MacPorts community would appreciate the contribution ;)
2) Update the [CompileOnMac instructions](http://www.freecadweb.org/wiki/index.php?title=CompileOnMac/es#MacPorts_Dependencies) on the Wiki to include MedFile as a dependency.  It seems the HomeBrew instructions are a bit out of date with the 0.17 dependencies but the Travis.yml documents the dependencies for HomeBrew users who want to build from source.

If we want to install MedFile in Cmake, which again is non-standard for FreeCAD, then at a minimum, this should be changed to check to see if MedFile is already installed before installing it.

@ianrrees, comments?

I agree with @bblacey - this should be handled by the package manager.  Thanks for mentioning that medfile recipe - have been meaning to follow up with getting that pulled in to Homebrew.

  1) It seems inappropriate (especially in the context of FreeCAD) to have cmake go and fetch things that it thinks are necessary .  The usual model is to run cmake after getting dependencies, so it's more appropriate for cmake to warn/error when there are missing dependencies.
  2) Scope could be improved - this change should at least be conditional on the modules that use Medfile.
  3) The comment about "A proper way would be to build all FreeCAD..." doesn't belong in source code.  If you think there's a better way to build all FreeCAD, then by all means work to implement that change, but the source code is not a discussion forum.

This issue with MacPorts and Qt4 came about several months ago when there was some movement in MacPorts to support Qt4 and Qt5.  I haven't followed the situation, but from memory there should be some other way to help cmake find the appropriate qmake.

It seems to me that unconditionally modifying external environment variables (which could easily have been set intentionally) to get cmake to work is a much less flexible approach than passing in a command line argument.  The real problem here though is that MacPorts has broken qmake's typical build process...

I've tested this with a typical Homebrew install with clang 7.3.0 - seems OK.

FWIW - we've been able to build Robot on MacOS for ages.

There are serious bugs in
Py::Object edgeWalker(const Py::Tuple& args) and
Py::Object findOuterWire(const Py::Tuple& args):
1. If the parsing in PyArg_ParseTuple fails then "pcObj" is not a valid pointer but still undefined. Thus, accessing it to create the exception message causes a segfault
2. In general inside PyCXX based functions you should avoid FreeCAD exception types but use PyCXX exception when doing type checking, otherwise the raised exception is a bit confusing. Alternatively you can extend invoke_method_varargs and directly convert Base::TypeError to Py::TypeError
3.  In the above two functions you should not explicitly check for the list type because otherwise you make its usage again quite unpythonic since it won't accept other sequence types like tuples, numpy arrays or other containers. Instead you should only do a type checking when accessing the items of the sequence and raise an exception there if needed.
Error handling changed to Py::Exception/Py::TypeError

1. The libarea changes are big, and might break something. Since I don't use libarea I cannot judge. It would be good if other Path/libarea users could test this before this is merged.

I haven't looked at the code yet, just played around with the actual functionality. Interesting indeed ...

My notes in random order:
* It seems features are left behind when deleted. I had significant problems setting the "workplane" once I had the WorkArea, so I deleted several attempts, some of which reappeared later on again. Not in the tree, but in the 3d view.
* Section planes have to align exactly with the model height levels. In other words the algorithm only sees what falls on one of those section planes. Nothing inbetween, no angled surfaces ...
* I don't understand the "thicken", I see a lot of potential there but I'm not sure what it actually shows me since I'm not looking at the actual path

Thanks for the appreciation, everyone. I really loved how FC is going these days. And I firmly believe in its potential to be the ultimate CAD/CAM for everything. On the other hand, I am just an amature in the CAD/CAM/CNC world. My motivation is to try to find a reliable way to construct 2D shapes in FC, and then generate gcode from it (which I still haven't got to yet).

As for the pull request here, FeatureArea comes very handy to construct 2D shapes, much reliable than OCC in this regard. And I think there is a missing link between the CAD model and CAM toolpath. Say the user already have a model built in FC, he still needs to perform various steps before being able to use Path.Feature to generate gcode (really, what are the recommended steps in Path mod? Can someone kindly point me to some links please? I haven't got time to search for instructions yet:).

And let's not forget about Path.Area, FeatureArea is good for hands on testing of various librea capabilities. But, Path.Area, I think is the one more suitable for Path developers here. It is essentially a FC specific python wrapper for libarea, I can expose more function if necessary. Eventually, I think we can just get rid of area python module, and directly use Path.Area here.

Oh, forgot to mention this. Path.Area abstracts the actual 2D library from the code that's using it. What it does right now is to iterate through OCC shapes, convert each edge to libarea vertex, call libarea function to perform operation like Union, Difference, Offset, Pocket etc, then convert the result back to OCC shapes. With this pattern, it is not that difficult to switch to a different 2D library, say, [GEOS](https://trac.osgeo.org/geos/) anyone?

@mlampert, the workplane doesn't have to be any shape belonging to the children of the FeatureArea. It can be any other planar shape. The UI needs some work. The key is to realize that two mode of selection is required. 1) Select the hosting FeatureArea by clicking the item in treeview. 2) Select workplane, holding the CTRL and click a face or wire in the 3D viewer. The workplane is internally used by BRepAlgoAPI_Section to perform section, and it only provides a direction, the actual section plane is displaced to be within the boundary box of the FeatureArea children shape.

The macros are because the warnings only show when a class is declared that uses override at least once, for every method that is overridden but doesn't declare that it is an override. Ah, I understand it now, thanks for the clarifications! This was one of the things I wanted feedback on :)

I set `CMAKE_INSTALL_DATAROOTDIR` to a full path to be able to actually have a working system install.
Because the `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX` is implicitly used when installing the modules it's currently not possible to do a system install when passing a `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX`. Case in point:
```
if("${CMAKE_INSTALL_COMPONENT}" STREQUAL "Unspecified" OR NOT CMAKE_INSTALL_COMPONENT)
  file(INSTALL DESTINATION "${CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX}/Mod/AddonManager" TYPE FILE FILES
    "/home/simon/src/simonvanderveldt/freecad/src/Mod/AddonManager/Init.py"
    "/home/simon/src/simonvanderveldt/freecad/src/Mod/AddonManager/InitGui.py"
    "/home/simon/src/simonvanderveldt/freecad/src/Mod/AddonManager/AddonManager.py"
    "/home/simon/src/simonvanderveldt/freecad/src/Mod/AddonManager/AddonManagerGui.py"
    )
endif()
```
Say one would set `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr` this would obviously fail/be incorrect because `/usr/Mod` is not the correct directory.

So I thought it made more sense to set `CMAKE_INSTALL_DATAROOTDIR` to a full path so that one doesn't have to pass a `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX` and that way a system install would be possible.
If someone wants to install it locally I one can pass `CMAKE_INSTALL_DATAROOTDIR="${CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX}/usr/share"`
I know this is not optimal, but right now the CMake setup is broken for system installs when passing a `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX`.

What would be the preferred thing to do? Adding an output to show the path as suggested by @yorikvanhavre is a simple thing to do.

Obviously in the long term the libs should be installed to a proper path so the `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX` can actually be used for it's intended purpose. That'll be a lot of work though.

The PR suffers from a couple of problems:
* PyInt_Check cannot be simply replaced with PyLong_Check because it breaks valid Python2 code when e.g. the passed number is really an int and not a long. This error has already come up with previous PR's where the same mistake was made.  Instead it should use PyLong_Check for Python 2&3 and PyInt_Check only for Python 2.
* InterpreterSingleton::init probably doesn't work correctly on all platforms. The argv argument is a list of UTF-8 encoded strings.
Unfortunately, the Python docs don't say anything about the encoding of wchar_t on the various platforms but on Windows wchar_t is a typedef to "short" and thus is two bytes long. On this platform the UCS-2 encoding is used and thus one needs a conversion from UTF-8 to UCS-2. Just widen each char to a wchar_t won't work. 
On UNIX-like systems wchar_t is a typedef to "int" i.e. is 4 bytes long and UCS-4 must be used.

The Python docs, however, suggests that for decoding/encoding the functions Py_DecodeLocale and Py_EncodeLocale should be used. See also: https://docs.python.org/3/extending/embedding.html#very-high-level-embedding

Here is an overview of the variables used with automake: http://www.gnu.org/software/automake/manual/html_node/Standard-Directory-Variables.html
Here datarootdir is set depending on ${prefix} and I think this PR should follow this suggestion because then a local "make install" won't be stopped from working.
And a packaging script can overwrite the default value to point to /usr/share

You have to be careful with implementing your own version of a function to check if two vertexes are considered to be equal or not. Have a look at: http://opencascade.blogspot.de/2009/02/topology-and-geometry-in-open-cascade_09.html

In OCC a vertex itself already uses a tolerance and if another vertex lies inside this "sphere" they are considered to be equal. With BRep_Tool::Tolerance you get the vertex' tolerance.
Now it can happen that your custom function considers two vertexes identical while OCC considers them different or vice versa.

I don't know if it in fact causes problems as things are now but I just want you to know of potential problems.

@ulrich1a - you can easily update a push request including changing the commit message with `git commit --amend`.  If you want to try and learn, simply do the following:

When the editor opens, change the commit message to your liking.  FYI, you can also use `git commit --amend` to modify files in the commit if you do a `git add <file>` after you have edited <file> and before you use `git commit --amend`.  

To update your pull request, you push your branch with force update because amending a commit changes the git history and requires a force-update on GitHub.

So, in this case, if you simply wanted to modify the commit message to add the Mantis id, do the following

```
# Switch to the branch for your pull request
git checkout pullrequest

# Amend the last commit
git commit --amend
<Edit the commit message to add the mantis id and exit the editor with save>

# It is also good to update your branch with any changes from master before pushing to GitHub (makes merging by the repo managers easier)
git pull --rebase upstream master

# Update Github with the changes to your local branch
git push -f origin pullrequest
```

At this point, if you check your pull request on GitHub, you will see your changes.

This PR doesn't fix the root of the problem but simply hides by stopping the chain of notification at a certain level. The real problem is fixed in a2dd176

I disagree. My fix is a fix for the root of the problem, because notification chain should be stopped there. Reassigning links is absolutely unnecessary, and an object that has the link touched whereas it shouldn't be. 
My opinion is that the notification system is broken by its very concept, i.e. making a copy behave as if it were a reference. (EDIT) and consequently causing trouble when applied to real reference.

> I disagree. My fix is a fix for the root of the problem, because notification chain should be stopped there.

No, it is only a workaround and hides the problem. The real problem is that it must not happen that inside the dict of PyObjectBase an attribute object suddenly is considered as parent object or vice versa. This is what the above commit fixes. The same problem could re-occur on low-level data classes then stopping the chain for PropertyContainers won't fix anything.

> Reassigning links is absolutely unnecessary, and an object that has the link touched whereas it shouldn't be.

Yes, here I agree that on this level the chain can be stopped. That's why I didn't close the PR. But I am not happy with some naming and the fact that the generated file generateModel_Module.py is manually changed. As soon as the file gets re-generated all changes are lost and will cause tons of build errors.

> My opinion is that the notification system is broken by its very concept, i.e. making a copy behave as if it were a reference. (EDIT) and consequently causing trouble when applied to real reference.

The solution is not perfect but what are the alternatives? Using real references everywhere as you suggest simply doesn't work and will cause crashes everywhere. A soon as the central C++ instance is destroyed (e.g. a DocumentObject) then all its memory is freed and if there is still somewhere a Python wrapper object for one of the properties or of its sub-elements  and it is invoked you may or may not get a crash. Have fun to find this kind of errors!

Another point is that e.g. to make undo/redo work properly it must be disallowed that the data can be modified from everywhere.

> generated file generateModel_Module.py

Aha, that's why it is so ugly! I didn't notice the file is generated. I'll try to rework it then.

> But I am not happy with some naming

+1, but I would like suggestions.

> The same problem could re-occur on low-level data classes then stopping the chain for PropertyContainers won't fix anything

Maybe disable it everywhere by default, and enable it explicitly in specific places, such as Placement and Vector?

> The solution is not perfect but what are the alternatives? Using real references everywhere as you suggest simply doesn't work and will cause crashes everywhere.

It is solved for DocumentObject by not destroying its Py counterpart, but marking it invalid instead. Sure, proper solution is going to be very long and boring. 

Another alternative is to implement it like it works in C++: have methods getValue/setValue. Which is somewhat equivalent of simply removing the notification system altogether. After all there is a bunch of places already where attributes return copies, and offer no notification update (e.g. PropertyLinkList: doing Group.Group.append(object) does nothing).

> Aha, that's why it is so ugly! I didn't notice the file is generated. I'll try to rework it then.

> I think, explicit template instantiations for every exception type are needed in Base/Exception.cpp

No, it's because of the export macro. Template classes must not have the export macro because the compiler generates the needed code at build time. See 33bed8d4128

Explicit template instantiation is usually done when the implementation is separated from the interface, i.e. the code is not in the header but in a source file.
This technique is only used when the template class makes sense for a few types. E.g. the Base::Vector3 class only makes sense for float and double but not much for int, bool, ...

Have you tested that this https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/pull/802/commits/441ba7526531b9d124dbab5ac7d73f813673c196 doesn't break the translation mechanism?

In order to keep things working it must fulfill these conditions:
1. when running lupdate/pylupdate then it must pick up all strings marked for translation and put them into the .ts files with the correct context string
2. when running FreeCAD the translation system must use the correct context string when requesting the translated string

I think this PR doesn't break the latter point but I'm not sure about the former since I don't know if lupdate/pylupdate is clever enough to recognize the default context string passed to the translate function.

Not really, `stage: Deploy dmg to GitHub Releases` contains a separate job, which is intended to be run after the `test` stage. It's a normal job with script/test stages inherited from global ones. There's also `deploy:` step within each job, but using it doesn't guarantee that the deployment process will run **after** all tests are confirmed to be successful (but stages do).

@peterlama

> So what is the advantage of completely separating the deploy process - is it just so the built-in deploy step and conditions can be used?

There are a few concepts here:
1. Build Stages
2. Jobs (build stages consist of jobs)
3. Steps/Hook points inside each job

Build Stages are sequential within a Build. If the previous Stage has failed, next stages are automatically canceled.

Jobs are bunch of build processed (containerized or virtualized). They run in parallel within a Stage they belong to. 

Steps within are sequential a job and executed according to the Build Lifecycle. [`deploy`](https://docs.travis-ci.com/user/deployment) is one of those steps (and it has it's own `before_`/`after_` substeps).

Based on above:
* if you set up step-level primitive (like `deploy`) on a root level of config, it will be populated to all jobs
* `deploy` will be executed independently, **regardless of whether any of other jobs failed**.
* you may end up in situation where one of jobs deployed its artifact and other failed to do so, which is inconsistent
* if you separate the job(s) with `deploy` into the last job, it will only run if all tests in all envs succeeded

> Also, what is the disadvantage of using after_success: for deploying the build?

* `deploy` is run after `after_success` stage
* it is semantically correct to use it
* it runs a special tool called [`dpl`](https://github.com/travis-ci/dpl), which:
  * has built-in support for lots of deployment providers, [like, for example, GitHub Releases](https://docs.travis-ci.com/user/deployment/releases/)
  * supports setting of various options for that providers
  * supports execution triggers, for example, you can configure it to only run deployments if you pushed a tag or it's a certain branch etc.
  * you can also use a sequence of different deployment providers, not just one

> I'm not sure I understand this correctly. Do you mean you want to update published binaries under the same tag when updating them? Could you plz add more detail?

Yes. For the master branch (Developer branch) we deploy assets from multiple places so it's important that the release tag remains static. As @bblacey has pointed out we deploy test builds for OSX for every merge to master automatically. If we tagged every release we could have 5 or 6 releases on a good day. In addition we also deploy AppImage builds to this same release tag from here: [AppIImage assets](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD-AppImage) as a cron job and Win builds that I create locally with build scripts. When we update the build dependencies we sometimes leave an old build with the older dependencies up in case there are problems. As a result the source tarbals aren't updated but it is worth the inconvenience not to have to check if a new release at the same version exists for all the assets coming from different places. 

For the stable release, 0.16.6712 at the moment, I think it would make sense to tag each "backport" release. 0.16.xxxx was released as 0.16.6700. We usually only do backports for crashes and very onerous bugs. These come from the [https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/tree/releases/FreeCAD-0-16](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/tree/releases/FreeCAD-0-16) release branch.

> Do you mean the Version.h file? That's exactly what I'm wondering about :)

Yes again, the SubWCRev.py scipt is run as part of CMake which generates the version.h file (it may update a place holder from the FreeCAD sources I'm not sure) and the version info is compiled in. When the user runs the application and navigates to Help > About FreeCAD info like this is presented

OS: Ubuntu 14.04.5 LTS
Word size of OS: 64-bit
Word size of FreeCAD: 64-bit
Version: 0.17.12124 (Git)

Python version: 3.4.3
Qt version: 4.8.6
Coin version: 4.0.0a
OCC version: 7.1.0
Locale: English/UnitedStates (en_US)

The version.h file looks like this after cmake (from the PPA) 
```
// Version Number
#define FCVersionMajor "0"
#define FCVersionMinor "17"
#define FCVersionName  "Vulcan"
// test: $Format:Hash (%H), Date: %ci$
#define FCRevision      "12140 (Git)"      //Highest committed revision number
#define FCRevisionDate  "2017/09/18 20:16:15"     //Date of highest committed revision
#define FCRepositoryURL "git://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD.git master"      //Repository URL of the working copy

// Git relevant stuff
#define FCRepositoryHash   "6ed14ed76a03d5040f3192a5f529a37d48dd0ce8"
#define FCRepositoryBranch "master"
```

So the version, branch, and hash are determined from this. The version.h file is written to the builddir/src/build sub-directory. This info is important on the forum for both help requests and debugging.

Hello,
Here is an example to show the use of the change I propose.

This model uses formulas to calculate to position of the different gears based on the position of the In shaft.
The macro I use simply sets the orientation and angle of the InShaft.
I manage not to set Angles nulls or multiple to 360°, but with the value 720°. If I do that is that I know that such an angle involves resetting the orientation to (0,0,1). 
The first video is recorded with the latest build on FreeCAD on Windows. The problem is the same on Linux with the daily build.
On can observe that the internal representation of the rotation of the In shafs varies from Angle from 0 et 360, back to 180, and then to 360 and the orientation is inverted when angle is going down. This is due to the internal coding of the rotation as a quaternion. When the angle is set to 720 then the axis of the gears is reset in the wrong direction and the behavior of the model becomes absolutely incoherent. This behavior is completely explained but is not the behavior an engineer would have expected when writing the formulas.

The second video is done under Linux with the latest git version amended with the pull request I propose. The rotation is internally coded in 2 ways: The quaternion as previously, and angle and axis to keep track of the exact value set. These 2 representations are kept consistent. The rotation C++ object provides the Axis and angle when requested, instead of the Axis and Angle reconstructed from the quaternion. When the quaternion is provided when requested. So there is no impact for the code.
On this video one can see that the gear box runs properly, the orientation is not reset, there is not alteration of the angle. That is the result I expected.
As I run Linux in a Virtual Machine it is a bit slower. Nothing to see with the change I made.

Some comments:
FemMesh::getEdgesOnly is extremely inefficient because for every edge you iterate over all faces until you find one with the given edge id. This leads to a quadratic runtime.
Wouldn't it be much more efficient to iterate once over all faces and store their edge ids in a set and then iterate over all edges storing the ids in a different set? The difference of both sets gives you the edge ids that are not shared by any face. The runtime will then be linear.

The issue is caused by the implementation of PropertyPlacementItem::assignProperty which computes the cross product of the internally stored axis and that of the rotation. If the cross product is the null vector then the two axes are parallel but they can still have different orientation. So, it's not enough to only check for the length of the cross product but also the dot product must be checked and if this is negative the internally stored axis must be flipped.

No. It is PartDesign.

If by "patching up basefeature instead", you mean deciding which one of the features should be used as basefeature. I considered it. However, because nothing guaranties that the features being used in the mirroring operation are the last ones (as in your example, but can be even worse, for example, features in the middle (like pocket001) that modify the original or the surroundings of the original). I think that there is no choice but to apply the transformation again also for the original in those cases.

In any case you are right about your example. The result misses Pocket001. The reason is that the support is not regarded to be "Pocket001", but the first selected feature. This can however be solved by forcing basefeature to be Pocket001 (so the previous feature in the list).

We need to:
1. Determine which behaviour we want regarding the "originals"
2. Then decide what to do with the base feature.

This PR is the first step for solving the problems of colors of the composed parts.
Il applies for the cut, fusion,  Booleans, compound, champfer and fillet parts. It will be generalize to other composed parts (pockets, etc).
The first commit adds two targets for creating more detailed documentation for py and cpp. It is very minor but helpful to understand better how the software is structured. There are for developers and are space consuming (12 Gb for the cpp doc). These two targets can be used as follow:

- make -j2 DevDocCpp

The second commit adds the generic class for derived parts.
The third uses these class for the different parts listed above.
The problems that are not yet solved are:

- When changing the color of a part the color is not reported to the parts directly or indirectly composed with this object.
- Changing the color to black of a composed part does not work for the objects present in the file before loading the file. This is due to history not saved, and therefore not loaded. This problem disappears when the object is recomputed. When the problem is detected by the code the object is marked to be recomputed, so F5 clears this problem. This can also be solved by marking to recompute the full document and F5, so all structures are recomputed and present in memory.

Coming the generalization to more composed parts.

Here is some more explanations:
https://forum.freecadweb.org/viewtopic.php?f=8&t=25505&p=213707#p213591

Usage:
When setting one of the composed parts to black (#000000), the colors used for this part are the colors of the composing parts. If the transparency is also set to 0 then the transparencies used are the transparencies of the composing parts instead of the transparency of the part itself.

If a color is set to something different to black, then this colors and the transparency are used for all the part.

I am happy you discovered the tree visualization view. I was unable to find it.

My first approach to this problem was to disable the tip handling (and it worked fine in my tests). I was however afraid of changing the design decisions of the viewproviders of (all) the features (other than those implemented in derived classes), as they might assume that the tip is on the insertion point. For example, if a feature were to rely on an body::insertObject call, then it may lead to unknown behaviour. I do not know of any such case. So it is a matter of waiting and seeing if there are bugs reported.

About the moving of the tip handling code to setEdit, it helped with restoring on abortcommand and undo. As a general idea, I think that "nothing" should be done in doubleClick() before calling the relevant commands (setEdit/unsetEdit), as then it is outside the transactions, and you have to take into account that some properties (changed outside those commands, which are reasonably consistently used across FreeCAD) may need to be restored manually, which becomes a source of inconsistency.

Here are a few things that should be fixed:
* The external smesh uses SMESH_INCLUDE_PATH but for the internal SMESH_INCLUDE_DIR is used which will then be empty. So the call of include_directories(${SMESH_INCLUDE_DIR}) has no effect.
Here it suffices to set SMESH_INCLUDE_DIR with set (SMESH_INCLUDE_DIR ${SMESH_INCLUDE_PATH}).
We could think about changing the variable name to use that of the external smesh.

* To avoid to clutter all modules with too much stuff don't add the include path in the top-level cmake file. The modules that need smesh (Fem and MeshPart) already set the paths.

* add_definitions(-DHAVE_NETGEN) must be removed. netgen support is still handled by the BUILD_FEM_NETGEN option. I have intentionally built my external smesh without netgen support so the above define will cause a linking error.

* add_definitions(-DSMESH_VERSION_MAJOR=${SMESH_VERSION_MAJOR}) is quite inelegant and as said above clutters the vast majority of modules with unneeded defines. A nicer solution could be to create a file SMESHVersion.h.cmake and build SMESHVersion.h at configure time which contains major, minor and build version numbers.

This causes the build to fail due to changes you did in C++ code.. You cannot join a qstring and a normal c string. you must do like this: QT_TRANSLATE_NOOP(...)+QString::fromUtf8("\n")

Rebased:
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/pull/1437

QT_TRANSLATE_NOOP(...)+QString::fromUtf8("\n") doesn't work either because creation of a QString from a plain C string is suppressed by setting the macro QT_NO_CAST_FROM_ASCII. This done to avoid that a plain C string is converted to a QString by accident and thus to force programmers to think about if the C string is supposed for translation, encoded, ...

A general note about fromUtf8:
If you can be sure that a string only is built of 7-bit characters then you shouldn't use fromUtf8 but fromLatin1 because it's much faster.
If you have a string that has only one character then you better use the QChar class.

Now from the above code changes in C++ you only try to concatenate the \n in SketchObject.cpp. In this case you can also just omit the newline character.

I anticipate that your latest change will fail too for exactly the same reason I mentioned above. As said in this case there is no need to add a newline at the end.

My note about QString/QChar or fromUtf8/fromLatin1 is meant to be a *general* note and doesn't apply to this concrete example.

During development, some problems raised that need transformation of the core.
It happens that in many situation calculations are done twice when a change occurs. 
To evaluate colors the history is needed but not stored. But history is evaluated during the execution of the operation on composed parts, that call the update of the colors.
I made some experiments to identify the changes to be done in the software to solve these problems, and doing this brought me deep into the code and the basic mechanisms on place.
I am convinced there must be a rework of the core to:
-	Avoid immediate calculation after propagation of the changes,
-	Avoid multiple calculation,
-	Avoid unnecessary calculation.

These change would lead to drastic improvement on performances, especially when animating a model. I really think it would really improve user experience and stability of the software, and anyway, without this change, the job around colors cannot be completed.
I have some precise thoughts about what should be done and how it should be done, but as this concerns the core the decisions should be made in collaboration with the designers of the software to be certain to address all aspects.
I noticed also that it is very long to convince to take PR with quite limited and circumscribed changes in the software that correct errors of the actual software. 
I am therefore certain a change that would touch the core would therefore almost impossible to have accepted, what is normal if this change is pushed with no preparation. It is also obvious that, as the software is quite vast, all the consequences must have been discussed to envisage all consequences and side effects. 
So that is why, unless we can setup a discussion on what could be the changes with the designers and have some sprints to experiment these changes, it is not worth for me spending time on that. So that is why I think this PR as it is should be closed.
To continue on that subject a discussion to decide the changes in the design needed should be set, and I am ready and would be glad to participate to such a discussion around the events management topic and behavior of the software. I would also be available to implement whatever could come out these discussions.
Regards
Pascal Garcia
PS: Before closing the box, I will write a document to record all I can on colors management, performances, and design aspects to improve.

@IchGucksLive git is pretty smart, and built for this type of thing. For example, the way git works is that you can [squash the commits all in to one commit](https://www.devroom.io/2011/07/05/git-squash-your-latests-commits-into-one/). This is typically done (AFAIK) in different cases, for example:  

- before submitting the PR
- if the user found a mistake themselves and corrects it after PR was submit (this can be problematic)
- once the PR has been reviewed and the reviewer has asked you to make changes
- once the PR has been reviewed and the reviewer squashes it for you before committing to master

_Note: If you squash all your commits in to one it will essentially delete the history or the process it took you to get to the final code you are submitting to the PR._

It's indeed a bit odd to have many new methods added to SketchObject just to have a convenient Python interface. Since the "analyser" member doesn't do anything else and to keep things a bit cleaner you can:
* keep the functions of SketchObjectPy but create each time a new instance of SketchAnalysis when one of these Python functions is invoked. This way you can remove the analyser member from SketchObject and all the methods. Also, this reduces possible side-effects in case of consecutive calls of validation functions unless you explicitly need this. But then it suffices to add a single method to SketchObject to return the SketchAnalysis instance.

* instead of putting the validation functions to SketchObjectPy you can create the class SketchAnalysisPy. In the long term this might be the better option since many new methods could be added. In order to invoke the validation functions from Python we have to add a single method to SketchObject(Py) to create and return a SketchAnalysis instance.

Nevertheless, I am going to merge the PR now and things can still be changed at a later time.

The changes about using references in the catch block looks okay to me. However, the double casts in the second commit look very ugly and I don't think that it's the correct way to fix them.

When looking at the Python API we have three different C functions with one, two or three arguments.
`
typedef PyObject *(*PyCFunction)(PyObject *, PyObject *);
typedef PyObject *(*PyCFunctionWithKeywords)(PyObject *, PyObject *, PyObject *);
typedef PyObject *(*PyNoArgsFunction)(PyObject *);
`
and the appropriate flags METH_NOARGS, METH_VARARGS or METH_KEYWORDS

Now e.g. for ConsoleSingleton::sPyMessage the function has three arguments but sets 1 (METH_VARARGS) as flag and uses PyCFunction as cast. So, the correct way to fix it is removing the superfluous kwd argument (which is commented out anyway).

I think that this once was made wrong in the initial manually written Python binding and the mistake was copied over and over again in many classes. But for example for our Python/XML generators this has been done correctly and there the compiler doesn't print any warnings.

So, the first commit can be merged but I would like to rework the second one to properly fix all the flaws.
Merged commit aa397ce66

With a9c4bcb all the mistakes are fixed where flag and number of arguments don't match.
Now the remaining warnings are due to how Python keeps function pointers. The second member of the struct PyMethodDef is of type PyCFunction and all other function types (PyCFunctionWithKeywords, PyNoArgsFunction) must be cast to it which now triggers the gcc warning.

This PR suggests this construct (PyCFunction) (void*) to suppress the warning but according to the Python ML this is not fully correct: https://bugs.python.org/issue33012#msg317853
Instead of (void*) it should be (void (*) (void))
Here is an example how pybind11 did it: https://github.com/pybind/pybind11/pull/1396/files
However, I would apply this fix only on the PyCXX code and for the generated swig-code I would simply suppress the warning with a pragma call.
I concur. I had not found the reference to `(void (*)(void))` but that is indeed better.  Thanks for the follow up and rework.

I can confirm the crash but I can't say for sure that the issue you mentioned is related nor that it's really a bug.
The actual problem is something else: the SoHandleEventAction class can grab a node which it will apply on all incoming events until it's released again. However, when grabbing or releasing a node it doesn't change the reference counter and thus it's possible that the hold pointer can become dangling and this is exactly what happens here.
When I start to drag then SoHandleEventAction grabs the dragger node and when pressing ESC to leave edit mode the SoHandleEventAction is not notified about this and its pointer becomes dangling and the application crashes as soon as it traverses the scene graph the next time.

Also, ignoring ESC events while a mouse button is pressed doesn't work in all cases. E,g, with a Qt5 build (with Qt4 this doesn't seems to be possible) I can move the mouse pointer to the Ok button, right click and release both buttons. The viewer doesn't seem to realize the release events so that the dragger is still active. Now I can click the OK button and the application crashes.

Looking at the Coin documentation I found a reliable way to fix the crash in the two cases. From the viewer we can access the event manager and from there we get the pointer to the SoHandleEventAction instance. There we can check if it has grabbed a node and if yes release it: fd2befe7a

> However, when grabbing or releasing a node it doesn't change the reference counter and thus it's possible that the hold pointer can become dangling and this is exactly what happens here.

Setting such a huge tolerance doesn't make any sense because effectively it's not easily possible any more to move a point somewhere inside a grid cell. If you want to achieve it you must always go back to the task dialog and tmp. disable the option.

And if you start to draw a new line you click somewhere but don't get any feedback that the first point is already accepted and when pressing twice an error is raised that adding the line failed because both points are equal. In order to see the preview line you must move at least half a size of the grid cell along X or Y axis.

I think this odd behaviour will be confusing to many users.

Btw, I looked at the feature request 847 and changing the snapping tolerance doesn't do what the OP wanted. If you have a line where none of its endpoint is snapped it still won't snap when starting to drag it.
Merged.

Ok, it is a misunderstanding of what gridsnap should do. As I understood it, one point of having the gridsnap on may be precisely not to be able to move points inside the grid. Under such assumption, using 0.5 precisely prevents points outside the grid. When creating a new line, with an appropriate grid size, as soon as the line passes 50% of the grid size, you get a line segment of exactly one grid size measure. Of course using inappropriate values of the grid size leads to unusable behaviour. Because endpoints of lines cannot be outside the grid, when dragging points snap to the grid. Of course, if one creates a line without snap on, outside the grid, then sets snap on and drags, it won't align.

Of course, if weak snap, as currently implemented in FC is how it should work, this PR makes no sense.

Regarding the ticket:
Dragging an endpoint of the line works perfectly with weak snap. 

I am not sure I will implement dragging the edge and trying to snap the endpoints.

I am not using the binary package and I am playing on Linux so probably I don't have the full picture. Moreover my experience with pip is limited to installing a few binary packages on Windows.

There are two problems, the first is providing deps when building from source and the second one when installing a binary.

In the second case, usually on Windows, the deps are included in a single-file installer together with the main application. This solution provides a smoother user experience but eventually may create other problems (archives bigger and bigger, multiple copies of the same dependencies installed on the system if not managed correctly, etc.). On Linux, instead, the deps are typically provided by distributions, each one with its package manager (there are even distributions like Gentoo that have a package manager which install the binaries compiling them from sources on-the-fly). I am speaking about all kind of deps, not only python packages. Furthermore I don't have experience at all with building installers on Windows.

The requirements.txt recently committed might be related to both problems. When starting from sources, we can offer an additional solution to install the dependencies to the user by using pip but he/she must still be free to choose another way. When building an installer, it could be used to prepare all the dependencies to be shipped together with the main application. Or it could be used also at runtime by the installer itself to automatically install the dependencies.

The `‘QString::QString(const char*)’ is private` error that shows in the CI buillds logs usually means this: You have a [QString](http://doc.qt.io/qt-5/qstring.html), and you are trying to add a C string to it (basically just a double-quoted text). You can only add another QString to a QString (that is because it's private. If not, apparently Qstrings would be able to do that conversion automatically, but I haven't fully understood all that yet). 

So instead of:
`QString message(QObject::tr("Rotation:")+" ");`
you need to do something like this:
`QString message(QObject::tr("Rotation:")+QString::fromUtf8(" "));`
(The result of QObject::tr is already a QString)
Note that this is only for QStrings. When you are dealing with a stream, where you add stuff with <<, it is able to swallow C strings directly.

Basically the way to solve these things is to look at the CI logs, find the error that made the build stop (usually near the end of the log), fix that error, push, wait for the new build, fix the next error. This is obviously much, much faster when you compile yourself.

Inheritance correspondence:

Geometry
- GeomPoint
- GeomCurve (GeometryCurvePy)
- - GeomBoundedCurve (BoundedCurvePy)
- - - GeomBezierCurve (BezierCurvePy)
- - - GeomBSplineCurve (BSplineCurvePy)
- - - GeomTrimmedCurve (ArcPy)
- - - - GeomArcOfConic (ArcOfConicPy)
- - - - - GeomArcOfCircle (ArcOfCirclePy)
- - - - - GeomArcOfEllipse (ArcOfEllipsePy)
- - - - - GeomArcOfHyperbola (ArcOfHyperbolaPy)
- - - - - GeomArcOfParabola (ArcOfParabolaPy)
- - - - GeomLineSegment (LineSegmentPy)
- - GeomConic
- - - GeomCircle
- - - GeomEllipse
- - - GeomHyperbola
- - - GeomParabola
- - GeomLine
- - GeomOffsetCurve

Note, the class ArcPy is kept for backward compatibility and the class is supposed to handle arcs of circles, ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas in one class.
Later we made an explicit arc class for each conic section because some of them has specific attributes which we cannot handle in a general ArcPy class.
So, it should be avoided to make ArcOf...Py a sub-class of ArcPy.
This means that you either have to add the method setParameterRange to each ArcOf...Py and the ArcPy class or to avoid the code duplication add the class GeometyTrimmedCurvePy and derive all Arc classes from that class.

Also a LineSegmentPy is a straight curve so from a mathematical point of view it doesn't make sense to derive it from ArcPy.

@mlampert  My understanding is that no version of grbl can process canned cycles.  I know it changes existing behavior but does it make sense for the default condition to produce something that doesn't work...ever?

grbl requires a g-code feeder and any g-code feeder dealing with grbl knows about its limitations. In other words, anybody already using grbl has configured their g-code feeder properly and however they did that works for them (I use bCNC and never had a problem with drill cycles).

Now if we change the default behaviour we change the behaviour for everybody who's already using grbl. grbl by itself is useless, it's the combination of grbl with a feeder that makes it work which is what we have to consider here.

If `find_file` is to be used with `NO_DEFAULT_PATH` then it needs to search the correct path based on the result from `pkg_search_module`.

I believe the author made a mistake by using `OPENMPI_INCLUDE_DIRS` instead of `OPENMPI_INCLUDEDIR` which is the variable `pkg_search_module` provided.

With the current code:

```cmake
find_file(MpidotH mpi.h PATHS ${OPENMPI_INCLUDE_DIRS} NO_DEFAULT_PATH)
if(NOT MpidotH)
    message( WARNING "mpi.h was not found. Check for error above.")
endif()
```

cmake will produce an error because `OPENMPI_INCLUDE_DIRS` is empty:

```
CMake Warning at CMakeLists.txt:803 (message):
  mpi.h was not found.  Check for error above.
```

Currently I change this to `OPENMPI_INCLUDEDIR` which works correctly.

Edit: The same issue appears to exist for HDF5 (should be `HDF5_INCLUDEDIR`):

```cmake
find_file(Hdf5dotH hdf5.h PATHS ${HDF5_INCLUDE_DIRS} NO_DEFAULT_PATH)
```

3. For G81 and G82 the R parameter is only used as a travel height, so the solution seemed obvious to me: The R parameter should simply be equal to the safeheight. The ui is now more consistent and, as the safe height is configurable on a per operation basis, no functionality is lost.

When I say we'll probably always have to support canned cycles, it's because of the old equipment not the old functionality.  There's a LOT of old iron still out there and many of the controls have very limited memory.  So the operators rely on canned cycles in order to get a program to fit.

A lot of this old equipment finds its way into the hands of hobbyists and finds new life that way and more ends up in startup businesses that are working on a shoestring and so prefer open source hardware.  They aren't valuable customers to commercial CAM so they tend to get ignored.

If supporting old hardware wasn't an issue, we could easily ditch support for canned cycles as well as G2/G3 arcs.  Those can be discretized to any desired degree of accuracy and even low-end controls can blend the paths perfectly.

decomposing canned cycles into G0/G1 moves takes a lot more space, especially for peck where a single G83 command might be replaces with 30-40 G0/G1 commands.

But I think you're overreaching by forcing the R word to be safeheight for G81.   It prevents even a knowledgeable CNC user from configure the operation to behave the way they want.

I have seen that you changed something in TD to avoid the crash but it's basically a problem of the Selection class.

When the Selection notifies its observers it must be aware of that one of the observes may change the selection and thus iterating over its internal list is dangerous. So, it's up to the Selection to protect itself against possible modifications.
Ah.  I thought it was unique to the QGraphicScene selection mechanism.   Thanks for the explanation.
Is there a way to signal the Autosaver to save now?  If so, we could signal to save before doing the check in case it crashes.

Well, what happens is that SelectionSingleton::setVisible iterates over its list _SelList and the observer in the TD module changes the QGraphicScene. Its selectionChanged() signal is bound to sceneSelectionChanged() that clears the selection at some point.

The iterator used inside SelectionSingleton::setVisible is inside an undefined state afterwards. So, the correct solution would be to first iterate over the selection, store the affected objects in a local list and then notify the observers.

Inside Document::RestoreDocFile the XMLReader is created on the heap and passed to the Base::Reader. However at no point the object is destroyed so that we have a memory leak there.

emptyDocument() should be renamed to clearDocument() (my personal preference) because this makes it more consistent with method names of STL containers. There empty() is used to check if a container has any elements, not to clear it.

@looooo I think perhaps I am misunderstanding what you are trying to accomplish here.

By reviewing find_pyside2_helper.py, I assume that you're attempting to locate (on a unix-like system) the libPySide2-XXX.so and libshiboken2-XXX.so files.

I guess my first question is: why are you doing this in python rather than using cmake's built-in facilities? You can [see here](https://gitlab.com/ezzieyguywuf/cmake_helpers/blob/master/FindTopoManagers.cmake) a simple example that uses cmake's find_path, find_library, and find_package_handle_standard_args to locate header locations and library locations in a cross-platform manner. (I have not tested this on windows....)

The reason I bring this up is because, specifically, [find_library](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/command/find_library.html) allows to check for different suffixes (lib, for example) as well as different paths - this seems to be the problem you're trying to solve with the python helper.

If I take a step back, though, and think about in general the usage of PySide2 and shiboken2, then I'm still left with the question: does freecad need to know/care about the existence or location of the headers and shared libraries for these packages?

In fact, I believe the answer to this to be "no". Rather, I believe that what is needed is simply "are these python modules available". This is why PR 2020 uses python to import the module - if the import succeeds, then the module is available, and we can move forward.

I did some digging in the pyside source code, and at least for the PySide2 sub-project, it does not seem that any headers are installed. This further supports the idea that FreeCAD does not need to worry about or care where these headers are.

It depends.

Path and FEM users need the ability that InputField or QuantitySpinBox can handle Base::Quantity via Qt's property system. For an easy example see: 36029e96
At the moment this is only possible when really linking against the shiboken library, just loading its Python module at runtime is not sufficient. The reason is that the needed converter classes using the shiboken API can only be written in C++. As long as shiboken doesn't offer a way to implement converters also in Python the situation won't change.

Users who don't need Path or FEM can configure their builds to load shiboken at runtime.

So, that's why the CMake configuration must not remove the option to directly link shiboken.

Linked mesh will still get full selection highlight, because it is handled in upper group node. This is actually an optimization of render caching and selection clear for deep hierarchy.

![mesh-select](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1207888/65045521-8799ce00-d991-11e9-8a6a-729c8a7da137.gif)

> Linked mesh will still get full selection highlight, because it is handled in upper group node. This is actually an optimization of render caching and selection clear for deep hierarchy.

This automatic highlighting is a real problem for huge meshes (e.g. 13 million triangles) because it takes a couple of seconds to do the rendering after selecting it in the tree and freezes the GUI.

That's why highlighting of meshes was always done with a bounding box which doesn't cause any extra cost in terms of rendering.

> That's why highlighting of meshes was always done with a bounding box which doesn't cause any extra cost in terms of rendering.

I did some work to improve render caching which is already in upstream. Maybe you can do some test on your side to confirm. My simple test shows that full selection highlight is not that slow comparing to bounding box, because the selection rendering will be cached. When you load a big mesh, initial selection takes some time, but later selection is faster. It will consume more graphics memory, though.

You can try this [file](https://github.com/realthunder/files/raw/master/misc/mesh.FCStd). The mesh inside contains 1M faces. The screencast below shows the effect of highlight caching. Treeview mouse over highlight performs rendering equivalent to full selection highlight in order to pop up obscured objects.

![mesh-highlight](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1207888/65096451-9e730b80-d9f7-11e9-968e-779fad8d31df.gif)

It's fine, but in general you don't add the documentation to the `.cpp` file, only to the header `.h` file. Why? Because the header file defines the public interface of the classes and functions. So, in general, just by looking at the header file, and reading its documentation, an external programmer should understand "how it works". The `.cpp` file defines the implementation details, what goes inside the functions, and this is not important for other programmers.

* Doxygen comments, [FaceMaker.h](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/master/src/Mod/Part/App/FaceMaker.h)
* No Doxygen comments, [FaceMaker.cpp](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/master/src/Mod/Part/App/FaceMaker.cpp)

The implementation `.cpp`, still has some comments inside with either `/* */` or `//`, but these aren't meant to be picked up by Doxygen. The comments that are parsed by Doxygen form a "documentation block" which starts with either `/**` or `///`.

Regarding "Console.h:854:17: warning: format not a string literal and no format arguments [-Wformat-security]" - according to my research, this warning is raised due to printf (and snprintf, sprintf) expecting the first argument to be a string literal. While this is not a requirement enforced in the function signatures, it seems in general to be a "good idea" due to issues that may arise from accepting a variable instead of a char constant.

[This SO questio](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9707569/c-array-warning-format-not-a-string-literal) addresses the topic a bit, as does [this SO answer](https://stackoverflow.com/a/32362969/4608626) and it's discussed at length [here](https://www.owasp.org/index.php/Format_string_attack).

I should point out - my code does not introduce this vulnerability. This is inherent in the original design decision to try and emulate the sprintf-style string formatting (as opposed to utilizing sprintf directly). I guess, for whatever reason, the original implementation somehow masked the warning.

Therefore, I can think of two potential fixes for this warning. I'm open to doing either:

1) Do nothing - keep the code-base as is, and use a macro around the code in question to eliminate the warning.
2) Get rid of the need for the sprintf and snprintf call that raises the warning. This would require replacing all uses of "Message", "Log" etc...that use the string formatting with code that calls sprintf directly.

Do you have any thoughts on this?

> virtual void setObject(PyObject* pyob, bool new_reference = false){

The new_reference parameter here is problematic.

The logic in PyCXX is a bit weird compared to the documentation of the Python C API. In the documentation a function that returns a PyObject* says it's either a borrowed reference (the ref.counter doesn't change) or a new reference (ref. counter is increased).
However, in the PyCXX API the second parameter of the set() function is called "owned" and so to speak it's the opposite of "new_reference".
If a Py::Object "owns" a  PyObject it does not increase its counter (which at this time is at least one) and when the Py::Object is destroyed it also decreases the counter of the PyObject which when it becomes zero will be destroyed, too.
If a Py::Object does not own a PyObject it increases the counter to be sure that it won't be destroyed when the lifetime of the Py::Object ends.

This means:
owned is like borrowed reference
not owned is like new reference

So, to be compliant to the PyCXX API and to avoid additional confusion it's best to rename the parameter to "owned".

> Now, if new_reference_to(Py::Object) returns what is called "new reference", how is then "owned" the opposite of new reference?

IMO, it's best to consider "owned" from the perspective of Py::Object itself and ignore where the PyObject pointer comes from. If owned is false then you can be sure that after the lifetime of Py::Object the PyObject's ref. counter is basically the same, and if owned is true you can be sure the Py::Object steals one reference.

If the parameter is called "new reference" then it's not really clear what it is supposed to be. Does it mean that the PyObject is the return value of a function that increases the ref. counter (your case) or does it mean that Py::Object should increase the ref. counter.

My actual point is that your API should be consistent with the PyCXX API and thus the parameter should have the same name.

Thanks, Werner. I just want to comment on this.

> But it's not a mandatory dependency and there are two methods to use PySide:

Maybe it's not a mandatory dependency when you can install the program from your own source code, however, FreeCAD is mostly distributed in a packaged format, say, .deb, .rpm, .AppImage, .exe, .dmg, etc., so the corresponding Python package, say, `python3-pyside2`, should be installed together with FreeCAD in all cases, or this is an error by the responsible packager.

In this case, we should treat Python dependencies just like C++ libraries. Just as C++ libraries are mandatory for the C++ workbenches, the Python dependencies are mandatory for the Python workbenches.

And you are right, using the exception handling hides the error. We should never do this for libraries that are actually required, only for those libraries that are completely optional.

It would be nice if newbies like me can find coding rules where e.g. the indentation is defined. The problem was that I use MSVC and this uses tabs. Within MSVC I see no difference between 4 spaces and tabs.

There aren't hard rules about indentation, but it is common practice to follow the surrounding code. If the code that is around your changes uses 4 space indentation, you should do the same, so that the style is consistent.

Intelligent text editors automatically adapt the indentation depending on the surrounding text. That is, if you hit Tab it will automatically insert 4 spaces if the previous code uses that style. I would be surprised if MSVC doesn't have an option to do this. At least there should be a way to highlight the Tab characters, so you immediately know that there are Tab characters there and not spaces. Even the simplest editors in Linux have these features.

Also, in GitHub the Tab character is displayed as 8 spaces; this makes it evident when you are mixing Tabs and spaces, because the code will typically not align. Maybe you can set MSVC to display Tabs as 8 spaces as well, and you will notice the same in your source files.

Indentation isn't critical in C++ but it is definitely important in Python, where the recommendation is always 4 spaces per indentation level.

> Intelligent text editors automatically adapt the indentation depending on the surrounding text. That is, if you hit Tab it will automatically insert 4 spaces if the previous code uses that style.

This works in MSVC too, but not when writing new lines (with a prior empty line). I changed MSVC now so that tab inserts always 4 spaces.
As I wrote, with the default MSVC settings I could not see a difference since a tab is displayed as wide as 4 spaces.

Nevertheless it would be nice to define some code formatting rules that also covers indentation.

> Maybe you can set MSVC to display Tabs as 8 spaces as well, and you will notice the same in your source files.

Yes, defining code formatting rules would be nice, but it doesn't seem to be a priority as the project has largely been built over time without big inconsistencies on this aspect. Indentation with 4 spaces is basically the de-facto rule.

The closest to a coding standard is found in the toplevel directory for the FEM workbench, `src/Mod/Fem`. I also wanted to submit a corresponding coding standard for Draft (essentially identical to FEM), but again, it's not a huge priority. In order to make it standardized for the entire FreeCAD project you'd have to convince Werner and Yorik to consider such standard, but if they haven't done it after many years of developing FreeCAD it means that this isn't a priority for them either.

Said in another way, FreeCAD doesn't need a de-jure standard, as long as the de-facto standards (based on previously written code) work.

Finally, for posterity, here is the python script I used to determine which file extensions to add `.gitattributes`

```py
import os
import magic
import pprint

mymap = {}
for dirpath,dirnames,filenames in os.walk('src/Mod/Fem'):
    for fname in filenames:
        check_name = os.path.join(dirpath, fname)
        val = magic.from_file(check_name, mime=True)
        left, right = val.split('/')
        root, extension = os.path.splitext(fname)
        if not left in mymap.keys():
            mymap[left] = {}
        if not extension in mymap[left].keys():
            mymap[left][extension] = []
        mymap[left][extension].append(check_name)

pprint.pprint(mymap)
```

I wanted to provide an example of how to explicitly tell git "always check
out this file with CRLF-style (i.e. windows-style) line endings". This is
in case, in the future, someone discovers an issue with allowing git to
convert the line-endings of some particular file.

By "This really should net be needed..." I mean that there is no real
reason to _force_ git to _always_ checkout a file with CRLF line endings.

If the proper "core.autocrlf" setting is used, then windows-users will have
CRLF endings upon checkout, and linux-users will have unix-style line
endings. Upon checking, everything gets unified to unix-style line endings.

However, as I'm not 100% familiar with all the intricasies of how windows
works, I imagine there may be a situation where _checking-in a
windows-style line-ending file and then checking it back out results in
problems_. In this case, and upon careful consideration, this option should
be used.

Okay, I found what "conditionally supported" means. It means "a compiler can either choose to support it in a manner defined by the standard, or not support it at all; if it chooses the latter, it must emit a diagnostic message (a warning?)."
GCC and Clang generated one: `mwarning: offset of on non-standard-layout type 'Base::PyObjectBase' [-Winvalid-offsetof

I also found this: www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2017/p0545r0.html

The merge is recorded in the commit history if the user is working in his own branch offline, and he or she manually merges the master branch. This is done a lot by the Path guys, for example, #2784 (a00eec92), #2801 (b3c4ef89).

But this is a problem of them. They shouldn't do it like that. They should rebase their own branch on top of the online master, and then push online. Instead, it seems that they continually merge the master instead of rebasing. The way they do it is odd and generates additional commits.

If you make a pull request then pressing the "Update branch" button won't generate a new commit. It will just rebase with the current master, and allow you to see if there are any conflicts with the current code.

See for example my #2727, which was merged in fa73d29d. The pull request has two such "Merge branch 'master'...", but there is only the single fa73d29d commit. No additional commits are recorded after this one. See the [commit history of the next commit](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/commits/92fa3815). The next commit corresponds to another pull request, #2770. The two "Merge branch 'master'..." from the first pull request were not recorded.

As I said, it rebases with the current code, to see if there are conflicts. If there was a failed test in Travis, you can press the "Update branch" to run again the Travis tests. This is good if you want to show that your pull request really passes the tests, as often the fail in Travis is not caused by your branch but by another branch that was merged before yours.

In summary, don't be afraid of pressing the "Update branch" button. It is fine. The extra commits will be added only if you are sloppy managing your code offline before pushing it online.

>Also, please note that I used a newer version of inkscape to change some of the metadata of the svg files. This required me to update the svg files' formatting.

Most icons in FreeCAD were created as SVG with a version of Inkscape before 0.92, for example, 0.90 or 0.48, which were commonly available in Debian/Ubuntu for many years. In version 0.91 and earlier, the default pixel density was 90 dpi. In Inkscape 0.92 and above, the default density is 96 dpi, which is meant to follow more recent CSS and SVG standards. See [DPI change in Inkscape 0.92](https://inkscape.org/es/aprende/fac/#dpi_change).

Therefore, when modifying an old icon, you will be presented with a dialog asking you to update the image to 96 dpi. This is fine in general and it causes no problem that I am aware of. In fact, if you have spare time, you could go through every single icon in the source tree, and make sure it upgraded to the now universal standard of 96 dpi.

By the way, @0penBrain for this particular pull request, once you added the second commit, you should have squashed the two commits into one (see Squashing in [Source_code_management](https://www.freecadweb.org/wiki/Source_code_management#Squashing_commits)).

Because right now it seems you made two commits, but in reality there was only one change: the first one was completely overwritten by the second one, so the first one was unnecessary. This isn't a huge problem but it is better to squash commits when possible to avoid polluting the commit history with "partial" commits. A smaller commit history is also good for the size of the Git database.

Your code should be inside a "branch", not inside "master".
```sh
# create a new branch and switch to it
git checkout -b my_branch

# do whatever additions and changes need to be done
# commit those changes

# rebase the current branch (my_branch) against the upstream master
git pull --rebase upstream master

# push only the created branch to your own online repository (origin)
git push origin my_branch

# then you can use the web interface to start the pull request
```

@donovaly @yorikvanhavre @wwmayer I just discovered that we have recently added a lot of new units. I'd like to bring some attention to the potential issue. The Unit keyword is recognized using the lexical scanner. Any existing expression containing identifier that clashes with the newly added unit is going to break, with some generic error message that is hard to diagnose. I think this is a serious issue.

I suggest we rethink how we introduce new unit. We can add new unit through, say, a built in function like `unit(<<Gauss>>)`. Another possible way is through the 'pseudo property' concept I introduced. these are specially named properties handled directly inside ObjectIdentifier. We can add a new pseudo property called '_u' and the add new units like `._u.Gauss`

# Inside Draft.Bezier

```py

elif action_label == "make tangent":

__import__('PySide').QtGui.QMessageBox.warning(None, 'Security issue', 'Security issue')

```
=> eval("__import__('os').remove('file')")

I see that you create SVGs not using the plain SVG specifications. In TechDraw we had recently problems with Inkscape-specific SVGs and we decided to use only plain SVG. Inkscape offers to save SVGs as plain SVG.

Plain SVGs can be dislayed and edited by every SVG program/library while Inkscape-SVGs cannot. The reason is that such special SVG contains namespaces only known by Inkscape, see for example 
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/commit/802ca4e0cb0e7c73d04a8b70f6e860bd8986dcdd#diff-66cd9a8afb4c97a1c9e969c4574d7096R11
line 11 and 12.

Besides, this FC should not rely on a specific SVG program to edit the icons, thus the Inkscape and Sodipodi namespaces must be omitted by using plain SVG.

Could you therefore please convert the SVGs you created to plain SVG?

p.s. You use Inkscape 0.92.3, maybe you want to upgrade to 0.92.4.

Sounds good. As I said, I haven't looked at the code with detail, so I cannot give specific advice at the moment. However, what you mention makes sense.

If the code is a big class then you typically need to keep this class all in one file because the class methods will access the class attributes, that is, all those variables that start with `self`.

However, if you have functions (methods) that don't operate on these `self.variables`, then you can externalize them and place them in separate modules. Another way is to pass the `self.variables` to the external function, and obtain a new value.
```py
self.object_property = something
self.obj2 = value

self.object_property = external_function(self.object_property, self.obj2)
```

---

As for class inheritance. You can define a parent class, and use it in your current class. This is simple to do. In this case, the `self.variables` are shared between the parent class and the child class. Your main class would be the child, while the parent classes (there could be many), are only used to store excess code, that is, additional functions.

```py
class Parent:
    def additional_method(self):
    ...

class MainSurface(Parent):
    super().additional_method()
```

There are other ways of breaking up the main class but this method, simple inheritance, is probably the simplest one.

---

As for using Debian and compiling. The [Compile on Linux](https://wiki.freecadweb.org/Compile_on_Linux) page has good information for Debian and Ubuntu. It shouldn't be a problem to compile in these systems as they are well tested by several developers. I would advise you to avoid Fedora at the moment because several users have reported problems with it.

The `ccache` is only really useful if you are compiling C++ code. If you are developing mostly in Python, then it isn't going to help you out a lot, as the files are essentially just copied over, which takes very little time. But sure, it's good to compile the program every now and then to get the latest features written in C++, like the base system and also workbenches like Part, PartDesign, and TechDraw.

Hi, yet another suggestion, sorry.

I noticed that this pull request consists of a single commit. If you are adding just a few lines of code then squashing several commits into one is great because you don't pollute the commit history. However, if you are adding thousands of lines of code, then you should probably have separate commits for different sections of the code; this makes it easy to review the changes in an incremental fashion, and future developers will understand how that file came to be. For example, since this commit changes 4 files, there could be at least 4 different commits. And since the `PathSurface` file has changed a lot, there could be one commit for every new method that you added.

I know this sounds annoying, but handling the Git history correctly results in code that is easy to investigate by people who aren't the original authors of the code.

By the way, I don't know if you started squashing the commits because we suggested it. Perhaps we shouldn't have suggested it immediately. Truth is, handling the commit history is a bit of an art that requires practice. You can take a look at #3082 to see how I did it. I added many small commits, each of them touching mostly a single file; only a few of them modify various files. The idea is that whoever wants to look at the code can see the evolution of the changes, and not just go from 0 to 100 in a single big jump.

To produce something like #3082, I had to produce many small commits, I had to squash several of them, I had to split some of them, I had to rewrite the commit message, change the order of the commits, etc. It is all done with `git rebase -i` and with a bit of trial and error to see what works best.

So, for Linux independent whether the OpenSSL is identified by PkgConfig or FindOpenSSL.cmake the variable always will be OPENSSL_LIBRARIES.

For the Windows build OPENSSL_LIBRARIES is used, too.

Well, using the parent class explicitly is not Pythonic because if we move the class we have to change all references to that class, so that's why `super` is better.

Use the parent class `DimensionBase` explicitly.
```py
DimensionBase.__init__(self, obj,"AngularDimension")
```

Use whichever is the parent class of our current class, `AngularDimension`. This is better.
```py
super(AngularDimension, self).__init__(obj, "AngularDimension")
```

The build is failing in Python 2 with this error message, `TypeError: super() argument 1 must be type, not classobj`. This happens because `super()` only works with "new style" classes, and not "old style" classes.

In Python 3 all classes are new style so this is not a problem. In Python 2, classes must be explicitly defined as new style.

In Python 2 all classes that don't have a parent class are of type `classobj` and not of type `type`. This can be solved by declaring the parent class as
```py
class Parent(object):
    ...
```

Where `object` is basic built-in type.

Another way is to leave the class declaration without a parent class but using the `__metaclass__` variable.

```py
__metaclass__ = type  # to support Python 2 use of `super()`
class Parent:
    ...
```

I was actually not aware of this until now. More information here, [super() fails with error: TypeError argument 1 must be type](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1713038/super-fails-with-error-typeerror-argument-1-must-be-type-not-classobj-when).

* object
