Before the big merge, there was only the attach() method in the view object proxy, not the object proxy. I added that to allow the proxy to override the C++ view provider type. The view provider type is normally determined by object's C++ API getViewProviderName(), and cannot be overridden by the proxy. I introduced the attach() method in proxy to allow the core to attach the proxy before creating the C++ view provider. The attach() method is only called if you ask for it, something like

```python
App.ActiveDocument.addObject('Part::FeaturePython', 'feature', MyProxy(), MyViewProxy(), True)
```
Please check the docstring of addObject() for more details.

Final words, it is actually rare for the need to override the C++ view provider type. So you guys probably won't need it. `ViewProviderLink` requires it because it borrows the visual from the linked view object.

>  `ViewProviderLink` requires it because it borrows the visual from the linked view object.

I mean, if you used it, it means we could also use it to add `App::Link` support to other objects, or not?

Link is pretty new so we haven't had a lot of time to use it in Draft and Arch. But in the future we will probably want to add more support for it in Arch as it really helps avoid copying objects; and it helps to reduce file sizes.

> I mean, if you used it, it means we could also use it to add `App::Link` support to other objects, or not?

Yes, of course you can use it. What I mean by my last comment is that besides `ViewProviderLink`, I don't think any other view provider requires this type of overriding mechanism.

I am completely in support of the feature.  
 
I do think it needs an alternate implementation - rather than completing each offset to final depth, I propose it complete each of the successive offsets at current depth before beginning the next depth layer. 
 
This proposal is suggested with the idea that chip removal is one of the two top priorities with such a feature improvement.  Based on this chip removal priority, clearing all the offsets at the current layer before dropping to the next layer will allow for better chip removal.  
 
The above proposal would require quite a change to the code in order to process all offsets at a specific layer, but I think the resulting operation would be a safer one for the machine and user.

I took a look and this is the current situation regarding Clang.

> -Wextra now enables -Wdeprecated-copy. The warning deprecates move and copy constructors in classes where an explicit destructor is declared. This is for compatibility with GCC 9, and forward looking for a change that’s being considered for C++23. You can disable it with -Wno-deprecated-copy.

https://releases.llvm.org/10.0.0/tools/clang/docs/ReleaseNotes.html

And as for Eigen, currently Clang 10 warnings are not addressed yet, and currently they are suppressing such warnings, when it comes to GCC 9+:

```
#if defined(__GNUC__) && (__GNUC__ >=9)
  #pragma GCC diagnostic ignored "-Wdeprecated-copy"
#endif
```

https://gitlab.com/libeigen/eigen/-/issues/1788

All in all i feel that it makes the most sense to suppress such warnings for Clang 10, for now. If somebody would introduce such warning in FreeCAD code, GCC should still be able to detect it.

Actually i now read Clang tends to pretend to be __GNUC__, hence the above approach, used on Eigen side, might suppress such warnings for Clang 10 too. As the changes were backported to Ubuntu 20.04 i will create an additional commit latter today and lets see how that goes.

@adrianinsaval, that was used in an earlier version of this code. I believe the reason for switching to using facets of the view tesselation directly was the desire to avoid repeated re-meshing when regenerating paths, since this re-meshing can be rather expensive. By using the view facets, that price is only paid once per session, rather than once per path operation generation.

The main downsides of using view facets I see are 
- affecting view performance, if the internal model is shown, and 
- the restriction on the linear deviation to 0.01mm, which is barely sufficient for high precision CAM work.

That said, using `tesselate()` also refines the mesh for subsequent `Part.getFacets()` calls. The lack of angular resolution support should not matter here, but we would need to find a way to avoid re-computing the mesh every time, even when there is already an existing mesh of at least the requested resolution.

I personally see step overs and breaks (the things handled by this code) in the same category, and with similar needs. I also think that we will use them more and more interchangeably as we are adding optimizations, such as processing cut regions in groups when strictly following the linear PDC direction would result in a lot of repetitive rapids and longer job times.

Do you have specific differences in mind? If we have no need to diverge right now, then I would prefer to keep the code unified for ease of maintenance. > I personally see step overs and breaks in the same category, and with similar needs. I also think that we will use them more and more interchangeably as we are adding optimizations, such as processing cut regions in groups when strictly following the linear PDC direction would result in a lot of repetitive rapids and longer job times.


I do agree that stepovers and breaks share commonalities (I would even say they are more similar than different).  However, there are differences that could benefit from handling each in a separate function. One reason is the number of unique cut patterns, that might increase later.  Another is that for breaks, given the cut pattern, one can know and predict the geometrical path of travel that must take place through the break to the landing point on the other side.  Whereas stepovers can be distant and perhaps require additional analysis to avoid collision - and this analysis potentially changes with some of the cut patterns.

> Do you have specific differences in mind? If we have no need to diverge right now, then I would prefer to keep the code unified for ease of maintenance. We can always diverge at a later point if we find a reason to.

Honestly I've never seen a file that Qt wouldn't cope with when saved as inkscape SVG, that would open better when saved as plain SVG. The difference between the two are basically all the additional attributes that inkscape adds to objects in order to be better editable in inkscape. But it's the essence of XML (and thus SVG) to allow custom attributes, and Qt handles it properly by skipping unknown attributes. So the only real advantage in saving as plain SVG is reducing the file size a little bit. But I don't see an reason why not either...

> Honestly I've never seen a file that Qt wouldn't cope with when saved as inkscape SVG, that would open better when saved as plain SVG.

This is not about Qt but about other programs around. We already had this case this year: the SVG export from FreeCAD could not be viewed by the browsers Chrome and Firefox.

The reason is non-plain SVGs contain style links such as
`xmlns:sodipodi="http://sodipodi.sourceforge.net/DTD/sodipodi-0.dtd"`

In the case we had, the browsers complained about that such an URL because it could not be reached thus the style to be used to display the SVG was not available.

So every SVG file that is used to be later exported as SVG should be plain SVG to avoid such cases. So icons are not effected but files for drawings, sketches etc.

> Still I have a personal problem with Draft.Point: it has a placement. It's shape is always located at it's 0,0,0.

Mmm. I'm not sure about this. Last time I checked, the Point does have a `Placement` but this is updated whenever you update the X, Y, Z properties. The `Placement` is actually hidden; if you show it you can see that its position corresponds to `App.Vector(X, Y, Z)`.

A different behavior is seen with `Part::Point` from the Part Workbench. This object has both a Placement and X, Y, Z properties; the final position is the sum of both, `Placement.Base + App.Vector(X, Y, Z)`. I noticed this when I was looking into the `Draft PointArray` tool.

The PointArray tool actually uses the Placement if it's found, and then X, Y, Z, if available, so the result is the same. However, I actually prefer to use the X, Y, Z values because it is explicit what is required from a Point. The Placement property has Position but also Rotation. The Rotation can be neglected as a Point naturally only has Position. So, by modifying X, Y, Z, it's more evident that you only need to change these values. In the past the PointArray would use also the rotation of the Point but I think this is strange because you would rarely care about the rotation of a point; you normally only care about its position.
Yes, we can leave it like this. I was just annoyed I could not change directly it's placement but had to change its coordinates instead, making it a "special object" compared to the other Draft ones.

@mwganson : AFAIK when a PR is merged, commits are just pushed to the master as they are.
To squash/fixup, you have to use interactive rebase called with 'git rebase -i COMMIT', where COMMIT is the first ancestor of the first commit you want to deal with.
So in your case, your branch was created from master commit cd53410, so you can run 'git rebase -i cd53410'
But it may be easier to make reference to your own commits. In your case your first commit is 6b26bef so you can enter the equivalent 'git rebase -i 6b26bef\~1'.
Finally another way is knowing you have done 4 commits, you can enter 'git rebase -i HEAD\~4'.
Then everything is quite well explain on the text editing you get. If you want to squash (merge commits + merge commit messages) a commit with its parent, replace 'pick' by 's' or 'squash'. If you want to fixup (merge commits + discard commit message of fixup commit) a commit with its parent, replace 'pick' by 'f' or 'fixup'.
Of course you can chain several subsequent fixups/squashes.
For sake of completeness, it is possible to move up/down a commit in the list (this is especially useful for fixups).
Let's say that in your case, the file you accidentally added was introduced with your first commit (I didn't check), your rebasing could look something like) : 
pick 6b26bef
fixup 83711b6 #The 4th commit actually fixes the 1st
squash c357859 #Could be 'pick' if it has sense it's a separate commit
fixup 6545f0f

As it will create non fast-forward changes, after using an interactive rebase you have to force push. I advise to use 'git push --force-with-lease' (rather than a brutal '--force') so it stays safe.

It should not be named "Part" nor "Part Design", because it doesn't have properties that are specific to these workbenches. The properties are general.
* "General" refers to the automatic calculation of boolean operations; this mostly affects Part.
* "Shape view" refers to the tesselation level; angular deflection and deviation are properties that all `Part::Features` have, not only objects from Part and PartDesign.
* "Shape appearance" refers to the visual properties of the object, shape color, line color, line width, vertex color, vertex size, bounding box color, two side rendering (lighting); again these are properties that all `Part::Features` have, not only objects from Part and PartDesign (also Draft, Sketcher, Arch).

Yes. The thing is the loading process of FreeCAD works in mysterious ways. If I remember correctly, the initialization modules, `Init.py` and `InitGui.py`, are passed to an `exec()` function. They aren't loaded as regular Python modules. This is the reason inside these modules, `FreeCAD` is already defined from the calling environment, as well as many other things.

When you use flake8, it doesn't detect that `FreeCAD` was imported, and will mark it as an error. But the actual FreeCAD program doesn't have a problem with it because `FreeCAD` is in fact imported before this. Look for the files called `FreeCADInit.py` and `FreeCADInitGui.py` in the source code which contain the basic initialization code.

In Draft and Arch, I prefer to be explicit about this, and actually import FreeCAD, but this is just for consistency in the file.

What you see is what you get, man. I've had to sit for months waiting for my pull requests to be merged. Join the party.

What do you mean "real" unit tests? Imprecisely language like this is not helpful.

Unit tests are defined all over FreeCAD; they subclass Python's `unittest.TestCase` class to be able to define small tests; you can test anything you want, the creation of a line, the movement of a line, the creation of a solid, a particular function, etc. When you submit a pull request, the unit tests are automatically run albeit without the interface, thus `FreeCADCmd -t 0`.

Locally in your computer you can run the entire set of unit tests, including graphical components, with `FreeCAD -t 0`. You can define as many unit tests as you need. One of my first contributions was reworking the unit tests of the Draft Workbench so we could test every object in the workbench; see #2668, #2727, #3005, and the `src/Mod/Draft/drafttests` directory. I wanted to do the same with Arch, but I haven't had the time, as I put most of my effort on refactoring Draft.

But yes, personally I think we could improve and add even more unit tests, especially for the most useful workbenches like TechDraw, PartDesign, and Path.

> What do you mean "real" unit tests? Imprecisely language like this is not helpful.

I mean unit tests that run independently of FreeCAD. For python scripts it means that FreeCad, FreeCadGui, Part, etc modules are stubbed so that the unittest can be executed with pure python. The benefit is that CI feedback loop is much faster (seconds rather than minutes or hours) as you don't need to compile the whole source tree.

Though, I'm not sure if it is feasible, as FreeCAD architecture seem to heavily depend on Qt slot/signals which are hard to mock out.
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/pull/3786

Moreover, I don't see unittest coverage being meantioned as a requirement when creating PRs. It only says you need to run existing ones, not cover newly introduced code. So there's no incentive to increase coverage. And as a concequence, there's no incentive to measure coverage. This lead to crashes after non-trivial PRs being merged.

Regressions and crashes lead to reviewers hesitant to merge PRs due to the fear. Which in turn leads to slow improvement and rare releases. Slow pace of development hurts FreeCAD community as contributors and users lose the patience (life is short) and turn to more vibrant communities (e.g. Blender BIM).

Some developers and users stay, but they rely on the core FreeCAD functionality exposed in python API to develop add-ons. This leads to fragmentation, as the PRs that get merged might change the behavior that add-ons rely on to function properly. Which leads to add-ons being unstable too. Which further leads to people leaving.

Some day there will be a crisis. If not already, as 0.19 release is being pushed further and further.

f2770a4169 be careful when sorting headers alphabetically. After the block of 3rd party headers the very first header should be the one that contains the class declaration of the source file, i.e. in this case TaskFaceColors.h should included before SoBrepFaceSet.h. Violating this rule is considered bad practice.

In C++ it's considered good practice that a header file is self-contained, i.e. it includes all necessary headers or uses forward declarations so that the source file that includes this header doesn't need to include other headers beforehand.
By changing this order the risk raises to hide the fact that a header is not self-contained.

In one of your other PRs you ran into exactly this problem. By changing the order of headers you got a build error because one of the header is not self-contained. You hided this fact by changing the order inside the source file. The right way would be to fix the header that is not self-contained.

> Could we also multiple inherit WallGuiTools from Wall object or from the ViewProviderWall to have directly access to WallGuiTools's methods from within the wall?

I think multiple inheritance is generally discouraged. Composition is preferable and easier to comprehend.

Here's the domain model as I see it:
- Wall is the UI-independent model of the architectural entity, has a base axis (a vector with first_point and last_point) , an extrusion direction, height and width
- Wall view provider is the 3D-engine specific implementation of GUI view of a wall (pivy.coin nodes), provides mapping of the wall model to a graphical scene, contains display options unrelated to architectural entity (visibility, colors, lines, etc)
- GUI tools represent user intent and manipulations with a model (e.g. move vector points)

Implementing this domain model in a single object is technically possible (using multiple inheritance), but I wouldn't call it a good design. User intent to manipulate an object should be modeled as a separate entity. So that when you add more ways to manipulate the object (e.g. swap the first and the last points of a vector), you only touch the "tools" part of the code. And when you add more ways to model the object (e.g. using 2D curves or profile rather than vector), you only touch the UI-independent model (since you may already have tools to manipulate 2D objects such as curves or vector).

So, we have to compose these 3 domain entities somehow. Since view in FreeCAD is implemented as a `.ViewObject` property, the easiest way to implement tools to manipulate the object is to do the same: attach tools as a property of an object.

> to identify which Vertex has been moved I'm comparing the coordinates of the Vertexes got from getSelectionEx with every Vertex in the Shape....

The returned value of getSelectionEx is a list of SelectionObjects. For a SelectionObject you can access the methods HasSubObjects, SubElementNames, SubObjects. So with HasSubObjects you will know if a sub-shape is selected or not, with SubElementNames you get the internal name like Vertex1, Vertex2, ... or Edge1, Edge2, ... or Face1, Face2, ...

From a SelectionObject you can access PickedPoints (I am not sure if it's that you use for the comparison) but you must be aware that the point coordinates are how they appear in the 3d view. So if a shape is part of some nested Part containers or a body the point contains the placement transformation(s) and thus it's difficult to identify the actual point on the shape.

Today I ran into a crash due to the changes of DocInfo::getFullPath(const char *)

You used the function std::mismatch to check if the path name starts with "https://". Now in my case the argument is an empty string and according to https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/mismatch this leads to undefined behaviour. In the documentation you find the comments:
> If no mismatches are found when the comparison reaches last1, the pair holds last1 and the corresponding iterator from the second range. The behavior is undefined if the second range is shorter than the first range. (until C++14)

> If no mismatches are found when the comparison reaches last1 or last2, whichever happens first, the pair holds the end iterator and the corresponding iterator from the other range.  (since C++14)

Since you used the overloaded version that only needs three arguments the second container must have at least first2 + (last1 - first1) elements. But because the second string is empty this always leads to undefined behaviour independent of which C++ standard is used.
With MSVC I get the error: Expression: cannot seek string iterator after end.

Since the intention is to check if the string starts with "https://" and you already have a QString it's much easier and faster to use QString's startWith method.

According to your comment:
> TODO: build a far much more resilient approach to test for an URI

You can use the class QUrl which has the method isLocalFile.

Some remarks:
* The AttachExtensionPython is always added if the selected objects lacks of the AttachExtension. Since this is done automatically and affects any kind of object you selected wouldn't it be nicer to pop-up a dialog and ask the user beforehand?
In case the user does this on purpose and don't want this dialog to pop-up each time a check mark could be added to not show the dialog any more.

* Currently we have two implementations of the attachment task panel. One is written in Python and is accessible as command within the Part wb. The other one is written in C++ and is accessible via the property editor. When using the latter then the attachment extension is not added

* Originally the execute() command was not designed to call the execute() method of its parent class. Now sometimes a class invokes the method of its parent class and in most other classes it doesn't. IMO, this will lead to quite some confusion and inconsistent behaviour.
Currently in FEM and TechDraw there are many classes that invokes the parent's function and there it's obviously on purpose which is OK.
In Part it's done for the PrimitiveFeature classes but it only hides the actual bug. IMO when executing a feature then the document must make sure to also always execute its extensions. It shouldn't depend on how the execute method of a feature is implemented.
That's why I recommend to move the code from DocumentObject::execute() to DocumentObject::recompute()

UIso and VIso (and many others) are virtual methods of OpenCascade's abstract Geom_Surface class. At the very beginning when implementing the Python wrapper classes we haven't implemented a wrapper for Geom_Surface and thus implemented its virtual methods in all derived Python wrapper classes. This led to a lot of code duplication and made maintenance more difficult.

That's why also a wrapper for Geom_Surface has been added and this made the implementation in various sub-classes obsolete.

@vocx-fc 

Yes, this function is only used by `exportIFC` function. I always call recursively here because it's a normal behaviour how `draftobjects.clone.Clone` work. 

### Let's first understand how `draftobjects.clone.Clone` works:

Suppose, I create a sketch at (100, 0, 0) point and then pad it (let name of object is **Base**), so this **Base** object placed at (100, 0, 0) but `Base.Placement.Base` is (0, 0, 0). Now, I create a clone object (name **CloneOfBase**) on **Base** object, this **CloneOfBase** object placed exactly at the same point and taking **Base** object shape as origin point and when we set placement to (50, 0, 0) then this placement is from **Base** not from global origin.

Now, I again create another clone object (name **CloneOfClone**) on **CloneOfBase** object and `CloneOfClone.Placement.Base` is (50, 0, 0). If we change placement to (0, 0, 0), then this **CloneOfClone** placed exactly same at **Base** object. So, internally this object also taking **Base** object as base shape.

As, this check `get_type(obj) == "Clone" and obj.Objects:` is for `draftobjects.clone.Clone` object and that's why I always search base object recursively.

This doesn't work either. Either write QString::fromLatin1("xcb") or QLatin1String("xcb").
QString has an overloaded constructor to directly pass a C string (https://doc.qt.io/qt-5/qstring.html#QString-7) but we have disabled it on purpose by setting QT_NO_CAST_FROM_ASCII.

This is because in FreeCAD we have to work with many string classes (C string, std::string, ...). By forbidding the direct conversion the developer is forced to think about it if the string is 7-bit ASCII or a unicode string e.g. encoded as utf-8.

There is no double namespace definition!
The statement `using namespace Gui` means that the namespace is **used** but doesn't **define** it. Without this line we would have to write the namespace as prefix to every constructor, destructor, function and so on: `Gui::FileDialog::FileDialog`, `Gui::FileDialog::~FileDialog()`, ...

A namespace is defined with `namespace Gui { ... }` and the function `dontUseNativeDialog` is inside there on purpose to reduce the risk of conflicting double declarations. Removing the `namespace Gui { ... }` moves `dontUseNativeDialog` to the global namespace.

An even better way is to use an unnamed namespace because then the compiler creates a unique name and thus avoids any possible declaration clashes. ceccc212b

For more details:
https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/namespace#Unnamed_namespaces
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/357404/why-are-unnamed-namespaces-used-and-what-are-their-benefits

I add verbose tool tips to many commands because often there is very little documentation about them in their corresponding wiki page (or anywhere else). Therefore, the tooltip serves as a way of documenting the tool in the same place it is defined, that is, the documentation is close to the definition, and is less likely to rot over time; this is what I've been doing with the tools of the Draft Workbench. I think if the wiki documentation was very complete, then a verbose tooltip would not be necessary because the user could always refer to it, however, that is currently not the case so I think this is a good compromise.

> What's the point of "to determine its curvature"? A constraining non-boundary edge for sure has an impact on the shape of the surface and thus to its curvature but this is true for all edges.

You are right in general, however, I'm thinking about those who are learning to use the software and who may not be experts in 3D modelling. I tested the functions with many simple three- and four-edge closed wires, and regular polygons. Essentially, you will always get a "flat" face in space; obviously this face may not be parallel to the base XY, YZ, XZ planes, it may be oriented in any direction. So, if we have this "flat" face, we can add a non-boundary vertex or edge away from that face to determine its "bulge", that is, how much it curves away from the original face. See the wiki, [Surface_Filling](https://wiki.freecadweb.org/Surface_Filling).
```
        c
a ------------- b    if a and b are points lying on the boundary of the surface,
                     the non-boundary c point indicates if there will be a bulge, and how small or large
```

I think the `Part.Arc` method, or one of those, also describes arcs in terms of a bulge, which determines the radius of curvature of the arc.

I think if you are experienced with modelling, then it's quite clear that any edge will naturally affect the final shape of the surface, however, I think that for beginners, having this concept of "curvature" is helpful to understand what the non-boundary constraints do. See also the scripting example in [Surface_Filling](https://wiki.freecadweb.org/Surface_Filling).

I understand this. However, when I rewrote the wiki pages, there was no information on how to use the tool. So, I had to test it, look at the code, test more, etc. I had to do all this because there was no documentation. A new user will be in the same situation; he or she won't have an indication on how to use the tool (in my opinion, the tool is not very intuitive), and thus adding a longer explanation will allow most users to start using the command without taking their eyes away from the program; often reading the tooltip is enough in such cases.

In my opinion, this is a good compromise between providing full documentation (using [Std_WhatsThis](https://wiki.freecadweb.org/Std_WhatsThis)), and just adding a very short text that doesn't mention anything special ("Creates a curve on a mesh"). In my opinion, we should try to "squeeze" as much information as possible in the tooltip, to teach the user quickly. For commands that are very intuitive, this is not necessary, but for commands which are a bit more complex, this is helpful. This is a personal opinion, of course; now that I've written the wiki documentation, then such a long tooltip is maybe not necessary, but I do ask you to consider how helpful it is to have the command definition, and the short documentation in the tooltip in the same place. The code is also self documenting, which is great for future maintenance.

So I can remove the word "curvature" but please consider that sometimes we need to use laymen terms to describe things.

@wmayer quick question, is there a technical reason why the text fields in 4499508 aren't translatable ?

No. There is no reason to not translate them. In order to do that the macro QT_TRANSLATE_NOOP must be used.
So, instead of writing
`openCommand("Add horizontal constraint");` it could be `openCommand(QT_TRANSLATE_NOOP("Command", "Add horizontal constraint"));`

Then in the undo/redo dialog class the string must be translated with `qApp->translate("Command", text)`

Important is that the context string "Command" is used everywhere because otherwise not all strings will be translated.

However, it is not clear to me what caused the regression. You made the bounding box now tighter and this works, but what made it so wide?

> However, it is not clear to me what caused the regression. You made the bounding box now tighter and this works, but what made it so wide?

I think it's a Qt library change at some point in time.  It was stated somewhere that if one wants tight positioning, one should use QGraphicsSimpleTextItem instead of QGraphicsTextItem.  Only the latter supports rich text editor, and thus bounding box calculations for it are considerably less accurate.  My current belief is that in some recent Qt version the QGraphicsTextItem bounding box hase been relaxed, and I could think at least of three reasons: (1) Improved performance for rich text rendering, (2) Reserving space for some weird unicode characters, e.g. integral sign, note key, oversized f, etc.  (3) Improving the standard FC font.  I think adding support for characters in a particular font would increase the Qt bounding box without any program changes, if some really tall characters would have been added to the font.  Fonts are difficult!

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9208489/tallest-unicode-character

> Just to assure: did you test that with your PR the tolerances don't hit the dimension line, for combinations of small and large font sizes with line widths?

I did test with a combination of various font sizes, and everything worked.  The new bounding box trimming is calculated in a Qt function which checks the actual plaintext against a given font for a tight box (luckily Qt supports this fully), but this does not work with rich text.  Luckily, TD dimension labels are plaintext, so everything works.  Note also that the tight bounding box is very (too) tight, so the code calculates a "trimmed" bounding box of reasonable size between the relaxed bounding box and the tight one.

I forgot to test with different line widths.  The old line width logic is untouched, so everything *should* magically work, but you are correct that this should be ascertained and tested, thanks!

CAVEAT EMPTOR:  Although I believe this PR works fine in other regards, I realized there is one problem:  The original Properties under- and over-tolerances in TD are not Distances, but Floats.  This causes the problem, that when changing the unit system for the document, all the dimension values are converted, but the tolerance values stay the same (e.g. tolerance +0.5 mm becomes +0.5 feet), which is obviously patently incorrect.  This PR fixes the problem by using the same UnitSchema conversion for tolerance values as for the actual Dimension value.  However, a new problem arises, namely the user-inputted tolerance value is always interpreted as mm (the internal FreeCAD unit), which is quite cumbersome for Imperial drawings etc.

The correct fix would be, in addition to this PR, to obviously use a PropertyDistance instead of PropertyFloat for the UnderTolerance and OverTolerance, so that they could be inputted with units.  However, I have no idea if it'd possible to make this change backward-compatible.  The PropertyFloats UnderTolerance and OverTolerance have presumably existed for a while, already.  Despite that, I really think this conceptual error should also be fixed, in addition to the fixes in this PR.

When using the package search engine of Ubuntu then none of the packages of Xenial (2016) have their metainfo.xml file in the metainfo directory, it's still appdata:
https://packages.ubuntu.com/search?searchon=contents&keywords=metainfo.xml&mode=&suite=xenial&arch=any

With Bionic the majority of packages have moved these files to metainfo now:
https://packages.ubuntu.com/search?searchon=contents&keywords=metainfo.xml&mode=&suite=bionic&arch=any

When searching files of the form appdata.xml then they are still used a lot:
https://packages.ubuntu.com/search?searchon=contents&keywords=appdata.xml&mode=&suite=groovy&arch=any

When I got the package instructions of e.g. Fedora right then an appdata.xml is used for the main application and metainfo.xml is used for add-ons: https://docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/packaging-guidelines/AppData/

So, this means that our appdata.xml file shouldn't be renamed but installed to a different directory on newer systems.

Now we can ignore the default install location for Xenial and thus have the risk that the meta information won't be shown (any more) because it will expire in a few months anyway or we can add a new CMake variable called CMAKE_INSTALL_METAINFO whose default value is "metainfo" but can be overridden by package maintainers of Xenial to be "appdata".

This PR must then be adjusted accordingly:
* it should use the variable CMAKE_INSTALL_METAINFO if we still want to support Xenial
* It should revert the change to rename to appdata.xml file (if I got things right)

Here is how KDE handles it:
https://community.kde.org/Guidelines_and_HOWTOs/AppStream
In a lot of way we aren't fully leveraging the AppData/MetaInfo aspect of FC. Should I open a ticket to explore this?

https://forum.freecadweb.org/viewtopic.php?f=17&t=53193

Just in case people are not aware what this file actually does:

There are three applications (that I know of) that use this file to display information to the user:

1. https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gnome-software
2. https://invent.kde.org/plasma/discover
3. https://flathub.org

In case an app has no such file, GNOME Software and Plasma Discover fallback to the *.desktop file.

I doubt that people who use PPAs / back-port repositories for older distros, install these through such software center applications. And I guess more and more people are moving to AppImage, Flatpak or Snap and are not affected by this change anyway.

@kisolre you don't need to redo it. It can be fixed like this using a terminal on your computer (I'm writing this from memory so there might be an error in the instructions):

Add freecad's repository as a remote (maybe you have done this already, if you have, just run `git fetch`):
`git remote add upstream https://github.com/freecad/freecad.git`

Create a temporary branch (but don't switch to it)
`git branch tmp`

Make sure you have created the temporary branch but still have on your master branch checked out with `git branch` 

Reset your master branch (which you are now standing on) with:
`git reset upstream/master`

Cherry pick your changes:
`git cherry-pick 30656e64` <--- the number is a shortened version of your commit's SHA identifier which lives on the tmp-branch. If you have more commits, cherry-pick each one the same way

Now your master branch will have your change on the latest freecad master branch

Fix the amend thing luzpaz asked you, run:
`git commit --amend`
This will let you change the last commit message (if you have multiple commits, do this after each cherry-pick)
Prepend `Sketcher: ` to the commit message

Now you're ready to push your fixes, but since you changed the history, git will complain... so add `-f` to overwrite what you have on origin:
`git push -f`

This pull request will update since it's linked to your branch.

Once you've verified that everything is like you want it, remove the tmp branch:
`git branch -D tmp`

There are other ways to do the same thing, but I think the instructions above are the easiest way to follow if you aren't that used to git. `git rebase -i upstream/master` would be a better way, but in my opinion it has a higher chance to screw things up if you're not used to git
You might be interested in read this article: https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Tools-Rewriting-History

The wiki includes a nice set of instructions for forking, branching, editing, rebasing, and submitting a PR, here:
https://wiki.freecadweb.org/Source_code_management

Notes to self:
- delConstraintOnPoint with false argument is only used for trimming and filleting. When trimming a line containing a vertical/horizontal alignment on an end point, it appears reasonable not to transfer the alignment constraint as a user can be expected not to want another geometry to follow the trimmed geometry. When filleting the point, it is expected that the user would like to continue alignment where the corner was, but the corner has moved, so sometimes not transferring would be the wanted behaviour and sometimes transferring would be the wanted behaviour. A default of not transferring appears reasonable.

- Magic number: 500*Precision::Confusion(), depends on the physical length of the sketch. Different if working on a road blueprint or a nano-machine. Will likely affect trimming in the second example. This magic number is used to correct for a deficiency either on seekTrimPoints or in the solver which does not achieve sufficient convergence. It fixes the behaviour (at least in a range of cases), but it does not fix the root cause.

Besides this, we have a general layout issue with tolerances I'll open a forum thread to find a solution. Just as reference, here is what e.g. the ASME norm Y14.5 2018 defines as layout:
![AcroRd32_eASeHof6nu](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1828501/103174414-39e16600-4862-11eb-9eec-fa64200b965c.png)

>     2. It's a bit hackish to use the sign of the undertolerance to trigger the feature.  Maybe add a tolerance Property to use bilateral tolerancing if possible?

That was my first thought but how to achieve this? The norms require bilateral tolerancing if under- and overtolerance is the same. But as user you are lazy and only want to enter one value. But then we need a way to handle the case that e.g. the undertolerance is zero and not because the user is lazy and only input one value.

This is how I came to the implementation of this PR:
- entering only one value means the zero tolerance is really zero
- entering the same value triggers automatically the normed bilateral output
- by entering the same value with different signs you can override the bilateral output (I bet some users want this for some reason)

What would be your proposal to improve this?

> What would be your proposal to improve this?

OK, we could do this:
- we add a new property just named "Tolerance"

Well, I implemented it as I proposed and adapted the PR accordingly:

-----------
the common rule is that if a dimension has equal over- and undertolerance, they are output on the same line as the dimension concatenated using the ± character.

This PR does this.
(It also uses a more self-explaining function name.)

Note that this is not just cosmetics, it is even standardized in the GD&T norms. The issue is also described in the Wiki: https://wiki.freecadweb.org/TechDraw_Geometric_dimensioning_and_tolerancing#Formatting_2
also:
* use one format specifier for tolerances since the norms don't allow a different format for the over- and the undertolerance
* some code optimizations like a self-explaining function name, remove unnecessary/outdated comments
-----------

This is the output (contains the changes from #4203):

![FreeCAD_ZouxKGoHKa](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1828501/103247768-55369900-4968-11eb-8c1a-6603bba3e454.png)

The benefits:
* if the tolerance is equal, you can just input its value to the Tolerance property, if you have unequal tolerance values, you can enter them as always -> we achieve norm-conform output
* existing documents will stay as they are since an explicit over- undertolerance leads to the two-line output
* if people prefer the two-line output also for equal tolerances, they can get this by filling the over- undertolerance properties

I also fixed the issue that FC allows different form specifiers for the over- and undertolerance. It would be strange to have the overtolerance with e.g. %.2f and the undertolerance with %.1e. With this PR there is one format specifier used for both tolerances.

I think this is a handy and intuitive solution that minimizes the workload (only on value to input for equal tolerances and no time-consuming additional toggling of options.

The output is still not completely as in the norm but it should go in anyway since the changes of the PR are necessary in any case.

For the future, this is how the norm proposes the output:
![AcroRd32_eASeHof6nu](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1828501/103174414-39e16600-4862-11eb-9eec-fa64200b965c.png)
and this is what we get with the PR:
![FreeCAD_CMVtISG3cX](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1828501/103248632-c88dda00-496b-11eb-8568-686696f626df.png)


So the position of the '0' must be left-aligned plus the space of a '+' sign. The unit must stay right-aligned. However, this tis fine-tuning that can be done any time later.

This is quite an ambitious and somewhat invasive change to Sketcher and right before the upcoming release.This type of change needs to be discussed on the forum ([example of discussion](https://forum.freecadweb.org/viewtopic.php?f=10&t=51716&sid=4cb8601fc5010f7ca8a387d8dc3ec727)). > IMO, this is an awkward workflow in some cases. It's fine as long as you only change the Tolerance property directly after creating a dimension. But it increases the work when switching from unilateral to bilateral tolerancing because you have to make sure that Over/UnderTolerance is 0 before the value of Tolerance is considered.

But how often do you have in real life that you first specified an equal tolerance and then change to an unequal one, maybe once every few drawings. Then, you need to set 2 values to zero. However, the main use case (about 80 - 90%) in a drawing - are equal, bilateral tolerances.
With my solution, you just have to enter your tolerance to the field that has this name and you are done - as quick as possible, no option can accidentally bet set wrong and existing drawings stay as they are, see also below.
What I should however do to improve the PR is to disable the Tolerance field when there are values in the Over/undertolerance fields.

> If you e.g. have a look at the scale function of GIMP you will see two spin boxes and in between a toggle button with the symbol of a chain link. If the chain link is locked the two scale values are always synchronized. This means if you modify the height value the width value is changed automatically and vice versa. If the chain link is unlocked you can freely change both values.

That is what also @aapo proposed. But there is a major issue why I do not support this:
- how do then get a two-line output for equal, bilateral tolerances? This is the output is what we have at the moment. If we don't provide this feature, all existing drawings would change - this would be a big issue because the tolerance feature with the two fields is in FC for a long time now.
So we could make the chain option OFF by default, the existing drawings stay as they are, but then you will have in future for every equal tolerance to perform two actions: adding the value + setting the option. But for example some of my real-life drawings have dozens of tolerances and it always annoyed me that I have to spend so much time in getting them by filling 2 fields.

So the question is of we keep existing drawings or not. Changing existing drawings make them more norm-conform that is what I like, but I also know that "automatic changes" that can even not be reverted will cause problems in companies because every change in a drawing has to get a new revision (I think this is normed as well) no matter if it is a pure editorial change or not. So the danger is to open an existing drawing, press save because you just changed something in a model (e.g. a construction sketch) and without noticing you get a changed drawing.

To summarize:
- having a chain option, when option by default OFF, existing drawings are preserved but all future drawings need 2 actions to get a tolerance
- when option by default ON, existing drawings will be changed and it won't be possible to get the two-line output for equal tolerances (not-norm conform, you you might have your reasons)

Therefore I think my proposal is more safe and provides the minimal possible workload for future drawings and therefore the better compromise.

1. setValues() is executed with the new datum value.

3.        => the latter triggers SketchObject::Onchanged()
4.  Path(not performing transaction, not an internal transaction, property which changed is Constraint, is a managed operation)
5.  => Constraints.checkGeometry
6.  => As geometry did not change at this point same result as the previous check before changing the datum (so a valid state)
7. => solve() is executed (just after setValues()).
8. => If solve returned an error is != 0 so Geometry is not updated and Constraint is touch().
9. => the latter repeats 3-6.
10. => getValues() returns the same list as before (1) but with just one datum value changed. I do not see how it can be empty.

I could see a problem if all this is executed with Constraints not having a valid state. But in such a case, before (1), the function would have returned because of an invalid state.

The way I implement extent wrt direction was intentional and probably is a case of defining what is meant. If I set up a start and end extent and then select _Reverse Direction_, I interpreted that to mean the end point becomes the start point of the path, not that I want to change the geometry of the which end gets which offset.  Maybe there are some unstated assumptions about particular usage cases going on here.

Where the offset is applied is a function of how one has defined the geometry of the slot and one would not expect this to jump when deciding to change cutting direction.  If I have extended a slot in order to start with the tool outside the stock and then decide to cut from the other end, I would expect to have to adjust my extensions accordingly, not to have the software double guess why I did what I did and try to think for me.  That kind of artificial unintelliegence usually has be screaming at the monitor. :x

Maybe the terminology is unfortunate since the extent adjustment is geometry based and tagging them as "start" or "end" when that frame of reference can flip is not optimal. Would the same offset be suitable if transferred to the other end when attacking from the other end? That depends on the entire model, the stock and how the machinist wants to do the job.  I don't think the software can or should attempt to anticipate that. 

Either some non specific labels like _Extent offset 1_ and _Extent offset 2_ could decouple from path cut direction, or clear documentation that "start" will be the end of the path when selecting when _Reverse Direction_ is selected.  That seems self consistent.

Starting at "start" when selecting reverse direction is self-contradictory in one sense anyway. It's now _Reversed_ in relation to what ? There is an implicit direction to slots which is not obvious to the user and is unrelated to what the user may consider that start point.  In that sense an essentially arbitrary and neutral  _End 1_ and _End 2_ would be perfectly suitable and there would be no expectation that it would move when selecting _Reverse Direction_.

I think clear documentation of expected behaviour is the preferable solution. 

This needs to be consistent with straight slots and needs to be clearly documented. 

Thanks for pointing out the inconsistency between straight and arc slots in the way I implemented this.

Here are the points I remember off hand.  I think there will be more as I work more with the machine and FreeCAD.

1) All text must be in uppercase.  That includes comments, gcodes, etc...

2) Several of the default options were reversed because Fanuc requires the opposite values.  This could have been resolved another way (calling the other post with options, or something like that)

3) header is different.  It needs to be:
`%`
`Onnnn (visible comment)`

Where nnnn is the program number.  To solve this, I put the filename (without .ngc) in that place.  So if saved as O1000.ngc, that line will have O1000.  The comment on that line is what is visible within the controller GUI, so it ideally would have the job name and freecad file name.  Right now I just have placeholder text in there since I couldn't see how to get that information.

4) It merges canned op sequences, so this:
`G83 X0 Y0`
`G80`
`G83 X1 Y1`
`G80` 
becomes
`G83 X0 Y0`
`X1 Y1`
`G80`
For this, I just skipped G80 if the next command was the same canned op.

5) It supports rigid tapping (though I am just getting to where I can test it).  A G81 or G83 is converted to a M29 G84 sequence (with some other settings) if there is a tap as the tool.

I think that is all of it right now.

I'm willing to merge this because it works as intended.  However I find the feature a bit confusing and potentially dangerous so I encourage additional work on it. 

I would rather see the logic merged into the helix feature because it could be useful for creating conical pockets. 

Here's why I think it's confusing: 
I don't understand what is gained by adding this kind of entry to the adaptive clearing.  Does it improve finish? speed? 

Here's why I think it's dangerous in present form: 

The user can specify a very large cone angle (~45 degrees),  This results in 100% tool engagement radially as the cutter starts to descend. That's normal and unavoidable.  
However, Since the cone is much larger than the tool, a 'stem'  is left behind in the center.  As the tool descends, the axial engagement on the tool increases with each step down because the tool is cutting more and more of the leftover stem.  
The result is that the load on the tool increases continually.  A user might monitor the cut for the first few minutes and conclude that it is cutting well, but the load will potentially increase to the point of failure.


![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/538057/105728494-d3e40f00-5ef1-11eb-9853-2655ca954dbe.png)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/538057/105728971-55d43800-5ef2-11eb-839d-335325f389e4.png)

If you want to proceed with merge, please let me know.  I'll go ahead but please document the feature fully on the wiki.

The example is a bit constructed but nevertheless demonstrates what can happen.

Create a cylinder solid and out of its faces create a compound

```
s = Part.makeCylinder(3,10)
c = Part.Compound(s.Faces)

doc = App.newDocument()
part = doc.addObject("Part::Feature")
part.Shape = c
```

The cylindrical face has id 1 and the planar faces the id 2 and 3.

Now if you replace the compound with a new compound whose first face is invalid
```
line = Part.makeLine(App.Vector(), App.Vector(10))
line2 = Part.makeLine(App.Vector(10), App.Vector(10,10))
wire = Part.Wire((line, line2))
face = Part.Face(wire) # broken face as it's not closed
c2 = Part.Compound([face, s.Face2, s.Face3])
part.Shape = c2
```
you end up with an object where both planar faces now show id 1, instead of 2 and 3

The PR fixes this issue.

@luzpaz Not particularly. It goes under general clause "Make all pixel graphics vector or available at various pixel density" and "Scale all cursors and icons (multiplying them by devicePixelRatio) ".

We can fix markers in various ways:
- providing more sizes for them so that we have more detail and they would be "crisper" and "rounder" on HiDPI display.
- "blurring" markers, thus providing sort of anti-aliasing: add alpha channel and various shades of red to xpms
- converting markers to SVG and rendering on demand

So it needs both higher resolution and smooth edges (AA). Anti-aliasing is not included in HiDPI roadmap, I suppose, as it's a different concern.

As markers are part of Coin/Inventor API it's hard to render them from SVG.

Also, Coin3D doesn't seem to support HiDPI by itself. That is it has no concept of device pixel ratio, it's just DPI which doesn't even affect the font size (fonts are rendered at 72 ppi, thus 1:1 ratio between pixels and points). So probably needs a separate HiDPI roadmap just for Coin.

@Vanuan
I don't think AA is an HiDPI issue. The improvement with AA is much more visible on low DPI devices. (I can't even see any jagged edges on markers on my HiDPI ~2016 macbook).

> * providing more sizes for them so that we have more detail and they would be "crisper" and "rounder" on HiDPI display.

This would be the fastest route

> * "blurring" markers, thus providing sort of anti-aliasing: add alpha channel and various shades of red to xpms

Alpha channel is only supported with indexed markers and index channels doesn't use the color information from materials.
Maybe we could add support for alpha markers (SoAlphaMarkerSet?) in upstream coin3d instead?

> * converting markers to SVG and rendering on demand

I don't think we would need to render vector graphics on demand. Instead we could render just the markers sizes we need to the coin marker system. That way we could use the current pipeline we use today.

@hyarion 

Regarding range-based for loops, I am not a fan of rewriting code that works without a sound reason. I need to see a clear advantage. For example, using move semantics implies rewriting code that works, but may have an advantage (clear advantage depends on the particular case). I would only introduce them where it makes sense and is appropriate. I tend to maintain code style if I am modifying something in the context where other kind of for loops are used. I have seen modernisation efforts that make code more obscure and peer developers complain about it. Change costs time also for those who work in parallel in a project. That said, I tend to use range-based for loops in new code. I mostly use C style loops only when I need index-based operations. I sometimes use iterator based loops when I am using STL functions operating on iterators. They are three tools in the toolbox. I do not consider a mistake to use one or another. Any C++ developer should be able to read and write the three of them without problems.

Regarding auto, I do not see a clear advantage of using it for basic types (e.g. bool/int). Sometimes I do. As good as it is that you do not have to change code when changing type, it is that you may be thinking you are using a type when you are actually using another one. For most new code, I use auto for more complex types, unless I really want to show intent. One thing I have realised about extensive use of auto, is that "grep"-ing the code seeking for a certain type stops being as effective. Most IDEs have tools to find the use of a function, but in projects as big as FreeCAD some of them do not work properly. Grep works perfectly but does not perform type deduction on auto. However I think that is is not a reason not to use it. Again, my view is that it is a tool. Not using it is not a mistake.

Other examples of modernisation are smart pointers. I am all for smart pointers... where it makes sense. It is not uncommon to see heavily upvoted stackoverflow replies telling to use a plain pointer in specific situations instead. Then even where it would make sense, if one should rewrite the whole application, usually even strong supporters tend to relax and understand that legacy support is there for a reason (there is a fool's day prank about removing pointers from c++ in the internet which is hilarious). Smart pointers are a tool (a cool one I must add), to be used in appropriate situations.

When I review code, I rarely comment on style things. I believe every developer has his/her own style. Some people systematically leave spaces after parenthesis, others never do. I know that some companies and even some communities have a very tight policy on formatting and will reject PRs just because of formatting. I believe every developer should be given a certain degree of space and choice in selecting style (or tool). I do not need that code appears to be created by a single individual. IMO the most important thing when it comes to choice of tools/style, aside from the code actually working, is intent. It must be clear what is being done and why. The best documentation is easy to understand code. Then, after this, code maintainability. Then, I respect developer choice. If I ask for a change, I justify why and you will not see a mere code styling among them. I try to apply this to myself too, so I bound myself to the same rules I would like enforced. I respect other developer's choices. Of course, if somebody starts systematically using things like goto label without a really good reason (and there are good reasons and use cases where it is a good solution, if no the best), that is guaranteed not to be merged by me.

Regarding the examples you put forward, a space after a parenthesis in an "if" or "for" comes likely from the editor (kdevelop). I have noticed this when doing search and replace. Not sure about if it also does it when changing the name of a variable. I have historically tended not to leave spaces after the parenthesis unless I am listing the parameters of a function (in declaration, definition or even use) and I am using a multi-line style for clarity. Then I align all to the first tab after the parenthesis. Similarly, in multi-line "or" or "and" logical operations, I tend to align operators  (||, &&) at the end to the next tab. I do this to increase readability. Other developers systematically introduce a space after each parenthesis. I am ok with both styles and I require no change for mere stylistic reasons. I do not quite like asymmetry, so I would prefer that if an space is introduced at the beginning it is also introduced at the end. If I realise that, I would change it together with the next commit. I am not a hard-liner of styles.

Yes, I am rather lax (in the sense of permissive) in code styling. I am thankful when the editor takes care of most of it and I can be left to produce actual code.

A last word, you will see an evolution in my coding style and use of tools, which follows my own development as a programmer, specially after I read Scott Meyer's effective modern c++ and code complete by Steve McConnell books, and also as I gained more knowledge about FreeCAD itself. Things that I did 5 years ago, I would do them differently today.

As a summary, IMO PRs just rewriting code that works without a clear advantage are lost time for everybody. Any change costs time. I think there are better ways to use time. Of course, if a PR does not improve functionality, but involves clear improvements in structure or architecture, that is a gain for everybody.

Since Py3.8 a pyd file does not any longer respect the PATH system environment variable to load DLLs it depends on. Instead os.add_dll_directory() must be used to add all needed DLL search paths.

What may happen here is that not all DLLs are copied over from the Libpack and thus the Fem.pyd file cannot be loaded. One way to fix this is by setting the environment variable FREECAD_LIBPACK_BIN that points to the bin directory of the LibPack.
The other way is to find out which DLL isn't copied over.

Can I suggest you look at PR which got merged to Path recently and associated forum thread.

https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/pull/4201

wmayer suggested in the thread that it should not be necessary to do INCing and DECing if we remain inside the CCX code wrappers. I have not analysed this PR but maybe you could consider if that is pertinent. 

That PR itself was concerned with very wasteful copy on read when using Pdict. This was causing _heavy speed penalties_ in Path where a read reference to a Pdict ( which was unchanging in the context ) was made inside a loop. 

Python programming would expect such a read reference to simply return the pointer and inc the python refcount. However, Pdict destroys the existing Pdict, creates a new one and copies all the same content back in tuple by tuple. 

To avoid this I made Pdict member in the class and kept track of whether it had been written to. Thus reads can just return a pointer where appropriate in a typical pythonist way. 

This seems to be necessary evil in trying to hack together code in two languages with such different memory allocation strategies.  Pdict gives python access to the underlying C++ data structures but it can be very inefficient due to language differences. 
https://forum.freecadweb.org/viewtopic.php?f=15&t=50583&start=30#p457914

It may be worth looking at whether this gives a performance hit in this context. 

It probably will not matter on trivial test shapes but in some kind of complex, multi-faceted shapes ( perhaps derived by importing other formats into FreeCAD ) it could cause significant slowing. 

The issue is more general than Pdict but this is one instance where I can point you to an issue and a solution.


Here is a direct link to wmayer's comments on use of CXX. 
https://forum.freecadweb.org/viewtopic.php?f=15&t=50583&start=10#p436736
and
https://forum.freecadweb.org/viewtopic.php?f=15&t=50583&start=30#p457641

@abdullahtahiriyo , it is nothing against you, it is that we seem to have an artificial deadline not communicated properly and not as result of a vote. Now we don't even have a string freeze to give translators a chance to translate and find typos.

My point is that FC has no visible structure. There are no release plans, it is unknown who makes decisions and what base. The developer community is even ignored (see e.g. the thread about more mergers where key people like @wwmayer not even wrote a single post). Now some persons (I still don't know who in what communication platform) decided to have a feature freeze (I know @yorikvanhavre because he announced the feature freeze). Features are pushed out of the 0.19 release without any discussion or at least hearing of the developers who contributed the feature.
Now it seems, there is an arbitrary deadline to please a certain Linux distri, but well, it is still not clear if this is really the deadline for FC 0.19. There was no clear statement nor a vote/poll.

Since a year I constantly post that we need a feature-freeze phase. A phase in which we have time to properly document, test and polish the new features. I never got any reply why this won't happen. Now we have a feature freeze but since this announcement luckily some pending new features are still merged, but this is not what I think is necessary. We need a release plan so that everybody knows **_in advance_**: 
* Until date A new features are accepted for review,
* date B is the last day to merge new features, what could not be merged before for different reasons, won't make it into the release.
* Then there have at least 2 weeks for documentation and testing. Then on date C we make a string freeze, release a beta version and give translators 2 more weeks.
* Than on date D there is a release candidate.
* A week later when no mayor regressions are found, we release on date E.

This is the case for other big projects like LibreOffice (https://wiki.documentfoundation.org/ReleasePlan/7.1) and not too hard to implement. And sure, plans can change and also for big projects like LO this happens frequently. But apparently their release process gets rid of release flame wars and this alone would help a lot.

Ok, found a little bug that I introduced. No biggie. Fixing it now...

The function TaskSketchBasedParameters::exitSelectionMode() calls onSelectReference() to clear the selection gate and there is a call to hide the base object.

So, far there are only these two sub-classes that use exitSelectionMode(): TaskHelixParameters and TaskRevolutionParameters.
The latter works a bit differently compared to TaskHelixParameters because for a groove it doesn't show the base shape and the transparent red part but it directly shows the final result. So, there it makes sense to hide the base shape as otherwise you won't see the difference.

For the helix it's bad as you only will see the red part.

A more elegant solution is to add two virtual functions: e.g. startReferenceSelection()  and finishReferenceSelection().
As argument both get the pcSketchBased and prevSolid (see onSelectReference) as argument. The default implementation does what TaskSketchBasedParameters does and the overridden function in TaskHelixParameters can ignore the prevSolid argument.

There are several examples in the codebase where that mechanism is used (it is not something "new"). Sure it could go somewhere in the wiki.

Basically it is used when a property gets renamed or the type of a property changes. In those cases, when an older file is read, the old property is read and the data migrated to the new property in those functions. This way, even if the property changed name or type, backwards compatibility is provided for those files. Of course, if afterwards the file is saved, it will be saved with the new property (name and type), so there is no forward compatibility with versions not knowing about the new property.

In this case, it is not necessary to do this because those "older" properties were present, but not used at all. There is no expectation from a user of opening an "older" file and getting a specific behaviour.

However, there is one thing that should be cleaned-up sometime:
The function calls ReferenceSelection, onSelectReference and addReferenceSelectionGate now carry up to six boolean as arguments which makes it quite error-prone to set the correct values from the calling instances.

A more elegant solution is to use an enum combined with Qt's QFlags class. This QFlags can replace all the boolean and has two benefits:
* in the calling instances the various enum values must be explicitly written that makes it easier for the reader to understand the purpose
* whenever a new type should be supported only the enum must be extended and the function that handles the new type. The argument list of all other functions doesn't need to be extended any more

> OK but why doesn't it cause a problem with boost 1.67 and MSVC? Is it then compiler specific or a limitation of boost?

I am not entirely sure, but `noexcept` changed in C++17 -- in earlier versions it was not actually a part of the function's type, but in C++17 they made it a part. So in a formal sense, trying to bind a noexcept function someplace that expects a potentially-throwing function is a mismatch now, and it wasn't before. Of course, it seems like the bind should still work (in a similar way to const-ness... if your function is more restrictive than required it's still OK), so it may be that some compilers are magic-ing it, and some are not. Or maybe Boost has some magic of their own. BTW, What is Boost::bind providing that we don't get from std::bind?

If I may not follow your order:

> If I understand correctly, FEM's material is currently implemented like some kind of group that references other objects

Yes, in FEM, the material points to the objects (parts etc.) made of it, whereas, in Arch, the object points to its material. That's an illustration of the lack of harmonization I mentioned in the last post...
Personally, I give my preference to Arch implementation. First, as far as I know, in major CG/CAD applications (Blender, AutoCAD...), objects reference their materials, so in a POLA approach I would not reverse the paradigm. I find FEM implementation less readable, as you have to open every material to know which is the one of your part. And the same in code: you have to loop through all materials to find the material information of a given object. So, I would personally stick to Arch and Part approach: the object points to its material.

> shall we add the Material property to every Part object?

But Part has already a Material property ([here](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/master/src/App/Part.h#L56))! The trouble is that it is rather unusable (and likely most unused) because it is of wrong type, compared to Arch "standard", and on top of that it's hidden. I posted a PR to fix that a few days ago ([4503](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/pull/4503)).

> how shall we handle multiple solids inside a body?

Yes, this is the key question, or more generally: how to handle containers and components. To me: we could have a Material property to whatever object for which it makes sense. It includes Part, Body, Link... And then, we could have a convention: the subcomponent's material, if any, overrides the container's material.
So, if we have the following:

CompoundObj (Material#1)
|-- SubObj1 (No material)
|-- SubObj2 (Material#2)

...we should understand SubObj1 has Material#1 and SubObj2 has Material#2.

L) This is the expected behaviour. There is no direct inter-curve tangency support for conics, and this is effected using a tangency-via-point (see extended info in the tangency constraint) and two point on object constraints with a newly added point.

M) This shows how the point on object constraints above are necessary for the construction to work. If they are not removed, the result of adding the extra point on object on the endpoint is the expected result.

O) This is indeed a very interesting case. The tangency that is rendered when going to click the second point of the line may actually relate to the first point, or to another curve that the line touched when going from the starting point to the end point. There's only one thing specifically that I want to see changed:  Please re-tab the file using spaces instead of tab characters.  Mixing spaces and tabs is the great evil of python and makes working on the file later difficult and prone to errors.  Anytime you're working on Python, you should have your editor set to insert spaces instead of tabs.

There are some other formatting conventions that should be followed but which I'm not a stickler on. We generally follow PEP8  formatting.  That's the 'pythonic' way of doing things.

The file is over-indented.  You should use 4 space indentation.

There are other whitespace issues like trailing whitespace and missing whitespace around operators.

If you use a PEP8 delinter like Flake8  your editor can show this stuff and usually fix it automatically. 

PEP8 is also picky about line length and complains if you're over 80 columns.  I ignore this unless the lines are over 100 columns. Even then, only if it makes sense.

Same thing with block comments and aligning lists:  common sense prevails over rules.

Hm, looking at this again, it seems like the rendering behavior might actually be intentional? Looking at how default windows are defined, it seems only the frame gets a rotation value, but the glass has no rotation defined. This ensures that only one floorplan symbol arc is produced, but to also ensure that the glass actually rotates when opening>0, it must inherit its `rotdata` (but not `hinge` and `omode`) from the previous component. I guess it also makes it easier to define rotating parts if you just need to define rotation parameters once.

It does actually seem that this is [documented](https://wiki.freecadweb.org/Arch_Window) as intentional ("If you defined a hinge in this component or any other earlier in the list, ..."), though maybe it could be made a bit more prominent. Also, this requires a specific ordering (all static parts before moving parts) and there is currently no way to reorder components, so reordering might be something to consider as a feature.

So, I guess my first commit actually problematic, but I guess the second commit is still useful (since without it, I think you cannot really manage to create a rotating frame followed by a non-rotating glass, since the second component will use the same values still in the gui elements).
