Ok, here goes. I can't really comment on gitkraken (I always use the commandline since there it is, to me, clearest what happens under the hood and you can always use all features, rather than the subset exposed by the GUI), but I'll try to also explain the concept so you can find the same thing in gitkraken.

First off: I think it would be good to first further update the code to look like you want it to look (e.g. generalizing the getObjectInfo stuff), since you'd otherwise need to make those changes twice later.

*Intended commit history*
Then, to plan what we want the commit history to look at eventually, I think something like below. Note that I'm just talking about what the resulting commits should look like, not yet about how to get there from the current history. So the starting point of the below list is the master commit you started from.

 1. Remove all the empty `pass` functions
 2. Remove the event parameter from `startEditing` (you added this commit last, but since `evaluate_context_menu_action` already has an `obj` and `node_idx` parameter, I think you can do this change earlier, preventing the intermediate breakage by removing references to `edit_command.event` before removing the variable itself).
 3. Remove the ` App.DraftWorkingPlane.restore()` line (I do not really understand this change, but you mentioned it should be its own commit?)
 4. Introduce a `getSpecificObjectInfo` function and update the original `addPoint` function to use it (or whatever other approach you choose to extract the object-type-agnostic code from `addPoint` so it does not have to be duplicated).
 5. Split out `addPoint` to multiple `add_point` methods in the `GuiTools` subclasses (and replacing the call to `addPoint` in `evaluate_menu_action` with a call to `obj_gui_tools.add_point`).
 6. Rewriting `evaluate_menu_action` and `display_tracker_menu` to use the new callback structure, and rewrite all GuiTools subclasses to also adapt (you could split this into two commits for clarity, but then the first commit would break things, which is usually not a good idea, so I'd keep this as one commit, unless you want to add the backward compatibility wrapper).
 7. Add the `reverse wire` command

*Basic approach*
Given that most of these changes are pretty independent, the basic workflow I would choose here is to:
 - Reset you branch back to the original master commit you started working from. The default "mixed" flavor of the `git reset` command resets your branch and the index/staging area but not the working copy, so this would put you in a position where you would have been if you had done all the coding in your checkout, but not committed any of it yet. On the commandline, this would be `git reset origin/master` (assuming that you `origin/master` still points to the commit you branched off from, if not you might need to rebase first, or replace `origin/master` with the SHA of the branch-off point).
 - Now, you can use interactive staging to select a subset of all your changes and create a new commit for that. You can do this for each commit to be created in turn. On the commandline, you would use `git add -p` for this, but I suspect that in kraken you can do a similar thing in e.g. a diff view where you select lines of the diff to be staged. On the commandline you can even edit the to-be-staged diff in a text editor (useful in case you need to commit one change in a line but not another, or in adjacent lines), but if Kraken doesn't support this, and you'd need it, you can always just revert one of the changes in the file manually, commit that, ^Z in your editor and commit the other change.

Note that especially the `git add -p` / interactive staging is IMHO a very powerful tool, which allows me to have a much improved workflow where I can (in a lot of cases) just focus on coding and making things work first, and then still be able to split the changes in proper commits at a later stage (sometimes at the end, somethings I already commit things halfway when I'm confident that a particular change is somewhat complete and will be included in the final history).

*Additional work for commit 4 and 5*
This approach will not work for all commits above. In particular, number 4 and 5 need to make changes to code in `gui_edit.py` that is already removed in the current PR (so with the above approach, that code will be gone from your working copy already). For this, I would suggest first making a backup copy of `gui_edit.py` and then use `git checkout` to throw away all uncommitted changes from `gui_edit.py` (or alternatively, only throw away a selection of changes, `git checkout` has an interactive `-p` option too). After this, you should again have the original `addPoint` and `evaluate_menu_action` code, so you can make changes to those and commit that (this is the part where you'll need to do some manual code editing, and will be writing/copying back some code that will be thrown away again in the next commit, but that's ok). After you created these two commits, you can restore your `gui_edit.py` backup again, and start interactively committing the rest of the commits.

*Verifying commits work*
Note that you might want to verify in between that your separated changes actually work. One easy way for that is to first commit them (even when you're not entirely sure that you got everything, you can always amend the commit later) and then use `git stash` to stash away all uncommitted changes, so you can test the code as you committed it. Then unstash and continue with the next commit.

*Interactive rebase and fixup commits*
One additional thing I would want to point out, in case you haven't used it before, is the interactive rebase in git. Though rebase is intended to be used to "rewind" a number of commits you made and "replay" them onto another starting point (e.g. a more recent version of the master branch), you can also rebase on top of an earlier commit in your existing history (instead of some newer master version), so you end up rewinding to that earlier commit, and then simply replaying the same commits on top of the same earlier base commit again (i.e. nothing changes). But if you then use rebase in interactive mode, you can select which commits should be replayed in which order. This allows you to easily reorder your commits or remove some of them.

Even more, you can tell git to squash some commits together in the process, which means it becomes very easy to fix mistakes later: If you already committed something, but spot a mistake in it, you just make a new commit with just the fix, and then use an interactive rebase to move that "fixup" commit backwards in history to be right after the original commit, and then ask git to squash them together into one commit, as if the mistake never happened.

Git even automates a part of this process using `git commit --fixup`, which marks such "fixup" commits in such a a way that the commit message indicates what previous commit they are fixing, so an interactive rebase (with `--autosquash`) can automatically reorder and squash them. I use this workflow often where I put fixes for earlier mistakes into such fixup commits, but do not do the interactive rebase right away, but wait until some later point (so I can rebase/squash a few of them at the same time to save time, or so I can push out the fixup commits to a PR so reviewers that already saw the mistake can see the fixup more clearly before I make both disappear again). Since  git remembers for me which fixup is meant to fix which mistake, I can easily postpone the actual rebasing/squashing since I do not have to remember :-) Of course if multiple commits touch the same code and you reverse their order (i.e. a fixup commit that fixes a mistake in code that was modified again after the mistake commit), such a rebase is likely to cause conflicts, so be prepared to fix some conflicts along the way (but knowing how to fix conflicts is useful in any case, of course).

*Force pushing*
One word of caution, though: All this rebase/fixup (and also the reset + recommit stuff) rewrites history, which is typically not appropriate once commits have been merged to master, or some other branch that is intended to have some stability. If you rewrite history on a branch that you already pushed somewhere, you'll have to force push to overwrite the previous history, which means that pulling from such a branch might cause problems (since as far as git is concerned, the original and rewritten commit histories look like separately developed commits which happen to touch all the same code, leading to conflicts). Force pushing is not acceptable for master usually (though this is a matter of convention, git doesn't care), but for pull request branches, this is usually ok (people pulling from PR branches should pull carefully, though again, project-specific convention might differ).

*Commit messages*
One additional advantage of splitting code into different commits, is that you can use each commit's message to more specifically motivate the changes in that commit. In this particular case, some of the changes may seem meaningless when the commit is viewed in isolation (i.e. commit 4 would split off some code into its own function which is then called only once), but makes sense in the whole. What I usually do for such commits is explicitly note this in the commit message (e.g. something like "This commit prepares for splitting out the addPoint code into multiple versions in a future commit, reducing the amount of code to duplicate when that happens").

In that case, I'm not so sure this PR is something to be merged in master. I'm not sure what the policies in FreeCAD are, but from a software development perspective, I would not put references to externally installable plugins in the core code like this, since that creates a particular dependency on that external code that is hard to track and does not scale well (what if a doze more of these addons would be created?).

Instead, in cases like these, an often-used approach is that the core code provides hooks, callbacks or signals of some sort, which can be used by the addon to do the right thing at the right moment. This means that the core code stays generic: It just offers an interface to be used by any addon that wants to (or maybe none), while the initiative, and the burden for version compatibility, stays with the addon.

I'm not sure how this should work in this particular case: The various arch objects could offer specific signals or global callbacks or so, but I guess some FreeCAD-wide solution would make more sense. Maybe the proxy-support is actually the existing mechanism for this, but that would require making a subclass of e.g. ArchWindow and set the object's proxy type to that subclass. Alternatively, I think there is the concept of object extensions, that could probably be used without needing to replace the object's proxy type (but not 100% sure if they can be defined in python too?)

One thing that came up in the thread, is why is this ToDo class needed at all? @carlopav suggested that it is unique to Draft and that e.g. Arch does not actually use it (at least not for committing changes). From what I've seen, it looks like the problem is that when inside a coin event handler, changing the document (which probably changes the coin datastructure as well) causes coin to crash (I've seen a case where coin is looping over a list to emit events and it looks like the list is changed or deleted, causing a crash, see the forum topic for details). That would make sense, but then I wonder: Why is this only a problem in Draft? Do Arch and other WBs solve this problem differently? If so, should draft be changed to do the same, instead of cleaning up the ToDo class like I did here?

> Can you help elaborating your idea, or maybe there is available tutorial on similar cases?

The general idea of my suggestion is like how the signal / event handlers work, where the generic code just exposes a signal or event and the addon registers an event handler for such a signal or event. I'm not sure how this same thing is done within FreeCAD currently (and I wouldn't recommend inventing some event handler structure just for this case, AFAICS FreeCAD need *less* complexity and fragmentation, not *more*). Maybe there are existing events available already, accessible from Python, but I'm not sure.

As for my more specific suggestions of using a Proxy subclass, or object extension, I'm not yet familiar enough with FreeCAD to offer a more specific direction here... IIUC object extensions can be added to an object, and each extension can provide additional functionality for an object. One aspect of this is that when e.g. onChanged is called on the object, it is *also* called on each extension in turn, which can then take additional actions as needed. This kind of thing seems like would be appropriate for ArchSketch.

Hoever, from a quick look over the source, I suspect that an object extension (i.e. like the existing attachment extension, which you would add to an existing object using e.g. `obj.addExtension("Part::AttachExtensionPython")`) can only be defined from C++ (there is an DocumentObjectExtensionPy class, but I think that is only intended to support accessing a C++ extension object from Python, not defining one from Python, but I'm not quite sure.

> I have nothing against using optional functionality from addon workbenches, after all it's not different than checking for Python libraries, 

I'm not sure I agree with this entirely. When including an (optional) library, you subsequently making specific calls to that library, which has a clear and well-defined interface and control over what happens and is supposed to happen remains with the FreeCAD core.

With a fairly free-form call to e.g. `ArchSketchObject.ArchSketch.setPropertiesLinkCommon`, this is not so well-defined. What does that function do exactly? When should it be called? What happens if FreeCAD or the ArchSketch WB is changed later, how is compatibility arranged? Can we ever remove these calls again later? What if ArchSketch has different requirements in the future (i.e. what if in addition to `setPropertiesLinkCommon`, some extra things need to happen when called from `__init__`, but not in `onDocumentChanged`? This now requires changes in FreeCAD core, which would break older ArchSketch versions as well).

So *if* you would accept something like the current form (instead of moving to some extension object or other more generic event handler style method as I suggested vaguely above), in addition to the conditions posed by @yorikvanhavre (which I agree with), I would also suggest to make the interface more clear and well-defined. In particular, this could be done by calling e.g. `ArchSketchObject.ArchSketch.ArchWindowInit`, `ArchSketchObject.ArchSketch.ArchWindowOnDocumentRestored`, etc. In other words, name the methods based on when they should be called, rather than what they *do*, so it is more clear from the FreeCAD core perspective how to treat these calls in the future, and preventing needing changes in FreeCAD core when changes are made to ArchSketch. For more forward compatibility, you could even consider moving this stuff from ArchWindow to ArchComponent (even less chance for changes needed in FreeCAD core in the future if ArchSketch is extended), but that would also make the performance impact of this change more pronounced.

> I have nothing against using optional functionality from addon workbenches, after all it's not different than checking for Python libraries, but it should be made very clear and silent if the user doesn't want to install anything. So I would suggest 1) encapsulating all ArchSketchObject functionality in only one place, not (as much as possible) spread all over the code, 2) add very clear comments in the code about what is going on and where to find the needed modules and 3) do not print anything if the module is not there (or maybe some discrete information somewhere IF it makes sense for the user to install the addon)

Not a good sign when people starting fixing code without understanding underlying concepts.
CSG is NOT a file format it is scripting for creating graphics objects as such it needs to be parsed rather than treated as a file format. importCSG parses the CSG file with a python version of lex, when objects such as cube etc are encountered they are placed on a stack, that is the way a parser works. When the parser encounters a boolean the objects it is to operate on are already on the stack. Colour is set in the ViewProvider ( Parts do not contain colour information ). There is currently no stacking of colour information so importCSG has to make a decision based on the objects being operated on. i.e. the objects that the boolean has tool and base set. I've run into problems with the `--return-to` command today ... it doesn't work.
It generates the code after the postamble:
```
[...]
(Begin postamble)
M5
G17 G90
M2
G0 X0 Y0
```
But M2 is the End Program command and as far as I could find (on [linuxcnc](http://www.linuxcnc.org/docs/html/gcode/m-code.html#mcode:m2-m30) and in [The NIST RS274NGC Interpreter - Version 3](https://www.nist.gov/publications/nist-rs274ngc-interpreter-version-3?pub_id=823374)), code after M2 is to be ignored. And my machine (Sainsmart 3018 Pro) seems to be following this rule, ignoring the return-to command.

My suggestion would be to maybe move the return-to command above the postamble? The best position in my opinion would be right after the M5 or right before the M2 (I tried moving the G0 command there and both worked fine), but since the postamble is a block by itself, moving it above (while the spindle is still on) would probably be the easiest way to solve this.

The FC storage policy, as I understand it, is to put new data in some new XML element tag, so that older version software can skip it and continue loading. And it works well regardless of whether the content of the element is saved inside XML or not, which can be proven by opening files saved with my branch in current upstream. My concern with the XML is that it is currently a very clean and neat structure, with limited (that's relative, of course) changes over the course of the file's life. So it makes it both easily human-readable and predictable. This turns them pretty good for diffing, as it produces rather small and understandable diffs. Since obviously we must thrive to integrate FCStd file as best as we can in version control systems, this is a precious quality.
Your proposal introduces "coded" structures inside it, which can AFAICS inflate pretty much (large pieces of texts), and turn diffs much more complex and harder to understand by humans. So placing them into separate files/structures makes sense in my opinion... I might be wrong there of course

> Frankly speaking though, I don't really understand the concerns here. The above changes still leave the same XML element tag in the document. The FC storage policy, as I understand it, is to put new data in some new XML element tag, so that older version software can skip it and continue loading.

This argument is true even if the data is stored in an external file and only referred to in the XML file (like the BREP files are stored). Doing this way will also silent all criticism about the "neatness" of the initial XML file being disturbed.

Also, about the ElementMapping algorithm itself, it looks like a lot like a binary tree (or a B-tree if you include the operation itself and it maps to more than 2 sources elements). Once you consider it as a binary tree, you can see that there are many shortcut that can be done to reduce the size of the mapping simply by using references to node instead of storing the complete path. You'll have to store the whole tree once, and then only make a reference to a node as its name.

For example, when you get this: 
```
Face2;:M2;FUS;:T2:5:F;:M(Face6;:M(Face2;:T2:5:F);FUS;:T1:5:F,Face6;:M2;FUS;:T1:5:F);RFI;:T2:21:F
```

It's like you add this pseudo binary tree:
```
             [RFI]
          /          \
[ Face2...]       [ M(Face6...] 
```
which is more like:
```
             [RFI]
          /          \
     [ FUS ]       [ FUS... ] // Not expanded, but you get the idea...
    /      \         
[ Face2 ] [M2]
```
Thus, if you store the highest tree once, and only use an ID for the node, you won't need that complex naming parsing anymore (IMHO), and the name above would only be the ID for the RFI node (can be a number)

When we add a new function on our object, only a small part of the tree is *invalidated* and only this part requires a rebuild. Since it's a binary tree, finding the part that's invalid is easy, since it'll be located as a root node of the last modified object and should only affect *one* leaf of the tree.

As for the ID, it can be better not to create them randomly or linearly, but instead, make them bit by bit (for example, 1 is left, 0 is right). So, let's say you add another function on your object, the previous root node had ID (1001101), the new root node with the new function will have ID (11001101), that way, with a single bit mask operation, you can see which part of the tree to rebuild/rescan. In our example, it'll be the left part, since the right part (01001101) is the same as the previous root's ID.

> Just a question here, why don't you try to recompute automatically when one function breaks (like a Fillet) and _only_ if it fails recomputing (meaning a user intervention is required), mark the function as error (with the `!` icon) ?

Because the algorithm cannot decide if the deduced the element is actually what the user wants. For some limited cases, where the same shape with the exact same geometry can be found in the modified shape, then it will auto correct the references


> You'll have to store the whole tree once, and then only make a reference to a node as its name.

It is actually implemented that way (sort of). The long name is for illustration only. In normal operation, [StringHasher](https://github.com/realthunder/FreeCAD_assembly3/wiki/Topological-Naming#string-hasher) (actually, it's more like a string table) will be enabled, and [here](https://github.com/realthunder/FreeCAD_assembly3/wiki/Topological-Naming-Algorithm#hashing-element-name) describes how the element history is stored and referenced using `StringHasher`.

When recomputing, FreeCAD will automatically sort the objects in dependency order, and only recompute the ones that are changed. The same applies to generating the topo names. For example, the names for the shape of a `Fusion` object includes names of the shapes of its base and tool objects, which are taken directly if they don't need to recompute.

> Because the algorithm cannot decide if the deduced the element is actually what the user wants

But... The user hits "recompute" button and has no choice here. If the algorithm fails, what can the user do ?
So it's more like a Pavlov's behavior (do action, press button, do action, press button...). If the algorithm is not sure about the change, and the recompute does not fix it the way the user wants it, she will have to fix it manually anyway, so why still requiring the user to press the recompute button ?

If I understand your algorithm, you still need to expand the hash and recompute it back when a dependency is updated. I don't know if it's a long process or not (probably not), but by using a tree and only node's ID, you'd skip this step. 

You are right that it's a similar behavior and I don't know the code enough to find out if using string was actually required or if it's overkill. It's just that encoding the complete operations as a (long) string does not seem the most intuitive way to do it. You know better than me, so it's probably the best solution, but it looks complex.

> But... The user hits "recompute" button and has no choice here. If the algorithm fails, what can the user do ?

Well, the expected response from user is to double click the object marked with error to edit it. At the time of entering edit mode, the algorithm will try to make some guesses, and present the result to user for visual inspection. The user can either hit OK to confirm or make manually changes. Or, if no guess can be made, the editing task panel will highlight the missing references.


> If I understand your algorithm, you still need to expand the hash and recompute it back when a dependency is updated. I don't know if it's a long process or not (probably not), but by using a tree and only node's ID, you'd skip this step.

The expansion is only required for reverse history tracing, when there is any missing element, and only for that element. For normal name generation during recompute, it just combine the existing names from the dependency to form new ones. The new name is shortened into integer IDs by storing the combinations of depending element names into a global string table, so the length of the name is under control.

The TaskDlgAttacher is used on 2 places. As a member variable within TaskPrimitiveParameters class and once as the base class for TaskDatumParameters. I did some testing with current HEAD in master.

For TaskPrimitiveParameters and I have found following:

1. If a new primitive is created, a new transaction is started by the openCommand("Make additive XXX").
2. If an existing primitive is edited by double-clicking, a transaction is started by the ViewProvider's doubleClicked() method.
3. If an existing primitive is edited by selecting "Edit primitive" from right click tree view context menu, no transaction is started at all => this should be fixed.

In TaskPrimitiveParameters case the TaskDlgAttacher::open() is never called, thus it has no effect.

For TaskDatumParameters the situation is a bit different. Because TaskDlgAttacher is its base class, open() is always called. My testing covered these situations:

1. If a new datum object is created, now the transaction is started 2 times - once by openCommand("Create DatumXXX") and once by openCommand("Edit attachment") in TaskDlgAttacher's open().
2. If an existing datum object is edited by double-clicking, again transaction is started twice - once by ViewProviderDatum's doubleClicked() and once by TaskDlgAttacher's open().
3. If an existing datum object is edited via selecting "Edit datum" from tree view context menu, the transaction is started only once - by TaskDlgAttacher's openCommand("Edit attachment") in its open() method.

Thus my suggestion is to drop openCommand("Edit attachment") from TaskDlgAttacher, however we must somehow ensure a new transaction is started when "Edit XXX" from tree view's context menu is invoked.

> That said, I am still unclear on how the undo-redo system works here. As far as I can tell, a "command" can get committed without actually calling "commit" if, say, a new command is opened.

Exactly - when a new command is opened, all pending transactions are committed. That's the current implementation.

I don't think it's supposed to be compiled -- it's one of those weird machinations we go through to get Qt's translation facilities to produce the strings we need. This change doesn't affect the compiled executable, just the output of `lupdate` (which it turns out ignores preprocessor directives).

Using Qt_TRANSLATE_NOOP doesn't do anything at compile time (Normally, we use translate() or tr()). Qt_TRANSLATE_NOOP allows the text to be translatable (picked up by lupdate), so its translation is available to FreeCAD, but the text is not translated immediately, but by another mechanism of FreeCAD somewhere else. This is mostly used in places where you still want to keep the english string (for example stuff that needs to be written to a FCStdc file), and FreeCAD will translate it itself, when needed.

So best I could get for now: files when loaded by `freecad xxxx.FCStd` only store the filename by relative path. The loading happens here: https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/2fd71242ba4a302aaeb70bb5dce4e9652eee5e44/src/App/Application.cpp#L791. I believe somewhere in that initialization we should make the file path absolute. I'm hesitating in just putting a `boost::filesystem::absolute` or similar here because there is a parameter used in `App::Application::openDocument()` called `paths`, and that could mess with a few things.

Alternatively, I could just try to run `boost::filesystem::absolute` during save time, but that sounds like a patchwork solution, and could anyway not work if the parent path no longer exists (the reason I made this change in the first place).

Yet another alternative: just remove that path making entirely, but I'm not really fond of that. Apart from avoiding the bug itself, that line allows the user to make an arbitrary `./path/to/file.FCStd` without having to make the parent folders separately.

We should consider creating parameters on access with Get.  This will grow the config file, but will it be a noticeable reduction in peformance?  Perhaps this in itself could be a parameter.   Problem with that is once the config file is grown there is no ungrowing it without deleting it and rebuilding on restart.

There are parameters that the users know nothing about because either they haven't read the documentation or because the parameters are not documented.  For example, did you know there is a way to underline the active body or make it bold or italic?  It would be nice to be able to browse the parameters and know every option available is in there for a particular workbench.  Does Spreadsheet have other parameters available than these 3?  I have no idea without searching through the source code.

As to putting the creation in the module startup, if that is done then they are created with every initialization of the module.  This way they are only created when an import or export is done, which is very rarely for most users and is very little overhead compared to the actual import/export.  We could test to see if they are already there before creating, but that is probably just as costly in performance as just simply setting them.

There is merit to the notion that if they are worth creating there should be a settings page in preferences.  This is true, but reality is there isn't one until somebody creates one.  The delimiter, in particular, not so much the other two, is really needed for spreadsheet import/export in the Gui.  This was a fairly quick thing to code, much needed, and if not ideal, it is at least a step in the right direction.

@mwganson that was just an "open remark" and moreover a personal opinion that I was unsure is a good one. :) 
For sure it should absolutely not prevent PR merging. And it doesn't affect the deep respect I have for anyone contributing too. 👍

The pull request is a request to pull from the submitters repo into the target.  Therefore only the submitter can rebase and squash his commits.  It's a pretty easy operation but they need to do it since we can't do it for them.

Agreed on all counts, and I'm happy to merge as-is, potentially with the other suggestions re:string handling that @0penBrain has made. @mwganson is it your plan to incorporate those other suggestions?
I will incorporate the suggestions on the string handling.
After this is merged I will add a preference page in edit -> preferences for this workbench.  But before it is merged I am wondering if we should have separate parameters for importing and exporting?

Truthfully, IMO in an idea world we'd prompt the user for the import settings every time: I get data in all sorts of formats, for me I can't just set the variable once and be done with it. For export, I can, though.

(Also, I've got to ask... of all the changes @0penBrain suggested I thought the removal of the double-conversion of the "tab" text was the "for sure" change -- why did you decide to keep the `char*`->`std::string`->`QString` conversion?)

Just an oversight.

I'm making progress on the settings page.  I'm thinking a combobox is the way to go for the delimiter.  That way the user can select from "tab", "semicolon", "comma", or enter a custom character.  A line edit should suffice for the other two.  I don't think these should be translatable.  Maybe it would be better to use "\t", ";", and "," instead of whole words, like "tab", but then again "\t" is kind of a programmer's thing.  Tab is the only one that can't easily be entered in a text field.

I was also thinking about a dialog during import/export after finishing with the preferences page.  The current preference can be the default in the dialog.

@berndhahnebach The basic idea is that sometimes Qt Designer rearranges (or fails to rearrange) the .ui files, so small changes to the UI (particularly grid layouts) can cause very large diffs and misleading output from `git blame`, and difficult-to-review PRs. The idea is that if we always normalize the UI files with this script before submitting a PR, the diff will actually only show the real changes. But of course that means that the UI files in the current repo must first be updated.

I think this PR is in some ways a "proof of concept": I'm not sure we want to make this change until GitHub and/or GitLab support ignoring commits in blame (git already has this feature, but these web UIs don't use it). Or we could just add these commits to a `.git-blame-ignore-revs` file, and figure eventually GitHub will catch up :). Then we can Black all of our Python, too 😉 .

Consider this example:
```
doc = App.ActiveDocument
doc.FileName = "C:/ディレクトリ/ファイル.FCStd" # It's the Japanese for Directory/Filename.FCStd
doc.save()
```

When passing a C-string to boost::path then internally it only widens the string to wstring but doesn't perform the conversion from a UTF-8 encoded string and thus the path name will be garbage.
So, for Windows it's important to directly pass a wstring this is already converted from a UTF-8 encoded.

This got me a bit further in my attempt to build FreeCAD on Apple M1.  I've been following the instructions on https://github.com/hyarion/homebrew-freecad-deps with the following changes:

- `brew edit hyarion/freecad-deps/nglib` to change `v6.2.2007` to `v6.2.2104` (which includes https://github.com/NGSolve/netgen/commit/dbe894fea373e7048a8ed8d7c3606a794fe57705)
- Homebrew on Apple M1 lives under `/opt/homebrew`, not `/usr/local/opt` as is the case on x86_64, so I've updated the `cmake` command line accordingly (see below)

In the FreeCAD source directory I've then:

```
mkdir -p build
cd build
cmake \
        -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="\
/opt/homebrew/opt/qt@5/lib/cmake;\
/opt/homebrew/opt/nglib/Contents/Resources;\
/opt/homebrew/opt/vtk@8.2/lib/cmake;\
/opt/homebrew/opt/pyside@2/lib/cmake;\
/opt/homebrew/opt/python-boost/lib/cmake;\
/opt/homebrew/opt/coin3d/lib/cmake;\
/opt/homebrew/opt/icu4c/lib;\
" \
        -DBUILD_QT5:BOOL=ON \
        -DUSE_PYTHON3:BOOL=ON \
        -DPYTHON_EXECUTABLE=/opt/homebrew/bin/python3 \
        -DPYTHON_EXECUTABLE=/opt/homebrew/bin/python3 \
        -DBUILD_FEM_NETGEN=1 \
        -DBUILD_FEM=1 \
        -DBUILD_FEM_NETGEN:BOOL=ON \
        -DFREECAD_USE_EXTERNAL_KDL=ON \
        -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release \
        -DHOMEBREW_PREFIX=/opt/homebrew \
        -DBUILD_WEB:BOOL=OFF  \
       ..
make -j8 -i   # ignore errors
```

The author probably didn't save the external files in the correct order, that is, save the external documents first before the depending document, which FreeCAD will automatically do when saving the main document. As mentioned in the 'big block of comments' I mentioned earlier, the Link will mark itself as 'touched' if it detects the linked document has changed its `LastModifiedDate` property. If you do a recompute, save the file, close all, and then re-open it, it won't prompt for save again when you close it.

Have a look at https://doc.qt.io/qt-5/i18n-source-translation.html
Basically Qt offers these functions for translations:
* tr() : this marks strings for lupdate and translates them immediately. In C++ the context is the class name but in Python it seems to use the string `@default`
* QApplication::translate() : does the same as above but you must explicitly set the context
* QT_TR_NOOP : only marks the string for lupdate but doesn't translate it.
* QT_TRANSLATE_NOOP : does the same as above but you must explicitly set the context

The _tr() function is only able to translate strings but it doesn't mark them for lupdate. So, as soon as a string will be changed we won't be able any more to add them to the .ts files.

The "holdup" is pretty simple: +17,032/−2,492, and 100 files changed, but spread across only 38 commits. In essence, the work of reviewing a PR grows exponentially with its line count -- a reviewer has to keep a lot of details in mind, and really understand not just the code that they are looking at in the moment, but how it relates to all of the other changes in the PR (at any moment some of which they haven't even looked at yet!) ...whereas the work of writing that code is closer to linear, because you sort of progress through it step by step, and already know both what you've done already and where you are headed (usually, more or less 😄). So there's a huge disparity when a PR gets this big. There is really only one person alive who has the technical chops to merge this particular PR, and that's @wwmayer. It's absolutely on his radar, but there are only so many hours in a day. 

The good news is that we have recently brought onboard two additional mergers (myself and @donovaly) who can help with the more straightforward PRs, hopefully leaving more time available to bring the "big guns" to bear on this massively more difficult problem.

I did not try to understand this thread. I am just answering the question. In the following I am not implying you should support single points in sketches at all. I am just answering the question on whether points can be made "defining points".

As @adrianinsaval rightly points out, since end of last year it is indeed possible to have points visible in the 3D view, outside of edit mode in a Sketch. Unlike the rest of the geometries, that are by default "defining" (normal geometry that define the profile of a sketch) unless you have the geometry insertion mode toggled to insert construction geometry, points are always enter as construction points regardless of the insertion mode. 

This apparently inconsistent behaviour is justified because: 1) 99.9% of the times a user expects a construction point regardless of the insertion mode; and 2) the introduction of the feature is meant to respect the legacy operation of the sketcher, in which there were only construction points.

However, if it is relevant, this behaviour is only possible for single points (geometric points created with the geometry point). It is not possible for "points" that are not geometric points, but endpoints of a geometric object. The reason is that geometric objects are either normal or construction, but not partly normal, partly construction.

To have a defining point: 1) select the point creation tool in the sketcher, 2) create a point, 3) Select the point, 4) click the toggle construction button. The color of the button will turn white (from typical construction point color, red). If you now exit edit mode, the profile will show you a point.

@Roy-043 
The whole project tries to transfer the tools of TechDrawTools.FCMacro into C++ source code. This has been desired by several users.

The user interface IMO is essential.

Actual situation:
1. The user creates lines, e.g. using the "Add Cosmetic Line" tool.
2. The user creates centerlines using "Creates Center Line", one by one, selecting the decorations once more at each use of the tool.
3. Then the user selects several lines and starts "Line Decoration" tool to change their decorations.

New situation:
1. The user **first** selects the needed line decorations using the "SelectLineAttributes" tool.
2. Then he creates the used lines, using any one of the several tools. All created lines having the needed decorations instantly.
3. Additional, if there are old lines, having not yet the needed decoration, you can change them using the "ChangeLine Attributes" tool.

The user interface in  the existing TD tools "Line Decoration" and "Create Center Line" is not very practical when creating technical drawings.
You are able to select any colour and any weight. This should not be. A technical drawing using 10 different colours and 10 different line weights looks like a single text page using 10 different styles of lettering. Furthermore it does not correspond to the technical standards.

Please have a look at:  [](https://wiki.freecadweb.org/Macro_TechDrawTools)

There I tried to document the macro. You can see the window used by the macro. My aim is to copy the appearance in the macro , but to have the fields one upon the other, to hold the dialog window in the Combo View is as small as possible.

I noted in my first comment that I don't like this direction.  It is increasing our technical debt with regard to 2.5D bias.  Right now, the bias is minimal in drilling but it only gets harder to remove with more features.  I know people want features but the fastest way to get new features is with maintainable and well designed code.  I suggest this PR should be closed in favor of a more intentional and long-term design.  Here's what I propose:

I've started the process of refactoring the circular hole processing architecture.  The first step is to abstract out the logic of producing drilling and helical gcode into a 'generators' and make it testable.  The first one for drilling is done and merged with PR 5154.

The next step will be to make the drilling operation use the new generator in the conventional way.  I have a feature branch in process and invite testers: https://github.com/sliptonic/freecad/tree/feature/drill-refactor  This will add no new functionality.

After that, the next step will be to similarly abstract and remove the shape generation logic. The drilling operation will only be responsible for moving from target to target and calling the generator for each.  When that is done, the drilling operation will be able to process each shape independently at any Z level (and at any orientation).

It's considered bad practice (code smell) to use user parameters to control the behaviour of low-level classes. If there is no real use case (any more) to auto-rename the passed property name then completely remove the code to do so.

If it should still be allowed to auto rename properties then add an argument to the function to make the intention clear. Currently, if a programmer wants to do it, first of all he must even know this parameter exists, then he must change the value and as last step restore the old value.

But the general problem is that the behaviour is almost unpredictable because depending on the value of the parameter custom Python features may work on one system and fail on another system.

A further special problem is the use of the static keyword:
```
    static ParameterGrp::handle hGrp = GetApplication().GetParameterGroupByPath(
            "User parameter:BaseApp/Preferences/Document");
```
The object hGrp will be used for the whole lifetime of the application and will never be read again. However, if in the parameter editor the group is renamed by the user, a new group "Document" is created and the user changes "AutoNameDynamicProperty" there, then DynamicProperty::addDynamicProperty() keeps reading values from the wrong parameter group.

> Well, although FreeCAD has 'system.cfg', but no code is currently using it,

The system.cfg is a different story and it was added by the project founder. I don't know what the original intention was but I assume it was supposed to put it into a directory where users only have read access (such as All Users on Windows or /etc/ on Linux) and that only contains application-specific settings. The way it is now it's pretty useless.

> The way I see it, parameter editor in FreeCAD is like registry in Windows and sys filesystem in Linux, which exposes low level settings for power users (and other modules through API) to control low-level system behavior.

With the consequence of all sorts of side-effects. I don't how many hours I spent to locate problems with functions that are affected by environment variables and to make things consistently working on all platforms, e.g. all the locale specific settings.

So, IMO for all low-level stuff we should try to avoid possible side-effects to guarantee consistent behaviour.

> I discovered the auto renaming problem because I made a mistake in my addon module by adding property without checking the existence first. And I only discovered the problem when I saw many auto renamed properties in one of the user files while dealing with an unrelated bug. This makes me think that the silent renaming is a bad behavior.

I fully agree on this and because you said it's impossible inside Python to determine the actually used property name the affected custom Python features are pretty useless. That's why I think the whole renaming stuff can be entirely removed sooner or later.

Existing project files with unexpected property names should still load fine because the names are stored inside Document.xml and the __init__ function of a Python feature with the addProperty() calls won't be called anyway.

> This problem applies to the parameter observers as well, which is why I think there is code there to not remove the group if there is any reference to it. I haven't tested it, though. I know this because I actually recently made a few changes to the parameter API in my branch related to this problem.

> Just realized that you're talking about renaming the parameter group, not removing.

Both can cause problems. I have seen use cases where two config files are merged into one by loading (a part of) a second file into a group of the already loaded file. If the group is not empty and there are attached observers then very funny things can happen directly inside the DOM document of the xercesc library. In some cases some removed nodes still somehow have a link to the document and when saving the document it can corrupt the XML structure.

> Still though, the renaming problem applies to those parameter observers as well. Maybe we should implement rename as copy, remove, and then add.

Two years ago I fixed several of these issues but before I could make more changes my PC died. Luckily, I still have a back-up of these changes and I should have a look of what can be merged.

Most of the currently used observers are only attached temporarily and thus the chance for problems is rather low but if a group is assigned to a static object the chance for problems is much higher.

> Yeah, it does cause problem like you mentioned. I guess adding property is not really performance critical, so changing to non static is not that a big deal.

If we should keep the possibility to restore the old behaviour then we have to consider two cases:
* should it be possible to decide for each container to allow the renaming then a non-static class member would be needed
* does it suffice to either enable it for all or for none then a static boolean should be used and set only once

So, in summarize, the ideal solution should provide a configurable color setting from both stylesheet and FC preference/parameter, and yet be able to provide a default value that is usable in both dark and light theme.

Here is my proposed solution:

For each color option, there shall be two FC parameters, one integer (or string) for storing the color, the other boolean to let user choose whether the color can be overridden in stylesheet. The two parameters can have the same name (or not).

Expose the color option to stylesheet by defining a `qproperty` in the relevant widget. It is actually quite tricky to determine whether the current stylesheet contains any setting for a `qproperty`. If not handled correctly, then the color from the last stylesheet may be wrongly retained when switching to another stylesheet witch didn't have the setting. I made a recent [commit](https://github.com/realthunder/FreeCAD/commit/14062dcce9d6d9547d1b0364d87b485a166791d6) in my branch in attempt to solve this problem. It works like this. Two boolean flags are used. One used in [property setter](https://github.com/realthunder/FreeCAD/blob/14062dcce9d6d9547d1b0364d87b485a166791d6/src/Mod/Part/Gui/TaskAttacher.cpp#L467) to flag whether the property has been written. The other flag [copies](https://github.com/realthunder/FreeCAD/blob/14062dcce9d6d9547d1b0364d87b485a166791d6/src/Mod/Part/Gui/TaskAttacher.cpp#L1121) the first flag when handling `QEvent::StyleChange` event, and then reset the first flag.

The actual color is applied in response to `QEvent::PaletteChange` with a timer, because of another potential complication, which is to provide a default color that is usable in both dark and light theme. My commit above (which deals with the green or red message in TaskAttacher) also attempts to solve this problem by [checking](https://github.com/realthunder/FreeCAD/blob/14062dcce9d6d9547d1b0364d87b485a166791d6/src/Mod/Part/Gui/TaskAttacher.cpp#L425) on the button text color. If the color hsv value is greater than 128, then consider it as bright text, and the default green message color is lighten to make it more visible in dark theme. This method may or may not be applicable to auto tuning of other widget color.

Each (flat) face has (a) normal vector, but there is no well-defined base to make an axis from that vector. The "normal axis" of a sketch has such a base: the sketch's origin. But for a face, there is no "origin". A seemingly obvious choice would be the face's center of mass. However, for all but symmetrical profiles this is highly arbitrary, sensitive to changes in the profile's shape, and lacks a way for the user to control it. (Introducing ways to control it would essentially recreate what we already have: attach a datum axis to the face and use the attachment offset to control it.)

Yes. And TD in general needs a thorough review. I once worked to fix the mess with pages and its displayed childs but I felt I could only cure symptoms, not the main causes.
In my opinion the main issues with TD are:
- TD is slow. Even with relatively simple assemblies and parts, it takes quickly ages (Wandererfan and Klaus, the maintainer of A2plus, once tried to improve the situation but both can no loner work for FC and I don't know enough about the underlying problem.)
- no other WB is recompiled so often when code in FC changes by MSVC. So there must be a lot of unnecessary dependencies.
- there are many hacks in the code Wandererfan was also aware of but never had time to look at. He told me that he took over the code from someone else and often does not understand these hacks as well.

Long story short, when you see strange code, any improvement like this PR is highly appreciated.

> Yes. And TD in general needs a thorough review. I once worked to fix the mess with pages and its displayed childs but I felt I could only cure symptoms, not the main causes.

A general rework at this point is difficult and actually not needed because the basic design still looks OK to me. A good idea always is code-refactoring where big functions are split into smaller ones. This automatically reduces duplicated code and may fix inconsistencies.

> TD is slow....

For this we should have a good test file that eventually could be added to the examples directory. In a second step a profiler must be used to identify the code parts that are called too often.

> no other WB is recompiled so often

TD depends on many other extension modules like Measure, Part, Spreadsheet, Drawing and Import. And of course it depends on the changes of the other modules.
A re-compile may only be needed if there are changes in header files but if only source files are changed then a re-linking is sufficient.

> there are many hacks in the code

I have seen many cases where inside the constructor of a class certain things are checked and if not fulfilled the further initialization is aborted and a message is printed. To avoid possible crashes the affected methods are full of checks not to call the null pointer member variables. In some cases the better alternative would have been to throw an exception in the constructor in order to clean-up the whole instance.

When changing only the mode, a recalculation of the derived values should not be necessary -- they should have the right value already. For me it looks like your issue is the following:
- The last recompute of your model was done *before* applying my patch (that's why *Angle* is still 0°)
- Now, the first change *after* applying my patch is the change of the mode. This change triggers a recompute and now the wrong 0° *Angle*  is a primary input, so the *Growth* is correctly calculated to 0 mm.

I guess there is not much I can do here. I cannot change an inconsistency from the past. A single recompute (prior to changing the *mode*) fixes this by ensuring all properties to be consistent again.

Performing the calculation when the mode is changed won't help here: I will only see the new mode, but to resolve the original inconsistency I would need the old mode, too. Without this, I don't know whether to trust your *angle* or your *growth*.

* I change the *mode* to "pitch-height-angle" (having #5254 applied, too, this makes *Angle* writable). *Growth* gets calculated to 0.0mm; which is correct, because *angle* is (wrongly) 0.0°.

That logic may have been flawed but the developer included it for a reason.  Unfortunately, the logic was buried within a larger function and had no unit test corresponding to his expected use-case.

This PR removes that logic and replaces it with a hard-coded value.  Now the function will perform as you expect but may break for use-cases he had in mind that you are not considering.

Then write a unit test that returns the correct value under the original and new cases.  Then, in the future, when this code is modified again to accommodate another use case, it will not break for the cases you're considering now.  The unit tests will exist to prevent that.

> The real solution is to get the correct error/warning/log setting at each point in the code IMHO.

We should distinguish errors from warnings.

Concerning warnings:
The best solution is to issue warnings when the users needs them. The PartDesign Helix feature is a good example. You are warned on creation of a helix that it can be self-intersecting. You only get this warning, if this is geometrically possible.

Concerning errors:
The optimum is to design the UI so that the user cannot do anythings wrong, e.g. not enter negative values when this leads to errors.

Personally, I try to achieve both and made a lot of PRs to improve the UI in this respect. However I am pretty sure we will never reach the optimum. Take for example the addons. Every addon can issue a warning and we cannot take care of the UI of every addon.

Many thanks. I only commented on a very minor style issue since I first can compile next week to give useful feedback.

> I am not that experienced with Python, but why do you use: `if direction is not None:` Instead of just: `if direction:` ?

Although effectively in the case of Base.Vector we can use `if direction:` without inconvenience, the code style guide proposes avoiding the use of booleans in a situation like this : https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0008/#programming-recommendations

 
>     1. If `direction` is orthogonal to `axis` the function should return `None` IMO. You should not use the `axis` in this case.

Using `None`  generates a segmentation fault in Coin. Another option is to use a Vector made up of `nan`, but this generates some unexpected behavior in the 3D view. Therefore, to avoid these problems, I decided to use axis as the direction of the projection in this specific case since it allows a good workflow when the direction of the view is changed.
 
>     2. If `direction` is a null vector there is a division by zero error. I am not sure if, or how, that should be handled.

It should be the responsibility of the programmer not to pass a null vector as the direction of the projection.

> should be just 2 different ways to construct the same object. I believe you when you say they don't, but it seems to me they should produce the same object.

It is not exactly the same. The former creates TopoShapePy that is the base class of TopoShapeVertexPy, TopoShapeEdgePy, ..., TopoShapeSolidPy and the latter creates the corresponding Python object to the underlying shape type.

> Otherwise it could lead to some very subtle bugs difficult to fix.

The point is that OCC itself isn't very strict in this regard. There are many functions that e.g. only accept a TopoDS_Face but in the function interface it uses TopoDS_Shape. As a convenience the Part module offers a function cast_to_shape that returns the correct Python wrapper to the underlying shape type.

> Passing in document name dot object name is a bit peculiar, but it works.

No idea how it's possible that sub-directories of /Users/jonas/Library/Preferences/FreeCAD/Mod are in the sys.path.
From QStandardPaths we use the four paths:
* GenericConfigLocation that points to ~/Library/Preferences on macOS
* GenericDataLocation that points to ~/Library/Application Support on macOS
* GenericCacheLocation that points to ~/Library/Caches on macOS
* TempLocation that apparently is a random path on macOS

The sub-directory for FreeCAD of GenericConfigLocation can be obtained with App.getUserConfigDir() and that of GenericDataLocation with App.getUserAppDataDir().

I tested the github action i mentioned above, at 2nd glance it is not as promising as i thought after all. 
2 reasons: 
- codespell uses a dictionary of misspelled words and the possible corrections. This means that there are inherently few false positives.
Check-spelling uses a dictionary with correct words, which means that all special words, abbreviations, etc. would have to be included in a list of allowed words. In the case of FreeCAD this is about 10000 different words with several regex, which is hard to do, because CamelCase etc. is not everywhere.
- codespell is a command line program. Anyone can use it locally.

> and Fusion appears indeed to be a standard in the maker scene. As I implemented it, it works almost the same as in Fusion.

Well, if it's considered as state of the art I can accept the functionality but this is independent on how it's implemented.

For example, to avoid to put all possible options into a single feature class one could split things into one or several DocumentObjectExtension classes or just normal helper classes. This is a bit of extra work but in the end pays off because it reduces code duplication and makes code more reusable.

> You spoke about a "god" class, but I only implemented what part Extrude for years.

God class is one of many possible code smells (see https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_smell) and it is independent from the functionality of an application that the end user sees.

Especially when looking at your changes of ProfileBased::generatePrism() there are now another two arguments (and the eight we had before were already more than enough) but inside the implementation there is a big if-block where all the new code goes to and the else-block contains the old code. This doesn't only make the function fatter by a factor of 3 but also complicates its use for possible new features because for having ten parameters it's not easy to figure out the valid values.

All this could be easily avoided by creating a new function.

The second thing is that ProfileBased::generateTaperedPrism() is almost identical to the code of Extrusion::makeDraft(). So again a big block of duplicated code that should be avoided. This can be fixed by moving the code to a helper class that can be reused by Part::Extrusion and PartDesign::FeatureExtrude.

In the forum thread (the original, as well as the second: https://forum.freecadweb.org/viewtopic.php?f=10&t=65171&start=30) there is consensus that the feature is useful and welcome, but there is considerable hesitation around the implementation that leads to BSpline surfaces also when it can be avoided. 

Also, it would be good if the feature supported inner wires from the start. 

I propose that the first approach is that the pad is modified to have taper using BRepOffsetAPI_DraftAngle.  
The Loft based method can be used as a fallback for cases that are not supported by BRepOffsetAPI_DraftAngle, mainly extruding sketches that contain bspline curves, or extruding sketches with arcs in an arbitrary direction.  I have posted a proof of concept for how BRepOffsetAPI_DraftAngle can be used in FeaturePad here:
https://forum.freecadweb.org/viewtopic.php?f=10&t=65171&start=30#p560960

An advantage of the draft approach is that inner wires are supported automatically.

The class Property has the private member myName that is by default set to null. The class itself doesn't offer methods to set the name from outside but instead there are two friend classes PropertyData and DynamicProperty that set a name when adding a property.

While for DynamicProperty::addDynamicProperty() it's guaranteed that myName cannot be null this is not the case for PropertyData::addProperty(). However, the latter is used with the macros ADD_PROPERTY() and ADD_PROPERTY_TYPE() and I am not aware that somewhere a feature passes a null pointer when registering a property. Nevertheless, to be 100% on the safe side PropertyData::addProperty() could be changed to print an error or throw an exception if the name is null.

So, normally it should not happen that for a property myName is null. In case it is unexpectedly null then it's an indication of a deeper problem elsewhere. The only allowed case when myName is reset to null is in DynamicProperty::removeDynamicProperty().

Modifying getName() to return a valid string in case myName is null makes the reported crash disappear but it also makes it impossible to find the actual reason for the crash and thus I recommend to leave it as it is without checking beforehand if the change would break anything else (e.g. if it's explicitly checked if getName() returns null and handles it accordingly).

And as it seems the problem has been resolved in the meantime as with current master the crash doesn't occur any more. However, it would still be interesting to know the real reason for the crash in v0.19 and what has fixed it in v0.20.

> Should it be changed there also ?

Yes. Thanks for the hint. Searching for `catch(...)` in the current code base shows that it's used too often and this should be reworked where not appropriate.

> Can you give some more explanation on this in order to improve next contributions ?

In many articles about coding guidelines it's considered bad practice to always handle exceptions with `catch(...)` because it may hide a deeper problem. The expression parser throws a Base::Exception (*) in case of a failure and only this should be handled. In case any other exception type is thrown the `catch(...)` swallows it and since it's not reported one would not even notice that there is a problem somewhere.

(*) IIRC the parser in the past has thrown Base::Exception but now it throws Base::ParserError. So, in the corresponding catch handles we should use Base::ParserError instead.

This change was explicitly requested in the forum by several people. The rationale for this is sensible - tapered extrudes are made for molded parts of molds and to de-mold parts the inner taper must have the opposite angle than the outer ones. With the same angle for inner wires, the taper feature is quite useless for practice.
Of course the change will be documented. However, this only affects when extruding as non-solid since for solid inner wires never worked..

The existing code is OK.
In most tools an object (cosmetic line, dimension etc.) must be selected.
_checkSel executes two checks:
1. check if a valid "container" (= view) is selected. If failed: "Selection is empty"
2. if check 1 passed, check if an object is selected. If failed: "No object selected"

In case of PositionSectionView only the "container" is used, check 2 always would fail in _checkSel

@mwganson Indeed commit history is a bit weird. You can try `git pull --rebase upstream master` then check with `git log` how it looks. If it's correct you can `git push`.

If it's not correct there, you have to look at `git log` what is the SHA of your commit then you can try following :
```
git checkout master # got to master branch
git pull --ff-only upstream master # update
git checkout -b tempBranch # create a temporary branch
git cherry-pick SHA # cherry pick your commit in the temp branch
git push --force origin tempBranch:part_loft # overwrite PR branch with temp branch
```

At this step the PR should be OK. Then a it of clean up : 
```
git checkout part_loft # switch to old branch
git branch -d tempBranch # delete temporary branch
git fetch origin part_loft # fetch remote branch to index
git reset --hard origin/part_loft # reset working copy
```

HTH

"How shall the code line look like ?"

If it is really a check for a floating point number being zero, it would be this: 
if (abs(uu * vv * ww) < Precision::Confusion())

If the values of uu, vv and ww are approximations, and you expect the error to be larger than Precision::Confusion (1.e-7) then you could use DrawUtil::fpCompare(float1, float2, tolerance).

It's because I build constrain contextually on top of ToolSettings. And I made further improvement of toolsettings on that ConstrainContextuall branch.

When the user selects only the base object, and then clicks the fillet/chamfer toolbar icon, currently (in this PR) all the edges are added to the list and the UseAllEdges property is set to True.  This is useful if the user wants only to do for example 96/100 edges.  He can disable UseAllEdges in the dialog and remove the 4 unwanted edges manually.  But would it be better to just add Edge1 in such cases and set UseAllEdges = True?

Here is my reasoning.  UseAllEdges = True offers protection from TNP, but if the user makes changes and now the base object has fewer edges than it had when the dressup was first created and the user toggles UseAllEdges to False, then the dressup will fail until the now no longer existing edges are removed from the list.  If only Edge1 is in the list box, then when the user toggles UseAllEdges to False the dressup will not fail (usually).  We must have at least one edge or else there can be a crash.  This is why you cannot remove all the edges in the dialog; you must always leave at least 1.

In the case where the user wants to chamfer 96/100 edges he can still use the add all edges context menu option, and then remove the other 4 in the dialog.

> BTW, I had a look how to use ViewProviderSketch in CommandDoc.cpp but can't sort it out. Using it creates forward declarations.

You cannot and you mustn't . The design is that the core provides the basic infrastructure but it's up to the extension modules to do then the actual work. The core is not interested in what exactly an extension modules does and how it does it.

As a consequence you are not allowed to implicitly or explicitly add a dependency of an extension module to the core system. In this case it would not even work technically because SketcherGui links FreeCADGui and now you can't make FreeCADGui to also depend on SketcherGui as this would be a cyclic dependency and thus impossible to build the libraries. 

Please keep in mind: everybody is free to use the core system and e.g. implements his own Sketcher extension module. When doing so the core must behave the same independent on how the extension module is implemented but this wouldn't be possible if you added a dependency.

If you want to do something in an extension module but the core doesn't provide the basics then the way to go is to add a virtual function to a class in the core (here ViewProviderDocumentObject) and override this function in the class of the module (here ViewProviderSketch).

I have taken a look to the modifications to ViewProviderSketch. 

1) The modifications originating in OpenBrain's commit should consider the review of OpenBrain's PR. That PR will be merged before this. This PR will need to be rebased on that one.

2) I do not favour data members with public access specifier (save for exceptions by design, such as properties). This has the potential to lead to very strong coupling and kills separation of responsibilities. It further leaks implementation details.

3) Although I have not looked into the whole with the necessary detail, it appears as the ViewProvider is being used as a carrier to store variables it should not even be aware of.

These issues are not problems that cannot be solved. However, they are serious issues that need to be tackled before merge. After OpenBrains' PR is merged and this is rebased, we will take a good look how we can solve them.

@PaddleStroke 

I think it would be great if you take a look to the comments I have made in OpenBrain's PR.

I think it is important that we all have a common understanding of the responsibilities of each component and the architectural barriers in place to prevent these responsibilities from spreading over different components (and where no specific barriers are set for flexibility and avoid a too complex design and mostly YANGNI, but special care should be taken so that responsibilities and delegations are mantained, this is the case of EditCoinManager and EditConstraintCoinManager, for example).

The menu bar is recreated every time a workbench is activated, so a command added to the StdWorkbench menu bar (similar to Part_ColorPerFace, for example) will be lost with every workbench change.
For Python-based workbenches, things are slightly different: the StdWorkbench menu is created the first time the module is activated, and future activations use a copy of the StdWorkbench menu bar created the first time.
So, in any case, the command is removed from the View menu bar with each activation.
If the command needs to be accessed from workbenches other than Part, the easiest way is to add the command to these specific cases.
For example, for Python-based workbenches:
`import PartGui`
--> add `"Part_SectionCut"` to workbench command list.

Thinking about this more.  I don't think we should do the M5 here at all.
Even though the Path Commands are very nearly gcode, they are not, in fact, gcode.  The Path Commands are an intermediate structure that will become gcode at postprocessing. 

At the time that the tool change commands are added there are two things that are required:
We need to know WHICH tool we're changing to (tool number)
We need to know what to do with the the spindle (On/off,  forward/reverse,  how fast)
Both of these come from the Tool Controller.  

At post-processing, those things get translated into gcode that is specific to the machine. The specific gcode commands will likely invole many other things like: stopping the spindle,  transiting to a change location,  retracting to the top, etc etc.  

For this reason,  I think the M5 command to stop the spindle is a machine-specific thing that should be added by the postprocessor.  For example,  my machine doesn't need an m5.  If a tool change is called, it automatically stops the spindle.

On the other hand, if we do an M5 here, it means the generator of the commands has to know the context.  That means keeping some kind of state object around and passing it from operation to operation and tool change to tool change.  That will get ugly pretty fast.

Thoughts?

> Apropos Wiki, here are the main limitations I have with splines: https://wiki.freecadweb.org/B-Splines#Limitations If you are in the mood, being able to insert and remove control points would be very valuable.

I am more than willing to improve (and in the process, learn about) B-Splines, especially inserting control points. But there are some limitations:
1. I'm basically only exposing routines already available in OCC (from [`Geom_BSplineCurve`](https://dev.opencascade.org/doc/refman/html/class_geom___b_spline_curve.html) which doesn't really have an insert pole function.
2. Even if there were such a function (or if we were to make one), this will result in the shape of the B-Spline changing unpredictably. 

However, addition/removal of control points correspondingly needs an addition/removal of knots in the knot vector, so as such both of these are equivalent. Addition of knots (including increasing multiplicity) can be done safely without altering the shape of the spline, but this also changes the control points that controlled the affected part of the curve. There is a link to some resources for how it's done in #5311 or related pages. By "[inserting] and [removing] control points", what you really want is to be able to change only some parts of the B-Spline, but this is an inherent limitation of B-Splines that we have little control on the actual points _on_ the curve. There are some other curves that allow a bit more control on that (don't quote me but possibly Chebyshev polynomials), but no doubt with their own drawbacks.

@0penBrain 

Commit 1 is not correct because you are assuming an order in the complete geometry array different from the actual one.

When generating the complete geometry array, the external geometry elements are added using a reverse iterator:
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/f179acf0625354dd79af7cc2d298206702beaede/src/Mod/Sketcher/App/SketchObject.cpp#L7192

I think you modified the code assuming that the element stored next to the last element of internal geometry is the external geometry with index -3, but this is not the case. The last element of the complete geometry array is GeoId = -1. So the third from the end is actually the one with index=-3.

Does this make sense?

Edit: Some extra information that may be helpful.

This std::vector<Part::Geometry*> format for complete geometry predates my involvement in FreeCAD.

Because of the different in indexing formats, I recently created GeoListModel (which is a template generating GeoList and GeoListFacade), which provides many member functions to work with this geometry model seamlessly including using directly GeoIds.

I have not modified SketchObject (yet) to use GeoList instead of std::vector<Part::Geometry*>. The intention is to do it to avoid errors with indices and increase code readability and maintainability.

Thinking about this further a good solution could be to do the same as with "display modes" of the view providers.

So, there can be a virtual function getEditModes() that returns a list of strings and these strings are saved with the QAction instances when creating the context-menu. setEdit() must be changed where the second parameter that currently is an int will be replaced with a string.

This avoids the difficulties with int's as described in the older posts above and a string automatically is a speaking name and thus easier to memorize when used in scripts.
Another big advantage is that there is no need to register values in the base class ViewProvuider like it's currently done with the EditMode enum.

First of all I wonder what's wrong with the current behaviour? If you copy a selected sketch it is copied to the clipboard and can be pasted into a second FreeCAD instance. This is a global mechanism and works for all object types.

The only difference to your suggestion is that it's not an XML format but very similar to FreeCAD's FCStd file format. If you want to use a different file format you cannot use the general Copy command because there is no way to figure out if the FCStd or XML format is supposed to be used.

If you want to support the XML file format I recommend to add a new command to the Sketcher workbench to bypass the general mechanism. 

At least for the Paste command you could eventually use the global function. The class MainWindow allows to register so called "url handlers". You can make a subclass of UrlHandler in SketcherGui and register it with getMainWindow()->setUrlHandler(). Your Copy function then has to create a MIME object that holds a url with the scheme name you choose with setUrlHandler().

This is not to copy a sketch, but to copy géométries inside a sketch and
between sketches when in edit mode.

This does not seem to do the right thing because what we need is what e.g. LibreOffice does:
Let's take for example LibreOffice:
![Inkedsoffice bin_JcXHowWOVp_LI](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1828501/153736093-23bde678-0c61-431b-9951-7d933222d1bf.jpg)

The language defines the rules. So German uses comma as decimal separator, English dots. etc. So all we need is an option when one uses FC in English, that one can also takes the decimal sign the language/locale defines.

What you do is to use in every case a special English style and not the decimal character defined by the language. For example in Farsi or Arabic, the decimal separator is neither a comma nor a dot.

So we need in my opinion a simple lookup list. We have the info here:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_separator#Usage_worldwide

In the preferences, we add an option. By default it is on, then the language's decimal separator from the lookup list is used according to the chosen language. If the option is turned off, the dot is used when the lookup list says for the language it would be a comma or U+066B. If it would be according to the language lookup list a dot, then the comma is used.
