Le dim. 17 juil. 2022 à 19:37, JanneK ***@***.***> a écrit :

> Spontaneously, I'm against the idea of having multiple "modes" if we can
> solve the issue by more aligned means (but still allowing for some
> flexibility in the end).
>

I don't think you can avoid multiple modes...

The complexity grows quickly in terms of getting every mode to do the right
> thing in every situation, every change would wherever (dress-ups) need to
> be confirmed to work for "workflows" that may or may not be used.
>

But the situation is not that bad because there are really only two path
computation modes!
First one is offset by tool diameter (theorical or actual), ie path
controls tool center.
Second follows part/feature contour, so called "on the line", and path
controls tool contact point.

Then, wether and which comp type should be output is just an option read
and interpreted by PP:
First mode, no comp: G40 in program and/or op header and that's all;
programer uses actual tool dimension in CAM, control has no clue.
First mode, comp: G41/G42 before compensated path, G40 at the end; CAM uses
tool dia, tool dia is 0 in control and control only uses wear.
Second mode, comp: G41/G42 before compensated path, G40 at the end ; CAM
uses contact point, control uses tool dia (not 0)+wear, ie actual tool
radius.

"Dynamic" mode is just a variation of the last one on the way the radius
data is obtained.


Is it not possible to fixate the super-set (G40/41/41.1/42/42.2) as the one
> and only "FreeCAD-way",
>

It is, and not only FC's one 🙂
But you have to provide the 4 "modes" to cover the different situations and
work habits.

and provide clear instructions/helpers on how to create PPs that result in
> the same...end result?
>

I don't really get what you mean here 🤔

> PP receives path points/move that it translates into G-Code moves,
corresponding to either the offset or the on the line path, optionally
wrapped into comp start/stop messages that it tranlsates into G41*/G42* and
G40.

It's the CAM programmer job to choose between those 4 universal scenari, ie
the one suited among those supported by his control, and the PP's one to
output it in the specific machine idiom.

This way, even the built-in "simulator" should/could work according to this
> complete set as a "professional machine". A correctly working PP should
> thus, if implemented correctly produce the same output as the simulator
> does.
>

This is a must indeed

Each set contains the "fixed tools" from some tool-dictionary, and the
> particular wear value for that individual specimen in that set.
>
>
See my other message for other, more advanced cases.

Now, when FreeCAD calculates the paths, it will always *only* care about
> the tool dimension (NOT the wear) to calculate proper offsets (and number
> of passes, like in a pocket).
>

CAM indeed does not not handle wear per se -BUT for machines without CRC,
programmer will have to adjust tool dimension and regenerate to take wear
into account.
Wether to offer a dedicated field for this case is more a UX choice. Of
course, supporting wear data in tool library would be nicely beneficial for
those users as this would ease reuse of wear data between jobs.

In a "hobbyist"-machine, the PP will have to ask FreeCAD for offseted-paths
> (?) to compensate the tool paths at the time of the gcode-generation.
>

All path computations should happen in CAM. PP is "just" an advanced
translator between generic PP input commands and control specific language.
Thus, provided the simulation is accurate, the very same CAM path, ie same
set of intermediary commands, post-processed by specific PPs for different
machines should deliver identical parts, true to simulation.

In each and every case, regardless of controller, the end result will (or
> is supposed to) be exactly as simulated in FreeCAD.
>

Absolutely

The workflow is the for everyone, the only thing that differs is whether or
> not someone has to change the wear in FreeCAD and regenerate the gcode, or
> if it can be done directly in the controller.
>

Yep.
I'd add that for the dynamic scenario, it would be nice to have the option
to output the D address value as a parameter. Operators will be grateful 😉

It's a design decision way back at the beginnings of FreeCAD... Basically App should work fully from Python, untranslated, and free from any Gui / Qt or localized elements. All the localization and translation should be done in Gui, so the App part would behave 100% identical, no matter the platform it runs on.

Of course later on this has been flexibilized a bit, there is some QtCore stuff in it, but I think the general idea is still valid.

> Regarding reverse IMO it is a valid and useful feature for all modes except through all,

It is, I suppose, depending on how we define "mode". If "midplane" cases are considered different modes it's not valid there.

> and I'm not sure if we need that mode for revolutions at all since it would be the same as a 360deg angle mode.

"Through all" only exists for grooves (subtractive revolve). For additive (just called revolve), it's replaced by "to last", which is actually non-trivial. This distinction I copied from pad/pocket, where making a pocket through the last face is simpler than padding to that last face, but still non-trivial since the length of the pocket depends on the size of the body (we pocket till the end of the bounding box). Technically we don't need it for grooves either, since we can just set the groove to 360. But removing it disturbs the enum commonality between additive and subtractive forms, that's allowing for some code reuse (at least when the superclassing is completed). This is not quite true. See https://github.com/coin3d/coin/blob/master/src/nodes/SoAnnotation.cpp#L34 and https://mevislabdownloads.mevis.de/docs/current/MeVis/ThirdParty/Documentation/Publish/OpenInventorReference/classSoAnnotation.html

If you have an FEM project with two pipeline objects then the objects might be ResultPipeline and ResultPipeline001 and you can only see the former.

One hackish solution could be to move the second pipeline object from the scene graph and insert it in front of the first pipeline object.

Another solution is to use the mentioned SoAnnotation node. As mentioned in the links rendering of geometric objects may cause some weird artifacts and this happened here too. However, by adjusting the SoShapeHints node I get the rendering working correctly.

Here is the Python test code:
```
from pivy import coin

view = Gui.ActiveDocument.ActiveView.getViewer()
node = view.getSceneGraph()
child = node.getChild(1).getChild(0)

anno = coin.SoAnnotation()
child.addChild(anno)

vp = App.ActiveDocument.ResultPipeline001.ViewObject.RootNode
anno.addChild(vp)

# fix the rendering
action = coin.SoSearchAction()
action.setInterest(action.FIRST)
action.setSearchingAll(False)
action.setType(coin.SoShapeHints.getClassTypeId())
action.apply(vp)
path = action.getPath()
hints = path.getTail()
hints.vertexOrdering = hints.CLOCKWISE
hints.shapeType = hints.SOLID
```

This statement is not exactly true, as [Blender](https://blender.org) has excellent support for Collada too. Furthermore, FreeCAD has ATM little to no support for textures, at least internally (some addons provided partial support). So in any case, there would be little you can do with textures in FreeCAD.
If you need to work with textures, I would suggest to use Blender instead, which has proper, extended and state-of-the-art tool for working with textures. (Note that there is good import/export between Blender and FreeCAD). Otherwise, unfortunately in FreeCAD itself, there is nothing we can really do at this point, as usable textures support is not something that will likely be integrated anytime soon.
One thing could be interesting, is to see if the materials defined in the collada file also define a color, apart from a texture. Then we could do something...

FreeCAD actually has enough support for materials to make it work well enough for my purposes.  That's actually how I was able to do a previous conversion of a different model.  But it was a painful process, because A. on one of the models, it had a whole-object surface that had to be omitted from the export, or else it "wins" over everything else, and B. you have to manually reassign each of the different surfaces to have a different material in FreeCAD before you export, because FreeCAD lumped them all into the same material during import.

The current released version of Blender had major problems with every .dae model I've tried so far (which is admittedly just a single-digit number of models).  Maybe Blender is still using an old build of pycollada.  No idea.  But it definitely fails to import these files in the latest released version (missing surfaces).

The only thing that handled this particular file completely correctly was MeshLab, which is a tool that I first learned about in the thread that led to this bug.

The limited support for materials in FreeCAD isn't a big deal, but I would expect the import to at least map different materials on input onto different FreeCAD materials so that you don't completely lose that structure when you import and re-export.

When building the shared libraries then the linker sets the RUNPATH inside the binaries so that they can find the shared libraries they depend on.

However, when installing the libraries then the RUNPATH entries are removed again and out-of-the-box shared libraries cannot be found any more. Thus, you have to set the environment variable LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

In CMake you set the library directory to /usr/lib/freecad/lib. Now have a look if the shared libraries go directly in that directory or /usr/lib/freecad/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu

It would be good to split the changes and make one commit for each category.

* 1st commit is for Part primitives

* 3rd commit add a new function ensuring a fallback to internal precision+unit in case the user unit schema would zero a non-zero value
For example, if your unit preference is 'Imperial decimal', using a quantity of '1 mil' would be converted to '0.00 in', that gives an invalid object. In this case, the new behavior falls back to '0.0254 mm' to ensure a valid solid is created. Notice that for values correctly handles by user unit schema, it still rounds to user selected precision. Eg. '0.12345 in' will be converted to '0.12 in' if you're using a precision of 2 decimals.

@grubertechnic See 0c7e521ff5

I had a look at the code base and found only two occurrences of **this** rotate() method. It's in circ_placements and polar_placements which both are functions of Draft's array module.

So, I wonder whether we should really keep the faulty implementation (added with 3fcbf71fb5280) which from a mathematical point of view doesn't make too much sense or at least has a weird behaviour. And since its documentation explicitly mentions `This method is compatible with TopoShape.rotate()` but in fact isn't it must be considered as bug.

Given that there is no other function using rotate() I think we should fix it and adjust circ_placements and polar_placements accordingly.

Then there should be written some unit tests to ensure the compatibility with TopoShape.rotate:
```
# Use this as the base for a proper unit test
import math
from FreeCAD import Base

box = Part.makeBox(1, 1, 1)
box.Placement.Base = Base.Vector(10, 10, 10)
box.Placement
box.rotate((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), 90)
box.Placement

p1 = Base.Placement()
p1.Base = Base.Vector(10, 10, 10)

p2 = Base.Placement()
p2.Rotation.Angle = math.radians(90)

# p3 is equal to box.Placement
p3 = p2 * p1
box.Placement

p4 = p1 * p2

p5 = p1.copy()
p5.rotate((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), 90)

# p5 is equal to p4 (but actually should be equal to p3)
p4
p5
```

EDIT:
There is a certain risk to break external Python scripts if we don't support the faulty behaviour. But when adding the comp parameter that by the default shows the old behaviour we should print a warning to discourage people to use it and fix their code instead.
Otherwise it could happen that people use the default and wrong behaviour in new code and are not aware of the issues and thus never fix their code.

Then in a future release we could remove the support for the old behaviour (but leave and ignore the comp parameter).

> Shouldn't this be fixed then directly in Base rather than introducing a workaround?

IMO yes. The current behaviour of Placement.rotate() is a bug because the doc string clearly says it's compatible with TopoShape.rotate() but in fact it isn't. 
So, we should check the FreeCAD code base where this faulty rotate() function is used (I only found the 2 occurrences in Draft's array module) and fix the broken rotate() function and its occurrences.

The only point to consider is how much the broken function is used in external Python scripts where we have no control over. But I can hardly imagine that it's used that much because of its weirdness.

To be 100% safe in the other PR an optional parameter `comp` is added that by default shows the faulty behaviour and to get the correct behaviour it must be explicitly set.

This bug hits FreeCAD 0.20 and makes working with FreeCAD unreliable. Also verified is still a bug in FreeCAD weekly AppImage from 10th-August-2022.

Position x: 28'9+3/4"
Position y: -13' 7+1/4"
Position z: 0

When focus/defocus each of those fields the result is follows.

Position x: 28'9+3/4"
Position y: -12' 4+3/4"
Position z: 0

All subsequent focus or defocus results in position y being evaluated and self-modified because it is evaluated as this bug issue report describes.
-11' 7+1/4"
-10' 4+3/4"
-9' 7+1/4"
-8' 4+3/4"
and so on.

This should not be possible from UX perspective because user entry of formulas "f(x)" is a different action than typing in a literal value. Yet we have this impossible expression placed in the literal value entry and evaluated so self-modifying every focus or defocus.

Attempting to purposefully move this literal into the Formula editor 
Position y f(x): -13' 4+3/4"
there is an error "Failed to parse expression". It can only be entered as:
Position y f(x): -(13'+4"+3"/4)
however this is not actually valid when accepting and leaving focus, the error is:
`16:19:32  Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
<class 'SyntaxError'>: ('unterminated string literal (detected at line 1)', ('<string>', 1, 105, 'App.getDocument(\'documentname\').Sketch060.setExpression(\'.Placement.Base.y\', u\'-(13\' + 4" + 3" / 4)\')', 1, 105))
`

What is successful:
Position y f(x): -(13*12"+4"+3"/4)

There are a few problems in FreeCAD handling of unit literals here.

1. Negative sign is represented naked without parenthesis when editing unit literal and for display
2. Unclear handling of complex units for editing
3. Display should not be the same as entry for complex units, but if it is going to be the same at least make it the same and have it be valid!

Position y f(x): -13' 7+1/4"
should instead on editing and display be
Position y f(x): -(13' 7+1/4")
however the 7 in this example is ambiguous. It should be more explicit as
Position y f(x): -(13' 7"+1/4")
yet this is still not allowed since the unit literal 13'7" is variously accepted or not accepted throughout FreeCAD (Spreadsheet, formula entry, literal entry, BIM field entry) and results in inconsistent behavior at input. So we should insist on consistent behavior as
Position y f(x): -(13'+7"+1/4")
and that is unfortunately not valid though either, let's try something else
Position y f(x): -(13'+7"+1"/4)
this is accepted by the formula editor however there is an error
`16:57:19  Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
<class 'SyntaxError'>: ('unterminated string literal (detected at line 1)', ('<string>', 1, 105, 'App.getDocument(\'documentname\').Sketch060.setExpression(\'.Placement.Base.y\', u\'-(13\' + 7" + 1" / 4)\')', 1, 105))`
okay let's try something else then how about
Position y f(x): -(13*12"+7"+1"/4)
Yes! That is accepted and computes.

Wait a minute why though? This does not make sense to me. Why would 13*12" be accepted but not 1/4" ?

But forgetting that one moment and focus on a problem here: it is still an error of application, as it gets converted to a display string that is then again evaluated, so is no longer the same value. The objects are not in their correct places!

Anyways...

Let us see:
Position y f(x): -(13*12"+7"+1/4")
Position y f(x): -(13*12"+7"+(1/4"))
Position y f(x): -((13*12")+(7")+(1/4"))

No these are rejected.

The only user workaround I can find is as follows
Position y: -13' 7+1/4"
must be entered by the user again as
Position y f(x): 0"-(13*12" + 7" +1"/4)

Anything else does get mangled.

Maybe. Unfortunately the spec doesn't explain well what the exact meaning is of icon or generic-icon. But it helps to look at some existing files under /usr/share/mime/packages. There I have e.g. openscad.xml with this content:
```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<mime-info xmlns="http://www.freedesktop.org/standards/shared-mime-info">
   <mime-type type="application/x-openscad">
     <comment>OpenSCAD Model</comment>
     <glob pattern="*.scad"/>
     <icon name="openscad"/>
   </mime-type>
</mime-info>
```
Now when looking for a file openscad.png then it's located e.g. in /usr/share/icons/hicolor/48x48/apps/openscad.png (and also available for 64x64, 128x128, 256x256 and 512x512). New files with the extension .scad won't show the openscad icon but that of text files.

Then in the same directory there is the file freedesktop.org.xml (with a few thousand file extensions listed) then for all entries of generic-icon the name attribute is a mime type, e.g.:
```
  <mime-type type="application/x-partial-download">
    <comment>Partially downloaded file</comment>
...
    <generic-icon name="package-x-generic"/>
    <glob pattern="*.wkdownload"/>
    <glob pattern="*.crdownload"/>
    <glob pattern="*.part"/>
  </mime-type>
```
Now when creating a file test.crdownload it immediately shows the icon /usr/share/icons/elementary-xfce/mimes/48/package-x-generic.png

I don't know anything about this interpreter information... but is it even relevant to have inside FreeCAD?

Yes, this information is relevant for running the `fcinfo` script from within a shell which is the case when using it as a diff helper for Git as described at [Enabling human-readable diffs for FCStd files with the fcinfo utility](https://wiki.freecad.org/WebTools_Git#Enabling_human-readable_diffs_for_FCStd_files_with_the_fcinfo_utility).

The line changed in this PR is the so-called [shebang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shebang_(Unix)) line is used by Unix shells (Linux, macOS, ...) to select the program for executing this script. It's common practice to have shell scripts are marked as executable (as `fcinfo` is) and start with such a line. So after checking out the FreeCAD repo you could directly execute `fcinfo` from your favorite shell and Git.

On Linux and macOS, and Windows the Python 3 interpreter is called `python3` in contrast to Python 2 which was just called `python`. Python 2 has been deprecated a while ago and #6143 removed the compatibility support for it. So we should consequently use the actual Python 3 interpreter `python3` for running the `fcinfo` script.

Hello, you seem frustrated. Let me explain why we have this guideline in place:
1) historically freecad has had very long release cycles with very few backport minor releases. Many bugs get fixed in the dev branch and may not get backported to stable. Therefore bugs may be already fixed in dev. It creates a bug triage nightmare to handle redundant bug reports. 
2) historically, the forum is the fastest way to get bugs confirmed and fixed. Many bugs will be fixed on the spot.
3) The forum is a spam target, first time postings are automatically moderated and pending until OK'd by a moderator. After that, the poster can post freely.  

If you want to report bugs, consider also running the development version of FreeCAD (at this time it's v0.21.x That way you can confirm that said bug is not present in the bleeding edge version. Of course you need to make sure you backup any important projects before you open them in development because they may not be backward compatible (when you open them in an inferior version). 

We are all unpaid volunteers. We have things set up this way to save time for triagers, testers, and devs. If you still are not satisfied, perhaps you can step-up and become more active in the community to be able propose and change the current workflow. If not, that is understandable as well.

While thinking back on this, I don't think **setBounds** is a good name choice.
It refers to the bounds() method, that returns parameters and is common to all surfaces.
While these methods are specific to BSplines, and deal with knots.
setKnotsRange(), setKnotsBounds() or setKnotsInterval() would be more accurate, IMHO.
Opinions ?

@LarryWoestman You will have to merge the different commits. All typo fixes should be in 1 commit. All f-string fixes should be in one commit. All commits making tests should be in 1 commit per file. It would also be nice if you could split it up into multiple PRs. Tests could be it's own PR, minor fixes like typos and f-strings it's own PR, refactoring it's own PR.

That is my recommendation and it will probably need some git skills - in this case I could help review some of the PRs. But it is really up to @sliptonic who is Path responsible - if he don't mind 1600 line PRs, then no problem.

I think setBounds is accurate given the signature. Only the first and last knots are given, and the ones in the middle appear to just be scaled to that range.

However, the topic is different if there already exists a "setBounds" function for other curves (I see that there is a setRange() in some cases) that actually keeps the same parametrization but changes start and end params (effectively changing the shape of the curve). AFAICT a function like this wouldn't make sense for a spline because of it's piecewise nature.

To further complicate the matter, there is a setKnots() function in OCCT that can specify a different sequence of knots. AFAIK that can change the shape of the spline.

So to summarize: setBounds isn't inaccurate, but if a function with the exact same name doing different things exists for other curves, it should be renamed; and, alternative names you suggested can add it's own kind of ambiguity.

If we have to rename I suggest something like "scaleKnotsToBounds()".

@benj5378 Part of a larger effort to update the code base closer to C++17 best practise.

> does the appimage fail in wayland? 

The AppImage version always runs under XWayland. My impression is that it only has the XCB platform plugin for Qt compiled in. On startup I don't get any messages about missing platform plugins.

The distribution version will run under Wayland, but I can force it to run under XWayland by specifying `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb` on the command line. However, the issue arises whether I start it under Wayland or not.

> AFAIK freecad itself doesn't have support for wayland and always runs under xwayland

I think this depends on the AppImage and whether it has the QT Wayland platform plugin compiled in or not. If it has only the XCB platform plugin, then it will only support XWayland. This is a common issue with AppImages. 

The distribution-provided FreeCAD version supports Wayland because it uses the system's Qt libraries, which include the Wayland platform plugin. Whether the issue with invisible vertices here depends on Wayland is an open question, but since the issue appears no matter whether I start the distribution-provided version under Wayland or XWayland, I have my doubts whether Wayland is really the culprit.

@marioalexis84 Thank you for raising this. I tried it as part of the modernization effort. Both are legal so it becomes a question of local coding guidelines (which we do not have here).

if(ptr) relies on implicit conversion from the type of ptr to boolean which does save some typing and arguably is easier to read. 

OTOH it is a relic of C, which doesn't have bool types. Current tools (e.g. cmake-tidy) and the language itself (e.g. explicit keyword) reflect a trend to making everything explicit. Fewer surprises. Less hidden bugs.

See also: [https://releases.llvm.org/13.0.0/tools/clang/tools/extra/docs/clang-tidy/checks/readability-implicit-bool-conversion.html](url)

The documentation to [PyArg_ParseTuple](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/arg.html#c.PyArg_ParseTuple) says:
> Parse the parameters of a function that takes only positional parameters into local variables. Returns true on success; on failure, it returns false and raises the appropriate exception.

Although technically it returns an int semantically it's considered a boolean. If clang-tidy raises a warning then we should think about setting AllowIntegerConditions to true.

`semantically it's considered a boolean`

Yes, in the context of **C**  that is correct. The python API code is for C. But in C++ context it clearly returns an int.

Setting cmake-tidy AllowIntegerConditions to true would apply indiscriminately, and hide C style relics which we should be striving to replace.

The main issue with a large C++ code base full of `auto` is that you don't know the type your are manipulating without digging into the code (which you might not have), example:
```
 auto f = some_func();
```
If you don't look at `some_func` signature, you don't know what `f` is, so you don't know if you can write `f->` or `f.`.
It increases the burden since you have to jump everywhere to find out what was this type. 
Sometimes you have an IDE that can resolve the type, but most of the time, you don't (or it's making errors).

Worst, the return type of `some_func` can be hidden also, so you might have to dig into a function you haven't written to understand what it does and whatsoever (if it's using `-> decltype(some expression)` for its declaration, good luck figuring out what it is).

Please refer to [this answer](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/6900459/the-new-keyword-auto-when-should-it-be-used-to-declare-a-variable-type) for other people opinions.

`auto` is very useful when it's local (doesn't leak outside of a scope), or to write generic code (when dealing with STL's internal/external meta programming).  In this PR, I don't see why it's a benefit, since it's not coherent (why are you replacing `A* b = new A*` but not `C* c = (C*)ptr` ?) and it's partial (so you end up with a mix of different behavior, some functions with auto , some without in the code base). 

Typically, in such code:
```
QMap<QAction *, std::function<void()>>::iterator it = d->triggerMap.find(a);
```
It's exactly where using `auto` would be useful to declare `it` since the type of the iterator is not very important and easily deducted from the right expression.

So as a rule of thumb, DRY ok, but only if it doesn't increase the code readability. 
Most of the PR is in this case already.

Look, I don't disagree with you. I disagree with Herb Sutter which is, in my opinion, correct for what he does, but not for real world applications. Sure, in a STL only codebase, or a codebase that's truely generic (like a library) you should use auto everywhere you can. If you write a C++ application from scratch, only using generic C++ dependencies like STL or boost, then yes, he's completely right. 

But for a real world large application that has to deal with mixed C / C++ library (like FreeCAD), with binding between Python, Qt, OpenCascade, OpenInventor, etc.., you have ten different coding convention where **none** of them are generic (maybe Qt is the closest one to being generic).  

In all cases, his message isn't "use auto everywhere" (since it's impossible), but "using auto makes your code more generic/maintainable/beautiful". 

In this PR, you're using `auto *` for pointers but not for all of them. This is inconsistent. Either use `auto` for all variable (inc. pointers) but make sure to cast to the appropriate type. Then you'll realize that the DRY principle doesn't really apply:
`QComboBox * p = new WidgetCombo(x)` => `auto p = (QComboBox*)new WidgetCombo(x)` isn't any better IMHO.

What HS said here would  have been to write `auto p = WidgetCombo{x}` or `auto p = make_unique<WidgetComboBox>(x)` or even better `auto p = WidgetComboBox::make(x)`. You don't need to know what WidgetComboBox is here, and you *guess* that `make` is a static function that's creating a `unique_ptr<WidgetComboBox>`.  Please notice that all these rewrites change the type to manipulate from a `QComboBox *` to `unique_ptr<WidgetComboBox>` which isn't storable in a `QComboBox *` array anymore. Unless you use a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<QComboBox*>>` and so on, you're STL'izing your complete codebase. 

See what I mean ? This is a lot more work, since Qt isn't written this way. 

Anyway, there are multiple place in this PR where `auto` make sense and code easier to read, but many where it's not the case too and I invite you to fix them, not by rewriting the lines where the variables are declared but the code that makes use of the variable so it can deal with auto. One example is for the `QComboBox*` above, where it likely possible that a `WidgetComboBox *` variable would work as well (so it avoid a useless cast): `auto p = new WidgetComboBox(x)` **is** more readable that `QComboBox * p = new WidgetComboBox(x)` but the required fix is likely few lines below where `p` is being using/stored/manipulated.

What was happening before was that a second hlr thread was starting before
this face finding thread was complete. So even though we checked
geometryObject at the top of the routine, the other thread could modify
geometryObject while extractFaces was processing.   In the current
implementation, geometryObject is only invalid for the execution of two
instructions.

In a perfect world geometryObject would be protected by a mutex to
completely eliminate the possibility of it being invalid.

The problem is that the get/set interface expects you to modify a whole attribute, for example if p.Parameters is a list, you can get a list or set a list. Not set a subelement of that list.

This is a problem met elsewhere in FreeCAD, I'm not really sure how to approach it. When you do p.Parameters['F'] = 200, you are basically doing: Set 200 to the element F of the result of operation p.Parameters, which actually creates each time a new Python list from C++ contents. The python list is a representation of an internal C++ list, not the list itself.

So I'm not sure what should actually happen there, since that python list is actually an independent copy of the C++ one, and I see no way to do it otherwise.. But I'm no C++ expert, and the C++/Python interface is a whole world on its own, there might be something I'm not aware of..

Yea, I can help you re-do this PR. There are a few issues that potentially block it from a structure point of view (no idea about the feature itself).   
1. You made your changes directly on the FreeCAD master branch, for reasons that are not obvious at first, this is problematic. You need to fork your own branch off of the master, make changes to said fork/branch and then propose those changes in pull request.
2. You are `git merging` instead of `git rebasing` which introduces a whole lot of 'noise' in to your changes. When you rebase you're taking your solely intended changes and adding them on top of HEAD (or the tip of the branch, in this case FreeCAD master).
3. This is not easy at first but think about how the `git log --oneline` will look when you're applying the changes. It's customary to name the code/workbench you're modifying in the git commit summary: `[FEM] added critical strain ratio functionality`. Note this is separate than the githib PR summary you see at the top of the PR page like this one.  
4. It's also good form to separate commits that aren't necessarily related to the goal of the PR. In this commit you refactored some syntax and you also removed your name from the code comments. Those could be either 2 separate commits or combined in to their own commit like `[FEM] Code cleanup`. That way if just one of the commits is causing breakage, it can be reverted an not effect the other (causing more work for merge devs or yourself when fixing). Or vice-versa, the commit that works could be `git-cherry-pick`ed conveniently. 

I'm happy to walk your though how to redo this PR if you want. I can also redo it for you but you wouldn't get the recognition per se in the git log since the code will be associated to me. But what I can do is explicitly state that I'm resubmitting your PR (which attributes the code to you in the title or commit body).

This Pull Request adds macOS QuickLook previews and icons to FreeCAD.

The patch in _Info.plist_ makes *.FCStd files known as filetype `org.freecad.fcstd` to the system. The actual QL plugin source code is located in _src/MacAppBundle/QuickLook_ and is installed in _FreeCAD.app/Contents/Library/QuickLook_ using CMake `install` in the file _src/MacAppBundle/CMakeLists.txt_.

FreeCAD needs to be built as a full macOS app (`brew install --with-macos-app freecad@0.20.1`) and the installed in the `/Applications` folder. A restart of _Finder_ may be required to get QL icons.

The bundle must be moved to `/Applications`. This should be enough for macOS to pick up on the file type. You can check that by running 

```
qlmanage -m | grep freecad
  org.freecad.fcstd -> /Applications/FreeCAD.app/Contents/Library/QuickLook/QuicklookFCStd.qlgenerator (0)
```

If it does not, use Finder to throw the bundle in the Trash and then move it back into `/Applications`. If it still has not picked up on the new type, a reboot may help. If it still isn't there, `/Applications/FreeCAD.app/Contents/Info.plist` wasn't installed correctly by the CMake script.

If the manager was found, you may need to restart Finder (Option-Rightclick, and select "Relaunch" in the menu).

If all that still fails, you can at least check with `qlmanage -t some.FCStd` and `qlmanage -p some.FCStd` if it created thumbnails and previews.

3. There are cases in the code where an iterator has been used, but const_iterator could be used instead, but to change it might be considered beyond the scope of a refactoring PR.

4. In some cases making range-based loop from a auto'd loop that has been set to cbegin() and cend(), my IDE (CLion) pushes `auto var`, whilst in others it happily makes `const auto & var`. I'm struggling to understand **_why_** (or is IDE just stupid), but I have read that in some cases (int, short string, even pointers?) and depending on what is done in the loop, this actually **_saves_** some copying and hence is to be preferred. I see many quite recent cases in the existing codebase by senior devs that are not so fussy about const-ness on auto.

Sure thing: in order...
1. First, the core developers do not all agree perfectly about `auto`: I prefer more of it, and Werner less, for example. Your example shows a case where I believe we do all agree, however, and that is with C++'s (extremely verbose) iterator types. For other uses, though, it's a tough sell to suggest a sweeping, multi-thousand line code change that has only lukewarm support from reviewers (and in some cases active opposition), and only marginal benefit to the codebase, considering how much time it takes to review those changes. A case like 1a is much harder to reach consensus on, so a big change to that sort of thing is probably a non-starter. I'd be fine with that line, but I suspect Werner would not, for example.
2. This space intentionally left blank.
3. I'd love to see whole series of PRs dedicated entirely to `const`-correctness. It is far, far easier to review highly focused refactoring changes, so don't combine those with anything else.
4. Your suspicion about why there is sometimes that difference in the loop construct (that sometimes it's cheaper to make the copy) is correct, or at least it is often _true_ for small POD types. Whether that's what your IDE is doing or not I don't know, but CLion has a very good reputation, so I'd guess so.

So it boils down to this: huge changes with low perceived benefit basically have to be non-controversial, and to make reviewing easier (and more likely to actually happen) they shouldn't be mixed together. Every time I have to "context switch" when reviewing slows me down, and on a 2000 line PR that really matters. You can see the timestamps on that last review: it literally took me all day (I mean, I had customers, and taught a class, etc., but it was still a lot of code to look at).

There are still two problems related to the use of `SoBrepEdgeSet` in the Arch workbench:
A crash  with `ArchBuildingPart` and a raised `AttributeError` with `AchSectionPlane`.

The reason for this behavior is that the `Draft` objects edited in this commit and the previously named `Arch` objects are `App::FeaturePython` (or `App::GeometryPython`), but not objects from `Part` workbench like `Part::FeaturePython`.
Therefore, at object creation time  when the document is loaded, the `PartGui` module is not imported and the `SoBrepEdgeSet` data is not initialized.
The crash is generated because `coin.SoType.fromName("SoCustomType").createInstance()` returns `None` if the data for `SoCustomType` was not previously initialized.
Then, trying to add `None` using the `addChild` method of `SoGroup` Coin objects leads to a crash, while trying to access attributes leads to an `AttributeError`.

> this is a red flag: why should this be any argument ?

Don't exaggerate, I know that FreeCAD veterans don't like comparisons with commercial software and that FreeCAD will never compete with that software but sometimes it's good to take a look at current standards in the CAD industry. After all, they were established by experts following the needs of users and are meant to make the designers' lives much easier.

> no, it's **EXACTLY** the same per definition: con-centric means coincident centers. 

Even if the concentric constraint internally works on centers like the coincident constraint, there's still a difference in the way they are used - concentric constraint is applied to arcs/circles themselves and coincident constraint is applied to their centers. The implications of this difference (and thus the advantages of concentric constraint) are listed in the referenced thread. Also, from what I know, concentricity and coincidence are not the same thing when 3D space is considered (this is also explained in that forum thread but is not relevant for the Sketcher since it can't handle 3D geometry - I just want to clarify that they are not necessarily the same by definition). And finally, whether you like this argument or not, all the commercial CAD programs offer both types of constraints and they do it for a reason.

> This issue should be closed as _solved_ and not burden already limited developers time.

Marking this FR as solved would be misleading for the reasons mentioned above. As a trade-off, it could be changed to something like "[FR] Possibility to apply the coincident constraint to arcs and circles themselves" since this would bring the advantages of concentric constraint to the Sketcher and would be sufficient at least until 3D sketches are introduced.

New features are welcome but I highly recommend to discuss them first with the community in the forum. For example the Hole feature is an essential one of FreeCAD and heavily used. Up to now there was no need for a depth as you implemented it because when you later manufacture your part you use a countersink grinder. This is wider than the hole. So manufacturing as I see in your screenshot is a rather uncommon countersink.
Therefore please start a discussion and @ me there (I am "@uwestoehr" in the forum).

Another aspect why in this case we cannot say, "well nobody is forced to use a feature, we just provide it", is the complexity of the hole dialog. This is a real beast and I spent countless hours with it already because it allows so many combinations and every combination must be checked if it is allowed or not. Therefore adding more functionalities is not trivial.

Also don't forget that the hole feature must fulfill different standards/norms.
So when FC creates as countersink must be possible to manufacture with the tools given in the different norms. Of course for e.g. 3D-printing one can manufacture almost everything but for this the hole feature is not designed. For these applications we have the pocket feature and since FC 0.20 you can with it also create tapered pockets directly.

Hello guys,

Please allow me to chime in and support that feature as this is really how
a hole for a countersunk head screw should be done, specially when screw
diameter increases.

Without the top counterbore for the cylindrical part of the countersunk
head, you'd have to make inadequately big countersinks to get the head top
flush with part surface.

This is also why countersink bits have those weird diameters and that small
vertical cutting edge: they correspond to screws head dia and allow for
that small top counterbore.


If the hole tool is becoming a UI maze, maybe adding pre-configured
shortcuts for most common types could be a valuable help.

standard cylindrical holes?

@MisterMakerNL :point_up:

The first commit fixes the synchronization problem of the cell span in `PropertySheet` and `SheetTableView`. The cell span changes are only notified when recomputing, while the user interface (i.e. `SheetTableView`) response to changes one cell at a time. After the first commit, it is reversed in the sense that the per cell span change notification (via signal Sheet::cellSpanChanged) is done immediately on change, while UI accumulates the changes and handles them in batch using a timer. This solves potential conflicts in update, e.g. with your example, where two consecutive rows having cell spans, after removing the top row, the lower cell span change may be signaled first, causing span overlap in the upper row in `SheetTableView`.

The second commit fixes various missed span adjustment after change.
* `PropertySheet::Paste()` handles undo/redo, where there were simply no checking on span change, thus no change notification. 
* `PropertySheet::pastCells()` handles copy/paste. Adds the logic for  property handling of pasting cell with span.
* Then there is also extra handling of adjusting row spans when removing intersecting columns, and column spans when removing intersecting rows. Using your example file, instead of removing rows, removing columns that intersects the row spanned cells shall shrink the span, or otherwise adjusting cell content might be hidden by the span.
3D Rendering Performance Enhancement, perhaps? This is not limited to STEP files, but any big models.

> I wonder about all the hardcoded filter values

There should not be magic numbers in the code (e.g. item(3)). The general approach to counter this, is to use an enum. In the past I tended to use legacy enums for this, because of the need for conversion to int. Lately, I prefer to use a class enum and make the casts explicit wherever there should be converted to an int. Strong typing without implicit conversions is way less error prone and leads to lesser amount of bugs (the compiler is leveraged to unveil typical legacy enum bugs).

It has been accepted in the past, to have hardcoded UI entries matching an enum order (or an enum matching the hardcoded UI entries). This has the problem of synchronisation when making changes. That can generally be solved by adding the filters when building the dialog (if possible at the constructor), instead of leaving them in the UI. It still requires maintaining a second synchronised string array or a function to generate the strings. However, keeping two spatially close classes (enum and static array) in code synchronised is way easier as opposed to having to jump over different files. My current preference lays on the latter, as I do not know better.

There are some third party libraries providing support for stringifying enums. There is no language support yet in c++17 or c++20 afaik.

Bottom line: Magic numbers need to go. A class enum should be used for that. I will accept a synchronised enum to the hard-coded filter strings. I will accept a synchronised enum and a static string array (can be done constexpr, see SketchGeometryExtension for an example), and populating the filter on construction.

Let me know if you know better.

It is important that you know the reasons. And the alternatives. 

Moving ElementType to cpp file is probably the lesser of all things, but the reasons are as follows. Header files define what needs to be known by other classes to use the classes defined in them. ElementType is an implementation detail. No part of the classes of the header file use it (e.g. take it as a parameter). It provides no information to a user of the class. There is a principle called encapsulation, which basically says that classes provide an interface to users and encapsulate the implementation. The encapsulated code may well change without users ever noticing it from an interface point of view. I could even go one step further and say that ElementType is misleading to a user. This is because the user may know the public available Sketcher::PointPos, which shares some members. Why one and not the other generates questions, that can only be answered looking into the specific implementation chosen for the class. In fact Sketcher:PointPos is a counter-example. It is an enum which needs to be known to users and it is defined in a header file. 

When enums are necessary for the client (the user of the class), they need to be in the header. it is also possible to make them into the class definition as a public member. Then the decision is about the coupling between the enum and the class. For example Sketcher::PointPos is separate because, although it is essential for the Constraint class, it is useful in many other classes, without direct need for Constraints. Many times the boundary is not crystal clear. And what appeared to be tightly coupled evolves to loose coupling or vice versa. Code evolves.

I hope this helps understand why I did it.

@0penBrain 

Ok, lets look into it.

First we need to define what would be inside that shared pointer, so that we can compare apples to apples. The easier way to compare would be assuming the shared pointer will have QIcons inside.

The shared pointers would need some structure organising them, so that we can get the one we need from the geometry type, position, ... . There are basically two ways to do this. A first one is to use static if/else branching. The second one is to use a map. It is a well known substitute to use a map instead of if/else branching. There is indeed a trade-off, a very small performance hit (searching in maps, specially small ones is extremely efficient), against code maintainability and scalability. So, with both shared pointers and with what we have, we need to select one of the two strategies. Running exactly the same performance/maintainability trade off.

Although the class we use does not use dynamic memory, but actual objects, it is very similar in terms of what it offers. It manages the lifetime of the resources, the icons, the allocation of resources takes place once and it ensures the user gets references (which is equivalent to a pointer). So, basically it shares the resources through references, it is kind of a factory of shared smart references.

If the emphasis is in the fact that four calls are made, the four calls are very lightweight and should not have any impact. If we structure the smart pointers the same, we will have the same impact. If we organise the smart pointers in a different way, then we should be able to do the same with the references. So it begs the question: Could be change, for example the map, so that we can get the four icons we need with a single map search?

I think we may be able to. The interface of the class somehow changed over time, and it is no longer necessary to provide the Icons one by one, so we could reorder the map, so that a Base::Type key retrieves a map of colormaps, with key being the GeometryState, and retrieving a tuple of the icons of edge, starting point, endpoint and mid point. However, as the getMulticon function operates on a single subelement, returning a tuple of colormaps of that single subelement, the initIcons function would be more convoluted if the map is changed and considerably less readable. Yet, that function gets called just once, so if there were an performance hit, that is one way to go.

In this case, I do nothing it is worth it as a trade off (performance gain negligible, less readable code). However, if any of you wants to do the exercise from an educative standpoint, we may then compare the performance gain and the readability of the resulting code.

A couple of possible examples of "too big for a single PR" are the work I am doing on refactoring the postprocessors and the work that realthunder has done with sensitivity to change that is trying to be merged right now.  I think that the characteristic that makes it hard to decompose those types of things into more manageable pieces is that lots of functionality has to change before the changes start working again.
In the case of refactoring the postprocessors some of the changes cause git to mark pretty much every line of the postprocessor code in multiple files as "changed", which makes any potential reviewer's job hard.
I think it is possible to chop a "big" change into "fragments", but they are often not functional until many "fragments" get comitted, and there is extra work involved in making sure that each fragment is able to build and be tested individually. 
I do think that having a very clear statement of the problem that needs to be solved is important for any change.

It is possible to write additional tests one test at a time, with a clear problem statement and a simple PR.
Where it gets "big" is when you move a lot of code to new places, or even just reformatting whole files to match the formatting standards.  Some changes might work as a single PR if they are a focused change even if they end up changing a lot of lines of code.

I read the articles about _optimistic merging_.  I agree that it has benefits, in principle.  However, to make it work, at least three things need to already exist:
1. There needs to be good test coverage and a strong value in the culture for writing/maintaining those tests.  You can't optimistically merge if you don't trust that the test suite will catch regressions.
2. There needs to be a high value for _minimal solutions_ and discipline in the issue->PR process.  If PRs are routinely submitted that are large, unfocused, or not grounded in a known issue, then optimistic merging leads to conflict.
3. There needs to be a shared understanding of the big picture.   You don't need a 100-point roadmap of every feature for the next five years but everyone has to agree on what is important, what's trivial, and the goals of the project.

Based on that, I think _Optimistic Merging_ is something we should work toward but not something we can embrace at this time.  

There's a third way that might be more achievable in the short term.  Let's call it "Reviewer Moderated Optimistic Merging"  The idea is to split _process correctness_ from _code correctness_.  In this model, the maintainers focus on the process but we make that process require sign-off by certain domain experts who comment on _code quality_.  It would work like this:

1. Maintainers are selected based on a history of successful PRs.  They don't need to be expert in any area but have to be comfortable reading code. They are instructed about the process.
4. A PR is submitted.  It's tagged by workbench(s), etc.
5. A maintainer, inspects the PR and invites review by any/all people that he thinks will have input. Those reviewers can invite others.
6. a reasonable time is given for review.
7. The contributor's job is to answer/address any concerns raised by the reviewers.
8. The maintainer's job is to referee, keep the process moving, and click the button when no concerns are left unaddressed. If reviewers make what C4 calls 'value judgments' the other reviewers and the maintainer can step in.

### Example:
Someone submits a PR to make Path Job use links.
OpenBrain takes it as the maintainer.  He invites me because it's a Path thing.  He also invites RealThunder because it involves Links.  Maybe it involves a bit of code I don't understand so I also invite another reviewer.
After a week, I've signed off on it because I'm just awesome that way.
Realthunder shows a better way to do something and the contributor updates the PR.
The third reviewer declines to comment.
OpenBrain merges the PR.

I'm glad you dropped optimistic merge. A couple of comments.

1. Including "Optimistic Merging" in the name implies a derivative of C4 version, but it is significantly different: C4 is faster than CI, this is days, and is not actually optimistic as it demands a traditional review first. Suggest "Moderated Merge".

2. If a moderator wishes to make 'value judgments' they become an "interested party" and must pass the moderator baton.

Here what happens when I switch from one subitem to another one **from a different element** (probes start with `>>`, times are in milliseconds, the triggering event is the LMB press)
```
20:29:20  >> ElementItemDelegate::editorEvent // 1666808960323
20:29:20  >> TaskSketcherElements::on_listWidgetElements_itemPressed // 1666808960323
20:29:20  10.0289 Selection.cpp(1620): Clear selection
20:29:20  10.0331 Selection.cpp(1277): Add Selection sketchtest#Sketch.Edge5

20:29:20  10.1857 MainWindow.cpp(1370): update actions
20:29:20  >> ElementItemDelegate::paint // 1666808960813

```
20:33:53  >> ElementItemDelegate::editorEvent // 1666809233129
20:33:53  >> TaskSketcherElements::on_listWidgetElements_itemPressed // 1666809233129
20:33:53  282.835 Selection.cpp(1620): Clear selection
20:33:53  282.837 Selection.cpp(1277): Add Selection sketchtest#Sketch.Vertex11
20:33:53  282.985 MainWindow.cpp(1370): update actions

"style guide" can be any human readable document stating format rules. It is not necessarily the reference that an enforcement mechanism is required to comply with.

A "policy" in this case is more correctly like the decision to require auto formatting and perhaps to define the required mechanism.

For C++ clang-format is a human-readable statement of rules designed to be parsable by an enforcement mechanism. It is explicit, and any change therein has immediate impact. A descriptive text e.g. a wiki entry, on the other hand, is not explicit and changes therein not only have no direct impact but can easily be out of step with a reference document.

So I agree with @WandererFan that the reference document for C++ in FC be the clang-format file in the project, and that a separate explanatory style guide be left for another time.

As an aside, the clang-format on FC is based on LLVM. There are many base styles out there.

For python, Black seems to be popular. It is self-described as a strict subset of PEP8. So whilst Black does have a descriptive text, there is not an accessible or changeable ruleset. Looks like "take it or leave it", and they say so.

First off, if the intent is for only a single set of default colors, we should first discuss and decide on a light vs dark theme before going to far down the rabbit hole with colors, and color theory and analysis of the current state of such in FreeCAD.

An interesting albeit slightly biased analysis in favor of a dark theme:
https://www.venturus.org.br/en/darkmode-and-the-benefits-for-the-user-experience/

Multiple sources also indicate that dark UI trends dominate in preference polls with ranges between 85%-92%. That's actually a lot higher than I expected to see.

That being said, ui/ux aesthetics is a deep and nuanced subject.

I would sum up light vs dark as such:
Light Theme
Pros:
  -More professional looking. Industry software is 
  almost universally shipped with light default themes
  -Light themes tend to look better in brightly lit 
  environments compared to dark.

Cons:
  - Light themes are less versatile and cause eye strain 
   in low light settings. (ie. a home office in the evening)
  - Blue light from light themes can be disruptive to the 
   circadian rhythm when exposed at night.

Dark Theme
Pros:
  -Very trendy right now among users and UI/UX 
  designers
  -Reduces eye strain during long work sessions
  - More versatile in varied lighting conditions

Cons:
  - elegant but not necessarily 'professional' looking
  -Does not perform quite as well in will lit settings as light themes
  - may be more challenging to find a suitable color palette to meet FreeCAD's needs.

In terms of tools for designing around contrast, color and vision impairment a simple tool/test one can do is take your sample colors and load them into image editor of choice. Photoshop, gimp or Pixlr and then completely desaturate the image. If there is still a high contrast ratio then you are good. If not, further adjustment is necessary.

In the [Property editor](https://wiki.freecadweb.org/Property_editor) the step size for the Transparency is 1%. Apparently you never change the transparency of objects there, but my guess is that many users do. I rarely use the appearance dialog. Note that the step size there is 3% (not 5%).

So we have 1%, 3% and 10%. The 1% step size may not be a deliberate choice on the part of the programmers, but in general step sizes are small rather than big. See f.e. the https://wiki.freecadweb.org/PartDesign_Preferences#Shape_view preferences (step sizes 0.01% and 0.5°).

I think 10% is too big for the transparency. But for consistency whatever is decided should also be applied to the Property editor.

> In the [Property editor](https://wiki.freecadweb.org/Property_editor) the step size for the Transparency is 1%. Apparently you never change the transparency of objects there, but my guess is that many users do. I rarely use the appearance dialog. Note that the step size there is 3% (not 5%).

Yes, I use the appearance dialog all the time. However for me the step is 5 %, I will have to investigate why it is 3% for you.

The property editor is sadly treated stepmotherly . For example for TechDraw the step sizes were almost different everywhere from the dialogs. For the dialogs people took care and used reasonable values, for the property editor only the default, which is "1", independent of the unit. So the property editor must be adopted to follow the counterpart in the dialogs. (For TechDraw I hope I fixed all cases, if you see there a mistake, please tell me.)
For Part and PartDesign checking the spin buttons step consistency is since a while on my ToDo list.

> So we have 1%, 3% and 10%. The 1% step size may not be a deliberate choice on the part of the programmers, but in general step sizes are small rather than big. See f.e. the https://wiki.freecadweb.org/PartDesign_Preferences#Shape_view preferences (step sizes 0.01% and 0.5°).

The step size must depend on the use case. For the angular deflection 0.5° make a difference while for the transparency 0.5% is not visible by human eyes.

Here with the transparency I think we agree that a step of 1% is not sensible because this difference cannot be seen and using the buttons dozens of times to get the desired result, leads to the effect that the buttons won't be used at all - users will use the slider (if there is any) or input the number directly. But the main benefit of the buttons is that you save the time to leave the mouse, move your hands to the keyboard and type.
What I learned from the ergonomics point of view that clicking a button 5 times is quicker than input a value while clicking it 10 times can be as time consuming as inputting the value directly.
Therefore in this case the question is still for me if we should go with 5 or 10%.

I can only tell from my use case and this is to make objects in most cases half-transparent, sometimes a bit more, sometimes a bit less. So with 10% I have to click 5 times while with 5% I would have to click 10 times and then would probably choose to input "50" directly and not using the buttons. But I think the step size should be so that the usage of the button has a benefit.
However, my use case is maybe special, so I will not insist on the 10% but that it should be at least 5%.

What is your use case, what transparency levels do you need in practice?

Extending

A couple of problems.  This solution adds properties to the stock object.  However, it doesn't add them to existing stock objects when the document is restored.  So if any future functionality actually relies on reading those properties, it will fail for jobs created before this was implemented.  

I assume the intent is to easily get to the stock size so the machine operator can rough-cut material to load in the machine.  The existing functionality of PathSanity provides this information for exactly this reason but doesn't require us to add properties.  Can you please comment on the use-case you have in mind that isn't met already?  In other words, what is the 'problem' being solved by this change?

It's that there _is no function_ to add a binding to at all right now: even the C++ doesn't provide simple access to "what is the highest row used?" and "what is the highest column used?" So I'm proposing that we write the aforementioned four functions in C++ (which will be fast), and then write Python bindings to those (which will be easy). If they are going to be called a lot, we may need to be more clever than just a brute-force approach, though. Even the C++ will slow down on a large enough data set.

> What is the point of the nameless namespace ?

The traditional way is to use static functions because they are only visible within a translation unit.
See: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/15235526/the-static-keyword-and-its-various-uses-in-c

The modern way is to use anonymous namespaces where the compiler creates unique namespace names to avoid name clashes.

> Why using inventor API rather than the same at both places?

Actually, in all places when we have an SoEvent we use the methods this class provides and avoid to mix two APIs too much.

The next thing is that the signature of `mouseButtonPressed(int Button, bool pressed, const SbVec2s &cursorPos, const Gui::View3DInventorViewer *viewer)` is a design flaw which leads to the use of magic numbers (e.g. for Button) and it suppresses some extra information that might be needed here and there.
So, long story short: at some point this must be cleaned-up and an SoMouseEvent should be directly passed. Then one could consistently use the Inventor API in the implementations of the sub-classes.

It's not necessary for you to do anything else, I am happy to squash and merge on my end, but if you are interested in learning, the operation you want to do is an "interactive rebase" which you will use to "squash" the commits and then "force push" the resulting single commit, overwriting the original commits. On the command line, it goes like this (in the case of two commits being combined into one):
```
git rebase -i HEAD~2
```
This will pop up an editor window that lists your two commits, looking like this:
```
pick 3952f7393c Update SoFCOffscreenRenderer.cpp
pick 549398b340 Add default quality to JPG export 
```
There are some instructions in a comment section below, but what you want to do is change the second `pick` to `squash` (or just `s`):
```
pick 3952f7393c Update SoFCOffscreenRenderer.cpp
s 549398b340 Add default quality to JPG export 
```
Save the file and close it. Another editor will pop up offering to let you create a commit message for the new, combined commit. Set it to whatever you want (probably just the commit message you wrote for the first commit). Save and close. Finally, you have to overwrite the commits in your branch to just consist of the new commit:
```
git push -f
```
If you refresh the GitHub page for your PR, you'll see that there is now only the single commit.

To help support this effort I'd like to help rephrase this as a problem:

### Problem: Summary 
UI (particularly treeview) elements consume a large amount of screen space in efforts to support displaying large amounts of relevant information while modeling.

### Problem Description:
In many common workflows, including those adapted from similar software, being able to have the tree view always displayed is considered desirable. In FreeCAD's current implementation TreeView is embedded in the Combo Panel and is not always visible while modeling. When it is separated it creates another full panel which obscures additional horizontal screen area reducing functional access to the 3d view.

### Proposed Solution: 
Apply panel transparency changes from @realthunder, including stylesheet changes to allow separating treeview while maintaining increased visual space in the viewing area. Unlike the "Glass" addon, these changes also allow for 'click-through' of the transparent areas of a panel and allows for simpler visual customization of the tree view through stylesheets in support of preference pack creators for unified visual UI/UX integrity. Default panel configurations should not be changed.

Please read all and most of all excuse my English. 

Just to be all on the same page I thought I'd give some examples of the overlay while actively using it on a  small project. 
The most important thing to note here is that @realthunder 's implementation doesn't actually remove or modify the current state of the UI but instead just extends the functionality taking advantage of some QT capabilities. 

In fact, on start the interface is indistinguishable from FreeCAD master  the only difference being the highlighted icons in the image bellow. Note that I just didn't want to reset all my personalisation to default for the screenshots but this is just how master would look when using split tree and properties view 

![Screenshot_20221109_210637](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/26909793/200930872-c45993e5-b5c1-43e1-a490-f5fae28227c4.jpeg)

I think that the first image in  @PaddleStroke  post was not the best to showcase the improvements that the OverlayUI can bring to a workflow. And now that we talk about it, there are so many so called "workflows" and there are also entire books written about man/machine user/interface interaction so I'm sure we will not be able to invent anything new here. The best workflow or user interface disposition is the one that better suits individual user's needs. This is where the OverlayUI shines. In giving yet another option to the user at setting the UI based on it's own needs. And this is IMPORTANT to understand; I (the user) have diferent needs based even on screen size or aspect ratio. 

I , personally,  use a different disposition of the UI on my laptop than on my   ultra wide monitor. Why? Differences in cursor travel distance, font size related to my declining sight, difference in gaze shift etc etc ..... so different needs from even the same user. 

This is why I also think that the OverlayUI implementation from Realthunder would be a emprovement for FreeCAD's UI as it ads another layer of customization that could help users adapt the software to their own personal needs all while not modifying nothing that isn't already a default now in master. Note that the actual first and last cell

x x x x
x x x
x x x   <-- cell in max range is empty; it is in max range because it's row is max row)

The Python wrappers seems to cover what we need. Of course, I have no idea if the underlying C++ code is bug free or not. That is up to them.

Munther

- regarding the zoom out, I think it's because you zoom to a point that
dimensions where greater than 32bit long. At this point I think grid is not
going to be the only issue.

- for the zoom on object that is far from origin, this is indeed not ideal.
The problem is that we can't increase the grid overall dimensions linearly when you
draw something far away from origin (how current grid is doing) because
then if you zoom in a lot you would have billions of lines. So the only way
would be to draw lines only on the viewer area. But then you would have to
redraw the grid lines everytime you move around. Which may be acceptable
actually.

For that we would need to know the viewer position in coordinates : minx
miny, Maxx, Maxy. Not sure how to do that.

@PaddleStroke 

I did not check this case by case with actual code execution (it worked on my head following your comment). The code is not equivalent semantically.

In my code, if item->isSelected() == true && selected=false there is a single execution of setSelected(false). In this situation, in your code there are two executions of setSelected(false).

Aside for the call redundancy, the idea was to encapsulate the hack within a single block. This situation (and this situation alone), is the one triggering the 0.5 seconds delay we want to fix. This is what new code would need to avoid. The encapsulation attempts to convey this idea to a future developer reading the code.

The blocker was there to avoid emission of signals due to selection change, as in this PR selection is handled via item pressed. I am unsure if in practice anything is blocked at all, due to not slots currently being attached in our client code (I do not know if there is some additional blocking in QT itself).

@0penBrain 

I agree we need to be aware of suboptimal choices.

I am unsure what to do (and welcome feedback).

The minimum is a comment in the code. This we have.

@PaddleStroke 

I just shortly did a very quick read of the code. I see you have introduced a legacy "enum". 

In general, we should not be introducing legacy enums in the code anymore, but use enum class instead.

The reason is that enums get implicitly converted and does not offer a strong type comparison, which is error prone. A legacy enum can be thrown anywhere where an int is expected and it will compile. Conversely, if you use enum class, you will have strong type checks, and it will require an explicit static_cast to int if you ever need to use it as an int. The compiler will protect you from wrong usage. 

I have sometimes doubted whether to go "enum" or "enum class" when there is a strong need of conversions. Explicit conversions are more verbose. When there are many, code may become difficult to follow. Lately, I systematically opt for the enum class. Sometimes I create a member function with a clear name encapsulating the static_cast, so that resulting code is more readable.

For item #2,  The policy says nothing about that.  How would you judge whether a contribution will stand the test of time?  Discussion of implementation can be had in the PR prior to merge and as long as the contributor is willing to improve it, there's no problem.

### Problem Description:
In many common workflows, including those adapted from similar software, being able to have the tree view always displayed is considered desirable. In FreeCAD's current implementation TreeView is embedded in the Combo Panel and is not always visible while modeling. When it is separated it creates another full panel which obscures additional horizontal screen area reducing functional access to the 3d view. Glass addon is similar but inferior due to several related issues listed above. Largest issues with Glass add-on, it only affects tree view. It creates a transparent background over the the viewport which is visually appealing but does not support mouse through clicking in clear areas, lacks customization of tree item display through stylesheets, the way treeview items are currently constructed makes selected feature highlights take up the width of the panel rather than restricting the highlight to the text only.

As I have stated above, the paraemeters were changed several times, and changed back to the original. So naturally everytime the model was remeshed and rerun.  The problem is if you do something to the mode and changed back to the original state, FreeCAD can not give the original results. The can cause serious problems.

In meshing programs there are certainly radom seeds, especially for freee meshing. But the random number is usually psuedo, not really random. This is to ensure persistent results. So if Gmsh will produce different results every time even when the inputs are the same, then maybe we should notify the developer of Gmsh.

Another possibility is the inside parameter of CAD may be different. Either way, the discrepency is not permissible. In some industries, there are even regulations enforcing the consistency of results from FEA program. The bottom line is, an engineer program should produce the same result when then inputs are the same. Otherwise it will be considered as "unstable".

I really don't think this prblem can be ignored. In fact we have tried to use FreeCAD FEM for testing some design algorithms, and it produces different result everytime, even with the same input, on the same computer.

wanted to fix it.
- I struggle for a day to put it in VP sketch because of some weird
architecture (VP sketch inherit from the grid object, which makes a lot of
sense I'm sure...)
- Then I'm told this is a no go, and by saying that you imply that my code
is not acceptable. You even say that I'm disrespecting Abdullah who cleaned
the VP sketch.

 Before cleaning VP sketch, everyone was adding things directly to VP
sketch. So for years it was acceptable for everyone, including Abdullah, to
do what I have done. Yet now it's not.
I think you guys are asking me quality standards that you didn't met when
you started merging stuff in master. In other terms, you raised the bar.

And so you are forcing onto me this extra work that you yourselves haven't
done in your earlier days.

I willingly spend months working on freecad, which is probably not smart
but somehow I can't help myself, but at least I'd like to be able to draw
the line when I think it is not worth it.

Lastly, raising the bar and this quest for perfect architecture is imo bad
for the software. FC have limited workforce, and spending 90% of it on
making the code perfect is not the best. Especially when sketcher is still
lacking things like offset, or very simple things like copy paste or
dragging.

I have read somewhere criticism on freecad that said that the issue of FC
is that it's written by passionate devs who overdo the code to the
detriment of software capabilities/UI. And I think the grid is the perfect
example: perfect code architecture but bad user experience.

There should be a balance between getting things done, and done well for
the user, and making perfect maintainable code. And while I'm maybe too far
on one side, you are imo far to the other side and should sometime question
yourself if you're not overdoing it.
On my side I of course question when my code sucks and try to make it
better.

> You're talking about good code architecture/cleanliness but this is a subjective notion. I personally think that this is counter productive complexity. It's harder to understand and no gain.

There is one point to keep in mind: something like _perfect code_ doesn't exist. Insofar I agree that at some point it's a subjective matter. But that only applies at the very end of a code-refactoring process and for everything before there exist some objective metrics to measure this: cohesion (the internal dependency) and coupling (the external dependency).  The goal of the code-refactoring process is to increase cohesion and decrease coupling.

The gain of all this is that it makes the code more reusable, flexible and extendable.

On YT you can find a talk from Robert C. Martin about code quality which is split into 5 or 6 videos and I recommend to at least watch the first one.

> Now big question, how to connect from vpSketch onChanged or updateData or onCameraChange to the GridCoinManager function createGrid.

Yep, this the touchy thing.
So in `EditModeGridCoinManager`, you will have all your functions relating to grid drawing. There you can have as much functions as you want, so you can make your code easy to work with.
In `EditModeCoinManager`, you'll add as member variable a pointer to a unique instance of `EditModeGridCoinManager` with something like : `pEditModeGridCoinManager = std::make_unique<EditModeGridCoinManager>(...`
Then in `EditModeCoinManager` you have to add a minimal number of wrapping functions. For example a `drawGrid` function that will call `pEditModeGridCoinManager->createGrid()`
Finally in `VPSketch`, an EditModeCoinManager is already instantiated, so you call `editCoinManager->drawGrid()`

The function getTempFileName() is supposed to return the name of a tmp. file. Therefore it uses some OS-specific functions that already create a handle of a tmp. file and release it immediately (Windows: GetTempFileName / DeleteFile and other OS mkstemp / unlink) just to get this name.

The problem is that when trying to open the file for writing there is no guarantee that in the meantime any other process already has access on this file. The consequence may be that the access will be denied or even worse the file will be (partially) overridden.

The better way would be to return a class object (e.g. TemporaryFile) where its constructor creates the file and the destructor releases it.

3. Introduce grid management tool in toolbar [this is the big part, can be more commits but one is OK]

The unit tests have failed because they exceeded the max. of 5 hours. This happened because the command line version is used and thus no QApplication instance is created and no GUI thread is running.

So, in other words the trick with the local event loop doesn't work in CLI but only in the GUI version. To make this working you have to split the tests that can be run in CLI and that require a running GUI.

The best way to keep them separated is:
* create the file TestTechDrawGui.py
* from TestTechDrawApp.py move these lines to TestTechDrawGui.py:
```
from TDTest.DrawViewSectionTest import DrawViewSectionTest
from TDTest.DrawViewPartTest import DrawViewPartTest
from TDTest.DrawViewDetailTest import DrawViewDetailTest
```
* in InitGui.py add `FreeCAD.__unit_test__ += ["TestTechDrawGui"]`
