5. Pad the sketch to 150mm
6. Create a datum plane with reference to the XY-Plane and offset it by 55mm (r2 of the pipe)
7. Create a sketch on the datum plane
8. Add a circle on the Y axis, 50mm from the origin and 20mm in diameter
9. Add a pocket to the sketch, "up to first" to create a hole in the pipe
10. Add a polar pattern to the pocket, 45°
11. Create a new sketch on the YZ-Plane
12. Draw a rectangle, height is 5mm (wall thickness of the pipe (55mm-50mm)), width is the hole diameter (20mm), horizontal offset of the lower corner is 40mm (circle distance - diameter / 2), vertical offset is 50mm (pipe inner radius)
13. Create a grove on the rectangle, angle is 45° (polar pattern angle), reference axis is the Y axis
14. Observe broken geometry

The leading dot is to indicate that the identifier is referencing a local property of the owner object (each expression must be owned by the object whose setExpression() is called). Without this leading dot, a current working expression may be broken in the future when you add an object with the same name as the property.

For example, `Constraint.Length` could mean an attribute named `Length` of the current object's property `Constraint`. Or, it could mean The property `Length` of an object named `Constraint`.

The leading dot is not needed for the indexer access because there is no ambiguity here. `Constraint[1]` always means to reference a local property `Constraint`.

I changed the way the side faces are drawn. First it was drawn using `GL_QUADS`, which draws a shape with four corners for each set of four vertices that are consecutively called using `glVertex3f()`. The side faces no longer consist of four corners so I changed it to `GL_POLYGON`, which draws a shape from the passed vertices. These vertices are defined here: https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/104dc424e82739b0b95d828136d8152f864e27fe/src/Gui/NaviCube.cpp#L662-L674
and then consecutively passed to `glVertex3f()` here: https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/104dc424e82739b0b95d828136d8152f864e27fe/src/Gui/NaviCube.cpp#L1117-L1121

@adrianinsaval
First it is important to understand that there is a base coordinate system at the center of the navicube. All faces and borders are drawn using this base coordinate system.
![base](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14298143/204132454-f5cb31bf-c542-4081-99d0-b57d048fa24b.png)
The top face is not rotated relative to this base coordinate system. All other faces are rotated for example: the front face is rotated 90 degrees about x. So if you were looking straight at the faces you would see this:
![top_front](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14298143/204132717-2a819a96-30ff-4181-ac87-cd43ac99d5ad.png)
However, for drawing it would be easier if all faces have the x, y and z going into the same direction regardless of which face you are looking at. Or in other words, you want to draw in the coordinate system of the face. The coordinate system of all faces looks like this:
![face](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14298143/204133042-19525398-df8e-4c6b-9424-e24f8a3d7592.png)
But remember that the drawing happens in the base coordinate system. So we need a transformation to transform between the coordinate systems. This already happens before the `addFace` method is called. The `x` and `z` that are passed into `addFace` are telling you how the the face axes are aligned in the base coordinate system. So for example the front face +y is aligned with the base +z.

Now about these lines:
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/104dc424e82739b0b95d828136d8152f864e27fe/src/Gui/NaviCube.cpp#L662-L674

What we are doing here is passing the points that we need to draw the border of the side faces. The order is drawn in the figure below (purple numbers). What we are actually doing here is three translations starting from the center of the navicube. First we need to translate to the plane of the face. `z` is the direction and distance to the plane of the face therefore we always start with `z`. Now we can look at the figure below with `w` the width, `h` the height, `g` the gap, `x` the x vector and `y` the y vector. From the figure you can see that the length of the vectors is half the width or height. 

![drawing](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14298143/204137030-148d4a25-db40-4d35-9b2d-d6e7073911f2.png)

To get the point in the bottom left we would need to translate -x and -y in this 2d plane. We don't want the bottom left point but we want point 1 to 8. Lets take point 1 as an example. You can see that point 1 is not translated by -x but by -x + the gap size.
Of course we only want to add the gap size in the same direction as the vector x. To change the length of a vector without changing the direction, you can multiply the vector. We know the length of the vector, the amount to translate and that the gap size is a fraction of the width:
$||x|| = 0.5w$
$g = 0.12w$
$x_1 = -||x|| + g = -0.5w + 0.12w$

Which can be written as a multiplication:
$-0.5w + 0.12w = -0.5w(1 - 0.24)$

Starting to recognize something?
The -0.5w is the existing vector `x` length which is then multiplied by `(1 - gap * 2)`
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/104dc424e82739b0b95d828136d8152f864e27fe/src/Gui/NaviCube.cpp#L647

Doing the same for y:
$y_1 = -||y|| + 2g = -0.5h + 0.24h$
$-0.5h + 0.24h = -0.5h(1 - 0.48)$

https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/104dc424e82739b0b95d828136d8152f864e27fe/src/Gui/NaviCube.cpp#L664

Thus resulting in a translation of `(z - x * (1 - gap * 2) - y * (1 - gap * 4)`.

Thank you for reviewing this PR, but I can't see your suggestions offer any technical improvement.

Input is a NodeType. NodeType is an enum of 12 elements.
Output is a FilterAction. FilterAction is an enum of 3 elements. Only two are used.

The code specifies a result for some, but not all, of the possible inputs.
Not all possible enum cases are defined so a default is essential.

As a default is essential, and there are only two possible output values, the logic can be reduced to specifying only the _non-default_ items. That's just two NodeTypes.

if-then-else-if-else etc could be used but gets ugly pretty quick and either a) repeats the retrieval of the input, or b) requires an additional variable, and denies code checkers the ability to ensure all enum elements are covered.

if-else with booleans isn't much better.

A switch is the perfect structure here as the input is evaluated once and all logic is contained entirely within the one switch statement. Code checkers can warn if you miss cases. Cases can be easily added etc. Cases of like output are simply placed together (no break between) and fallthrough to the same code. Simple and concise.

The original has an additional return after the switch statement. All cases have a return so this return is unreachable code. Note also the redundant break statements in the original.

The alternative is add an intermediate output result variable but that is unnecessary complexity.

Currently we have a design flaw with the feature classes Revolution and Groove. The class interface of both of them is identical and the only difference in their implementations is that the former adds material and the latter removes it. The result is that we have two implementations where 90% of the code is identical.

I think that the two classes should be refactored by creating a common base class with the same class interface.

As consequence all the code duplication can be avoided and the dialog class could be greatly simplified too because it's not needed any more to check for two concrete types.

We once had the very same problem with Pad/Pocket where a common base class was created.

Description of the Work

The DocumentObject DrawAuxiliaryView inherits DrawViewPart, with some added properties:

- BaseView - the DrawViewPart that this DAV relates to
- AuxiliaryDirection  - projection direction relative to BaseView. Used to calculate the absolute projection direction and rotation.
- ReferenceLabel - the text that appears in both the BaseView and the DAV.

A new graphics object (ex. QGIViewAuxiliary) is not required as the painting of the view is the same as a regular view.

QGIViewPart will need to be modified to draw the reference Text and arrow on top of the BaseView.

A graphics object for the Reference and Arrow will probably be needed.

The existing ViewProvider for DVP can likely be used, but need to confirm that changes to AuxiliaryDirection and ReferenceLabel can be detected in ViewProviderViewPart. If necessary, a light weight view provider can be derived as is done for sections.

A new command will need to be added to TechDraw/Gui/Command.cpp and TechDraw/Gui/Workbench.cpp.

A new task dialog will be needed to set direction (see TechDraw/Gui/TaskSectionView.cpp).

A new wiki page will be needed.

I’m currently struggling this now and can see valid reasons to model / not model. The former provides a quick visual reference check while giving the model a polished finished look. The later OTOH, could speed up the modeling process if it were to also update the model with the user defined countersink/counterbore specs In a dialog much like the thread tap in the drilling op. Thus achieving the polished, finished look of the former. 

Countersinks have a couple popular included angles depending on which screw spec is being used. The dialog should, much like typical mechanical drawings, request the depth and major diameter of the countersink including the angle. 

For CBore there are standards established for the size of SHCS and their corresponding hole dimensions. The dialog for it could simply ask for the screw size and model the specs for depth and diameter. If the cbore is not  a bolt head hole then it should allow for custom user defined dimensions for depth / diameter.

The answer to this could be as simple as “either can work”. Question: Should comments better be here or on the linked forum thread?
I'll put here few thoughs. 

First thought: there is no much expedience to speak about theme(s) before most elements are theme-able.
At first glance currently:
1. There is no any differentiation of line thickness and styles in Sketcher (thin, dotted, dashed, dash-dotted are needed). Probably similar issue for other WBs.
Custom line thickness/styles is crucial for improving UX, actually sometimes even more important 
than colors. Additional vertex styles should be available too.
(shoul it be a separate feature request?)

2. Some colors are hard-coded as well: Axes colors, selected item hover color.

Many other elements I guess too, just named what I noticed and wanted to tune first when I started 
to work. So regardless of light or dark choice, not much can be done with those.

Background : I prefer textured background to reduce eye strain. (another feature request I guess).
Otherwise solid color or slight radial gradient. 

My view on light/dark choice:
Light:
- I beleive it should be the choice for normally lit environment since it is physiologically predefined (dark 
objects and features on light background is how information is read by daylight creatures in general).
- It is de-facto standard for most systems in general.  

Dark:
- Looks kinda cool for some people.

The change basically is to produce a smart pointer. This smart pointer holds the responsibility to release the dynamic memory when it goes out of scope. When no exception happens, this smart pointer gets copy-elided to the caller of the lambda (effectively as if it were moved). When the exception happens, the stack must be unwound. This means that all local variables go out of scope, which means that the destructor of the smart pointer is called, and the memory released.

> If the case that I was thinking (user wants to wrap around but somehow we have `0 < v - u < confusion`) does arise, we can do the wrapping before generating the python code.

Exactly. This is what I was referring to when I was saying that the split tool (the UI part in your example) is responsible for translating the intention to the user when using the split tool into the trimming commands necessary for executing it.

> In my opinion that is the correct behavior, though an exception with a better explanation may be possible. The parameter itself is not known until within the `SketchObject::split()` method (only the coordinates of the point are passed). So any check will have to be done there. Further, The user will have to intentionally run this through console since it is impossible to pass the end point by pre-selection when in GUI.

About the message: 
Now the CADKernelError exception goes all the way to core, because it is not handled in SketchObject::split. The message is then not so meaningful. What you may do, is to catch CADKernelError exceptions in split(), report the underlying exception to console (to keep track of where the whole issue is originating), and then either provide your own meaningful message to console and tidy up or throw another exception with a more meaningful message (which will appear as the one you see, but with a better message).

About the behaviour:

The split command uses the addGeometry method at different times during the execution. Geometry property is changed on each call. This contrasts with other methods of SketchObject, where all the changes to the geometry property are done on a std::vector array and at the end the changes to the property are submitted. The first approach is more flexible. The second more efficient. Notwithstanding, the first introduces intermediate changes to the Geometry property. This means that, if the function is exited by exception after the Geometry property was changed, the execution of the command does not offer a transactional guarantee (i.e. that the operation will be executed in full, or not executed at all). I mean that the SketchObject split() function does not guarantee this. The UI function that calls the Python code does open a command and if an exception reaches it, rolls back any change (aborts the command). So, you will only see what I mean from Python: 

```
ActiveSketch.addGeometry(Part.BSplineCurve([App.Vector(-50,60),App.Vector(-60,70),App.Vector(-70,80),App.Vector(-80,90),App.Vector(-90,100)],None,None,False,3,None,False),False)
 
ActiveSketch.solve()

ActiveSketch.addGeometry(Part.ArcOfCircle(Part.Circle(App.Vector(-34.880920,77.786903,0),App.Vector(0,0,1),16.017876),1.635223,2.547379),False)
 
ActiveSketch.split(0,App.Vector(-89.9999999999999999999999999,99.9999999999999999999999999,0))
```

If you execute the code above, which will fail and exit with an exception, you will see that you end up with the original B-Spline and another B-Spline. Both essentially the same. This is because the one trim operation that failed is the second "part". If the split position trims first the exception-throwing curve, then nothing will be added. The arc is there in the code just to make more clear which B-Spline objects are newly added to the end of the list.

Generally the split() function works well and we are talking here just about corner cases.

What could be done differently in these corner cases? Well, when splitting a non-periodic, it should be possible to check at Python level that the two curves can be produced (at least a confusion check), if one cannot be produced, then the function may produce an error message to the console and return failure. In this case, no matter which point is selected, the outcome is consistent, even when the split function is asked to do something that it cannot do. In this case the original object would remain, which is basically what the user wants if one of the curves that need to be split is so small that cannot be handled by OCC.

Thanks for the feature request.  A couple of thoughts about this off the top of my head:

A user would create a tap tool using the toolbit system.  We don't have a standard tap tool shape but the toolbit system will support everything needed to create one.  This is pretty simple and is a good milestone task.

Spindle speed is declared in the tool controller so nothing should be needed there.  Calculating the feed rate is also an independent unit of work from the tapping operation. I would consider it out of scope for this feature.

The R plane and O plane should be derived from the safe height and clearance height properties common to all operations.  Some logic to derive it may be necessary but we should not need to add any properties to the operation.

That means most of what's required is already done.   A tapping operation should work on essentially the same kind of geometry as a drilling operation.  So we can copy src/Mod/Path/Path/Op/Drilling.py and use it as the starting point.  

The real logic, and it isn't very complicated, will be in a new rigid tapping generator.  I would start by copying /src/Mod/Path/Path/Base/Generator/drill.py.   The generator is actually quite simple.  The main part is a single pure function that takes everything needed to produce a single tapping cycle.  (Ignore feed rates for now).   The most important part is the edge.  This is where the tap will go.  One end of the edge is the start point and the other is the endpoint.  

The generator is very thoroughly tested.  In the case of drilling, the tests are in /src/Mod/Path/PathTests/TestPathDrillGenerator.py   Again, we can begin by copying that file as a starting point.  Writing the test cases first would be incredibly helpful.  To see how it works, you can do this at the command line:

`./bin/FreeCADCmd -t TestPathApp.TestPathDrillGenerator`

 So here's a work plan:

1.  copy the drillgenerator tests and adapt them to test a hypothetical tap generator.  Tests will fail.
2. Write the tapgenerator to make the tests pass.
3. Once the generator works, copy the Drill.py operation to RigidTap.py and adapt it to drive the generator.
4. Copy /src/Mod/Path/Path/Op/Gui/Drilling.py and adapt it as RigidTapping.py. If an icon is needed, do it now.
5. Tweak the cmake files to make all the new stuff install where it needs to be.

Yeah sure.
A Turntable is used to keep the world's Z axis collinear with the screen's Y axis.
The already existing Turntable orbit mode is only rotating on the X or Z axis depending on how you moved your mouse/controller.
```
SbVec3f dif = point1 - point2;
if (fabs(dif[1]) > fabs(dif[0])) {
[...] //rotate around the Z axis
} else {
[...] //rotate around the X axis
}
```
This is useful to create rotating animations of your object as you are sure to make a perfect circle around it.
Using it to work on an object is frustrating because if you move your mouse diagonally only one axis will be transformed.

The FreeTurntable that I added does not select an axis before applying transformations, both mouse's X and Y movements are taken into account. The goal is to replicate Blender's orbit style.

So the difference to the Trackball is the need for the world's Z axis to stay aligned with the screen's Y axis.
The FreeTurntable has a slight drift and it looses the alignment after some transformations but I couldn't do better.
But after using it for about a month almost everyday, it is not that annoying because each time we get perpendicular to a face, it realigns the Z axis.

For example,
Here, I started from the same face each time, and I rotated the object by moving my mouse diagonally for the same distance for both.

With the Trackball orbit style we can see that the Z axis is not aligned with the screen's Y axis:
![2022-12-19-07_23_42](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9805355/208361361-08af128e-8321-4c3c-8e17-e57858ae3bae.png)

And with the FreeTurntable orbit style, it still is:
![2022-12-19-07_24_06](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9805355/208361454-0b299506-495e-473e-a93c-84b52d1c5ee9.png)

That's because the Trackball takes the direct transformation between the last and current mouse position whereas for the FreeTurntable the transformation is divided into two movements: around the object and up/down movement both being relative to the screen's referential.

We generally try to build our operations to support LinuxCNC as a reference implementation.  Whenever possible, we push the quirks of gcode dialect into the postprocessors. Looking closer at the [LinuxCNC gcode reference](http://linuxcnc.org/docs/html/gcode/g-code.html). 

I see three related gcodes that we should probably support. 
G33.1 is Rigid tapping.
G74 Left hand tapping with a floating chuck
G84 Right hand tapping with a floating chuck.

I think all three of these can probably be addressed in the same generator.

See especially the warning in G33.1 about the coordinate position.  This is something the generator can check for and throw an error.  For example, the edge has different XY coordinates between the start and end points.   This shouldn't happen in practice and will be caught upstream as well but the generator can check and error if it gets through.

G74/G84 looks pretty simple.  The only difference is the righthand/left hand which controls spindle direction.  There are two ways to handle this.  The operation could have a right/left enumeration property.  The better way is for the tapping tool to have that property. 

The operation will need a dwell time property

G33.1 rigid tapping is different
it has two additional words
K - distance per revolution.  The generator should be able to derive this from the feed and speed.

I - optional spindle speed multiplier for faster return move.  To support this, we would need another property in the operation.  I'm inclined to NOT support this in the first version and wait for someone to complain.

At this point, I see the tapping tool being similar to a drill but also having a pitch, and handedness property.  Taps also have properties like whether they are bottoming.  Let's not add that now.

MeshFlatteningBoostPython.cpp is only built if the option BUILD_FLAT_MESH is set and FREECAD_USE_PYBIND11 is off. In this case there is a check for the boost python package while now boost python headers are always included even if not needed and more important without searching for the corresponding package.

Rigid Tapping G33.1 requires three specific hardware capabilities in the CNC:

- DC Spindle drive with encoder
- Spindle encoder Control board 
- Rigid Tapping Option in the controller (CNC has to support it)

G74/G84 cycles require a floating tap holder and manual feed/speed callout.

CNC controls that support these canned cycles handle the spindle direction by virtue of the call itself. They understand the need to dwell (optional) at the bottom of the tapping cycle, reverse spindle rotation until arriving at R height, then reverse rotation back to normal. The Dwell time is optional and is a needed input along with the G call and movements. 

I now have a working test solution for G84. It's very basic, no feed or speed calculations, just the ability to create a tapping operation on a series of holes with the ability to supply a dwell time. I removed the peck and chip breaker references as they do not apply. Path doesn't need to do anything much here, just spit out the G codes and dwell along with the movements. The Control handles the spindle requirements as mentioned. 

Including both G74/G84. I envision a user selectable drop down box with either option listed and output the code requested code. A better option would be to grab the user input and set the spindle rotation of the selected tapping tool by updating the tool controller direction. Would think this could also be done for feed rate and spindle speed? It's left up to the user to decide proper speed/feed rates to properly execute the tapping sequence based on thread pitch/spindle speed. 

G33.1 Rigid Tapping seems much more involved to me. Different command parameters have to be coded along with the required movements.

I found a fix to this issue that should be added to the export functions for models, if you export them individually at least..

Add the following line to model exports

__obj__[|index_var|].Placement.Base = FreeCAD.Vector(0, 0, 0)

Models are exported relative to world origin, not relative to their origin. So by setting the exported __obj__'s vector position to world origin, the model is exported relative to both.

I have a macro version of the export for .dae. I made it only export one model at a time. Export a model with the python console open in your preferred file format, see how it exports it, and add the above line to your __obj__[i]] gets exported at:

```
    def export_self_as_dae(model, model_folder, name):
        """
        export self as a .dae model
        """
        dae_folder = "%s%s.dae" % (model_folder, name)
        #documentation of importDAE
        # https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/d35400aae339d71d5fc8c7f767e3be17687fae90/src/Mod/Arch/importDAE.py
        try:
            import importDAE
        except:
            print("WARNING: collada likely not installed, attempting fix using freecad.pip util that comes with snap install assuming user installed FreeCAD via snap(where error normally occurs)")
            os.system("freecad.pip install pycollada")
            import importDAE

        __obj__ = model

        #Set the object's placement to be at world origin since models are not exported relative to their origin, but to world origin.
        #by setting the object's position to world origin, the model will be exported relative to it's origin.
        __obj__.Placement.Base = FreeCAD.Vector(0, 0, 0)

        importDAE.export(__obj__, model_folder)
```

I wanted to have a conversation with @wwmayer about it, but suddenly I was not available and then I forgot. This can be a good occasion to ask him about the limitations in place and the underlying reasons.

Python itself is written in C and doesn't have an exception handling like in C++. And since we do not know what happens inside the C code before and after it has invoked our callback function we cannot be sure that everything is in a consistent state when somewhere a C++ exception is raised and not handled by the callback function.

At least for older MinGW builds the application crashed in such scenarios.

So, the safe way is to convert a C++ exception into a Python exception in the callback function and then the calling instance (C++) that has invoked the function of the C Python API (in most cases) can check the returned value whether it's null or not.

Both ways are fine. When using PyErr_SetString you have to make sure to immediately return from the function with `return nullptr`. Using a PyCXX exception (or a sub-class of Base::Exception) does it do automatically for you.

My recollection is that all conics (circles, ellipses, parábolas and
hyperbolas) can be defined as the set of points the ratio of whose
distances from a line (I believe that is called the directrix) and a point
is some constant. For a parabola, that ratio is one. The ellipses and
hyperbolas correspond to the ratio less than one and greater than one,
respectively, or may be vice versa, I don't remember).  I think the case of
the point being on the line itself corresponds to a line perpendicular to
the directrix, because that gives the distance to the point equal to the
distance to the line, hence a constant ratio ( the case of a plane passing
through the vertex of the cone). So upshot is I believe the desired
"parabola" in that case is a line perpendicular to the given line.

I would prefer not to use 'View' mainly because in TechDraw we have drawing views. And the texts in annotations are not aligned with TD views.

'Camera' and 'Screen' can both work IMO. My main reason for choosing 'Screen' is that this is also used for the yellow labels:
`obj = App.ActiveDocument.addObject("App::Annotation", "Label")`
If 'Camera' is chosen here then the yellow labels should perhaps be updated to match?

Note that the Render workbench has camera objects.

Changing 'Screen' to 'Camera' would not be a problem.

Regarding your 2nd remark:

Objects from older files are of course converted. But once converted, files cannot be opened in older FreeCAD versions without issues. For example a Draft_Label in a converted file will not show its text when opened in an older FreeCAD version. I see no way to solve this.

We have had the same situation with sketches after an update. So what is happening here is not uncommon. If necessary a macro could be created to revert the changes made.

Since a curve is always a numerical approximation, with this method, the Helix calculation algorithm can return a geometric point for the helix outside the existing part. Once you did a recompute you can then inspect the resulting cells, edges and vertices of each voronoi diagram. There is one for each face, so there's an extra voronoi diagram for the dot of the 'i'.

Displaying all primary edges I did with this function:
```python
def vd_show(vd):
    for i, l in enumerate("KiItchen"):
       for j, e in enumerate([s for s in vd[i].Edges if s.Color == 0]):
           Part.show(e.toShape(), f"{l}{j}")
```

This'll run for a while - it's not very efficient. The `Color` values are defined in `Vcarve.py` in case you want to look at edges that have already been discarded (colored). There is a post processing stage after this which filters out all edges that are deemed to be "artifacts of linear approximation" for the op. So don't worry if it gets noisy. The main thing is that the edges that _should_ come out for the operation are there in the first place.

First of all, I can only confirm this.

The issue seems related to the code used in the `execute` function of the Wire object class. This function is triggered by a recompute inside the move transaction. This somehow 'breaks' undo-redo. There are two potential solutions:
1. Remove/fix the problem code in the `execute` function.
2. Do not recompute inside the transaction, but do so after the transaction has been committed.

See test codes below. The only difference between the two is the position of `doc.recompute()`.

Test code "undo_problem":
```
import FreeCAD as App
import Draft

doc = App.ActiveDocument

p1 = App.Vector(0, 0, 0)
p2 = App.Vector(10, 10, 0)
line = Draft.make_line(p1, p2)
doc.recompute()

delta = App.Vector(20, 0, 0)

doc.openTransaction("undo_problem")
Draft.move(line, delta, copy=False)
doc.recompute()
doc.commitTransaction()
```

Test code "undo_ok":
```
import FreeCAD as App
import Draft

doc = App.ActiveDocument

p1 = App.Vector(0, 0, 0)
p2 = App.Vector(10, 10, 0)
line = Draft.make_line(p1, p2)
doc.recompute()

delta = App.Vector(20, 0, 0)

doc.openTransaction("undo_ok")
Draft.move(line, delta, copy=False)
doc.commitTransaction()
doc.recompute()
```

As already mentioned, the code in ArchPrecast.py can create several objects. For all objects the handling of faulty values is currently:
1. When the object is created it does not receive a shape.
2. If the object already exists its current shape is kept. Which is confusing IMO.

Changing this behavior for Prefab Slabs only would not be consistent.

For a slab the current checks are:
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/780d8416e24d5d2ada1c9a9521171515489c820f/src/Mod/Arch/ArchPrecast.py#L560-L570

My proposal is to change this to (I have removed the unnecessary brackets):
```
        import Part

        if length == 0 or width == 0 or height == 0 or base == 0:
            obj.Shape = Part.Shape() # Null shape.
            return
        if width <= 2 * slant:
            obj.Shape = Part.Shape()
            return
        if height <= base:
            obj.Shape = Part.Shape()
            return
        if holenumber > 0 and (holespacing == 0 or holemajor == 0 or holeminor == 0):
            obj.Shape = Part.Shape()
            return
        if holemajor < holeminor:
            obj.Shape = Part.Shape()
            return
```
In this proposal a check for the value of SlabBase (base) is included. And in case of faulty values the result is always a null shape. `obj.Shape = Part.Shape()` would then also have to be included in the checks of other precast objects.

In case my suggestions to the modifications to Voronoi.cpp were not clear from the diff I quoted, may I state them here in words: getting an angle from $\rm{atan}(y/x)$ in angleOfSegment() may give the wrong angle, since, for example, $y=-1, x=1$, will give an angle that is the same as $y=1, x=-1$, however the correct angle for the first segment is -45 deg, while for the second it should be 135 deg, definitely not the same angle, eventhough the tangent  $(y/x)$ is the same for both. The function $\rm{atan2}(y,x)$ gives the correct result for both cases, as well as for the case $x=0$, so the extra tests for $x==0$ are not needed. May be for the colinearity test, for which angleOfSegment is being called, the ultimate outcome might not matter, but certainly one would not want for a navigation app, for example, to tell one to head 45 degrees south of east, whereas it should be telling one to head 45 degrees west of north (exaclty the opposite direction!) (Note that for some libraries the first argument to the atan2 is the x and the second the y, so one should actually check!)

Another suggestion: calculating how close in direction two segments are by taking the difference between their angles relative to some direction (as is done in colorColinear() is tricky; for example segments with angles 1 deg and 359 degrees are quite close to each other, but the difference is large; subtracting a PI from the difference does not solve the problem. The safe way is to take the dot product of unit vectors along the two segments (cos(thet) = u_1.dot( u_2) and comparing to the cosine of some threshold angle.
I apologize for sounding pedantic about this; I am sure you are aware of these points. The code dealing  with angles in Voronoi.cpp, though, is not quite correct.

I have found out where Vcarve.py seemed to be going into an infinite loop and have found a solution for it.
First try to carve the letter "H" in the attached file. Note the size is 10 mm. There is no infinite loop if the size is 4 mm.
[H_2003_10mm.zip](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/files/10339164/H_2003_10mm.zip)

With the 10 mm letter one of the edges sent to _getPartEdge(edge, depths)  was returning nan for edge.getDistances(). So I modified the code in Vcarve.py to

``` python
def _getPartEdge(edge, depths):
    dist = edge.getDistances()
    if math.isnan(dist[0]) or math.isnan(dist[1]):
        return None
    zBegin = _calculate_depth(dist[0], depths)
    zEnd = _calculate_depth(dist[1], depths)
    return edge.toShape(zBegin, zEnd)
```
and in the calling method _getPartEdges to
``` python
    def _getPartEdges(self, obj, vWire, geom):
        edges = []
        for e in vWire:
            partEdge = _getPartEdge(e, geom)
            if partEdge is not None:
                edges.append(partEdge)
        return edges
```
As to why edge.getDistances() is reutrning nan, I don't know. I am guessing the coloring algorithms in Voronoi.cpp might be passing an edge the is is_inifinte, but I have not checked that.

Note that I used the Voronoi.cpp version with the round() fix and my calculations of angles that I posted before.

> To get App AND Base working I had to link to FreeCADApp instead of FreeCADBase. Huh?

If you use classes from FreeCADApp, then you only have to FreeCADApp explicitly. CMake implicitly adds FreeCADBase because FreeCADApp depends on it.

> I have fmt installed (https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/pull/8077) into App, Gui and Base (might be hacky?).

The proper place is src/3rdParty. fmt allows it to be used as header-only library or to build a shared library of it. If other targets use fmt then nothing must be done if used as header-only, otherwise the shared library name must be added to the linker.

> I am finding it necessary to link fmt::fmt to tests, even though already linked to App etc. Seems strange.

Sometimes the handling of 3rd party libraries can be very confusing. On some systems it suffices to add it only once but on other system you have to add it to each target where you use it.

Do you install for the current user only (this is the default) or for all users? When starting FC from the installer, FC is of course executed from the user that executed the installer.

> It’s for catching a bad configuration and reporting a valueError in the Report View window. It doesn’t prevent the user from proceeding, just warns them of a mismatch.

Hm.  I like the idea of catching the misconfiguration but I'm not sure it belongs in the tapping generator to do it. There's at least three places it might make more sense.   

First would be the operation itself.  The op knows what TC is selected and it is where most of the op-specific logic lives. 

I suppose someone could make the argument that it belongs in the TC itself. After all, the TC checks if the tool should allow power.
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/master/src/Mod/Path/Path/Tool/Controller.py#L269-L276

The toolchange generator actually acts on that test.  expanding it to test for 'handedness' is possible but it seems like we're going down a slippery slope.  
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/master/src/Mod/Path/Path/Base/Generator/toolchange.py#L47-L63

I would suggest that it's the operation's job to check if the tool is appropriate to the task and throw an error if it isn't. It should never call the generator with an inappropriate set of arguments.

It's not that they don't work in general, it's that they are broken in various places throughout our codebase, and Qt no longer provides diagnostics. See @wwmayer's post here: https://forum.freecadweb.org/viewtopic.php?p=650866#p650866

As already indicated by Gene in the forum discussion, whatever happens here is data driven. > > The issue seems to be with the voronoi diagram construction. For a regular letter of the sample the `finite` `primary` edges of the constructed diagram look like this for `c`: and like this for the letter `e`: For the letter `h` I get this however: All of those edges get discarded afterwards in cleaning up the diagram - they are presumed to be `exterior` edges, which are either `infinite` or linked to an `infinite` edge. > > At this point I suspect that either I intruduced some memory corruption in the binding or the voronoi algorithm itself runs into some instability. I have conducted many tests on this issue to try to understand the cause of the error and the behavior for cases of a point on the same line as a segment. (1) If a point is on the same line as a segment (but ouside the segment), the vornoi algorithm produces the correct edge ( a line midway between the segment and the end closest to the input segment; not a parabola). (2) If a point is on the segment itself, the vornoi algorithm produces a line with one end a nan and the other and infinite. Mathematically, the "parabola" in that case should become a two lines perpendicular to the segment, on both sides of the segment. There is no limit to these lines. However, none of the letters tested pose this problem. I suspect, as @mlampert indicates above, the problem is with the vornoi algorithm (from the boost library) and not from anything done on the FreeCAD side. The following images show the vornoi segments, with and without rounding the input coordinates: With rounding: ![II_with_rounding](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/95139464/211874344-6ca250ef-b97b-4936-89e4-2c0fc5332763.png) Without rounding (the current FreeCAD code): ![II_without_rounding_annotated](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/95139464/211877217-c778305f-4fbb-4420-ba19-d559a3e27993.png) Note that without rounding the vornoi algorithm is producing edges that cross each other, without them sharing a common vertex. That should never happen. I believe these edges are produced by the vornoi algorithm itself and not by the post processing done in VornoiEdgePyImp.cpp. I am currently trying to compile boost1.81.0 and build FreeCAD with it to see if the problem is there too. If it is, I believe this is something that should be brought to the attention of the boost vornoi developers.

I have built my own Visualizer based on what's in Vcarv.py; I will take a look at your input files. The issue, though, is not that the inputs are slighly different for the two I's - that is expected. The issue is that Vornoi diagram for the second I is producing a voronoi diagram that violates the definition of a Voronoi diagram. The voronoi diagram is supposed to be made of distinct non-overlapping cells. The cells are supposed to share edges and vertices, not areas. That is, the edges of a cell can meet at a common vertex, but are not supposed to cross. But the edges for second "I" clearly cross where I indicated.
Afterthought: of course, the above assumes that the input is made up of segments and points that do not cross. Are you saying that after the scaling some segments overlap? I will check later.

We are probably very close to finding the source of the bug. Inspecting your files you will notice that the last segment is 0 length in one, and only 1 pixel in length for the other. If you examine the number of edges in the input string (or Vcarve model), you will find that it is 17, not 22. The extra edges come because several of the edges in the "I" are B-splines, and on Discretization produce  a few more segments and one (or may be more) have zero length. I thought
these zero-length segments are what is causing the error, but I modified Vcarve.py to remove zero-length segments and the "bug" (second I not producing proper PRIMARY edges) stayed.

_**HOWEVER**_, when I used int() in addSegments I noticed that segments for the second "I" do not close:


__(-24870, 6130)__, (-22796, 6155)  <- first segment

(-23948, 6769), __(-24869, 6130)__  <- last segment

For the first "I" the segments are closed. With round() of segment ends one gets for the second "I"

__(-24870, 6130)__, (-22797, 6155),  <- first segment

(-23948, 6769), __(-24870, 6130)__,   <- last segment,

So, with the round() the segments close. It is not clear that round() will always do this. A better solution is to make sure the segments close (on an integer grid) in Vcarve.py. You would not want to force segments to be closed in Voronoi.cpp, because that could be used to do a voronoi construction that has nothing to do with carving, and closing is not required (that's how I did most of my tests). In Vcarve the segments are created end-to-end, so it seems one should never an open curve, unless the high() and low() functions produce different results for the same point.

Briefly for now, might have time later to check the actual code:

All dark themes exhibit this issue currently. The text color is not defined via stylesheets or preference packs, and is instead chosen via the bar at the top. 

The DEFAULT color is black for all stylesheets, but can be changed individually. Additionally, only the default cell color is themed by the stylesheet, but can be overridden with the bar at the top as well.

The problem we would face, implementing these in PreferencePacks is, what to do when the stylesheet changes on a finished table? What do we do with all the colors set manually by the user?

Potential solutions include:
- Have the default font be "Automatic" and have it switch between a dark and light color depending on the actual cell color background (Like Microsoft Office) but not care about the chosen theme
- Have the default font be enforced by the PreferencePack. Overriding the color manually would make the chosen color stick forever, but without choosing anything, the PreferencePack would provide its color on pack change.
- Have the table be light in any theme (Not preferred, for obvious reasons)

I would like to see the second one implemented, but that would mean updating the code to read a new value from the preference pack, and have that value set for all preference packs. 
Solution one would be easier and faster to implement, but the color won't neccessarily match the theme fully.

---

It should be impossible to create a tapping operation with a drillbit TC or an endmill TC.  The tapping operation should check to see if you're using a tap tool.   That alone is probably enough for now.

I'm not an expert on tapping but it seems like there are exactly two criteria that the user cares about.  Two things that make a tap a 'tap';  The diameter and the thread pitch.  Yes, there are others like shank, flutes, etc. but these are the two critical ones.

**Thread Pitch**
The thread pitch should absolutely be included.  This attribute needs to be defined in freecad units and represented in user units so that the display follows the unit schema.  Take a look at how the other attributes work.  
I can imagine that In the future,  someone might want to improve the tap toolshape so that it renders accurate 'threads' in the solid model.  They would need the thread pitch to do it.

Moreover,  the thread pitch can be compared to the feed rate and spindle speed for a sanity check on rigid tapping. 

**Diameter**
I guess this is the major diameter?  1/4"  for a 1/4x20 tap or a 6mm for an M6x1.  This should be (and is) the diameter attribute in the sketch.

Looking forward (No need to act on any of this.  Let's get a first cut of the tapping operation done and merged.  But this is stuff to  think about):

The thing we don't know and can't predict is how the users will prefer to model tapped holes.  
Most will just add a cylindrical hole feature to the solid.  The tapping operation should work with this.  However, What if the selected hole is too small?  What if it's too big?  What if the model contains hundreds of holes of different sizes?  It seems like the tapping operation might need to get smarter about auto-selecting its targets.

On the other hand, some users will use the "hole feature" in part design.  This will let them specify the thread pitch, counterbore, diameter, profile, etc etc etc.  It will render accurate threads if the user wants to see them. 

The first iteration of the tapping op won't don't do anything with this information but it's an area for future improvement.  If there's more information available, the tapping operation can do more with it.  It could, for example, automatically select any M6 holes holes (and only threaded holes) if you select an M6 tap.

For empirical threads, threads per inch (TPI) is a key detail. One does not
consider thread pitch when selecting an empirical tap, it’s diameter and
TPI (eg. 1/4-20). Pitch can be easily determined however by dividing TPI by
1. A 1/4-20 tap has a pitch of .050”. That is one revolution of the tap
moves up or down .050”.

Metric threads do not use TPI, only pitch. An M6-1 tap refers to diameter
and the pitch (1). In this case one revolution of the tap moves up or down
1mm.

I can see the need to add both pitch and TPI attributes. Pitch for metric
and TPI for empirical.

App.ActiveDocument.Sketch009.Shape.getTolerance(1)

First things first, thanks for providing the Python code to make it reproducible.

The bug report is licit. The underlying problem is known. But I save the ticket as means to reproduce it.

The issue arises because the gradient of a constraint becomes zero in a specific position, so the constraint is detected as redundant. However, when activated the second time, it does not converge to exactly that specific position, and the gradient is very small, but not zero. Therefore it is not detected as redundant.

No "buts" there. Yes, it is a bug. But some "Howevers" :).

However, as @PLChris would say, that sketch does not comply with good sketching practice. One basic rule is that geometric constraints (the ones not having an associated value) should be preferred to dimensional ones (the one having an associated value, i.e. the magnitude).

So this:
![imagen](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5249162/212925026-564e248e-dd71-4358-b51f-ed5c0b188d9e.png)

Should rather be something like this:
![imagen](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5249162/212925791-a6badbb8-6b68-4c91-85e6-4728168a574f.png)

There are many different alternative (good) ways of constraining. The one making the sketch usually understands better what needs to be dimensioned, as he or she knows best what needs to be achieved. For example the lines defining the sector could also had been made just "equal".

Following these rules, issues like the one described are less likely to appear.

> * since I cannot test this right now, have you tested that files created with FreeCAD 0.20 will work fine (no warnings) also with your changes?

Yes, as stated in he PR's description. I also added unit tests for this scenario to backup my claim and avoid future regressions. Since the InvoluteGear has not seen any changes lately, I guess using only v0.20.1 as reference is enough, though.

> * please use generic file names without referencing a FreeCAD version

Why? Those files are explicitly from v0.20.1, to ensure compat with that very version. If I add new features after we have released a, lets say 1.0, and I add new features for a potential 1.1, I will add additional fixtures generated with 1.0 which will then have "v1-0-0" in their name. And once we decide that backward compat with v0.20 is not needed any more, we can remove the "v0-20-1" files.

> * please add tooltips to the UI file

Will do, but on a dedicated PR, together with translatability and single-source for property docs and task panel tool tips. As there are no tool tips for all the previous fields as well, I decided to group my PRs that way.
Is that OK for you?

> * can you please merge your different commits to one

Here I oppose. I have carefully crafted my commits to address one specific concern each. I explicitly did not mix refactors/cleanups with functional changes. And I stated the motivation behind each change in the respective commit messages.  
I see a benefit of *not squashing everything together*. Not only to ease your review, but also to enable sensible bisection in case of regressions or make efficient use of git's history (e.g. via blame/annotate) in the future.
To not repeat what others have already put together very nicely, please see [this excellent article by Chris Beams](https://cbea.ms/git-commit/) with which I couldn't agree more.

> I see a benefit of not squashing everything together.

Especially when running a Git blame this is a problem. It is often to find the PR that introduced the problem, rather than the particular commit This saves time for maintainers like me and usually the PR submitter has then already enought knowledge to check his PR.
Therefore we usually keep the commits per PR low. If we think having several commits is more suitable, we make several PRs. Sure this is a matter of taste, as a reviewer I only follow here what we usually do. If you insist to have the different commits, then I request you to split the PR to one PR in which are the commits where you add the actual feature and one where you refactor the code. Would that be OK for you?

This is one in a series of PR's where I am taking code from at least 4 postprocessors partially written by different people, combining them into three files, then trying to make the code more consistent and simpler.  This particular PR doesn't add any functionality but it should make the code more maintainable.  The long term goal is to enable much simpler postprocessor files with much less copied code in each postprocessor file and much more "shared" code in the three Utils*.py files.  This should make it easier to test and make changes to the code in only one place and affect many of the postprocessor files.  Future PR's in this series will continue the refactoring, add many tests, and add some new functionality.

This was originally checked in as one commit, but after looking at it, it probably should have been done as several commits, one for each type of refactoring that I did.  These were the important changes:

- Modified the create_comment function to look up the the comment symbol instead of passing it as a parameter.  This resulted in simpler (and shorter) create_comment calls.
- Added format_for_axis, format_for_feed, and format_for_spindle functions that returned a number formatted with the proper  precision.  This simplified the code and made it more obvious which type of number formatting is wanted.
- Refactored the "parse" routine to pull out the code that handled a group (a compound or a project) into the "parse_a_group" routine and renamed the remaining code in the "parse" routine into the "parse_a_path" routine which handles a simple path.
- Refactored the "parse" routine to pull out the code that added the parameters (sometimes called "words") to the outstring into a "add_parameters" routine.  This shortened the "parse" routine and reduced the number of levels of indentation needed.
- Simplified the "add_parameters" routine by waiting until the end of the main loop to output the parameter letter followed by the parameter number value instead of having the output scattered through the code.

Just following up on this from the #8064 discussion.  The problematic letters occur when the path discretizer aims for the terminal vertex (presumably it could be any vertex?) and misses slightly.  insert_many_wires() closes the letter's outline polygon with a little short segment.

If Vcarve round()s like your fix, that slight miss vertex and the target vertex end up identical so the short segment added by insert_many_wires() goes to zero length, which doesn't hurt anything as long as orthognalProjection() checks for zero length segments.

Boost's Voronoi sweep line algorithm truncates the coordinates it gets to integer values, so there's a reasonable chance the two vertices that were close in FC's floating point coordinate system end up separated by one or two Manhattan distance abscissa values in Boost's coordinate system.  There's a further chance that the separation induced by that truncation makes the letter's outline polygon in Boost's coordinate space contain self-crossings, resulting in garbage out of VoronoiBuilder.

> It's not that they don't work in general, it's that they are broken in various places throughout our codebase, and Qt no longer provides diagnostics.

After all only a very few connect() were broken. And for clarification there is no issue with Qt reporting failed connections, it was my bad by not setting a debug build.

Anyway, when searching the code base for SIGNAL (options: case-sensitive, complete words and *.cpp files) then there 55 hits:
* Gui/Application.cpp: must still be done but requires some internal changes
* Gui/DlgActionsImp: it's a bit tricky because the object is known as QWidget and that a pointer to a member function cannot be used
* Gui/PropertyPage.cpp: same here
* Gui/PropertyItem.cpp: this isn't easily possible because the connect() are used inside functions where the slot function is passed as function argument as a string. Since the arguments of the slot function vary it's not possible to use a function pointer
* Part/PropertyEnumAttacherItem: same here
* Web/BrowserView.cpp: it only affects the old webkit binding which isn't available in Qt6 anyway
* others: they are all commented code

Now the next issue is all widget classes with `Q_SLOTS`. Here the slot functions shouldn't be connected with `QMetaObject::connectSlotsByName` either because this is error-prone. Usually a slot method follows the form: `on_OBJECTNAME_SIGNAL`. The connection will fail if the object name or the signal name doesn't match.

I was working on a project today, and it just occurred to me that I had not run into the dreaded Copy delay like I had been for the last month.  I even tried it on the official release and I'm not seeing it anymore.

I think I found out what caused it on the Windows side.  @acpopescu , your troubleshooting led me to start looking at the Accessibility Settings in Windows itself.  I started looking through the System --> Accessibility options to see if anything might look like they would do anything.  I got down to the Clipboard section.  While in there I noticed a few settings for Clipboard history, syncing, clear clipboard data, and suggested actions.

I'm a paranoid and stubborn guy that doesn't like Windows telling me what to do or recording what I do, so I turned off the clipboard history and suggested actions.  To be honest, I didn't check to see if they did anything at the time as they really didn't seem to me like something that would have an effect and I was working in the shop at the time and didn't have time to deal with it then.

But since I wasn't experiencing the problem today when I got back to the office, I thought back to what I might have changed to cause it.  I first thought it might be a Windows update, but looking at the history there, nothing new showed up.  I then remembered messing with these settings.  I turned both the Clipboard history and Suggested Actions back on and low and behold the Copy problem was back.

I ended up narrowing it down to the Suggested Actions.  I turn that on, the Copy problem comes back (even without closing FreeCAD) and when I turn it off, I can Copy with no issues.  In fact, I have to wait for FreeCAD to become active again before I can turn the switch off.  But as soon as I do, the Copy starts working again.

WEIRD

Just arriving to FreeCAD from OpenSCAD which has some limitations but is a breeze to version in git, and I don't even feel like designing anything until I know how I can properly version things.

There's at least two incompatible ways I found:
- just putting the zip directly into git, optionally with some difftool sugar with [WebTools_Git](https://wiki.freecad.org/WebTools_Git#Limitations), which I don't find acceptable, I mean even LibreOffice has a Flattened version of their formats (FODT),
- using [a local smudge filter](https://blog.lambda.cx/posts/freecad-and-git/), and version the dumped output, but then anyone cloning the repo will need to configure it manually to get a usable file,
- some other rezip smudge implementations [here](https://github.com/callegar/Rezip) and [there](https://github.com/costerwi/rezip)), which keep the format as ZIP but with no compression, meaning people would still be able to use the file directly after a checkout at least, but don't separate the files inside either,
- and [someone mentioned me](https://tooter.social/@Nic/109805002368310172) realthunder's branch (but which one, there's 224 of them?), where you can save as unzipped folder. But if it's never merged upstream then people checking the repo will also need to install the patched version.

So there's 4 ways equally unusable to me right now. :shrug: 

While it's possible to use any of these locally and later convert the repo with something like filter-branch, once a repo becomes public it kinda becomes set in stone, as rewriting public git history is frowned upon.

Is there any plan for advancing on this?

Would contribution to WebTools to handle the smudge way be accepted?

Same for a patch that would allow disabling compression when saving files, to avoid having to use a smudge filter?
EDIT: Just got told one can already set the compression ratio in the settings. Just tried and it seems to work as intended, though it still uses the deflate method and not the store one, at least it doesn't compress. It'd be really nice to have WebTools propose setting it to 0 on install… I guess I'll go that route for now, along with a difftool.

Is the folder-based format decided yet? I wonder if a smudge filter could actually use the same format meanwhile… (seems not, they must output a single file)

My feeling is that the result is not especially useful. Where with OpenSCAD you are storing commands to create geometry, in FreeCAD you are storing the geometry itself (as BREP files). So while technically they are text files, a diff between them can't really be treated the same way. If you want a more OpenSCAD-like experience I think you'd need to write (or record) a macro that creates your geometry, and version that instead.

Gentlemen, I wrote a simple program importing ASCII STL file, completely mimicking this code. I used `std::regex`, `boost::regex` and `QRegularExpression`. I took `std::regex` code from this PR, `boost::regex`  from the FreeCAD code, the code utilizing `QRegularExpression` I wrote myself. Time elapsed:

|  | Small model | Large model |
| --- | --- | --- |
|std::regex |95 ms| 26 723 ms|
|boost::regex |87 ms| 24 368 ms|
| QRegularExpression |87 ms| 25 348 ms|

I used gcc 11.2 together with Qt 6.3 on Windows 10. The speed comparison shows that the difference between them is negligible.

I think it's time to reconsider this topic. Why does import depend on regex at all? If you look [here](https://github.com/sokunmin/stl-gcode-viewer/blob/master/model.cpp), [here](https://github.com/wangxinkuan/qt-stl/blob/master/model.cpp) and [here](https://github.com/vladkrylov/STLViewer/blob/master/STLParser.cpp), none of the developers use regex to import file. They use `QFile`, `QStringList`, `QString`, `QVector3D`, `QTextStream` etc. The usage of regular expressions is quite burdensome.

My proposition is to rewrite the import code using `QFile`, `QStringView`, `QTextStream` and `QByteArray`. It's a Qt application anyway.

Thanks for running those tests, it's good to see that gcc has improved their regex library. Can you also test clang and msvc?

Regarding the import code: is there an advantage to using Qt? My general impulse is to use C++ standard library stuff whenever possible.

That said, one way of checking that you have the correct functions underscored or not is to underscore all of them, and then run pylint and see which calls it yells at you about: it should complain about any non-self-prefixed calls to underscored methods. That's useful when refactoring big code where you don't know exactly what needs to be public.

I can recheck it on openSUSE 15.4; my clang and MSVC toolchains (MSVS 2019) on Windows are rather old.

The main advantage of Qt is portability. You may heard problems concerning `std::filesystems` and, of course, `std::regex` on different platforms that are absent in Qt. In case of import/export there will be some gain in speed or none at all.

Some programs can be written utilizing C(++)/Qt interchangeably. However, usage of regular expression in some parts of FreeCAD is extensive, like in src/Mod/Mesh/App/Core/MeshIO.cpp

In my point of view, it is better to write `stream >> fX >> fY >> fZ` instead of 30 lines of code utilizing regex. Some parts of MeshIO.cpp use C++ streams, some parts use regexps. I'll compare import of ACSII STL using regex and C++ streams, though, beforehand I think the latter is faster.

What a small world, I am also adding libfmt as part of the console refactor (to handle printf statements necessary for console). I am also confused by the documentation. CMake is also not my cup of tea.

This is what I did:
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/pull/8350

Basically:
1. Add to CMakeList ```find_package(fmt)```
2. For header only code, then the macro needs to be defined:
```
#define FMT_HEADER_ONLY
#include <fmt/printf.h>
```
Looking at this PR, I am mising the REQUIRED in the ```find_package```

As far as I understood, there are two ways of adding libfmt, either (a) as a header only library (which is what I did), or (b) pre-compiled. 

In the header only version, I do not think it is necessary to use "target_link_libraries", as there is nothing to link against (it is header only, it gets compiled together with the code).

In the pre-compiled version, there is indeed a shared library to link together with the code. I read that this reduces the compilation time quite a lot (as opposed to using the header only version).

In a project the size of FreeCAD, where libfmt has the potential to be used in several places, it would probably make sense to use the precompiled version (at least for Windows, which currently uses pre-compiled headers). 

On the issue of the libpack, if we are going for the header-only, the libpack (or outside the libpack the actual code) needs to be available for the compiler to compile it. If we are going for a pre-compiled version, then I guess the pre-compiled version needs to be added to the libpack.

I am unsure if we will end up with several copies of the object code of libfmt if we use the header only version at different modules.

First, I apologize for the PR taking so long.  Between launching Ondsel and the Fosdem meetup, I've been severely slammed.

In general, the code looks good to me.  I'm a bit confused why you're passing in the safeheight and clearance height.  The generator shouldn't have any need for them.  

The safeheight is mainly used for moving between targets within an operation.  But a generator only works on a single target at a time.  

The clearance height is mainly used to move between operations when a clamp may interfere.  Again, since the generator is only working on a single target in the context of a single operation, it shouldn't have any need.

If I were building the helix generator based on my earlier assumptions,  The helix would start at the startpoint.z and end at the endpoint.z.  The generator would return the tool to the startpoint before exiting.   From there, the operation would be responsible for getting the tool into position before and after calling the generator.

Here's my understanding ...

fmt comes in three different forms:
- source. Can be built to linkable object files
- package: includes compiled, linkable object files built for certain target
- header-only header files. Available from source or package

The headers can be used without linking. Just copy them to the project. #include directly to format.h. But there be dragons I don't fully understand. I can verify you do need FMT_HEADER_ONLY to silence weird errors. Werner pointed out that including format in a header file can cause lots of linking as headers load nested dependencies.

Object files need linking to the project and can be:
- created from source
- provided pre-built by a package manager(brew, vcpkg, etc)
- in the case of FC, provided by so-called libpack, pre-built for Windows (atm not fmt).

Package also includes config files for cmake's find_package.

My first PR attempt was source, rejected as don't want fmt source in FC.
My second PR attempt was package, rejected because fmt not in FC libpack.

I have used both methods, but technically it seems linking to a package is the way to go. The missing link is Windows support. Hence my question whether vcpkg is a suitable alternative source for Windows fmt package. No response here or on forum.

I do have quite some interest in adding this library too. Let's see if we can get some answers to be able to move forward.

Some clarifications/summary:
- Including the source in FC (either for header-only or to generate a shared or static library) should not be done.
- The package, at least the Ubuntu version, includes both the source and a static library (not a shared library, but a statically linked one, .a not .so). This means that, the package can be used directly in Freecad either for header-only (Option A) or for statically linked code (Option B). The package could also be used indirectly to generated a shared library as in the link above (Option C). However, no shared library is provided as a package, at least, in Ubuntu.

> The headers can be used without linking. Just copy them to the project. #include directly to format.h. But there be dragons I don't fully understand. I can verify you do need FMT_HEADER_ONLY to silence weird errors. Werner pointed out that including format in a header file can cause lots of linking as headers load nested dependencies.

The use of FMT_HEADER_ONLY is [indicated](https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt/issues/596) by the creator of the library. As linked above, according to the creator, the only difference between statically linked and header-only is compilation time (which is always precious). 

However, in any of these two options, it is indeed a concern for me that several separate copies of object code (compiled from source or statically linked library) may be ultimately be present in the binary. This prompted my observation and why I mentioned the option to compile the source to make a shared library (Option C).

Option C would require in Linux (and macos I think) to compile libfmt as a shared library and install it, which may also have strong packaging implications. We could invite Kurt to the discussion it we would seriously consider Option C (I do not see why bother him, if for other reasons we are not going in this direction).

I am not emotionally attached to Option A. For my specific case it was the lowest modification option to introduce libfmt at a single point to fix the specific issue with Console I was addressing, while waiting to see which was the agreed best possible way to use it globally. Now we have arrived to this point, so Options B and C are left.

Option B is straight forward (as in this PR).

This said, I can live happily ever after with any option, but, of course, I prefer the one that better suits our needs. This we need to resolve first. We need Werner's guidance:

@wwmayer Could you please weigh in on which Option you favour?

In practical terms:
- No matter the option in Ubuntu (and I think macos too), the package is the way to go.
- I am on your very same footing regarding Windows. I see the package can be obtained from vcpkg. However, I also see that in Windows developers use the Libpack. I do not have Windows. We need additional information of how our community is approaching this kind of issues (it cannot be it is the first time). Let's try to get some guidance here:

Could you please weigh in on which the Windows requirements are regarding this library inclusion? Do we need every single library into the libpack or we can live with a mix of libpack and vcpkg?

Hopefully, with those two questions answered, we can move forward. You can made the changes to your PR, if any necessary, get it merged and I can rebase on top and mark mine as non-draft for merge too...

The Debian package uses Python3.11 while the default on my system is Python3.10. However, when looking at the code https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/master/src/Base/Interpreter.cpp#L517 then the init() function for Py3.10 is different to Py3.11. To this function all arguments are passed that are already checked by Python.

In Py3.10 and earlier Py_SetProgramName and PySys_SetArgv are used but in Py3.11 they are marked as deprecated.

Thanks @sliptonic.
The operation can have multiple circular holes. Each hole may take multiple helices (the result is actually a circular pocket. (It was designed to make ring or annulus shaped pocked but the front-end hides this option). As you wrote the generator handles a single hole.

With my changes the redundant first move to the center of the hole is canceled. The opration moves directly to the start XY location. Then it's doing G0 to safe-height and G1 to start-height (where it can barely touch the work-piece). The retract is to the safe-height except the last helix of a hole that retract to clearance-height.
Moves between holes (of the same operation) are at clearance-height, as it was before my changes.

The clearance-height parameter is used mainly to eliminate two consequent G0 retracts to safe-height and immediately to clearance height.

* At least for LinuxCNC, probably for other controllers we **must** retract to safe-height before any horizontal move. This is because the controller adds a radius between linear moves. Safe-height must consider this radius.

However, it looks reasonably good.

There is one aspect that could be improved. The code is checking the parameter preferences on every function execution (hgrp + getint). This is unnecessary, as a parameter observer can update local variables used in the functions when they change. This leads to faster and more readable code.

You have similar code here:
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/b6af6c9330051dd1fdfbb96a61aaa8b7928698c1/src/Mod/Sketcher/Gui/EditModeCoinManager.h#L106
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/b6af6c9330051dd1fdfbb96a61aaa8b7928698c1/src/Mod/Sketcher/Gui/EditModeCoinManager.cpp#L76

Basically, this class does the following:
1. Initialise the variables to the parameter value upon construction.
2. Subscribe to parameter changes (and unsubscribe upon object destruction).
3. Modify local variables used in the actual algorithm when the parameters change.

A nested class can access private members of the outer class. So if you make the observer as a nested class, you can directly change local private variables of the outer class (the SnapManager).

Do you feel like making this improvement?

I tested the change on a 2560x1440 display, the highest resolution my monitor will achieve, it was in response to yet another report this morning https://forum.freecad.org/viewtopic.php?t=76070 It's certainly better now than it was!!

Current situation is that the generator does not know its boundaries and the op does not know what the generator is trying to do. The result is a possible collision. 
My changes are basically making the generator do almost all the movements, that's why it needs to know the heights.
My next suggested change (its in the forum discussion but I wanted to separate the PR) is forcing just the outer-most helix. It's useful to cut through circular holes (similar to profile hole but uses helix).

> This doesn't look like a friendly workflow. 😕

I think it is (is also my experience in 10 years with the lyx.org project). Let's compare both workflows:

Method A: Keeping existing bugs open until fixed in stable:
- for the developer it is one click to reopen the bug and some seconds to set the "Fixed for 0.21" label
- for the release manager it is just a dozen clicks to close about the dozen issues
- forum guys only have to be active once a user reports it, but can then quickly find the open issue and post this. In many cases users will not even post to the forum if they found the existing bug. So let's say for every user encountering the issue, half will find the open issue, so no work at all for the forum guys. For the other half, we need about 10 minutes each

Method B: keeping bugs closed, no matter if already available in stable release
- most users will post in the forum, so a lot of work for the forum guys to read the report, then to check open _and_ closed bugs, then maybe a short discussion why the issue is closed despite still in stable...

So in total more work for us with method B while. We used in the project www.lyx.org for more than 10 years method A and it worked well. (that time I was very active in the forum and therefore know how much time it can take to give support. This sums up over the year.)

Yesterday I did another test of this PR: If the absolute scale factors are equal but have different signs e.g. (1, -1, 1) then the function claims that the scaling is uniform.

> As I think you noted in the code snippet before there is no way to distinguish between scale(-1,1,1) and scale(-1,-1,-1) and a 180 degree rotation.

Good point! I try to solve this apparent contradiction.

Of course, a scale(-1,1,1) is a uniform scaling in the sense that it doesn't change the relations of lengths of a geometry but mirrors it. If we have (-1,-1,-1) then any two mirroring can also be considered as a rotation around a coordinate axis by 180 degree. So, it's a rotation and a mirroring. The geometric meaning is uniform scaling.

But for the algebra it seems to make a difference. If you write this you can easily see that both results are the same (it's easy to prove this generally):
```
M=App.Matrix()
M.rotateX(1)
M.rotateY(1)
M.rotateZ(1)

S=App.Matrix()
S.scale(-1,-1,-1)

M * S
S * M
```

Now if you write this then you will see that the results are different:
```
M=App.Matrix()
M.rotateX(1)
M.rotateY(1)
M.rotateZ(1)

S=App.Matrix()
S.scale(-1,1,1)

M * S
S * M
```

So now let's try to solve this contradiction:
If we have a scale(-1,1,1) then it's equal to a scale(-1,-1,-1) and a rotation. Let's call them T and R. Because T is uniform we know that S = T * R = R * T.

Consider M * S:
M * S = M * (T * R) = M * (R * T) = (M * R) * T

Consider S * M:
S * M = (T * R) * M = T * (R * M)

So, in other words when multiplying T from left then another matrix is used than multiplying T from right.

Resume:
It's correct to handle equal absolute scale factors with different signs as uniform scaling.

If T does uniform scaling and that's what I have demanded then T * R = R * T. In this context R doesn't need to be a rotation matrix but can be any matrix.
T is of the form
```
T =
|t 0 0|
|0 t 0|
|0 0 t|

and R =
|r11 r12 r13|
|r21 r22 r23|
|r31 r32 r33|

If you do T * R or R * T you can easily see that in both cases the product is
|t*r11 t*r12 t*r13|
|t*r21 t*r22 t*r23|
|t*r31 t*r32 t*r33|

which is equal to t * R             (t is a scalar in R) 
```

I'm seeing quite a few issues related to the LeadInOut dressup.  This dressup is some old code and the developer who wrote it is deceased.  I would suggest that this dressup be refactored.  

As a first step, the GUI and dressup logic could be (and should be) separated.   This will make the dressup conform to the same pattern as the boundary, dogbone, and tag dressups.  It'll simplify the code, reduce redundancy, and make it easier to work on.

The actual code that generates the leadIn and leadout commands could be further abstracted to generators. These would be pure functions that take a small number of arguments and return a set of commands.  It would then be the job of the dressup to call the generator and add the resulting commands at the right place.

When the generators are written, they should also be thoroughly covered by unit tests.  The generators shouldn't assume a dressup context but should be generalized for reuse.
