Two observations:
First, reading through the contributing policy I notice that the role, requirement, and process for maintainers is heavily biased toward the solution/PR side of the equation.  In fact, the process doesn't even mention maintainers in the context of issues.

Second, the process specifically (step 14) says the maintainers shouldn't make value judgments on the contributions.  That doesn't mean the process shouldn't have judgments.  It just means those judgments should happen WAY before the code is written.

Considering this together, it makes sense that the maintainers should have a much more explicit role in the issue creation.

Consider this recent example.  [Issues 8556](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/issues/8556).  
The original problem is really a non-issue.  The user is confused by the functionality.
That confusion is the real problem (the UI is confusing for image import)
The discussion evolved toward an improved problem description and some solutions were suggested.
With slightly more discussion, it should reach a consensus on a minimal improvement that solves the problem.

IMHO, part of the maintainer's role should be doing this.  They should be offering opinions and value judgment at the issue stage.  After all,  they are the ones who understand the big picture well enough to guide the discussion toward real improvement.
FYI, several of the [complaints raised at Fosdem](https://forum.freecad.org/viewtopic.php?t=75768#p658200) were about the image workbench, scaling, and display.

Requiring it is heavy handed.  It starts to feel very artificial to create an issue just to turn around and close it for some minor one-line bug.
This could be an area where the maintainers have more discretion.  For example, we might say Maintainers are encouraged to create issues but are allowed to create or accept a PR without one at their discretion for trivial changes.
This doesn't solve the problem since it opens up the can of worms about what is 'trivial'.

At a minimum, I would suggest that any change which affects the user interface, experience, or workflow is not trivial regardless of the size of the PR.  If the user sees it, it should be in an issue.

We could say something like: Creating an issue first is not mandatory, but understand that if you don't, you might create additional work for maintainers who need to assess if your PR fixes an existing problem, and might delay its handling

> We could say something like: Creating an issue first is not mandatory, but understand that if you don't, you might create additional work for maintainers who need to assess if your PR fixes an existing problem, and might delay its handling

Expressing a policy like that isn't a good idea.  It doesn't give any guidance to the people who most need it - the casual contributors.  If we're going to allow exceptions and freedom of action,  it should be for people who have experience.

The policy should be as black and white as we can reasonably make it.  Perhaps we could say what kinds of issues absolutely require an issue:  

1. Anything that affects user experience, user interface, or workflow.
2. Anything that changes a published API
3. Anything that affects document structure
4. Any breaking change to existing models.

We could also require that all first-time contributors MUST create an issue before submitting a PR.  this gets them started right and ensures they understand the default process.

> MUST create an issue

It's not that they must create an issue, but that their PR must address an issue. And it still feels new-contributor-averse to me: if your one-line PR fixes an obvious problem, then we're asking you to basically triple the amount of work it takes you to fix it. And that's not an uncommon first PR. So I'd be in favor of not having the special case for new contributors. A "thanks for the PR, it looks good, merging now. For tracking and discussion purposes, we would appreciate if in the future if you could create an Issue first" would suffice in many cases.

Therefore the license class must be changed to return identifier and url.

When filling the combo box pass two arguments to addItem(). The first one is the translated string as it's done now and the second parameter is the url. For "Other" pass an empty url.

In the slot function onLicenseTypeChanged() you get an int and with this you can access the second argument of addItem() with itemData(). Pass the value of itemData() to the line edit for the url.

But the color handling seems to me wrong too because in View3DInventor.cpp an unsigned long is directly passed to a QColor while in NaviCube it's split into its RGBA components and then assigned to a QColor. This will result into different color values.

Qt handles an unsigned int as ARGB while FreeCAD handles it like Coin3D as RGBA

```
>>> from PySide import QtGui
>>> col = 3806916480
>>> color = QtGui.QColor(col)
>>> (col >> 24) & 0xff
226
>>> color.red()
232
>>> (col >> 16) & 0xff
232
>>> color.green()
239
>>> (col >> 8) & 0xff
239
>>> color.blue()
128
>>> col & 0xff
128
>>> color.alpha()
255
>>> color2 = QtGui.QColor((col >> 24) & 0xff, (col >> 16) & 0xff, (col >> 8) & 0xff, col & 0xff)
>>> color.red()
232
>>> color2.red()
226
>>> color.green()
239
>>> color2.green()
232
>>> color.blue()
128
>>> color2.blue()
239
>>> color.alpha()
255
>>> color2.alpha()
128
>>> 
```
Additionally when assigning an unsigned int (aka QRgb) then the alpha channel will be ignored and always set to 255:
https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qcolor.html#QColor-3

> So since you mentioned only tangency and curvature, you just need cubic B-splines?

Yes (and bezier curves).

And to come back to degrees and tools, there are two approaches I am aware of:
1. Offer the spline tool in-command options to change the degree prior to creation
2.. Give the user a degree 3 and a degree 5 option for the spline. 
Degree 3 is the default for tangency constraints and is what you need to be a close match for SubD geometry (the NURBS based version of Opensubdiv), which is mathematically only able to maintain curvature continuity with itself (it is degree 3 math).
Degree 5 is what you need for curvature continuity. 

1. Gives the user more flexibility. For instance, in Rhino, I set my default alias to access a spline to CV and degree 5. I can access any degree by typing C3, ..., C9. 
2. Simplifies the interface for more novice users. The downside, however, is that if you need to do some hefty degree changes, you'll need give more input than with option 1. 

Then there is another creation method that I haven't brought up which is a spline through points (an interpolate through the clicked points spline). In Rhino, this type of spline is converted back to a cubic B-spline after creation. You'll lose the points you clicked, but you keep the same type of spline. From the top of my head I don't know whether there is another type of spline that lets you interpolate through the clicked points and that is capable of being converted to a cubic B-spline later (by the user). For most people, this is much easier to draw, because it gives most local control (as opposed to the CV Hull based cubic B-spline, which changes shape slightly as the CV you manipulate also affects the portion of the spline at the next CV).

What it also doesn't let you do is increase the degree of the curve, but retain its shape. This is mostly used in surface modelling, where you try to keep the degree of splines to the bare minimum. @0penBrain 

The current most important point of coupling is that the VPGrid is added to the same scenegraph as the VP on which it needs to be displayed. Moreover, the VP needs to add the grid node root before use.

The second most important point of coupling is that the VPGrid, having the root node in the scenegraph of the VP, is bound by all modifiers of it, which it does not control. So it draws in (X,Y,0), while the actual plane depends on the VP. To be able to interpret Viewer3D's global coordinates, it needs to be provided with the plane direction (not to be able to draw, which is probably what it should be, but to be able to interpret the information from the viewer).

Probably, the right way to handle this would be for the VP to configure the extension with the plane information where to draw (basically the placement of the sketch), then have the extension represent the grid on its own separate node.

On top of this is where the sensing needs to be built, because the grid reacts to the changes in the camera, so as to cover only the area that is needed. The challenge comes from where in the scenegraph the node of the extension is with respect to the node of the extended VP. I did some tests while finishing this PR, but I had lots of problems, as when adding the grid to the extension, the grid would not draw properly. Werner mentioned that something similar is implemented in the color bar. I have not had time to look at it. Eventually I will because I am interested in the potential offered by VPExtensions.

I think that before deciding on moving the sensing to an extension, we need to have the picture above clear. It may be that camera sensing needs to be implemented at the root class, VP and inform the extensions. I do not have a clear picture.

What I wanted to do here, is to decouple grid from VP, to avoid intertangling it, and eventually be in a position to work on what is described above.

> why not? isn't changing the active sketch the expected behavior? and didn't it behave like this before?

I do not think it is expected behaviour. 

I understand that some preferences are globally applied on change (for example language). However, when behaviour is specialised per object, a preference should be an indication of a default value to applied in the future by default. Nobody would expect that, let's say, I change all existing sketches in the tree when I change that I want a given grid size by default. Then,  why should a sketch in edit mode (should it be one) need to change to reflect a preference change.

From a functional point of view, if I just opened a sketch and realised that I am changing the grid constantly, I may decide which is my most used size and configure it, without necessarily being the case that my most used size is adequate for the current sketch.

Applying such behaviour mixes different responsibilities. Preferences indicating default values to be applied on creation and Editing controls/Properties indicating the state of a sketch being edited.

Preferences are for indicating preferences for the future, not for attempting to retroactively apply them. 

When some users expect to use preferences to change the active sketch in edit mode, something is clearly wrong. This was exposed in the discussion, when users want to move edit controls to preferences (to remove them from the taskbar). Edit controls are not preferences. Edit controls belong to the toolbar.

These are the reasons why I have decided to adopt this behaviour.

@adrianinsaval Slow tests should simply NOT be part of normal unit tests because unit tests must run fast so they can be run frequently during development. There can be thousands of tests and the idea is the whole lot runs in seconds. The faster the tests, the more often they are likely to be run, and problems detected long before a project build.

**I appreciate this is different to what some here insist unit testing is.** 

Having said that the unit testing framework (gtest) is quite capable of running slow (integration etc) tests. We just don't want slow tests to spoil unit testing.

Sooner rather than later CI should include unit tests. CI has less time pressure so conceivably could run both unit tests and slow tests.

@realthunder 

Does the following table and interpretation from the code look correct to you:

| postfix (elementMap key) | meaning       |
|----------------|---------------|
| `:H`           | tag (local)   |
| `:C`           | child element |
| `:X`           | external tag  |
| `:I`           | index         |
| `D`            | duplicate     |
| `:T`           | deprecated tag (uses decimal) |
| `:M`           | mod           |
| `:MG`            | modgen        |
| `:G`           | gen           |
| `:U`           | upper         |
| `:L`           | lower         |

(above edited based on RealThunder's feedback)

And anything else is most likely an operation.

(for ref: look through code in `ComplexGeoData.cpp`, `TopoShapeEx.cpp`, and `src/Mod/Part/App/TopoShapeOpCode.h`)

And so, the interpretation of the simple `Unnamed#Fusion.;Face6;:M2;FUS;:H1ab:8,F.Face10` (asuming Hashing turned off) would be

`Unnamed` = the documents name

`#` = doc / object separator

`Fusion` = object name

`.` = object / elementMap name separator

**MappedName portion begins**

`;` = elementMap entry prefix

`Face6` = the item's historic parent element name

`;` = elementMap entry prefix

`:M` = marker of modification
`2` = the object at index 2 (the third object)

`;` = elementMap entry prefix

`FUS` = modification was a fusion operation; see `src/Mod/Part/App/TopoShapeOpCode.h`

`;` = elementMap entry prefix

`:H` = This is a TAG
`1ab` = the tag's id in hex (would be '-' if it didn't have one)
`:8` = marker indicating length of _previous_prefix, in decimal
`,` = comma separator for next parameter for ':H'
`F` = This is a "Face"; literally the first letter of the actual name

**MappedName portion stops**

`.` = MappedName / element's name separator

`Face10` = the actual name for this element

I've been looking at the new importer code to get a better idea of the origin of the error there. The 'obj' in the traceback is an App::Annotation object. The importer initially converts DXF text into App::Annotation objects, and convertDraftTexts converts these to App:FeaturePython/Text objects. It appears that, when creating the App::Annotation, the LabelText is set by calling setValues (in C++) which expects UTF-8-encoded std::string(s). The fault appears to be in ImpExpDxfRead::OnReadText or ImpExpDxfRead::Deformat, which should behave differently depending on the AutoCad version from the DXF file; for newer versions the text can be used as read from the file, but for older versions the text must be UTF-8 _encoded_ before setting it into the LabelText property.

The point is when running FC in cmd mode then the creation of a document doesn't consider user settings (while it does when creating it in GUI mode). So, undo/redo is always disabled and must be explicitly enabled after the creation with doc.UndoMode = 1

> This must be already set when using the Test Framework?

No, there is nothing to be set beforehand. If needed UndoMode must be set for each created instance of a Document

> The question is about the constraints on the poles. That is done in addition to creating the poles. Biggest issue is to disallow adding weight constraints when they are not desired.

- With the legacy code, if the initial pole is not constrained, nothing is constrained.
- With the modified code, the first pole is constrained to weight 1 if it is 1. The rest are constrained if the first is constrained and they are the same value.

If the legacy code is fed a rational B-Spline, it won't constrain any pole.
If the modified code is fed a rational B-Spline, it may at best constrain the first pole to weight 1.

If you see an issue with rational B-Splines, then perhaps we should not do the modification. 

An alternative is to create a new function which does not constrain at all and move there all the common code. The current function will then be refactored to call that other function and constrain (either legacy or modified).

The caller is responsible for calling one or the other, depending on what is to be achieved.

We may also make the change now, and if the problem arises, then refactor. Give it a thought.

Breaking this into to planning parts. First, the general pattern:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    id1([Prepare])
    id2([Implement])
    id3([Integrate])
    id4>Enable]
    id5(Optimize)
    id1 --> id2
    id2 --> id3
    id3 --> id4
    id4 --> id5
    id5 --> id5
```
1.  (Prepare)
Create the supporting functions needed by element naming and the algorithm.
These are simply libraries with good unit testing to ensure they are accurate when used later.
**FreeCAD behavior is unchanged for users**
2. (Implement)
Create the naming-of-elements algorithm.
Create the ElementMap class.
Using the previous libraries, import the general algorithm that will _eventually_ be called by ComplexGeoData.cpp to have the more advanced naming.
Add the members to the ComplexGeoData.cpp class but don't use them. Simply add support for visibility in the Selection View and support for the _manual_ call via Python Console.
Using unit tests, verify that the naming is very predictable and reliable.
**FreeCAD behavior is unchanged for users**
3. (Integrate)
Migrate to v.22; contact other workbench maintainers.
Add the naming, but do not use it yet.
While the member values are set, they are not actually used.
**This stage will slow down FreeCAD and will make the naming visible on an element when selected.**
4. (Enable)
Use the toponaming so that the model is more resilient to upstream object changes.
**Users will start seeing increased stability.  Performance is still impacted**
5. (Optimize)
Selectively add optimizations to speed FreeCAD up again.
This could include: MappedName-hashing and IndexedName-int:string-caching.
**Repeat**

@Intuos5 There will always be continuity issues in a spline if you go to a high enough derivative. Degree 3 splines can only guarantee that the curvatures will be _continuous_, but not `differentiable (smooth)`, which is why there is a "corner" in the curvature graph. Discontinuity would mean the two lines do not meet at all, like so:
![Screenshot from 2023-03-04 16-31-24](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4316933/222896307-fd7859d5-dd95-44f1-8e2f-046edddd1266.png)

1. Use the B-spline creation tool.
2. Press "D" and enter 5.
3. Provide the "CV" points (note they are called poles or control points here).

The overall goal is to gather up code from many postprocessor files into some "shared" code that will help simplify all of the postprocessor files.  When you have all of the code in each postprocessor file, it is relatively easy to make changes since you are only affecting one postprocessor.  If you want to make changes to the shared code, you probably affect all of the postprocessors that depend on that code.  That usually isn't what you want.
By making all of the code that processes the "arguments" for the g-codes into functions you get at least two main benefits:
    You can change the order in which the "arguments" are processed from the postprocessor file ("A, B, C" can be changed to "C, B, A", for example).
    You can replace one or more argument processing functions with new ones from the postprocessor file.  For example, you could replace the function that processes the "Q" argument with a different function without affecting other postprocessors.
I agree that it is making the code more complex but I think it is in a good cause in this case.

This is an issue on if the parser should assume 1/2in means (1/2)in or 1/(2in). It seems the former is always the correct assumption, but the expression parser assumes the latter.

@CrashedAgain1859 I pushed an update to this branch, if you're able to give it a shot.
https://github.com/ConnorWorrell/FreeCAD/tree/SpinboxFractionInput

This modifies the input box text before it's passed to the expression parser to give the requested behavior. This assumption also makes it easier to handle units that are part of division, multiplication, and exponentiation operations, which this didn't do before. This should work unless 2 or more units are mixed together and this assumption breakes down, Eg (1in*1ft/1mm). In this case correct and explicit units are needed.

I think this is the requested and correct behavior, this assumption does lead to some interesting math:
W/ US Customary units:
- 1/2 -> .5in
- 1/2in -> .5in
- 1/2mm -> 19.685 thou
- 1/(1in+1) -> .5in
- ((1in+1in)/(1in*1in))*2^(1in+1in) -> 8in

At the moment it doesn't compile neither with MSVC nor under MSYS2 because the export macro is missing:
```
    template <LogStyle>
    void Notify(const std::string & notifiername, const std::string & msg);
```
==>
```
    template <LogStyle>
    BaseExport void Notify(const std::string & notifiername, const std::string & msg);
```

Besides that a nicer way that doesn't require the extra export macro is to add a private function 
`void NotifyPrivate(LogStyle category, const std::string& notifiername, const std::string& msg);`
and the implementation of Notify can go to the header file:
```
template <LogStyle category>
void Notify(const std::string& notifiername, const std::string& msg) {
    NotifyPrivate(category, notifiername, msg);
}
```

The failures are related to this PR and this line is the culprit:
`const char* licenseUrl = (paramGrp->GetASCII("prefLicenseUrl", url)).c_str();`

GetASCII() returns a tmp. std::string object and it will be destroyed after the call of c_str(). This means that licenseUrl is a dangling pointer and may point to a garbage value. Writing this garbage will invalidate the Document.xml file of an FCStd project so that it cannot be opened any more. This is then the reason for the failing tests.

The line must be corrected to:
`std::string licenseUrl = (paramGrp->GetASCII("prefLicenseUrl", url));`

IMO overloading the "Distance" Sketcher constraint for a concentric constraint is a hack. 

At solver level this implementation just sets a difference between radii. There is no guarantee of concentric.

Conceptually, any Python power user would expect that creating a distance between two geoids belonging to two circles would enforce such a distance also when the circles are not concentric.

If this Sketcher constrain would be reimplemented as "Concentric", I would argue that the coincident constraint is what makes the two circles concentric. I have problems to see the added value of "Concentric".

If the intention is to provide a distance between circles (which would lead to an offset between edges when their centers are coincident), then the solver part needs to be reworked to consider the centers of the circles in addition to the radii. So, basically the problem to be solved by the solver is that of a distance between edges of circles with centers at any positions. This problem will lead to an offset when the centers are concentric.

> However in Ubuntu 20.04 there is no shared library in the repositories.

If Ubuntu 20.04 works with the static library there is no need to switch to a shared library. The trick to build the shared version from the sources was to add this block to SetupLibFmt.cmake
```
if (MINGW)
    set (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS ON)
endif()
```

But BUILD_SHARED_LIBS is a global CMake variable that affects all calls of add_library() to always create a shared library.

I think it makes sense to overload the sketcher distance constraint to a case of circle to circle (1).

The problem with (2) is twofold: (a) I do not think it makes much practical sense a constraint "radius difference", (b) that constraint would not have support at sketcher level, so we would need to create a new sketcher constraint to map it. 

Now, you have invested quite so work in this. Do you feel like writing the solver constraint of (1)? 

You need a new constraint taking as parameters both center points, both radii and a fixed value (the offset or distance). You may use derivector to define a Vector between the center points. Your error function is the length of derivector minus both radii minus the offset. You can extract the gradients directly from derivector.

This is an example of how to use derivector:
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/1a0801a23f917f534d4dabe8c956df4cd206e2a2/src/Mod/Sketcher/App/planegcs/Constraints.cpp#L2519

There are two ways to code solver constraints. One is the Constraint P2LDistance way (without derivector). The other one is the one I linked above (with derivector). With derivector you do not have to care about the gradient calculation (you write one function and derivector takes care of providing the differentials for the gradient. Without derivector you need to provide both the error and the gradient functions yourself.

Derivector may seem a little bit odd at first, but it is very easy to build geometric vectors. My advice is to go the derivector way. But if you feel very much comfortable with calculating functions and derivatives, you may want to go the other way. The other way has more checking to be done. But I will review whatever path you decide to take.

Point to circle and circle to circle are likely to be doable with a same constraint, where the radius of the point is zero. But this you will see as you code it (perhaps I am not anticipating an issue).

Yes... the general case is more complex...sorry for that.

In addition, the circles can also be secant (one cutting the other).

I do not think it is possible to decide which distance is the one without actually comparing the four combinations (where the line joining the circles and its extension cuts both circles). So the four intersecting points.

There are at least three places where this needs to be calculated:
i) in CommandConstraints when calculating and applying the Acting Distance.
ii) in EditModeConstraintManager when drawing the labels
iii) at the solver when calculating the gradient and error function

for (i) and (ii), you may create a function in Mod/Sketcher/Gui/Utils.h to calculate the distance and return the points on the circle where the distance is minimum. These can be calculated using Vector3d.

Then, you need to calculate the same inside iii but using DeriVector.

One possibility for making this calculation is:
1) Calculating the inter-center vector using the centers V= C2-C1
2) Normalising the vector v = norm(V).
3) Then the four intersection points are:
i11 = C1+r1*v
i12 = C1-r1*v
i21 = C2+r2*v
i22 = C2-r2*v
4) Then the four possible lengths are:
L_i11_i21 = (i21-i11).Length()
L_i11_i22 = (i22-i11).Length()
L_i12_i21 = (i21-i12).Length()
L_i12_i22 = (i22-i21).Length()
5) Take the minimum of them
6) The intersection points leading to the minimum are the two points you are looking for, and the minimum length the distance.
7) For the solver constraint you have the derivector that lead to the minimum length, the error is basically the length of this vector minus the constraintvalue.

For those calculations using derivector, the ellipse constraint can serve as inspiration. For example: ```ConstraintInternalAlignmentPoint2Ellipse::errorgrad``` (as there emaj is a normalised vector that is afterwards scaled by the radius a, da).

Hope that helps.

I am a bit skeptic about Z88 in general. Z88Aurora is not OpenSource and the documentation is poor.

I extended support for Z88 already a bit last summer but stopped since Z88 can only perform mechanical analyses. The main feedback up to now was that FreeCAD's FEM misses multiphysics (acoustics in combination with heat etc.). Therefore I focused on Elmer. CalculiX can also perform much more than the thermomechanical analyses we support at the moment, but the problem is in my opinion the poor documentation and low user base for non-thermomechanical analyses.

Concerning the connection to the VTK post processing, this is now resolved in master. One gets now automatically a result pipeline so that one can change constraints recalculate and see the results as one defined the pipeline.

Therefore I don't see much room for a GSoC project regarding Z88. Personally I think the FEM workbench would benefit from more multiphysics. We have now support for electromagnetics, but other basic things like acoustics are still missing.
Thanks to the recent Elmer extension project, I think this could be a relatively easy task. One can copy the code for the electromagnetics equations and modify it for acoustics and elastics and other physical equations.
The challenge is hereby to catch the cases of multiphysics. So when you e.g. perform an analysis of a fluid that is heated and the fluid flows in an elastic pipe that is squeezed while the fluid is flowing, one must solve the different equation in a certain order. Ideally this should be done by FreeCAD because otherwise one would have to dive deep into the docs of Elmer for every case.

So for GSoC, I would either extend our Elmer support as easy project or extend CalculiX as medium task.

> I agree, let's use `std::string` instead. We can always change course later if we really have to, but let's try the cleaner path first.

There is a reason of using `const char*` here. It makes `IndexedName` an extremely light weight structure, which is important, as there can be literally millions of instances of this kind of highly repetitive data. Also note that `IndexedName` does not simply reuse the input string pointer, `IndexedName::set()` function will try to lookup the type from an explicitly supplied type array that is supplied by the caller, which is assumed to be persistent, and hence safe for reuse. If the type cannot be found, and the caller allows this 'unexpected' type, `IndexedName` will store the name in an internal `set` to avoid duplication.

Yes. The feature is a very basic of  visual layers. It will be much more powerful in the future. The reason why we get this now is twofold: (a) I need to remove the rendering order to improve the visualisation, (b) Removing the rendering order without providing anything else would be harder for users when dealing with overlapping geometry.

The basic solutions is to provide 3 layers. Layer 1 which is the normal Layer. Layer 2 which has a discontinuous line style. Layer 3 which is hidden (so the Hidden Layer). In terms of FreeCAD ability any layer has the functionality to hide and show itself, but this is not exposed to the user yet (will be in the future). So, in this interim basic solution, when you want to hide a geometry, you assign it to the "Hidden Layer". This can be done via the checkbox (as in constraints), or via contextual menu (there is an entry called "Layers" where you can select 1, 2 or Hidden).

Yes, I have realised that the constraints of the geometry elements stay. I have noted this for when I implement the extended support. I am not sure exactly how it will work yet.

It's a Qt bug, I don't know what causes it. Quick search showed that the message `QBackingStore::endPaint() called with active painter` introduced with [this patch](https://github.com/qt/qtbase/commit/2aa9908e24611fa6d321e694b8415ba7e8d364b0). `qt/qtbase 5.9.5 on Jan 12, 2018`

However, [it caused flooding](https://bugreports.qt.io/browse/QTBUG-66452) the console output with the aforementioned warning. `5.9.6, 5.10.1`
 
It was supposed to be fixed in [this](https://github.com/qt/qtdeclarative/commit/047f161b1a706e81034ccd8d4700a3126c16dfe4) patch. `5.11.0-beta1 on Feb 19, 2018`



Addition of `did you forget to destroy it or call QPainter::end() on it?` took place with [this](https://github.com/qt/qtbase/commit/86f91bf0f707e34392fbdf424d6914e7cf6bb4e6) patch. `qt/qtbase 5.12.5 on Jul 22, 2019`

Another bug with [similar warning](https://bugreports.qt.io/browse/QTBUG-83139) affecting `5.13.2, 5.14.1` on Linux, though, the bug [seemed to be unreproducible](https://bugreports.qt.io/browse/QTBUG-83139?focusedCommentId=506141&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels:comment-tabpanel#comment-506141) with `5.14.2`

I hope that update to `Qt 5.15.8` will fix this.

> is the intent in the following code to ensure that the QByteArray in the unordered_set has a unique copy of the data? Or is this doing something else?

@chennes `ByteArray::mutate()` is called right after inserting into `IndexedName::NameSet`. To avoid wasted buffer allocation, I use QByteArray::fromRawData() to wrap the caller supplied const string pointer to attempt an insertion. If it fails, no buffer deallocation is needed. If it succeeds, `mutate()` will be called to ensure its member QByteArray owns the string.


> is the following test an accurate representation of the expected behavior

The second test case shall fail. Because the last argument `allowOthers` is false, and since `EDGES_ARE_REALLY_GREAT` is  not in `allowedTypes`, `indexedName.getType()` will return an empty string, and `indexedName.isNull()` will return true.

@PaddleStroke 

There are some changes I would like to have in this PR.

UI Side:
- Snap To Grid is a preference that is in the Grid control.
- Snap To Objects is activated in a new setting in the ElementWidget.
- Snap To Angle is settable from a DSH, when Ctrl is pressed.
- Snap to Objects also on the Sketcher Settings Preference Page, where also an angle can be configured.

I think this is wide too spread and duplicative. Additionally, I think that the preference page should not be used for current editing tool status (i.e. to switch between snap editing modes). A preference is something a user wants to define as a default, as opposed to something the user is continuously changing to adapt to different CAD challenges.

While there are indeed different ways to handle UI, I think a solution to these problems could be to do something similar to the grid control. The button could be a general button to enable/disable all types of snapping. The widget in the drop-down, can have all these UIs above in a single place (Of course, including the setting of the angle steps, which the user can easily change, if for a CAD challenge 6º degree steps is what he or she needs). The icon of the command, could even change to reflect the snapping mode that "SnapManager" is applying.

This could also consider whether a "snap to Grid" enabling should perhaps enable the grid if disabled, or be greyed out indicating that without grid there will be snap to grid (I have no strong preference for one or the other, but just that the user is not mislead).

Architecture:

It is mostly ok. There is an aspect I have been reflecting on while reviewing the PR. 

(1) SnapManager is intended to be the box embodying the business rules for snapping. While other tools or the user can provide input edit mode preferences or requests, it is SnapManager the one deciding how to deal with them. In other words, SnapManager holds the status of what is being applied as snap modus. For this reason, I think it makes sense to have a enum class at SnapManager, that SnapManager can return to indicate the state (this could be used in the UI above to update the icon, for example). It can also be used by tools (e.g. DSH) to see if their request for a given snapping is being applied or not.

(2) When tools (e.g. DSHs possibly anglesnapping, or even the control at the beginning of this post, if angle snap will be used when dragging) communicate a configuration of a Snap Mode or request one mode, they are not setting a mode, but requesting a mode. The difference, be it semantic, reinforce that SnapManager will decide and the result may not be what the tool expects. I would then rename the functions setAngleSnapping to requestAngleSnapping. This is a minimal change, but full of conveying intention. If DSHs will request a mode in the future (e.g. object snapping during the duration of the DSH), it should also call accordingly.

These changes intend to abstract the contents of SnapManager from the rest of users, which do not need to know how snapping is being handled. This helps defer many decisions on the complete business rules.

I think that snap is one editing functionality and that it should have its icon on the Toolbar.

The argument for one toolbar icon can be applied to many other features. Most users likely do not use bspline knot increase/decrease, or even splines at all. Many do not use carbon copy. Others never import external geometry. Mirroring or arrays are other such features. If the Sketcher has snapping functionality, which now is being extended, it needs to have a centralised place where this is controlled.

No providing a button for it will make the feature worse understood.

With respect to the argument that grid snap is grid and should be with the grid. Well, grid snap is snap and should be with snap is an equally valid argument just on its face value. However, looking more carefully, there is a reason why snap disappeared from the grid VP extension, and is dealt with here. Snap to grid will be overruled in many occasions. This needs to be conveyed clear to the user. Snap to grid is not overruled because of the grid, but because snapping functionality is more complex than just snap to grid. When it will be overruled and how depends on other settings for snapping. Any extension in the future of the snapping functionality will only require more control of snapping in a single place.

With respect to the argument for snap to object, it is not one button for every snap functionality, but one single button for all of them. We do not know how many people will want to use it and how many will despise it. However, if it is not discoverable, then nobody will use it unless it is the default, or everybody will use it even if perhaps they do not want to if it is the default. 

Snap to angle. While we agreed to leave the snap on dragging from the first version of this PR, snapping does work with dragging and it is possible that it is implemented in the future (In fact probably should, specially if a polar grid is also implemented). Spreading the UI around will not help further development either. 

On another point, the Elements widget is already overwhelmed with functionality. That widget is for the geometry or operations with the geometry. An editing mode does not belong there.

It is very difficult to get feedback to improve a tool if the tool is hidden, difficult to discover or difficult to use. Conversely, it is easier to get feedback for improvement when all the tool is in a single place.

For Gui (which is the namespace of this file), at least generally, the translated notification is better. From a translation framework point of view, with a TranslatedNotification the translation itself is made at the source of the notification. This means that the developer has full control on the size of the context used for translation. Also, there are many translations that are already there (with whichever context the developers decided). Changing it to "Notifications" may not be advisable (I am not knowledgeable enough of Crowding, but changing a context perhaps makes troubles for translators).

Notifications, where translation is advisable (IMO always), share the context all over FreeCAD ("Notifications"). This means the context will be as big as all the possible notifications. However, this may cover a use case where it may not be acceptable to add a dependency on the translation framework, while marking for translation is perfectly acceptable. This is much more important though for the App namespace than for Gui.

Although the question is about notifications, the notification area listens to warnings and errors (as the report view does). These are not translated. If these are marked for translation with the "Notifications" context, the notification area will translate them. So, we can have the regular untranslated messages in the Report View, while having translated versions in the Notification Area.

I wanted it to be fully legacy compatible while providing a new flexible framework. So there are different possibilities. We will see how users and developers end up using it (I am often surprised by how features end up being used).

Ok so after a bit of digging and reading I think I have some answers:

From the Qt documentation of [fromRawData](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qbytearray.html#fromRawData):
> The bytes are _not_ copied. The [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qbytearray.html) will contain the data pointer.

> A subsequent attempt to modify the contents of the returned [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qbytearray.html) or any copy made from it will cause it to create a deep copy of the data array before doing the modification. This ensures that the raw data array itself will never be modified by [QByteArray](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qbytearray.html).

> Warning: A byte array created with fromRawData() is not '\0'-terminated, unless the raw data contains a '\0' byte at position size. While that does not matter for [QDataStream](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qdatastream.html) or functions like [indexOf](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qbytearray.html#indexOf)(), passing the byte array to a function accepting a const char * expected to be '\0'-terminated will fail.

So:
- Probably this is the reason for the unexpected/missing copy you have found
- The role of `raw` is to keep track of the `\0` termination. Not to signal that `\0` might be in the string (as I initially thought). The tests should be updated then.
- QByteArray is used to avoid copying data, for performance reasons.
- Having two separate variables for data and postfix is helpful in this regard: to avoid copying data, or rather copy only whats needed and leave alone the other variable.

Perhaps smart pointers could come in handy to better express ownership?

There are two aspects of the problem:
- first, we need to detect that the problem has occured and inform the user.
- second, the system should be able to recover from the broken state without user intervention.

In order to solve the first aspect, we need to know that the geometry being referenced by the dimension is not the geometry that was originally referenced.  This requires saving a copy of the referenced geometry for comparison.  Geometry is a relatively lightweight object, so saving a copy of an edge or a few vertices is not a problem.

Comparing geometry is a difficult undertaking - there is no "==" operator for geometry.  In a complete solution, we would need to consider changes in scale or positioning as well as actual changes in the geometry, such as a line becoming longer or a radius getting bigger. The problem has some similarities with feature detection in computer vision applications.

The general flow of the comparison process is: 
    geometric shapes > extract characteristics > compare characteristics > take action

The extraction of characteristics controls how "good" our comparison will be.  A simple comparison of line endpoints or circle centre and radius should be sufficient to detect cases where the geometry has not changed, but has been renamed.  A more detailed set of characteristics would be required to detect the situation where the geometry has moved.

Once we have detected a mismatch, we need to take action.  This may be just a message to the user, or an automatic replacement of the erroneous reference with a correct one. 

To automatically replace the erroneous reference, we need to search through the candidate geometries, extract the characteristics, compare to our saved geometry's characteristics and use the best match to update the reference.

Determining the best match can be as simple as selecting the first matching geometry or as complex as scoring each candidate and comparing the scores. 

The general flow of the replacement process is:

    candidate shapes > assign scores > rank candidates > update reference with best candidate.

Implementation details

DrawViewDimension 
    a new property to store reference shapes
    code to update stored reference shapes
    code to invoke comparison
    reference replacement code

DimensionReference
    code to deliver reference geometry for comparison
    
new GeometryMatcher
    perform the actual comparisons
    
QGIViewDimension
    display an indication of invalid reference

If I understand you well, you might be assuming that free is the eponymous C function.  However that function takes a pointer as argument. If there weren't another function taking a vector of constraint pointers as argument, the code would not compile at all.

The actual function called is this one:
https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/45001fa1601f98e8836f4eca6dcbed81907cb355/src/Mod/Sketcher/App/planegcs/GCS.cpp#L4821

This function iterates the std::vector and deletes an static_cast -ed version of the pointer and clears the vector.

As you know, clearing a vector will not release the dynamically allocated memory of the pointers in it. So explicitly deleting the pointers is necessary before clearing the vector. 

Leaving aside the fact that it is quite old code and things could be done differently (and certainly I will look into it with more calm), what it does ensure is that there is no memory leak when a constraint needs to be removed from the system. 
So I see no memory leak.

I say things could be done differently because, at least now, constraint has a virtual destructor, so if every inherited class provided an appropriate destructor (either the compiler provided default one, which will be virtual due to inheritance, or a specific virtual override where necessary), this type checking and deleting appears to me, at a first glance, it should not be needed at all (dynamic dispatch would do it for you), and then indeed there would no use of reusing the free function for just one constraint and the code could be simplified to a simple delete constraint, as there will be no need to construct the vector just to reuse the free function (which I presume was the intention of the developer here). So, there might be indeed an opportunity to improve the code so that it is more readable (with proper compiler optimizations, the assembly may  end up being the same, but code readability is important). But perhaps I should look into this after having some sleep, as now I have been almost 18 hours awake and I may be missing something.

Regarding your observation of ```addConstraint``` not allocating memory, it indeed does not, because it takes the pointer from specific functions which call it. These specific functions allocate with new the memory for the constraint dynamically. This pointer needs to be released. If what you mean is that constraints do not having any dynamically allocated memory of its own (i.e. data members), I think that is the case today (have not checked all of them), but it could happen in the future. Then, they should have an appropriate destructor, so that when delete is called on a base pointer, dynamic dispatch gets to the destructor of the specific constraint and memory is properly released.

Please, let me know if you think I am missing something.

Well, you're right that with absolutely identical edges it probably shouldn't matter because they can be re-swapped during dimension fixing if they happen to swap in OCC, but quite often the superfluous edges seem to be shorter parts of the "real" edges that fully overlap other edges.  The short and long arc parts of the same "real" arc are not freely swappable, and the short parts may disappear after OCC update, which may turn up to be a problem if the user has (accidentally) attached a dimension to a such short edge.  This happens especially with arcs and other round shapes when there are e.g. concentric circles in the 3D model that are flattened on top of each other in the projection.

All the suggested solutions have pros and cons. The Getting Started wizard, in particular, assumes that the user already knows what WBs the program has, what they do, and which ones the user needs, which is not necessarily the case, especially for new users.

A few thoughts.

When you are building a rocket, what do you need? Rocketry, Sketcher, maybe FEM and TechDraw. But definitely not Arch, or BIM, or Paths? When you are designing a house, you need Sketcher, Arch, BIM etc., but again, probably not FEM or Robot (unless you really, really need to). So there's context. 

Well, people have already figured out several ways to deal with context. One such way is workspaces that limit visible UI to just the features that belong to a particular context, with the rest tucked away but still fairly accessible. You can see this in multiple non-linear video editors like Kdenlive that come with a set of predefined workspaces yet give users the way to configure their own workspaces. For FreeCAD, that might mean having a context selector and dialog similar to Getting Started above for defining custom workspaces and managing all workspaces (factory defaults and custom ones), and a few other things maybe.

The tricky bit is figuring out the UI to choose context when starting a new project. It's easy when you add an extra step just for that. But the price is an extra step. Or you can do it similarly to what Inventor does: have a split button and multiple choices of what to create: a 2D sketch, a part, an assembly etc. And give 3rd party WB developers API to 1) plug into that split button menu, and 2) append a new workspace and set WBs visible by default (i.e. define context).

All this will become even easier after some internal cleanup, because it looks like users are not particularly fond of having two 2D sketching workbenches by default and would rather have just one. Which, again, removes the cognitive load.

> I don't know this in details, but I presume ob_refcnt should be 1 right?

Yes, it should be 1. In the meantime I found the root problem. It's hidden in the line `PyObject* item = (*it).ptr();`
The VectorPy class implements the sequence protocol by providing the method sequence_item(), ... Inside there it creates a double object on the fly with `Py_BuildValue("d", a[pos])` and at that point the ref counter is 1. The calling instance is the PyCXX function
```
        virtual T getItem( sequence_index_type i ) const
        {
            return T( asObject( PySequence_GetItem( ptr(), i ) ) );
        }
```
The function asObject() returns a Py::Object and it does NOT increment the counter. If the returned Py::Object is destroyed it decrements the counter to 0 and the double object will be deleted before checking its type.

Since according to the documentation of PySequence_GetItem it returns a new reference the PyCXX code is correct and the function to blame is VectorPy::sequence_item.

So, the problem is caused by creating the double object on the fly instead of holding it inside a list of tuple. This way the ref counter won't be higher than 1 and then it happens that it reaches 0. When it was hold in a list or tuple the function VectorPy::sequence_item would return an object with a ref count of 2 and this way it won't happen that the object will be destroyed too early.

So, the solution is to add a list object to VectorPy and store the double objects there. They will be destroyed together with the VectorPy object.

> Any idea why `operator==` doesn't just delegate to the `data` and `postfix` members, but instead jumps through hoops that may include constructing a whole new `QByteArray`?

The use of `data` and `postfix` in `MappedName` is considered as an implementation details. The reason of the separation is to improve memory efficiency. The same postfix may be attached to many, and sometimes all, resulting subshapes of a boolean operation. To most of outside caller, the `MappedName` is supposed to be treated as a single string. So, two `MappedName`'s are considered the same if their `data+postfix` are the same. One case where two `MappedName` can have different postfix is when the name is converted to a normal string and stored inside a property link, and then read back and converted to `MappedName` to query topological data, where the `postfix` information is lost.


> I think actually raw is used in the QByteArray sense: it purely indicates whether a copy has been made. The Compact function is used to ensure a copy, which is why it then sets raw false, even though it will happily copy null characters.

Yes, that is correct. In other word, `raw` means the data is not owned, and is not safe to store in the element map.

My feeling is somewhat opposite this.

There are several things to do to move the options to the new storage location, and the existing support code for the new location is the only part implemented. And a tiny part it is, changing one path string relating to the options storage location. If this were changed back to use the old location, in the future when a shift to the new location were done fully, it would be trivial to find and change back.

Right now it is just an impediment to other development, an unused stub of code that nevertheless needs to be maintained. If the change were harmless it would not be a problem, but right now the change breaks DXF import.

I would feel quite differently about this if there were a well laid-out plan in place to migrate the options location, with a list of where changes were required and what the changes might be, both in terms of code changes and UI changes. Would Import work differently depending on which workbench is active? What about "Open file"? Would there be separate options for Draft import and TechDraw import? Perhaps such a plan exists and I just haven't found it.

That being said, I do have a different fix for the problem, which changes `ImpExpDxfRead.setOptions` so that, when it is called, the settings that exist in the new options container will be loaded, but settings that do not exist in the new options container are left unchanged. The current behaviour is that settings that do not exist int the container revert to their hard-coded defaults. Because the current code is passing an empty container (`Mod/Import`), this forces all options to their hard-coded defaults. With this alternative proposed change, the options not in the passed container would stay at the settings read by the `ImpExpDxfRead` ctor from the `Mod/Draft` location.

The original issue was about the time taken to import a large file, and I'm not sure that turning the entire drawing into a single object or each layer into a single object would have much effect on the import speed.

Doing so would very likely speed up manipulating the imported drawing since the entire layer/drawing would be a single entity in the underlying topology package, but I'm not sure it would speed up the import itself. One would do almost as well to have a separate post-processing step (one the user invokes separately) that does the merging. This would also give the ability (with a UI for this command) to be more selective about what is merged and would also work for drawings imported from other sources besides DXF/DWG.

In any case if you want to do that, you could use a combination of the existing "Group layers into blocks" and "Use Layers" options:
don't "Group layers into blocks" and don't "Use Layers": Individual drawing objects as direct children of the drawing
don't "Group layers into blocks" and "Use Layers": Individual drawing objects grouped into layers as they were in the DXF file
"Group layers into blocks" and don't "Use Layers": All drawing objects grouped into a single compound
"Group layers into blocks" and "Use Layers": The contents of each DXF layer grouped into a single compound each

Essentially this would interpret "Group layers into blocks" (which I feel is poorly worded for what it does anyway) as "Combine sibling objects into blocks"

The first priority of the topo naming encoding scheme is to generate unique and stable names for geometry elements. Decoding and history tracing is a `good to have` feature, which is why there is no strict syntax definition. Another reason is that, for many cases, there are ambiguities when doing history tracing. You can't get back the source element even with a strict syntax definition. What we should guarantee is that a model done by an old version syntax will work correctly and can continue modeling with new syntax in newer release. The syntax change may break history tracing, which may affect how good the software can auto fix common topological changing problem. But that's acceptable, as long as it can detect the change and report the failure to user in a meaningful way.

With that in mind, you'll see that `TopoShapeOpCodes` is just a convenience to centralize all the model operation code. It's exact content is not that important. I prefer to make it in `Part` workbench, because currently only `Part` and other workbenches that uses `Part` make use of it. It is good not to have duplicate op codes, but not a must. So spread the codes in other workbenches shouldn't be a problem either.

> I will keep pushing for faster iteration in the future. It's unfortunate that we've caused people to rely on the development branch being stable. It's making us be too tentative about merging things. Faster iteration solves a lot of our problems and creates very few new ones.

Brad, here we have diverging views. 

I think it is very fortunate that people rely on master being reasonably stable. Because this ensures we get timely feedback. If master became unstable, (a lot of) people would stop using it and a lot of feedback would only come from (yearly) releases. Intensive testing of master aside, within release cycle corrections are vital for FreeCAD success.

New features are shaped by the fast feedback only because there is feedback. There is feedback because a substantial amount of users understand they can rely on FreeCAD master being reasonably stable.

Of course there is a balance between quality and merge rate. As often in life, virtue lies on the right balance.

Specific of this PR, Ajinkya generally produces good quality code. Some corner cases with unacceptable behaviour were detected. Other unrelated issues were detected. We (mostly Ajinkya) separated ones from the others. Fixed the ones relating to this feature (I presume). And as soon as I  have time (will definitely happen before the weekend), I will test and merge.

Some guidelines remain (this has nothing to do with this PR, it is just general information):
- A PR with well written code has much better chances of being merged early. It also puts a lower burden on the maintainer. For this, I recommend that every contributor critically reads their own code before making the PR.
- A well tested PR has much better chances of being merged early. It also puts a lower burden on the maintainer. For this, the contributor should have some minimal testing in place. Perhaps builds can be given for volunteer testers for some contributions as needed.

My approach may be perceived as egoistic as it leans toward maintainer time. Reality is that what I want is to merge right away. Review code once, test once and hit the button. This leaves more time available for me to review other PRs and to code my own ideas.

This does not mean I do no want to be consulted early if the developer sees impeding difficulties or have doubts about the soundness of the architecture being used. I should be consulted early to avoid loss to effort and frustration. It means that, when the situation is balanced, I can make an optimum allocation of resources, and often, life allowing, I can be reasonably responsive to all.

For times were I cannot be responsive, and other maintainers are not available or prefer to defer to me due to the nature of the PR, I would propose that contributors run development of different features in parallel, so that they are not stopped waiting. If the features are of different WBs, it may be better for diversification, but also several features of a single WB could work.

Ok indeed your part will not export correctly to DXF or DWG because none of the exporters outside CADExchanger is able to handle solids. Solids are actually encoded as ACIS/SAT blocks inside a DXF or DWG file, and that format is proprietary and undocumented, and therefore very hard to support by open-source projects.
So if you use the built-in exporter, only 2D entities are exported. I'm afraid at this point the only way to solve this is by using the CADExchanger addon, which can export a DWG file directly from the FreeCAD solids.

Yes, sorry, mixed my words. I meant "group layers into blocks". This is a remnant from a time when the Draft WB has a block object, which was basically redundant to the Part Compound object, so it ended up being removed.

A compound is an OCC term, it's basically a shape that includes other shapes, without any modification to these shapes. They can be lines, solids, whatever.
There is also a Part object named Part Compound, which allows to add other objects into it and produces a shape that is a compound shape of all its child objects. Basically like an autocad block.

In FreeCAD, creating many objects in the document is very time-consuming. DWG/DXF files typically have a large amount of small objects. Creating the shapes itself does not take so much time. Creating one FreeCAD object for each does. So "packing" all the little lines into one compound shape does speed up the import, a LOT.

Since the "group layers into blocks" option works again, you can easily see the difference if you turn that option on and try to import a big file. One object per layer already solves the problem I guess, but I think having another option to create just one object would be useful as well.

About texts (and dimensions), as they don't have an OCC shape, they can't be included in a compound shape. I'm not really sure what to do here..

What is even more interesting about the export side is that the C++ exporter looks for settings called "maxsegmentlength", "ExportPoints", "DxfVersionOut", and "DiscretizeEllipses" which the options UI does not set (these names to not appear anywhere in the FreeCAD source except in the C++ exporter).

The options UI sets "dxfmesh", "dxfExportBlocks", and "dxfproject" which are used only by the legacy export code in ImportDXF.py.

It looks like the C++ exporter is completely out of touch with the location of the options, or even what the options are.

At least on the import side, both the legacy and C++ code agree on the names of the options (but not on their location), although the C++ importer only looks at three of the dozen or so options.

With @wwmayer 's merging of #8997 the actual problem, per se, is fixed, and in that sense this PR could be dropped.

The changes remaining in this PR are:
1 - Updating the documentation string for readDXF to reflect that it takes a fourth options_source argument
2 - Changing the semantics of ImpExpDXFRead.setOptions() so that settings found in the given source are applied to existing loaded settings rather than to coded-in fixed settings to produce the new loaded settings.

I think item 1 is still worth doing, if only to keep documentation up to date with code.

Item 2 is a functional change, and I feel it is a better way to do things, but it could affect 3rd party code that tries to do importing because the import setting in the dialog would suddenly be applied even though the 3rd party code thought a different option set had been loaded (which did not provide settings for everything). This is an incomplete solution to the problem that there are too many pieces of code trying to load the settings, and is also related to the incomplete separation of the legacy and C++ importers (insofar as parts of importDXF.py are always called, and this decides whether to use the bulk of importDXF.py to do the import or to use the C++ importer to do most of the work (except for that convert_draft_texts thing)

Wouldn't the neural network edge matching be essentially the same as the scoring algorithm, unless you'd have much more extraneous neurons that you'd train with some test data.  The difficulty would be obtaining good-enough large set of hand-fixed cases, and probably the slowness of the algorithm if there are enough neurons.  Thus, I'd suggest to at least first implement the simpler scoring algorithm.

In general I guess the scoring algorithm should give highest scores for exact matches, high scores for edge type matches, and medium linearly adjustable scores for scaled for position differences, length differences, angular differences for straight edges, radius differences, etc, so that the score is highest when difference is zero, and probably go by difference squared type of scaling to reduce the score.  Spline scoring I have no idea about.

For solving the problem with the scoring algorithm, there are the difficult cases of scale change and the ISO count.  The scale change should probably be detected independently (there are two sub-cases, changing the TD scale and scaling the 3D model itself).  The ISO count case is more difficult, because an edge dimension might be split into a dimension with the end points at two different edges (you'd have to actually track the vertices to solve this).

I was referring to the C++ importer. You are right, the colors are never imported, even without grouping into blocks.

In the legacy importer, colors are indeed imported for objects individually, not when grouped.

DXF layers have a color property and that color is used for entities whose individual color is "ByLayer".
When making a Freecad Compound from a DXF layer it would be great if the Freecad color matched the color of the DXF layer.
Obviously DXF entities whose color is not "ByLayer" will not have their correct color when grouped in a Compound (it is often considered as bad practice to set entity colors individually in Autocad anyway).

Here are the python commands that i was using after the import as a proof of concept (it doesn't work 100%, sometimes the freecad object has not exactly the same name as the layer...):

```
import ezdxf
doc = ezdxf.readfile("file.dxf")
for layer in doc.layers:
    rgb_color = ((0, 0, 0) if layer.color == 7 else ezdxf.colors.aci2rgb(layer.color))
    fc_color = tuple(a / 255 for a in rgb_color)
    # print(layer.dxf.name, layer.color, rgb_color, fc_color)
    obj = App.ActiveDocument.getObject(layer.dxf.name)
    if obj:
        obj.ViewObject.PointColor = fc_color
        obj.ViewObject.LineColor = fc_color
        obj.ViewObject.ShapeColor = fc_color
    else:
        print("Layer not found", layer.dxf.name)
```

When a ViewProvider gets double clicked, this calls ```Gui::Document::setEdit```, which calls ```Gui::Application::setEditDocument```. The latter is responsible for setting the edit document (Gui::Application::Instance->editDocument()).

From there it gets to the hierarchy of ViewProviders ```setEdit```, ultimately ```ViewProviderSketch::setEdit```. Therefore, I think it should be expected behaviour not to have a ```nullptr``` editDocument at this function. 

The way to reproduce the crash in the issue (for which I am thankful to the author of the issue), shows that when reject is called, the editDocument becomes nullptr at ViewProviderSketch::setEdit. Because at this point the editDocument should be preserved and calling ->reject nullifies this pointer (when removing the dialog), then 
either:
- ```reject``` is not doing what it should by making the editDocument nullptr,
or
- ```reject``` should never be called at ```ViewProvider::setEdit``` because it is not intended for this use case.

Then the solution may be:
either:
(a) to modify ```reject``` so that it does not make the editDocument nullptr,
or
(b) to use another function, such as closeDialog(), i.e. what @xtemp09 proposes here.

> FreeCAD cannot have a non-admin privileges if the user has already admin privileges.

This is verifiable false. Please understand that in Windows there is a difference between being an admin (that is, being logged in as an account with admin privileges) and running a program as Admin.

Running any program while you are an administrator does not automatically grant it administrator rights. The rights have to be explicitly granted (Run As Administrator) or asked for (UAC Prompt). You can verify this yourself by running, for example, notepad and trying to save a file to C:\Program Files. Regardless of if you are an admin or not, your access will be denied. Then, run it using the Run As Administrator context menu option and you will be allow to save it.

When running FreeCAD normally (that is, after it has been installed and you launch it from the start menu or elsewhere), it correct uses the non-privileged role most normal applications use (the first instance of notepad in the above example). However, when it is launched at the end of the installation, it retains the admin rights granted to the installer, ie. without you having to explicitly use the Run As Administrator option.

May I express some concerns about this system here?

In Qt, when you close a window, the system **indirectly** notifies the window via _signal/slot_ mechanism by invocation of `onClose()` method. One can see here[^2] and here[^3] how dialog reacts differently on the same changeEvent.

In FreeCAD, a dialog **directly** closes or, rarely, rejects, another dialog. This approach opposes the Qt way and is officially discouraged.[^1] In my humble opinion, the system should use the Qt way. Who knows what kind of problems it can bring in the future.

[^1]: https://wiki.qt.io/How_to_Use_Signals_and_Slots



[^2]: https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/f1fc50595535ee5ae668a12f95bf0c28bffc9d63/src/Mod/Fem/Gui/DlgSettingsFemCcxImp.cpp#L128-L138

[^3]: https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/f1fc50595535ee5ae668a12f95bf0c28bffc9d63/src/Mod/Fem/Gui/DlgSettingsFemElmerImp.cpp#L89-L97

Done with Phase One!

I wanted to express my gratitude for all the hard work everyone put into phase 1 of this project. It was a massive undertaking, and you all went above and beyond to import/test/refactor RealThunder’s working code!

Now it is time for phase 2 and I can't wait to see what we can accomplish together.

While I have been researching what should be in this phase, I’m not the FreeCAD expert you all are; so I’m asking for help! I’m hoping to have all of the next steps laid out by Friday, and getting comments and suggestions from the experts is invaluable!

The general idea for phase 2 is adding the algorithm but not actually using it yet. The big goal is good consistent testing; and then updating/modifying that testing in phase 3 as we inevitably learn more.

Specifically, it will be adding the naming algorithm. Some of that is found in the ElementMap class. I suspect that will be step 1 of phase 2.

And, I was thinking this will also mean that we go ahead and add the `ElementMapPtr _ElementMap` item to the ComplexGeoData class with its supporting methods (and possibly TopoShape). However, those methods would not yet be called in the live FreeCAD code. They are only called by the testing files.

We might also want to add indirect support into the Sketcher workbench, but I’ve not really started looking at it to know what that would involve. **Any Sketcher enthusiasts around?**

Thanks, @JohnAD, your organization of the project has been invaluable, this is an excellent team effort. And aren't we **all** Sketcher enthusiasts?! 😁 Of course, @abdullahtahiriyo is really The Dude there.

@JohnAD 

Feel free to ask any questions you want about the existing code of the Sketcher. Hopefully, I should be able to answer most.

One issue that was "synchronised" in the past between RT's branch and master relates to the storage of IDs for geometry. The Sketcher uses ```Part::Geometry``` for storing geometry related data. 

Here I set strong boundary that any Sketcher related data structures should not pollute Part. 

From the many solutions possible, the one chosen was to provide support for what is called ```Part::GeometryExtensions``` (not to be mixed up with App:Extension, it has nothing to do). A Part::Geometry has the ability to store a number of extensions. This enables every module using ```Part::Geometry``` to see just a ```Part::Geometry``, and then every module will know about its extensions, which can be used to retrieve module specific data. This framework is also used to separate concerns between App (```Sketcher```) and Gui (```SketcherGui```), as some extensions carry pure visualisation data (scaling factors, visual layer Ids) while others carry core App data (identifiers, construction/nonconstruction, type of internal geometry, ...). 

All that is just to provide some basic background to where the geometry data is stored and why. 

So coming back to storage of geometry identifiers, ```Sketcher::SketchGeometryExtension``` is the extension where all the identifiers for regular geometry are stored. This includes the Id (getId) that is only used in RT's branch. In fact, while it exists in the class ```Sketcher::SketchGeometryExtension``` it is not even serialised during persistence (it is serialised in RT's branch only). This was done so that data is not inconsistent between RT's branch format and master, and to facilitate future migrations. So the piece of information here is: that extension is where regular geometry identifiers are to be stored.

To enable a transparent use of Geometry and ```SketchGeometryExtension``` at Sketcher level,, ```Sketcher::GeometryFacade```  was created, which is nothing but a facade to be able to access any relevant information about regular geometry directly, no matter if it is stored in the ```Part::Geometry``` or in the sketcher extension.

One meaningful difference between RT's branch and master that has some bearing in toponaming is external geometry. External Geometry comprises two aspects: (1) geometry aspect (Part::Geometry) and (2) link aspects (where outside the sketcher they connect to). This is stored as an internal array at SketchObject level for master, but it is (or perhaps was) integrated into geometry in RT's branch.

In master there is a ```Sketcher::ExternalGeometryExtension``` that was created to store the data necessary for RT's branch. It is unused in master. It was put there to limit divergence of RT's branch, so that in the future it would be easier to merge any development.

I think that is about what the Sketcher has as in-place regarding interfaces with toponaming code. Feel free to ask questions.

Unrelated to this interface, but related to code changes activity:
I am currently thinking about how to refactor the Sketcher to make use of smartpointers for geometry, so basically going from ```Part::Geometry *``` to ```std::shared_ptr<Part::Geometry>``` and its weak pointer counterpart. This means there are likely to be changes to ```Part::PropertyGeometryList``` and ```Sketcher::GeometryFacade```, which will call for quite some code changes all around (mostly within the Sketcher WB, other than the list itself), as that is the most used data structure in the Sketcher.

Those changes should not impact toponaming support, but depending on what exactly the current Sketcher toponaming support entails, they might lead to (easy to resolve but numerous) prospective merge conflicts.

In CFD, mesh quality is everything.   More mesh engines equal better meshing options.   For a lot of models with complex geometry snappyHexMesh creates a really good mesh.   Ditto cfmesh.   gmsh, it turns out, has an option (boundary meshing) that is very helpful for thin flow surfaces such as airfoils and heat exchanger fins.

The issue with importing a FEM mesh is the matching of surfaces in the FreeCAD model to the patches in the FEM mesh. I want to point out there are four approaches to using conda as a dependency management system, of which the `conda-devenv` approach is just one.

1. `conda build`:
    Running `conda build` with the appropriate parameters to not use a container and keep the build environment using the upstream `freecad-feedstock`.  This will go through the process of building FreeCAD, but also leave the environment with the dependencies installed.  This approach is not very clean and wastes significant time compiling a version of FreeCAD outside the development environment.
2. `conda install -c conda-forge freecad-devel`:
    I have a couple of PRs on `freecad-feedstock` that have been received positively by @looooo to create a new package `freecad-devel` that contains the build dependencies ([#87](https://github.com/conda-forge/freecad-feedstock/pull/87) and [#88](https://github.com/conda-forge/freecad-feedstock/pull/88)).   Unfortunately I cannot seem to figure out the magic to get the CI/CD system to build these packages.  I can build them locally without issue using both `conda build .` using the host conda install, as well as using the upstream docker containers via the `build-locally.py` script.  A con for this method is that it's unlinked with the FreeCAD source tree, so changes to dependencies would need to be managed in `freecad-feedstock` and not in `FreeCAD`.
3. `conda env`:
    Conda provides a means to exporting and restoring an environment.  Unfortunately there is no template functionality as there is via `conda-build` this means that each configuration of OS, CPU architecture, and software versions would each need their own env files that will need to be maintained over time.  By including the environment files, build dependencies can be managed via the same PR that adds or removes them.  The project [`mantid`](https://github.com/mantidproject/mantid) uses this approach, but only supports x86_64 architectures.
4. `conda devenv`: (this approach)
    `conda-devenv` preprocesses a templated devenv file to generate and apply an environment file.  This restores most of the `conda build` functionality not available in `conda env` to simplify OS, architecture, and versioning.  Unfortunately the templating engine is less expressive than `conda build` and is missing selectors for `aarch64`, `armv7`, etc, but it is sufficient for the majority of users.  This approach keeps the dependencies tied in with the `FreeCAD` source tree, permitting dependency management via PR.

My personal preference is towards a `freecad-devel` package, but the challenges associated with getting it functioning and maintained lead me to believe that `conda devenv` may be better, especially if the template limitations are addressed.

shapes = [obj for obj in doc.Objects if hasattr(obj, 'Shape')

Scalar tests use an absolute tolerance of 5 as the preliminary check.

Angular tests (directions) use a tolerance of M_PI / 10.0 as the preliminary check.

Bounding Box test is binary: +1 if boxes overlap, -1 if they don't.

The reason for the other problem is that the current state of all toolbars is saved when leaving edit mode. But because the toggle action is visible the function ToolBarManager::saveState() also saves the state of the editing toolbars. Later when quitting the application the toggle actions are invisible again and thus ToolBarManager::saveState() ignores the new state. This means that the user.cfg has stored the state when the editing toolbars were visible which isn't necessarily the last state.
