Well, all that you wrote is perfectly correct and I agree with it. But IMO this is looking at the problem from the wrong side. :wink: 

> The value of `double next = std::nextafter(8.2, 9.0);` is guaranteed to be different to 8.2. When writing with digits10 the text output is the same, i.e. when reading it in we have a loss of accuracy.

Which is excellent. We have an inner precision better than the one we display. This is precisely what we want.
Oppositely, your previous posts proved that using `max_digits10 +1` can't guarantee that all inputs aren't actually possible as `8.2` and its `nextafter` are separated by more than 1 less-significant digit.

> Also the value of `std::numeric_limits<double>::epsilon()` is guaranteed to be higher than the written 0.0

Again, I have no doubt that it internally is. And having displayed as 0.0 is excellent as this also proves that our display precision is compatible with internal precision.

> The documentation of max_digits10 says:
> 
> > Unlike most mathematical operations, the conversion of a floating-point value to text and back is exact as long as at least max_digits10 were used (9 for float, 17 for double): it is guaranteed to produce the same floating-point value, even though the intermediate text representation is not exact. It may take over a hundred decimal digits to represent the precise value of a float in decimal notation.

True. But basically we do the opposite : string -> value -> string. And in this case this documentation doesn't apply. It even is the "opposite", we have issues using a more than max_digits10 value to string conversion. Which is normal.

> So, this means when serializing a double as string then by using max_digits10 (which is even higher than digits10 + 1) it's guaranteed that the double converted from the string is equal. With digits10 we lose precision.

But we need to lose precision in our case. :wink: This is a tradeoff to ensure we correctly display the user input.

> So, the question is whether the change could cause possible regressions elsewhere.

I quickly checked and `toString()` calls seem to be only used for presentation so it shouldn't create any regression.
And anyway if it would, that would be an error made somewhere else in the code to use this IMO.
And well, admittedly it solves the bug seen on the forum. :wink:

> It seems like if both `_sid` and `stringID._sid` are `nullptr`, then the comparison should be `false` (because they are effectively equal), right?

Yes, you are correct. My mistake.



> `_sid` is a pointer, so it's checking whether the two refs refer to literally the same `StringID` object, not whether the two SIDs are equal to one another

`StringID` instances are supposed to be uniquely generated by `StringHasher`, so it is enough to only compare the pointer value. It does not make much sense mixing `StringID`s from different `StringHasher`s, which belong to other documents/objects, because even if they contain the same textual content, they are referring to different geometry.

Alright, I tested my assumption; `man 3 free` says:

> Starting in macOS 13, iOS 16.1 and aligned releases, free(3) fully zeroes many blocks immediately. This may expose some previously-silent bugs in existing applications.  In particular, read-after-free bugs may now observe zeroes instead of the previous content of an allocation, and write-after-free bugs may cause calloc(3) to return non-zero memory. MallocZeroOnFree can be set to 0 or 1 to explicitly disable or enable this zeroing behavior to aid in diagnosing such bugs.  Support for this environment variable will eventually be removed, and it should not be used by shipping software.

When running freecad with `MallocZeroOnFree=0`, the error is indeed gone.
So we're looking for a use-after-free bug here.

I'm up to my eyeballs trying to figure out some stuff at the moment, but I am happy to share some opinion.

The exercise here was to "fix" one tiny part of the system in isolation. I think this is the opposite to what should be happening. Each tiny part is part of the whole and if the fundamental design criteria are set for the whole then doing one part is relatively simple.

Design is part art, part science. There are people who are good at it, just like some people can draw while others (like me) can't. But most of us recognise really slick design, mainly because it is unobtrusive.

Programmers are notoriously bad. Witness how the discussion goes round in circles almost every time a change is proposed. But whose opinions do you listen to? Are they based on UI/UX knowledge? Can they explain in human engineering terms?

Users are useful but not perhaps in the way they think. Their frustrations are manifested in different ways and filtering these to identify underlying issues is not easy. For mine, there needs to develop a culture of respectfully listening to users and reading beyond their words. Old saying: "if you don't find the bugs, your users certainly will". Users are a tremendous resource, not to mention your customers. And there's a lot more of them than you.

It seems QT is capable of magnificent UI. How?

I think the deceptively simple question that really needs answering is "what are the defining characteristics of the UI we want to have", and then apply that consistently.

Use View3DInventorViewer::getPointOnScreen to convert 3d into 2d coordinates. But note, that the returned SbVec2s is in Inventor coordinates that begin at bottom left, not at top left. So, to get it in Qt coordinates you have to compute `y = height - y`.

There is currently nothing implemented to notify widgets. An option is to implement a special SoEngine that emits a signal when one of the fields of an camera node has changed.

> Do you perhaps have some hints how this should be done ? I mean the global architecture.

Adding a widget as a child of the 3d viewer works but you cannot rotate the widget as shown in your image. For that case you have to use the capabilities of the QGraphicsView.

In FreeCAD we have changed the Quarter code so that QuarterWidget doesn't inherit from QopenGLWidget but QGraphicsView which opens a lot more possibilities adding widgets to the 3d view. So, an alternative is to use a QGraphicsProxyWidget that contains the spin box and can be added to the QGraphicsScene.

The `StringHasher` can be considered as a table for storing unique strings. Although it works with any string, it is mostly optimized to store encoded element names (i.e. `MappedName`). I'll use a simple example to illustrate how element names are encode and stored in `StringHasher`.

Let's start from a box. None of its element name is encoded. So we have Face1, Face2, etc. When it is fused with another shape, one of its changed face will be named as `Face3;:M;FUS;:Hb:7,F`. Here, `Face3` is the source element name of the box, called as the `prefix` of the name and stored in `MappedName::data`. The rest of the name, `;:M;FUS;:Hb:7,F`, is store in `MappedName::postfix`. `StringHasher` is not used at the current stage. Well actually it is used to shorten names for those elements that are generated/modified from more than one elements (i.e. more than one source element), but it is out of the scope of this illustration.

Now, when the fusion shape is again fused with a third shape, the above face is changed again and now named as `#38;:M;FUS;:Hd:7,F`. The prefix `#38` is a `StringID` stored inside a `StringHasher`, obtained by calling `StringHasher::getID(MappedName)`. The 38 here is a hex number, acting as a key mapping to a string that is the source element name, `Face3;:M;FUS;:Hb:7,F`. If `StringHasher` were to naively store the string as it is, then each element name of the source shape will be a unique entry in the table, because the postfix contains a unique ID of each object, for history tracing purpose. Instead, `StringHasher` sotres the prefix and postfix separately similar to `MappedName`.

For prefix, if it is an `IndexedName`, e.g. `Face3` in this case, then only the element type string `Face` will be stored in `StringID`, while the index is stored in the returned `StringIDRef` in `StringIDRef::_index`. Flag `StringID::Indexed` is used to mark this case. The encoded prefix is stored in the related string ID vector, `StringID::_sids`. Note that this optimization is causing some problem during recompute and is later [restricted](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/140236c7747aecaedd7e199a05ee81c1081378d9/src/App/StringHasher.cpp#L266) to only names without postfix. I haven't got time look deep into it yet.

For postfix, if it is not already encoded (i.e. contains no `StringID`), it will be stored in `StringHasher` by calling `StringHasher::getID(QByteArray)` and the returned string ID put in the related string ID vector, `StringID::_sids`. Flag `StringID::PostfixEncoded` is used to mark this case. And `StringID::_postfix` will be assigned the text form of the `StringID`.

Finally, we get to the code you are referring to. For that, let's consider an extra fusion operation, which changes the face `#38;:M;FUS;:Hd:7,F` into `#71;:M;FUS;:Hf:7,F`. `#71` is the string ID that refers to the string `#38;:M;FUS;:Hd:7,F`, where `#38` is the prefix, and the rest is the postfix. For prefix that is also a `StringID`, it is stored in the related string ID, `StringID::_sids`, and marked by flag `StringID::PrefixID`. If the prefix is not only a `StringID`, but also with extra index (e.g. as mentioned above, `Face3` will only store `Face` as string ID, say `#2`, with index stored in `StringIDRef`, represented in text form as `#2:3`), then it will be marked by flag `StringID::PrefixIDIndex`. In both cases, the code will try to put the existing `StringID` in a predefined position in the related string ID vector, for saving/restoring purpose.

Let's talk more about selecting points outside the image boundary.  

In the vast majority of cases, the user is selecting two points inside the image.  For that reason, it's helpful to bound the selection points inside the image.  It makes it easier to position the points accurately.  

I can only imagine a single use-case where letting the user set points outside is valuable:   When the user has an image that is cropped so the target point they want to select isn't included but where the image still has enough information that the user can roughly guess where the endpoint should be.  That's a pretty rare case.   Are there others?

If there are valid cases, then 
1) We ALWAYS let the user select outside the image and this makes selection harder in the most common cases
2) We provide a control to turn on outside selection.  This takes up screen and the user has to understand what the control does.

If we're just including this feature because it's cool and _might_ be useful to someone in the future, I would suggest removing it until users ask for it.  The cognitive burden of understanding it is higher than the value of the feature at this point.

Regarding improving the selection of things I had a look. Here are my notes for reference. Please note that I'm not 100% sure about those.
 
- It seems that the selection rely on `View3DInventorViewer::getPointOnRay`.
This function seems to be getting a single `SoPickedPoint `with `SoRayPickAction.getPickedPoint()`.
- This SoPickedPoint seems to be processed in the different workbenches. For example in sketcher it is processed in : `EditModeCoinManager::detectPreselection`.

So the selection seems to rely on SoRayPickAction. From [its doc](https://www.openinventor.com/reference-manuals/NewRefMan1030/RefManJava/com/openinventor/inventor/actions/SoRayPickAction.html) we can read that it is also possible to get a list of points hit by the ray and not just one : 

> Callers can request the action to compute all intersections along the ray (sorted closest to farthest) by setting the pickAll flag to true. By default, the action computes only the closest intersection.

So this makes me think that by using `getPickedPoint` we only get the item that is the closest to the camera. Which would explain the strange behaviour you guys mentioned.

So I think we should instead get the list of points, then process this list in each workbenches to determine which feature to select. Then we can set rules like 'Points are prioritary on edges' and 'edges are prioritary on faces'.

If someone can confirm or deny or comment my assumptions ?

From my experience much of the pick behavior on icons and text seem to be on the painted pixels of the particular icon or text you are selecting, where I'd prefer a bounding box around said text or icon or even the centroid of it plus a select radius.  
This results in frustration trying to double-click on a dimension, but if my pick radius is small, I have to make sure my pointer is on the letter strokes to do that.  More than once I've double-clicked in the middle of a zero to, well, zero effect.

Like PaddleStroke said, but include the constraint icons to the class containing points for the selection priority rules.
Could do it with a icon/text centroid plus pickable radius and pick radius overlap, once they overlap it's a potential pick, then the rules would come into play on the click event.

The hand/eye coordination is 2D, so pick behavior, ideally, should follow that.  It would solve the foreground line picked over the slightly background line that is closer to pick center.  If far background geometry is desired to be pickable, in the case of wireframe, or transparent geometry, those could still be picked, but maybe using an ALT to a stack selection dialog.

Hunting to click this much makes me pine for Catia, and that's just sad.

In my opinion there are two good options to implement this. 
1. Make the pop-up appear at a fixed location on screen, like Krita (so you know where you should look)
2. Make the pop-up appear next to the cursor (which is where you are always looking)

The third possibility is what Triplus' Launcher does, which is add the search box to a panel. This is also what Qgis (Qt based FOSS) does. So perhaps it's possible to look at the Qt code for this. But, showing it in a fixed location always consumes UI space even if you are not using the command search. Which is why I think it is the lesser option of the three. You can indeed click on the search bar, but with option 1 or 2, you can still invoke search with a hotkey.

@Syres916, might I ask, why do you write in a very strange way?
```ruby
bodyMessageStream << ". "
```

To my poor knowledge of English, full stop is supposed to be in the end of a sentence. You write it separately, avoiding `QObject::tr`.

Why do you write in this way? How do you think it can be translated into Armenian, Bengali, Hindi, Hebrew and many other languages? When you write like this:
```ruby
bodyMessageStream << QObject::tr(Full sentence)
```
It can be translated. When you write like this:
```ruby

bodyMessageStream << QObject::tr(some fragment) << comma << QObject::tr(sentence without full stop) << full stop << QObject::tr(some fragment)

```

You put translator in a very difficult position. Some languages have differrent word order, different punctuation marks. Moreover, people at crowdin are supposed to deduce what you want to say. It's impossible to understand what you are trying to say looking at a fragment instead of a sentence.

@abdullahtahiriyo @AjinkyaDahale what do you think of this issue? should we keep it open? I'm inclined to consider this user error and close it. I believe the problem comes from having these horizontal and vertical distance constraints with expressions bound to the radius of the circle:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/36372335/232160355-88da2de1-79d7-4dcf-ba3d-28b780e055ff.png)

I believe when you change the radius constraint, sketcher tries to solve this before evaluating the expressions
If the value goes up the constraint is still valid even without updating the expressions so it is accepted then leads to the expected result once the expressions are evaluated.
If the value goes down the constraint is invalid in combination with the not updated constraints so the change is rejected before ever evaluating the expressions

I came to this conclusion after removing the expressions and then testing the behavior when changing the radius value without changing or after having changed the distance values manually.

To execute the sketcher tests only you can use the following command line
```sh
./build-pr9044/bin/FreeCAD -c -M FreeCAD-git/src/Mod/Sketcher -t TestSketcherApp.TestSketcherSolver
```
Replace `build-pr9044/bin/FreeCAD` by the path to your FreeCAD executable and `FreeCAD-git/` by the location of your source tree relatively to your current working dir.
`-c` (`--console`) avoids starting the GUI, which means you can run your tests *much* faster.
`-M <path>` (`--module-path <path>`) allows you to prepend a path to FreeCAD's module search path. I use this when working on python-only stuff to not having to recompile. You can omit this, but then you have to deploy your changed .py-files manually or you have to work outside of your source tree.
`-t <test case>` (`--run-test <test case>`) tells FreeCAD to execute the specified test case.

Note that in the first of the new tests, `testCircleToLineDistance_Driving_Passant`, the solver fails to converge.

Hi @chennes! I tried a different route.
The main idea is that the `stack` could contain things that are _just_ `SoNode*`s instead of _full_ `SoFCSelectionRoot*`. Therefore I changed the type of `stack` and I try to cast the node that is expected to be as `SoFCSelectionRoot*`, if this is not the case I behave like it did not exist. In this way it much less strict than my previous attempt, and obviously it does not trigger UB.

One relatively minor nitpick: I know _a priori_ that a pointer inside `stack` is _exactly_ a `SoFCSelectionRoot*` or just a generic `SoNode*` I am not really interested into. Therefore, just theoretically, instead of using a `SoNode*` and then doing dynamic casts, it could be possible to use a `std::variant<SoNode*, SoFSelectionRoot*>` and totally avoid RTTI. However doing so will surely decrease the readability of the code (`std::variant` is not exactly ergonomic to use), and at the same time we will double the amount of memory needed by `stack` because of a single bit of information, which would be a bit a shame.
I think that in this case maybe just using dynamic casts is good enough, but let me know what you think.

Thanks in advance!

I have found the real root cause of all this silliness:  the table cells are getting word-wrapped and it sees the colon as a breakable character. 
`
        self.form.toolControllerList.setWordWrap(False)`

The concise H and V are still beneficial but the reason it breaks on words and not chars is because of word wrap. Then obviously the wrapped bit is invisible because the rows only display one line. Qt adds the ellipsis to show it is truncated by being wrapped.  There should be some mention of this in doc of the elide functions and ElideMode . 

Once WordWrap is false you get character based eliding and a much more sensible and useful display.

> `1m 10 mm` is not supported syntax AFAIK, write `1.010 m` or `1m + 10mm` instead. Mathematical operations are supported in the input boxes so certain syntax rules are required. The parser was changed recently also so behavior for some of these situations might have changed in latest dev versions, however unsupported syntax will still fail.

Fractional data entry UX should be consistent across mixed-units. It is clear what the intent is of `1m 10+3/4in` or `3.2yd 20/4mm` even if these are silly use cases. These are user input & display data not simple mathematical operations. What is not easy to parse we should make easier to parse: bracketing for mixed-value statements?

`[3.2yd 10ft 3/4in 6m 4in]` => re-ordered to relative size of each unit `[6m 3.2yd 10ft 4+3/4in]`

`[3.2yd 6m 10ft 4+3/4in] * 4` => distribute the multiply `[24m 12.8yd 40ft 19in]`

optional type conversion heuristics between compatible fractional and decimal units
`[24m 12.8yd 40ft 19in]` => at 1/8th inch resolution `[24m 13yd 34ft 4.1 + 1/2in]`

unit-less zero
`[1m 10mm]` => positive method A
`0+[1m 10mm]` => positive method A
`0-[1m 10mm]` => negative method A

unary positive or negative within the brackets leading the value.
`[+1m 10mm]` => positive method B
`[-1m 10mm]` => negative method B

methods A and B reserved for whatever makes the most sense, for example type conversion heuristics on or off. The user should be able to express the value as "I entered this. Leave it alone, it's fine like it is." or as "Can you please re-shuffle this and make it better for me? Thanks." This is where "zero" needs to be unit-less, so you can do something like
`0+[+1m 10mm]` => ?
`0+[-1m 10mm]` => ?
`0-[+1m 10mm]` => ?
`0-[-1m 10mm]` => ?

`[1m 10+3/4in] / 3` => distribute the division `[1/3m 10/3+3/12in]`

Looks weird? Users do weird things and that is okay. They can fix their mistakes but we should not introduce new mistakes by assuming absolutely everything is a mathematical expression.

I don't know if we're using brackets already for anything, but something like this would be easy to convey to the user as "Tip: use brackets for fractional and mixed-unit values".

Edit: Non-unary plus and minus should be the same meaning as a numeric separator within the value
`[5'+3-3/4in]` => `[5ft 3 3/4in]`

* We can decide what context string is used for exceptions (e.g. "Exception")
* Mark then the text as `throw Base::ValueError(QT_TRANSLATE_NOOP("Exception", "Error: Result is self intersecting"));`
* In the dialog or wherever it's shown we translate it: `qApp->translate("Exception", exc.what())`

The whole point is to have a reliable context string

> while I was scrolling through I saw that CmdShapeInfo isn't being translated -- do you know if there was a reason for that

The command doesn't even do anything any more. It must be checked what happened to it, and -- if needed -- removed completely.

> Also, CmdPartSectionCut doesn't have its sGroup entry translated.

Having the group name marked for translation has the side-effect that for every command the same text must be translated over and over again. To reduce this extra effort we once have decided to not mark the group name any more but instead add the line `qApp->translate("CommandGroup", "View");` so that it must be translated only once.

So far this is only implemented for the core system and the Sketcher module.

So, not marking the group name for translation is correct and we should start to migrate all other modules, too.

I guess the tests are supposed to work with `std::vector<Constraint*>` and `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Constraint>`. Unless the tests need to access the value of the pointer, two things can be done to make things work on both:
1. Use `clist.cbegin()` and `clist.cend()`. (actually, probably I should make it `std::vector<const std::unique_ptr<Constraint>`... but it is a good idea, anyway, because you probably do not want to change the pointers)
2. Use `auto& constraint` in those "lambda functions", because `std::unique_ptr` cannot be copied.

>     (actually, probably I should make it `std::vector<const std::unique_ptr<Constraint>`... but it is a good idea, anyway, because you probably do not want to change the pointers)

So there's a lot happening here, and I'm trying to figure out how to approach this. Some thoughts:
1. We need to add a new parameter for the constraint, which for point-on-object became the value of the consttraint. If the constraint is between two splines and a point, this would have to be two values---not a problem since constraints can have two values. However, angle-via-point already has one value, viz. the angle between the curves.
2. The order in which the curves are provided matter. When calling the solver constraint creator, this order can get mixed up. So that also may be create unintended consequences.
3. There is currently an issue when drawing angle constraints: the angle is not drawn properly. This may be an ordering issue.
4. We need to tie point-on-object and angle-via-point so that they use the same curve parameter for the b-spline. So both constraints have to be made at the same time. However, this is different from how it works with other curves like hyperbolas. I've tried to avoid this as much as possible but this can still have unintended consequences, for example, if the same point is used for other constraints, some partial redundancy is detected.
5. The constraint depends also on the direction of the curves. A B-spline and another exactly reverse B-spline will behave very differently.

`Unit tests` come into their own when a large body of same are developed, each targeting a very small, isolated, "unit" of code. They run VERY fast. Because of the speed, a developer can run unit tests very frequently. This leads to the concept of TDD (Test Driven Development).

The problem though, is getting the code into so-called `testable` state. That is to say in a form where unit tests can be applied, which is dictated by dependencies, statics, singletons, complexity. Basically much of the stuff espoused by the likes of Uncle Bob Martin and others over the last 20 + years. FreeCAD is large, old legacy code, and in the main not `testable`.

As FreeCAD has not been written with unit tests in mind, the alternative is to perform so-called integration tests. These each encompass a range of classes, files etc in each test. Typically, due to the many dependencies, they run much, much slower.

FreeCAD has say 5000 classes etc. If each has say 20 tests, and they each take 20mS that is 33 minutes run time. They will not be run very frequently!

I have had well over 100 unit tests and cannot get the run time to register 1 mS. 

A **_single_** integration test introduced for metadata took variously from 8 to 120 mS.

Integration tests aare terrific, just keep them separate.

I implemented the high priority picking group in my branch, not the low priority, but the same principle applies. The scene of a FreeCAD document is grouped under a `SoFCUnifiedSelection` node. The picking is initiated in `SoFCUnifiedSelection::handleEvent()` by traversing a `SoRayPick` action down the scene node. I added a new group node at the same hierarchy as the scene node, and perform a picking traversal through that node before the normal picking. Similarly, low priority picking can be done by adding another group node at the same hierarchy and perform an extra picking traversal. But, that would involve some changes to the core, which I think is outside the scope of this PR.
Indeed outside the scope, I guess for now we make it unpickable (maybe optionally?) and then we'll see when we can work on implementing selection priorities in the core.

I agree that the current behavior of the attachment modes is inconsistent - but I don't think the best way to go is to change the behavior of App.Rotation(v1,v2,v3, 'XYZ') modes when the input vector(s) are zero. Zero vectors are of course invalid, as they are supposed to represent directions, so we are indeed free to do what we want with them. 

let

```
V = App.Vector
R = App.Rotation
vx = V(1,0,0)
vy = V(0,1,0)
vz = V(0,0,1)
def T(rot):
    print(f'vx->{rot*vx}\nvy->{rot*vy}\nvz->{rot*vz}\n')

```

Consider the rotation  R(vx, -f*vz, vy) where f>=0 is a float. Currently:

```
>>> T(R(vx, -f*vz, vy, 'YZX'))
vx->Vector (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)
vy->Vector (0.0, 2.220446049250313e-16, -1.0)
vz->Vector (0.0, 1.0, 2.220446049250313e-16)

>>> f =0
>>> T(R(vx, -f*vz, vy, 'YZX'))
vx->Vector (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)
vy->Vector (0.0, 2.220446049250313e-16, -1.0)
vz->Vector (0.0, 1.0, 2.220446049250313e-16)

```


So when f=0 the algorithm continuously reverts to the same rotation. However, with the proposed algorithm, 
 R(vx, 0, vy, 'YZX') would evaluate as  R(vx, vy, vy, 'YZX')

 ```
>>> T(R(vx, vy, vy, 'YZX'))
vx->Vector (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)
vy->Vector (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)
vz->Vector (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)
```

which would be discontinuous at f=0

I agree with your proposal

"I like to suggest that the "hint" direction instead uses the local axis corresponding to the last character."

but I think the 'fix' should be directed at the attachment modes - in the situation where insufficient references are provided to pin down the axial rotation.
 So, for instance, for 'OYZ', if no reference is provided for the Z direction hint, the local Z direction is used, as proposed. 

This still leaves the question of what to do if the Y-direction selected is the same as the local z-axis, thus providing no hint direction.  One possibility might be to do the rotation in the (y, newy) plane. App.Rotation(y, newy) - another might be to make the OYZ unavailable until a further selection is made.

Yes.  Continuity is not a particularly good argument.  
    It makes me uneasy to rely on undocumented behavior of App.Rotation(a,b,c, 'XYZ') for invalid inputs  (which includes not only zero vectors, but equal ones for the priority ones.)  to fix a higher level function.  What it does now is not unreasonable and who knows what code might rely on it corner cases.
   
 As  I said before, I would prefer the logic of the Attachment modes to be where ambiguities are resolved. But if we change the logic there, it could still break previously constructed models.   If we had an empty canvas, it could be done better, but it isn't clear to me that changing the behavior now, just to make things a little less arbitrary is a good idea.

 I think the typical user of the OXY-type Attachments makes the first two selections and if the result is as desired, stops right there. If not he/she adds a third reference.  That workflow is fine whatever we make the defaults, but changing those defaults breaks previous models.  Is it worth that price?

I agree it is a matter of luck if the code-chosen default determining the axial orientation is correct. But that is true whatever default is chosen.

A user wants to attach an object to a vertex with some specific orientation.

1.   He chooses the attachment vertex

2.  He chooses the direction to align one of the axes (X/Y/Z) of his object to.

At this point the axial orientation is not specified, so the code chooses one for the sake of definiteness.  If the object is axisymmetric, or he is lucky, he's done.  If this is not the case a third reference is required.

So what is the point of changing the default? Will a user be lucky more often?  Why would a user care exactly what the default is, in advance?  He can inspect to see if he needs a third reference or not.

What usually makes the review hard is if a commit changes too many different things on existing code. Sure, one could have split this PR into a few smaller commits but because the changes made to existing code are not huge it's OK for me, too.

I don't know if there is a clear definition for a checkpoint commit but when changing something big, I tend to make a lot of small commits. For me, these commits usually have big chunks of temporarily removed or added code that are not meant for a PR. The commits are useful so when I find an unexpected problem during development I can easily go back to previous commits to see which change is responsible for the problem. 

I think a checkpoint commit is just a commit that contains some intermediate code that did not make it to the final version.

To provide an example where Part Design Clones copying colour is preferred, I recently made a project which depends on parametric colouring by combining various monocoloured parts through boolean operations, thus parametrically persisting the face colours and allowing me to make edits to the model history without needing to manually recolour faces of the final model on every release.

Draft Clones create a non-parametric copy of geometry and colour.  Part Design Clones create a parametric copy of geometry with the added abillity to perform Part Design operations on the resulting Clone, but remove colour.  Links create a parametric link of geometry and colour and do not feature the ability to perform Part Design Operations.

Part Design Clones which create a parametric copy of geometry *and* colour would have been ideal for making iterative parts which preserve parametric colours.  Instead, as a workaround I followed a separate (and I believe unnecessarily convoluted) workflow creating multiple duplicate Links of the same source monocoloured parts to perform the same boolean operations on, but with one added part unioned here or one less part cut there.  If memory serves, it would have been significantly more straightforward to create one parametrically coloured part from boolean operations, and then clone that part to build upon it for the next iterative part as opposed to repeating the same actions in the feature tree multiple times.

So with that explanation out of the way, I would propose that parametrically perserving colour in Part Design Clones is just as important as parametrically perserving geometry, as parametric colours are (delicately) possible in FreeCAD; and in a case like the project described above, can be a defining factor of a part which needs to be carried through to its successors.

Feel free to explore the project [here](https://github.com/recursivenomad/ki-lime-pi-pico) (model source [here](https://github.com/recursivenomad/ki-lime-pi-pico/blob/main/models/RaspberryPi_Pico_Variations.FCStd)), and you can read through [BUILDING.md](https://github.com/recursivenomad/ki-lime-pi-pico/blob/main/BUILDING.md) for more thorough descriptions of parametric colouring and limitations therein.  My understanding is that this parametrically coloured workflow is fairly unconventional, so please don't hesitate to ask if you seek clarification on anything related to this workflow or project.

Thanks for creating the issue.  It's usually helpful to avoid 'feature request' and instead talk about a problem to be solved.  In this case, you've alluded to at least three different problems:
problem 1 - You don't know which tool to pick because there isn't enough information shown.
problem 2 -  Seeing tool details is slow if you have very large collections of tools
problem 3 - You have to repeat information multiple times to create a tool. 

The original design intent of the dialog was to allow the user to add tool controllers without interrupting the workflow of creating an op.  As such, the user may wish to keep the dock open for a long time, even the whole time they are using Path.  So it should occupy as little screen real estate as possible.

@knipknap's idea of adding a row  of meta-data below the description as shown in the image is interesting.  Realistically, the icons won't look that good.  More like:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/538057/236334114-63f26d04-89ba-4a01-af11-d530c0e486fa.png)

I'm not sure how useful that is.  It adds to the dock width but I can see some value.

The problem is that while this solves problem 1, it doesn't do anything for problem 2.  You can't sort based on the metadata like you could with a table of sortable columns.
In some ways it makes the problem of large tool collections worse because each item occupies more vertical space.  So you'll be scrolling a lot more to find items far down the list.

One possibility would be some kind of filter widget at the top of the list.  Something similar to the filters in sketcher
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/538057/236333430-0a398f28-03b0-4927-9d06-741ff04a1385.png)

A two part filter widget [filter type] [filter value] where the type is either shape, diameter, flute count, etc.  and the value is an input

I have seen that once.
It is caused by code like this:

```
const std::vector<vertex *> &points = all_points();
return points[leftmost_point_index()];
```

if leftmost_point_index() fails and returns -1 by convention, then the 
indexing operation will read from the vector element -1.
The element -1 probably stores the length of the vector, while the shape 
happens to have 0x30 vertices.

There is indeed a deeper problem. The Pad uses a shape binder as profile instead of a sketch. However, inside isFeatureMovable() it's checked whether the passed object (the Pad) is profile based and if yes its sketch is checked. Because the pad is not based on a sketch the returned object is null. This null pointer is then passed to the recursive call of isFeatureMovable() and caused the crash.

There are two things to fix:
* instead of getVerifiedSketch() the method getVerifiedObject() should be used
* if the returned value is null then isFeatureMovable() shouldn't be called at all because otherwise it will say the pad cannot be moved which isn't necessarily true 
* then there must be further checks for shape binders, sub-shape binders or datum planes and decided what to do in that case

Bad idea.  
The term 'tool'  is way overused throughtout all of FreeCAD.  It refers to a button on a toolbar.  Sometimes it's a dialog.  
It's confusing as hell.  That's why we're trying to avoid it entirely.  In Path, you have:

toolshapes - FreeCAD files that define abstract shape of tools like 'endmill'  'ballend'

toolbits - specific instances of those shapes.   This can be as generic or specific as the user wants.  It can mean "A whiteside 1/4" router bit part number 1234"   Or it can have 1:1 mapping of a toolbit to a physical tool in the user's collection.  Like  "The whiteside 1/4" bit with the blue sticker in the top drawer"  

toolcontroller - a _usage_ of a toolbit in a job.   A TC also carries the spindle speed and feedrate .
The user may have the same physical tool loaded into the spindle but run it fast part of the time and slower for other operations.  That's one toolbit but two toolcontrollers.

But in some environments (e.g. someone running a lathe) this will lead to several cells showing "n/a", and it may not scale in the future.
2. Go with the two-line UI from my initial posting. In this case I would define a priority for all known parameters and dynamically show only the first four or so. The UI wouldn't allow for ordering based on parameters, but filters could still be implemented.

I also thought of introducing the concept of "library types" - e.g. one for lathe tools, one for probes, ... and then show different columns depending on that. But I think in reality machine types differ too much to cover everything - there are lathes that use endmills, CNCs that support sawblades, etc. So a user would then have to choose tools from multiple libraries, depending on the tool type. Another drawback is that FreeCAD could not ensure that tool IDs are unique from this user.

So in summary, I still think option 2 (combined with the other UI and button changes that we discussed) would be best.

The solution is different depending on the exact solution.

If I remember correctly (but feel free to correct me as I talk from memory), the solution having the most support/or better balance, was to suggest constraint names based on sketch-wide uniqueness. In principle, only the UI would provide automatic naming.

I do not know (I would have to check), if it is necessary to always produce a unique index (over the whole history of the sketch), or if it is just enough that gaps are filled.

Horizontal1

==> New suggestion is Horizontal5 or Horizontal4?

This is rather important in the number of resources and accounting you need to make. It is a rather important design decision. If we need Horizontal5 and we set for the other, the code is very different (and it has bigger complexity and less performance). If we can do with Horizontal4, code is simpler. This is an important assumption to validate before starting coding.

I am not familiar with the state in which FC stays when having deleting a named constraint. So which behaviour depends on what we need.

So, two approaches for it, (a) keeping track of indices [Horizontal5], or (b) calculating an unique index per call [Horizontal4]. 

If (a) the only place needs to be sketchobject. The big drawback is that you will need to maintain an accounting that is seldom necessary. Keeping the accounting may be more resource intensive, complex and less performing (think of undo/redo operations too), than just doing the simple match of getting the next index. For this reason, I tend to favour a solution of type (b), if possible technically. In principle, I strongly prefer sketchobject over propertyconstraintlist, because a propertyconstraintlist can be assigned from one sketch to another. Then, the historic maximum value will not be sketch-wide of the sketch being assigned (which is the whole point of this). Also, if we set the scope sketch-wide, the responsibility should belong to sketchobject. Of course, it may be implemented in a helper class ("ConstraintNameAssistant", it may be a nested class) containing all data members necessary for the accounting, sketchobject must notify that class of all changes, including constraint name changes (the user may manually rename a variable matching the automatic naming convention), so that the class can ensure it always stores, for that sketch, the highest historical value per constraint type. It must also handle direct changes to properties from python, so on change, it must record a higher constraint index per type if the user provided one.

So, as it appears, (a) has some complexity (at least intellectually, codewise it may be one function that gets called in all right places), and introduces quite some overhead. In fact, creating a unique name per constraint FreeCAD-wide would probably be easier (just a atomic counter on the constraint class, possibly storing the counter value on save and restoring it on restore). A similar solution is present for geometries, see Part::Geometry (cpp file).

If (b), the place should be under Sketcher/App. Why? Because naming is not UI specific, we may want to have a name suggested for Python users or for FC console only. Which place then? Two main options (i) A new class, something like "ConstraintNameAssistant" (can be nested) or (ii) just a free c style function. I would put this on SketchObject.h (in both cases).

At the end there will be a function (possibly static if in nested class), something like: 
```std::string suggestConstraintName(SketchObject &, ConstraintType)```

Under the assumptions of b) all this function needs to do to produce a sound suggestion is to iterate the Constraint property of the sketch, for each constraint get the current name, match it against a regexp of automatic naming (of the right type), to calculate the maximum index present, and provide the next suggestion. This will NOT ensure that the index is historic maximum of the sketch (it is the assumption of (b)).

From these two subsolutions, (ii) is probably the easiest to implement, given that the Constraint property of a sketch is public. It is reasonably refactorable if you change mind later on.

Many behaviours are possible. It is possible not to allow negative distances for the constraint when toggling back to driving. It is possible to remove the restriction (but we have then to consult users if we change the behaviour of the normal point to distance constraint and ensure it does not break the normal work-flow).

> Please note that this was the pre-existing behaviour.

The pre-exiting implementation had some bugs. The constraint works by calculating the area of the triangle defined by the endpoints of the lines and one endpoint to the center of the circle, then dividing this area by the base length (giving the height of the triangle, which is the distance, and then correcting this distance with the constraint value and circle radius). The area is calculated using the geometric property of the vector product (cross product). While the absolute value of the magnitude is the area, the vector can point to -z or z, the differential was calculated without taking into account this. Depending on the direction of the vectors (the positions of the start and end points), the constraint would fail to converge.

It appears that `WorkbenchGroup::addTo` is called : 
- On app start for QToolBar and for QMenu.
- On every workbench change for QMenu only.

So actually the view/workbenches menu becomes correct (without the disabled wb) after this. And then it creates the index issue for the comboxbox (as the list is updated but not the combobox items).

Anyway I think the solution to this (and it will let us get rid of the need to reboot) is to call refreshWorkbenchList and refresh the qmenu and qtoolbar on saveSettings.

The problem is that we are not storing the leading ', the problem presents itself in several forms, if you input these values in a spreadsheet:
`'5C` | `''a` | `'1/2m` | `'5`
they show up like this:
![image](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/assets/36372335/423fa935-911a-4525-b933-b23d92ff5da9)
but only the last one is stored with the leading `'`, for the others it is discarded so when you reload the document they now show up like this:
![image](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/assets/36372335/61974087-9d9f-421d-8e69-c68b8987e76d)
and are now stored like this:
`=5C` | `a` | `= 1 / 2 m` | `'5`

notice how `''a` has now lost both `'` so it is not possible to have a string that starts with `'`

also, it's curious that only `1/2m` is evaluated and interpreted as numeric input but `1*2m`, `1+2m` or `1-2m` are all automatically interpreted as strings


As solution I think we should avoid ever discarding a leading ', I would guess this was done as an attempt at being clever and removing unnecessary ' but it's clearly being counterproductive.

> it has to be well-defined because of that.

Exactly.  I much prefer contract work.  Then the contract is defined in at least three phases:
Phase 1 - A detailed written plan.  the developer does the hard research and figures out what needs to be done.  Gets paid for delivering a plan that anyone else could continue with if the developer dies or quits.
Phase 2 - A working example.  The developer implements the plan and shows it working.  Gets paid for this.
Phase 3 - A merged feature.  The developer works with the community to get the code up to snuff and merged.  Gets paid.

In my mind, this spreads the risk equally between the person offering the contract and the person accepting it.  
It focuses the work down to deliverables.

Good software developers have three skills:  
problem solving
Coding
Communication

Those map fairly neatly into the three phases.

> Might I ask when will the modernization take place?

Some time ago I started to modernize parts of the code base but the pending PR for the toponaming always held us back to continue on this.

Now that the strategy of merging the toponaming code has changed (i.e. rewriting it from scratch and commit it step by step) gives us the freedom to continue on this. However, this still has to wait after the freeze.

> The source code of FreeCAD still contains old syntax for SIGNAL/SLOT

When I did the Qt6 port I got rid of most of the old SIGNAL/SLOT connects but there are still a handful of places where it's not trivial to port the code.

> C-style conversion

You mean C-style casts? I don't know if this can be fixed automatically with clang-tidy but at least clang provides a compiler flag to find all occurrences.

> boost::bind

All boost::bind can be replaced with std::bind. When doing so we also have to change the namespaces of the placeholders `_1, _2, ...`. If this is an issue that you consider as urgent we can do the replacement also for the release.

Recently I have tried https://clang.llvm.org/extra/clang-tidy/checks/modernize/avoid-bind.html that replaces binds with lambda expressions but clang-tidy did a very bad job because most of the transformed code didn't compile any more.

The plan of introducing this new property was to get away from the previous hacked behaviour which was neither G98 nor G99 but someone's personal trick to simulate all canned cycles as G99 behaviour while issuing G98 instructions.

The RetractMode is effectively a means of selecting whether you use G98 or G99 behaviour between holes.  If anyone thinks it is not doing that please point out the failure. 

If anyone thinks G98 was a mistake by those writing the standards and all holes should be rigged to do G99 using G98 commands maybe they could make their case for reverting.

OK, I investigated this a bit. The "problem" is indeed the selection mechanism.

Actually it can be summed up very simply : when mouse release event appears above an object, the object is selected and the event is consumed.

I see 2 possibilities to fix:
1.  Upgrade the selection mechanism. For example selection would only happen if both mouse press and release events occur above the same and/or within a defined radius
2. Add to FC new functions so that a feature can temporarily disable (then restore in previous state) the selection mechanism so it is guaranteed to receive all mouse events (unaltered).

Both have (to me) balanced pros and cons so feel free to give your opinion if one looks better to you than the other.

I can't easily test what you have done.  Basically you are doing a QR decomposition of the 3 x 3 submatrix into a rotation times a scale*shear.  Up to signs on the diagonal, this factorization is unique as long as the matrix has full rank (so it maps 3d into 3d). The cases we are worried about is where one or more scale-factors vanish and the column rank is 0, 1 or 2, not 3. I haven't pinned down to what extent the factorization then fails to be unique.  If the rank is zero (3D maps to the origin) then the rotation is completely undetermined - might as well make it the unit matrix.  If the rank is is one, then the rotation would appear to be undetermined up to a rotation around the image line.  I'm unclear about rank two.
  I would construct matrices by multiplying up a rotation times various less than full rank upper triangular matrices, and see if I could retrieve the rotation by the algorithm.

One problem with the "tool icons/thumbnails" I noticed during the implementation: The only way to display them is by creating a temporary tool in an active document. That is a bit ugly, because:

1. It is slow and prevents us from loading many icons at the same time. Definitely cannot be used to show a preview of each tool in a list.
2. It prevents the tool editor sub-dialog from being looked at when no document is open. And in the current implementation even the library dialog is blocked from being opened (which makes sense because of the aforementioned problem). That has bugged me numerous times when organizing/researching stuff in the workshop.
3. I think the library editor in general shouldn't manipulate a document, unless explicitly asked by clicking "Add toolbit to job". A document shouldn't need to be recomputed just because a shape in the tool library was edited/added/removed. So long as it is still in the job, of course. 

So I am thinking of the following plan to address these issues:
1. Decouple the tool editor from the open document by rendering the toolbit in a separate, headless FreeCAD instance. I have done something similar using "freecadcmd". It feels hacky though, though the current implementation isn't really better IMO. Not sure if there is a more direct way using the official API while preventing the user from seeing it. This would resolve the issue of not being able to open the library editor while no document is open.
2. Create static icons for the tool list and show those there. Even better would be if FreeCAD files had embedded thumbnails...

Is there a possibility to display the parts in a shaded view for all rounded edges and only display the hard edges with a line style? This would result in a shaded view combined with edges but without smooth edges.
![grafik](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/assets/6246609/f9122f4d-9afe-4fea-8bd0-0757c9faab7a)
Especially for complex cast parts like housings or when working with surfaces it is helpful to identify hard vs smooth edges. It allows to quickly see hard edges for e.g. a spotface or helps to see the continuity of a surface. Also, in complex parts, too many edges are more disturbing than helping but often you need to select or use the sharp edges for new features or as references.

In CATIA and NX, you can use a specific composite rendering style to shade the surfaces of an object with its edges, except the smooth ones. A smooth edge is an edge that does not break the continuity of the geometry, contrary to a sharp edge.
Different render styles are shown [here](https://www.3ds.com/fileadmin/3dxml/dircopy_official/PlrUserMap/plr-t-Player-RenderingStyles.htm)

When using surfacing or creating complex cast parts in Part Design which are set up with multiple positive and negative bodies (boolean) which result in a complex geometry this view / render style is very handy as it hides all (unnecessary) smooth edges and displays only the sharp / hard edges.
This is a not so complex casting model (housing) and even there the too many lines around all fillets are obstructing. Usually all negative parts for a e.g. a core are combined bodies which are then filleted and afterwards removed from the positive bodies.

> Could you please describe briefly what exactly does the tag do / mean?

I'm running from the context of the code, so it is possible my understanding is not full or complete. @chennes,  please correct me if wrong.

But it is my understanding that the tag is used to uniquely id an object/face/vector/etc .

In the simple case, it can be ignored mostly. But when a operation is involved, such as a union, this becomes more important.

So, if a cube (tag = 1) and another cube (tag = 2) are "fused" into a new shape (tag = 3); and you follow through the history of the new shape, you can identify the "current tag" (3) is different than the other objects (1 and 2). This helps prevent duplication of the same objects when serializing the toponame.

It's **very** possible that tags are used for other things also. I've been concentrating on naming.

Complicating things further, elements of an object, such as faces, vectors(lines) and points also have unique tags. Again, it is to distinguish between the items involved in any operation.

Using the example, you can detect that "Face1" of the first cube is different from the "Face1" of the second cube by looking at the Tags.

I understand.  I'm going to give a little more context here for the sake of others who might want to pick up the baton and run with it.
My preference isn't coming from a programmer's perspective.  It's driven by experience and seeing the issue in context.

First, as I mentioned, is the issue of translation.  In your second image, you cropped off the text 'Endmill' but still left the indicators S,H,D for Shank, Height, and Diameter.  These are arabic characters and will make no sense in non-arabic languages.  The use of text in images makes them impossible to translate.

Second, the artistically generated images look beautiful.  But they'll never exist for a user's custom designed tool. With the automatically generated images, a user can design any kind of tool and get an image that works exactly like the defaults. There's only a handful of tools that are used widely in milling.  Not true when it comes to woodworking where there is a never ending catalog of router bits.  

Going beyond custom bits, lathe work isn't too far in the future.  Lathe cutters also come in a huge range of shapes. There's simply no way to both create and maintain a catalog of images for them, especially with a small team of mostly volunteers.

Third, the big beautiful images look great in a tiled layout where you have room to show them.  The same images, however, are used in the icons in tree.  Those big images won't scale down to icon size and remain attractive.  That means we have to maintain TWO sets of images or use both drawn and generated images.  That sucks and is confusing for the user because the image for the same thing looks different in context.  Now instead of helping the user instantly recognize a 'thing' in the tree, they have to think about it.

Fourth, the generated images _can_ look better than they do now.  In fact, they have the possibility to blow the drawn images out of the water.  They currently look very plain because they're modeled with only the attributes needed to calculate tool paths.  That doesn't have to be.  If someone wanted to improve the Endmill.FCStd file and model the flutes, it would generate a better image.  It doesn't have to stop there.  In the toolbit creation dialog, we could update the image in realtime to reflect the parameters as entered by the user.  The toolshapes are FreeCAD models and we're literally IN FreeCAD!
I'm looking at the current state as one step along a road that leads to something the user loves.  I agree it is unattractive and can be (much) better.  But don't throw the baby out with the bath water.

Here's a file showcasing the algorithm that I believe we can follow for these cases:
[algorithm showcase.FCStd.zip](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/files/11647650/algorithm.showcase.FCStd.zip) (remove zip extension)

if last intersected surface is intersected more than once:
• extrude bounding rectangle of profile past body bounding box in the selected direction
• boolean common between extrusion and last surface
• the operation should result in at least two faces, pick the one furthest from the profile
• extrude profile past body bounding box
• slice apart extrusion using the face picked earlier, discard all solids beyond this face and use the rest as addsubshape
• perform union between basefeature and addsubshape to obtain new shape


we could use this also to offer a "far side" option for up to face operations that use faces like this

Or another possibility that might by simpler is to translate the profile outside the body bounding box in the extrusion direction, then make an up to first extrusion in the opposite direction and subtract this from an extrusion of the original profile

A multiple solid PartDesign Body is something different as an Part with multiple PartDesign Bodies. A PartDesign Body to automatic a boolean operation, a Part Container not. So when touching surfaces are included, the result is complete different.

Disclaimer for the examples: it is only considered the cases, where the models are build with PartDesign, not with other WBs.

Example a francis runner where a multiple solid PartDesign Body helps for modeling, but in the Part Container is in the end only one PartDesign Body.

Usually you start to make the runner crown and the runner bottom, since there are first given as parameter. But they are not touching or intersect so it is not allowed atm (singe solid rule). Then you create the blades and pattern them (and do the rest dress up). Then the end result is a singe Part Container with PartDesign Body with a single Solid. But while working, it has a for a certain time a multi solid PartDesign Body. Pretty the similar workflow is while making track wheels, fly wheels, ..... (rim and hub at first, then the rest).

https://forum.freecad.org/viewtopic.php?style=8&t=77004&start=30#p667104

An other example a Part Container with multiple Bodies. Welded parts. They are not boolean operated, but are still one part, since the one position in a BoM, handled while assembling as one Part, bought or manufactured (manufactured with maybe some exceptions) as one part and so on. Also in connection in a PDM or ERP they are handled different. When they are different in the ERP, the change requests are foredoomed. Here is an exapmple, but it still have the singe solid in Part Design limitation. For example i would make all welding seams (or all with the same welding addition) in one multi solid PartDesign Body. A similar build up but complete differt part, a roller bearing. It has multiple PartDesign Bodies, but is only one part (one position in a BoM, handled as one, bought as one, .....).

About font metrics, usually the 'm' is used to be the max width, while it is difficult to have a measure of the max "bounding box" of text.

usually capital M should be slightly less than "m", but a simple test of the "bounging box" will reveal the dimensions.

In Tex "em"  that is the width of the 'm' and ex that is the dimension of the 'x' are used as "font metrics" when typesetting things, 

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/2385829/what-is-the-difference-between-px-em-and-ex

Tooltip: Horizontal and vertical alignment

Tooltip: Height reference used for justification

Tooltip: Keep left margin and leading white space when justification is left

Tooltip: Scale to ensure cap height is equal to size

Currently the actual height of the text typically does not match the Size property. Depending on the font it is sometimes bigger, sometimes smaller than Size.

Tooltip: Fuse faces if faces overlap, usually not required (can be very slow)
Default: False
Not directly related to this issue. This is mainly for 'calligraphy' fonts where characters overlap intentionally.

**Tracking:**
Changed the type of this existing property to "App::PropertyDistance" so that negative values are possible.

scipy's interpolate  seems to handle periodic BSplines correctly and produces a result invariant o the choice of join point.

EDIT: It appears the BSplines need to be of odd degree to be symmetric.

```
import numpy as np
import math
from scipy.interpolate import make_interp_spline
import Part

def makePartBSpline(spl):
    u, c, degree = spl.tck
    poles = [App.Vector(*v) for v in c]
    knots = u.tolist()
    mults = [1] * len(knots)
    bsp = Part.BSplineCurve()
    polesfc = poles[0:-degree]
    knotsfc = knots[degree:-degree]
    multsfc = [1]* len(knotsfc)
    bsp.buildFromPolesMultsKnots(polesfc, multsfc, knotsfc, True, degree)
    return bsp

def makeknotvector(c, method = 'chordlength'):
    n = len(c)
    if method == 'uniform':
        return [i/(n - 1) for i in range(n)]
    elif method == 'chordlength':
        chords = np.array([np.linalg.norm((c[i+1] - c[i])) for i in range(n - 1)])
        chordssummed = np.cumsum(chords)
        return [0] + [c/chordssummed[-1] for c in chordssummed]
    else:
        return 'unknown method in makeknotvector'


ncirc = 13
rad = 10

#wiggly circle as per Chris_G
circ = np.empty((ncirc, 3))
offset = 1
for i in range(ncirc - 1):
    th = 2*math.pi * i/(ncirc-1)
    circ[i][0] = rad * math.cos(th)
    circ[i][1] = rad * math.sin(th)
    circ[i][2] = pow(-1, i) * offset

circ[ncirc-1] = circ[0]

degree = 3
u =  makeknotvector(circ, method = 'chordlength')
spl = make_interp_spline(u, circ, k = degree, bc_type = 'periodic')
bsp = makePartBSpline(spl)
Part.show(bsp.toShape(), 'Periodic BSpline')

#rotate the data
circnew = np.empty((ncirc, 3))
circnew[1:] = circ[:-1].tolist()
circnew[0] = circ[-2].tolist()

unew =  makeknotvector(circnew, method = 'chordlength')
splnew = make_interp_spline(unew, circnew, k = degree, bc_type = 'periodic')
bspnew = makePartBSpline(splnew)
Part.show(bspnew.toShape(), 'Periodic BSpline Rot points')
#yes - invariant under change of join point!

> It is more flexible IMO,

Really? What if you have to move a Body (or FeatureSet)? Then you are bound on the origin of the part and refactoring is much more work.


Also there is the Body (or FeatureSet) boolean workflow, when you have regions of interest, for example in injection molds (plastic or metal) or bigger castings with region with different sections/usecases. Here a really simple example of clips on a injection molding. It looks maybe at first really wierd, but it is really practically. If i want to move a clip, just move the Body (FeatureSet), all content moves with it, no adaption needed.
![2023-06-18_00-26](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/assets/109620914/a9663c24-ec50-432a-afae-940a7e584954)


Also if you want you can still refer to the part origin, for example for a draft.
![2023-06-18_00-34](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/assets/109620914/2f790786-9390-402b-ac2c-245a95558ed0)

Also very practical, the origin of the clip is in this example in the section of the counter part. That means you can model the Body (FeatureSet) with the origin in the section, now that it is nice!
![2023-06-18_00-34_1](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/assets/109620914/bedfe58f-5b0c-401c-ae8d-fa1d6ccb5140)

Also a good thing on welded parts, if you have several Bodies (FeatureSet) in it and see, that some Bodies (FeatureSet) must move to an other welding part, because it is better in construction, manufacturing, ..... then you move the whole Body/Bodies (FeatureSet) to the other Part and you have no dependencies to the old part (as long you do not refer something to it). And since the the placement was in the section, you just need to move the Body/Bodies (FeatureSet) to the section coordinate again and you are done. No need to change every sketch, pad, revolution, etc. Do not forget, if there is no origin of the Body (FeatureSet) all sketches/features refer to the origin of the part. This means when new destination the part have an other placement, which is in assemblies 99% the case, you have to edit all sketches/features according to the new origin, that is pretty much work.

Maybe on some people never need this, but for large and/or complex models, were you need structure to get an overview, it is a real lifesaver.

Profile is using some kind of polygon offset functionality in libarea. In case nothing is to offset, i.e. tool compensation is off and no extra offset is defined or extra offset = - tool_diameter/2, there is nothing to offset, and that is the problematic case, convention from libarea and of FreeCAD seem to differ. It looks like the FreeCAD code checks for this with case with "if not obj.UseComp:", but this misses extra offset without compensation or radius  + extra offset == 0, both these cases result in wrong orientation.

I really don't want to dig any further into libarea. IMO profile (and pocket) should use code like in adaptive clearing, without calling into libarea, but I'm not sure if that would have some drawbacks.

So I propose to change https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/master/src/Mod/Path/Path/Op/Profile.py#L355 to
```py
        if (obj.UseComp and self.radius or 0.0) + obj.OffsetExtra.Value == 0.0:
            if direction == "CCW":
                params["orientation"] = 1
            else:
                params["orientation"] = 0
```
which inverts direction iff case no effective offset is applied to the path.

C:

double test(int b) { return (b) ? 1.0 : 2.0; }

is perfectly valid C, nothing is type-cast, num != 0 returns 1.0, num
== 0 return 2.0. ?: is not a short-hand for if-then-else. 

äquivalent python:

def test(b): return b and 1.0 or 2.0


python "and" operator looks at first argument, if it evaluates to
False, first argument is returned, else the second. python "or" is the
opposite, returns first argument if it evaluates to True, else the
second argument is returned.

I don't know if it is silly or not, it is like it is, and IMO it is
quite logical to do it like that. see 6.11 in python docs
https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html?highlight=operator#boolean-operations

The difference to "if ... then ... else" in C and in python is that
those are statements whereas ?: resp (... and ... or ...) are
expressions, you can use expressions e.g. as arguments to function
calls, you can't use statements there.

python also knows expression-if syntax, that would look something like

def test(b): return 1.0 if b else 2.0

As already emerged in this threed the main addition brought by RT PartDesign model (which I think should be adopted also in FC master) is the possibility to have several branches of history tree (named featuresets by grubetechnic) in the same coordinate system.

This kind of RT Body model: 
- simplifies the cross-referencing between objects in different branches, 
- but it makes more difficult  moving a featureset into a different position.

In the RT branch it is possible (**not obligatory**) to have several  featuresets in the same Body (in the same coordinate system). I am using this option only when the first point is more important then the latter. 

Regarding the _Body_ term (which is the subject of this topic),  I would suggest to replace it with _Geometrical Set_. This term is used in Catia for a generic container that can hold any kind of geometry (multiple solids, faces, shells...). The _Geometrical Set_ of Catia is defined inside a Catia Part (in the same way of a FC Body in a FC Part).

IMO using _Part_ term for current _Body_ ( and a different name for current _Part_) would also be acceptable. This choice would be in better agreement with the step format exported by a current FC Multubody Part. In fact, in the export phase, this kind of part is always converted into an assembly of parts. It may be easily checked reimporting the step file in a commercial CAD  (such as Catia).

The current guide creates a `conda` environment on the command line, as we use `devenv` to manage dependencies in a cross-platform manner.  The Python extension detects this environment when you run the [`Python: Select Interpreter`](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/python/environments#_working-with-python-interpreters) command.

The VSCode CMake extension already provides a means to configure the environment prior to launching `cmake` through the ["environmentSetupScript"](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-cmake-tools/blob/main/docs/kits.md#general-options).  This is how the environment is currently being configured here: [.vscode/cmake-kits.json](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD/blob/master/.vscode/cmake-kits.json#L8C6-L8C28).

I do not believe that attempting to replace the CMake Tools extension with a set of tasks and custom scripts is all that worthwhile, and due to the incompatibility between the tasks and the extension will result in a greater request for support in the future.

A general philosophical argument is to keep source, build scripts, and documentation in the same repository so that they may be in sync at all times.  When checking out a version of source, there's no inconsistency with that version and the necessary version in the build and documentation repos.  Consequently, a means of building the packages within the repository would be a benefit.

Duplicating external code, however increases developer overhead and the likelihood of a synchronization error.

I believe a reasonable approach to make cross-platform package building from within the source tree would be to:

1. bring over the `FreeCAD-Bundle` repository into the main repository
2. use CMake's [CPack External Generator](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/cpack_gen/external.html#variable:CPACK_EXTERNAL_PACKAGE_SCRIPT) to call the platform-specific package generation script.

> I can see that might be an issue, however this seems to be the only way. Yes there's `environmentSetupScript`, but it also requires to pretty much hardcode everything for conda. There's no way to switch it off so to say. See for example

`conda` is the means by which all official builds are created.  Any other build means differ from the official builds; prioritizing these above `conda` can, and already has, led to a large amount of time in debugging developer environments instead of productive work on the project.  The wiki for compiling FreeCAD is already quite out of date for virtually all non-conda build instructions.  Keeping these document up to date, let alone actually diagnosing and resolving the many environment-specific issues that developers and would-be developers have is already a challenge.

For reference on how official builds and releases are performed: The official build script is in the [`conda-forge/freecad-feedstock`](https://github.com/conda-forge/freecad-feedstock/) with the Linux/macOS [`build.sh`](https://github.com/conda-forge/freecad-feedstock/blob/main/recipe/build.sh) and Windows [`bld.bat`](https://github.com/conda-forge/freecad-feedstock/blob/main/recipe/bld.bat).  After these artifacts are built, the [`FreeCAD/FreeCAD-Bundle`](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD-Bundle/) script is run to build the release artifacts then publish them as GitHub releases.  This is done [weekly](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD-Bundle/releases/tag/weekly-builds), but special tags are made for the [official release artifacts](https://github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD-Bundle/releases).

> * currently there's no windows configuration

This does not require a complete rework of CMake extension as a set of incompatible tasks.  Simply adding the configuration, including the environment script for Windows would resolve this concern.

> * using cmake-kits kinda feels against cmake's "automatic discovery"

This PR is about VSCode's integration, for which the Microsoft's CMake extension is already present and provides a means for configuring the environment prior to launching `cmake`.  From the command line the discovery of the toolchains within the environment is already automatic, so creating `cmake-kits` is unnecessary.  Rewriting the extension as a set of incompatible tasks feels against focusing on the VSCode integration.

> Moving everything to external scripts / tasks solves all these issues. They're quite simple really, they just call cmake configure and then build, so... "what could go wrong"
> 
> The only downside is that it's a bit less "polished / integrated" and we lose the problems panel output.

No, the issue is that running `CMake: Configure` and `CMake: Build` as well as their associated GUI buttons no longer work.  Instead this approach requires running `Tasks: Run Task` and selecting the newly created `CMake: Configure` and `CMake: Build` tasks.

I do not see any added value in moving from the Microsoft-supported CMake extension to an incompatible set of tasks.

However, there is considerable value in adding support in VSCode to the following:
* Windows build, test, and debug
* automated tests
* packaging

> Maybe in the former case the module doesn't get garbage collected?

It can only be garbage collected when its reference counter reaches zero. But this is very unlikely to happen and won't be achieved by removing it from the sys.modules dict.

The reason that it fails when loading FreeCAD as extension module (i.e. loading FreeCAD.so) is that it additionally may be created as built-in module. In src/App/Application.cpp there is a function init_freecad_module() that is used twice. 
When used in Application::setupPythonTypes() then beforehand it checks whether a FreeCAD module exists or not but in Application::initConfig() there is no such check.

So, this could eventually be the reason of this issue.

All attributes in SVG starting with `inkscape:` is not really SVG but just metadata convenient for Inkscape usage/editing, for instance `inkscape:pagecheckerboard="0"`. Therefore, we don't really want it to be included into our files. `inkscape:zoom="14.116667"` this for instance is data on your last zoom level in Inkscape I believe.

It's really not your fault as it were there to begin with, but it would be good to remove it. This is what I call "conversion", convert Inkscape SVG to Plain SVG. This can be done in Inkscape by using "Save As..." and then choosing Plain SVG as the filetype. This is like formatting and should be done by it's own commit.

> It's not clear to me why body->BaseFeature.getValue() != BaseFeature.getValue() is meaningful

If you look at the code you will see that this check is already in master. My change makes sure that the body's BaseFeature is only adjusted if it's already set to a value. This is to avoid that it's automatically set when e.g. restoring a project file where it wasn't set beforehand.

When you execute this code snippet you will see that the BaseFeature of Body is not set. Now, if you save the document and restore it you will realize that it's all the sudden set and this triggers the out-of.scope warnings.
```
doc = App.newDocument()

part = doc.addObject("PartDesign::Body", "Part")
box = doc.addObject("Part::Box", "Box")
part.Group = [box]

body = doc.addObject("PartDesign::Body", "Body")
base = doc.addObject("PartDesign::FeatureBase", "Clone")

base.BaseFeature = box
base.Placement = box.Placement
base.setEditorMode('Placement',0)

body.Group = [base]
body.Tip = base

doc.recompute()
```

> Did you even tried ? The behavior is very different. With master, dragging the Sphere to the Body is rejected. With this PR, it is accepted and BaseFeature is changed.

Adrian is right that this is not a regression and the behaviour depends on which master version you have used. If master is older than f4a8d94838 then the behaviour is different compared to after this change.

Before this change the creation of a clone did this:
```
doc = App.newDocument()

part = doc.addObject("PartDesign::Body", "Part")
box = doc.addObject("Part::Box", "Box")
part.Group = [box]

body = doc.addObject("PartDesign::Body", "Body")
base = doc.addObject("PartDesign::FeatureBase", "Clone")

base.BaseFeature = box
base.Placement = box.Placement
base.setEditorMode('Placement',0)

body.Group = [base]
body.Tip = base

doc.recompute()
```
And now it does
```
doc = App.newDocument()

part = doc.addObject("PartDesign::Body", "Part")
box = doc.addObject("Part::Box", "Box")
part.Group = [box]

body = doc.addObject("PartDesign::Body", "Body")
base = doc.addObject("PartDesign::FeatureBase", "Clone")

body.Group = [base]
body.Tip = base

base.BaseFeature = box
base.Placement = box.Placement
base.setEditorMode('Placement',0)

doc.recompute()
```

There are a number of tests that have multiple asserts. Where there is only one act this -may- be ok, but asserts on multiple acts are a no-no. A common rule is one assert per test. A test should only fail for one reason. When a test fails, if there are multiple asserts there is no way to immediately know exactly what went wrong, and when you start using the tests you'll soon discover how annoying that is. Yes, you'll finish up with a lot of tests - so keep em efficient.

Also, it is common for test names to be in the form Ensure_something_returns_a_value_of_0. This helps readability of these long strings. 

It is also better if the test name describes the expected behavioral result, rather than describing what it does. "cat_has_eaten_dog" is preferable to "testCat".
